item.title: synthmc: a precedent-based synthesizability score for transition metal complexes
item.description: Data-driven methods are increasingly being used for the in silico discovery of transition metal complexes (TMCs), ranging from machine learning models for high-throughput screening and generative models proposing new candidates to evolutionary algorithms for their de novo design. However, computationally discovered or designed TMCs are only rarely realized experimentally, in part because their synthesis is difficult and often not considered during the design process. At the same time, established synthetic accessibility scores for organic small molecules cannot be transferred to TMCs beyond their constituent ligands, as their fragment-based heuristics and molecular representations do not capture the influence of the metal center, coordination mode, and steric effects on coordinability. Here, we present synthmc, a precedent-based synthesizability score for TMCs that combines the precedent of ligands, coordination environments, and degrees of steric crowding in a reference corpus constructed from experimentally reported complexes in the Cambridge Structural Database. Evaluated on random and time-based validation sets, synthmc assigns, on average, lower scores to more recently reported complexes, consistent with their reduced precedent, indicating its ability to identify novel chemistry. We hope that synthmc will help to prioritize synthetically accessible candidates in high-throughput screening and generative design of TMCs and, more broadly, motivate the development of more comprehensive synthesizability assessments for TMCs, for example based on retrosynthetic approaches or expert evaluations.

item.title: Why Pairwise Force Fields Can Reproduce Ionic Conductivity but Not Solvation Shells
item.description: Pairwise force fields with scaled ionic charges are routinely validated against ionic conductivity or other collective transport measurements and used to interpret Li+ solvation and transport in battery electrolytes. We test this practice for 1.5 M LiFSI in dimethyl ketone with ab initio molecular dynamics, a fine-tuned machine learning potential, a newly developed polarizable force field, and a pairwise force field with charge scaling, compared with both Raman probes of the Li+ shell through computed bound-to-free cross-sections. The pairwise model reproduces the ionic conductivity, yet places 51% of anions in contact with Li+ (21% measured) and 4.8 ligands around the cation (4.0 from first principles). No adjustment of pair parameters removes the excess acetone, as ligand polarization is non-additive, costing a fifth ligand 22–25 kJ mol−1 of polarization energy, and favors acetone over the anion. The many-body models revise the experimental interpretation: Li+ moves vehicularly with a compact four-coordinate shell and ion pairing barely lowers the conductivity, which reflects the low viscosity of acetone rather than the fraction of solvent-separated ions. Agreement with transport therefore validates neither the solvation shell nor the transport mechanism, and we propose a validation protocol built on solvent-side spectroscopic observables.Pairwise v many-body paradigms for the study of battery electrolytes, and comparison with Raman spectra

item.title: Physical consistency and completeness in the data-driven modeling of microwave absorbing materials
item.description: Machine learning (ML) has been applied to the modeling of microwave absorbing materials, including the prediction of electromagnetic parameters and reflection loss (RL), yet the physical consistency of such models is rarely examined. This paper addresses two types of physical consistency problems in data-driven modeling: the physical inconsistency of predicted outputs and the physical incompleteness of input features. On the output side, we constructed a numerical integrator based on the Kramers-Kronig (KK) relation to test permittivity spectra output by ML models. The results show that none of the four examined spectra from three studies satisfied the KK relation, indicating that the model outputs markedly violate physical consistency. On the input side, we took a published MXene study as a case example. There is no thickness, which determines the RL jointly with other variables, in its feature space. Using physically consistent synthetic data, we conducted controlled experiments under two data settings and two partition schemes. It was found that without the thickness, the model captured only a limited part of the RL variance and could not distinguish the labels corresponding to different thicknesses. Adding the thickness restored the performance, with the R2 rising from 0.364 to 0.956 under the fullthickness setting. Finally, we further discussed three approaches to embedding the KK constraint into the modeling workflow. Our results suggest that physical consistency and completeness are necessary conditions for building reliable data-driven models, and that global integral constraints such as the KK relation cannot be learned implicitly from small samples.

item.title: Singlet-triplet superconductivity from repulsive interactions in a $p$-wave magnet
item.description: arXiv:2611.14609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by recent proposals of $p$-wave magnets, which host odd-parity spin splitting, we study electrons near Van Hove singularities with local repulsive interactions. We demonstrate how the symmetry of the $p$-wave spin splitting governs the competition among instabilities. Using a parquet renormalization group (pRG) analysis of a simple one-sublattice model of a $p$-wave magnet, we find that superconductivity is the leading instability over the entire phase diagram for purely repulsive interactions. The resulting superconducting state is generically a mixture of spin-singlet and spin-triplet pairing and approaches an equal-weight mixture when $T_c$ is small compared with the energy offset between each Van Hove electron and its inversion partner. Extending the pRG analysis to a more realistic two-sublattice model, we find that superconductivity remains the leading instability, while the sublattice degree of freedom leads to a competition among various singlet-triplet pairing channels and even a finite-momentum equal-spin pair-density wave. Our mechanism applies broadly to odd-parity magnets and opens a natural route to nodal topological superconductivity.

item.title: Steering Skyrmion Diffusion with Chiral Molecules
item.description: arXiv:2611.15253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiral molecules adsorbed on a magnetic film interact with its magnetization and can thereby alter the thermal motion of magnetic skyrmions. Here we develop a theoretical model in which an aligned layer of tilted molecules modifies the interfacial magnetic interactions according to its handedness. Within this model a skyrmion responds only to spatial variations of the coupling, so a uniform layer leaves its position unaffected, whereas boundaries and coverage gradients exert forces on it. Near a chiral region, these forces deflect the skyrmion transversely in a direction that reverses between enantiomers, which provides a direct signature of the chiral interaction. In extended periodic patterns, the same forces reshape the long-time diffusion, suppressing it in the direction in which the potential varies and enhancing it in the perpendicular direction. The net effect on the mean diffusion is set by the balance between the gyrotropic and dissipative responses of the skyrmion, as we show exactly for one-dimensional landscapes. Stochastic micromagnetic simulations and collective-coordinate calculations confirm these predictions and show how molecular orientation, spatial patterning, and skyrmion properties together determine the motion.

item.title: Periodic Trends in Oxygen Vacancy Formation Energies Across Binary Main-Group Metal Oxides
item.description: arXiv:2611.15297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The function of oxide materials, from solid-oxide fuel cells to solar thermochemical fuel production, depends on their oxygen vacancies. Their formation energetics have been mapped systematically for ternary perovskites, but reported values for the binary oxides, their conceptual and thermochemical building blocks, remain scattered across studies with differing computational methods. Here we report a systematic r$^2$SCAN density functional theory survey of neutral oxygen vacancy formation energies across 39 binary main-group metal oxide polymorphs spanning groups 1, 2, 13, 14, and 15, using the ShakeNBreak method to locate reconstructed defect ground states. The formation energies span 8 eV and decrease down each group and, for most multivalent cations, with increasing oxidation state. Both trends follow the reducibility of the cation. An interpretable crystal feature model is fit to these energies; its inputs are properties of the pristine bulk, with the reduction potential alternatively taken from tabulated thermochemistry. Retaining only its two dominant descriptors, the crystal reduction potential and the band gap, the model reproduces the formation energies with a held-out mean absolute error of 0.31 eV, lower than that of its four-descriptor parent model for transition-metal perovskites. The bond-breaking and stability terms of the full Born-Haber fit prove statistically null for the binary oxides, and the largest residuals identify the hosts where electron accommodation departs from the cation-reduction picture that the descriptors encode. The dataset provides a benchmark for machine-learning interatomic potentials, and the model estimates vacancy formation energies of main-group oxides from bulk properties alone.

item.title: Interplay of Pair Density Wave and Uniform Superconductivity on the Kagome Lattice
item.description: arXiv:2611.15354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the interplay between pair density wave (PDW) and uniform superconductivity on the kagome lattice within a single-orbital $t$-$W$-$J$ model near the $p$-type van Hove filling, where $W$ and $J$ denote effective pairing attractions on lattice sites and nearest-neighbor bonds, respectively. While onsite attraction favors zero-momentum pairing through the conventional BCS instability, nearest-neighbor attraction naturally promotes finite-momentum pairing due to the kagome geometry and sublattice interference. The model therefore provides a framework for exploring the competition and coexistence between uniform superconductivity and PDW order. Self-consistent mean-field calculations in a $2\times2$ supercell reveal that the uniform component reorganizes both the amplitudes and phase structure of the three $F_1$ PDW components, giving rise to superconducting states absent in the pure bond-pairing limit. A Ginzburg--Landau analysis identifies symmetry-allowed couplings that can favor this reorganization. The resulting states exhibit distinct charge modulations and quasiparticle spectra, while the chiral PDW undergoes topological transitions as the onsite attraction increases. Our results demonstrate how uniform superconductivity reshapes the order-parameter landscape and quasiparticle topology of a PDW state.

item.title: Competing lattice instabilities in epitaxially strained BaSnO3
item.description: arXiv:2611.15550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use density functional theory to map the lattice-dynamical landscape of BaSnO3 under biaxial compressive strain and uncover the hierarchy of structural instabilities. Our results demonstrate that the phase stability of strained BaSnO3 cannot be inferred from the softening of the polar mode alone. Instead it is governed by the competition among lattice instabilities and their anharmonic coupling to structural relaxation. Two-mode energy-surface analyses show that the polar and rotational order parameters interact predominantly competitively. While A- and M-point octahedral rotations become unstable before the zone-center polar mode and dominate the harmonic response for moderate values of strain, they are related to a continuous transition without anharmonic lattice coupling and a moderate gain of energy with strain. Large strain may induce a first order transition to a supertetragonal polar state. Once this state is stabilized, the magnitude of polarization and ferroelectric energy well depth are comparable to BaTiO3 under compressive strain. Furthermore, we discuss how an electric field or electron doping may tip the balance between the different modes and favor of the supertetragonal structure over antipolar and rotational alternatives at a reduced critical strain.

item.title: Filling and Sealing Carbon Nanotubes by Local Anodic Oxidation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are prime nanofluidic conduits and nanopores for studying matter under extreme confinement. Since most synthesis routes yield CNTs with closed ends, opening and filling strategies are required to access their interior for fluid and ion transport, whereas studies of the encapsulated species themselves may additionally require sealing to prevent their escape in dry or vacuum environments. Capacitively coupled local anodic oxidation (LAO) in an atomic force microscope (AFM) has been shown to cut individual CNTs at predefined positions, but whether cutting induces opening, filling, or sealing has remained unclear. Using spatially resolved micro-Raman spectroscopy, we find that LAO cutting surprisingly produces filled CNT segments that remain sealed under dry Ar atmosphere for weeks. The magnitudes of the blueshift and broadening of the innermost-wall radial breathing-like mode are consistent with water filling, pointing to the water meniscus condensed between the AFM tip and the substrate as the source of CNT filling during cutting. High-vacuum annealing at 140 {\deg}C releases the encapsulated species from some, but not all, segments, indicating a thermally surmountable barrier rather than re-formed end caps. This one-step cut-fill-seal capability offers a route to diameter-resolved studies of nanoconfined water and aqueous solutions, and to zeptoliter-scale sample delivery for vacuum-based analytical techniques.

item.title: Machine-accelerated extraction of experimental superconducting parameters for physical insight and prediction across thousands of materials
item.description: arXiv:2611.15627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: New superconductors could unlock next-generation technologies from nuclear fusion to lossless electronics. Machine learning can predict candidate superconductors but lacks validated experimental training data beyond the critical temperature. Here we present AutoSuperCon, a database of eight superconducting parameters, containing 20354 entries for 6793 superconductors. The data were extracted from over 47000 arXiv preprints using a large language model and validated against reference datasets ($R^2 = 0.96$ with NIMS SuperCon). Using AutoSuperCon, we show that median gap ratios rise from 3.6 in conventional superconductors to 6.4 in cuprates, 28% of upper critical fields exceed the Pauli limit, and critical temperatures lie below a ceiling proportional to the superfluid density. Further, we train composition-based predictors for the critical temperature ($R^2_{\log}=0.83$) and the upper critical field ($R^2_{\log}=0.69$), boosted by transfer learning. Within known superconducting families, composition alone is sufficient to screen candidates for both parameters. AutoSuperCon thus enables physical insight and data-driven discovery across thousands of superconductors.

item.title: Brute-force molecular dynamics simulation of aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$
item.description: arXiv:2611.15664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chalcogenide alloys such as the prototypical Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ compound are used in phase change electronic memories due to their ability to undergo a fast and reversible transition between the amorphous and crystalline phases upon heating. The amorphous phase is subject to aging that leads to an increase in the electrical resistance, which is detrimental to the operation of the devices. Using a machine learning interatomic potential, we have investigated the structural relaxations responsible for aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ in molecular dynamics simulations at temperatures slightly below the glass transition. The aging simulation, lasting about 100 ns, follows an equilibration of 24 ns at 400 K. During aging we observed an enhancement of the Peierls distortion in axial bonds which is a typical feature of these alloys that we relate to the widening of the electronic band gap computed within Density Functional Theory in smaller aged amorphous models. We also observed a marked reduction of the atomic mobility with an increase of the bond lifetimes during aging. However, we do not see a reduction in homopolar bonds, which are expected to be absent in the ideal aged glass and which should be removed on a much longer time scale.

item.title: A Hierarchical Harmonic-to-Anharmonic Framework for ab initio Screening and Mechanistic Analysis of Negative Thermal Expansion in ZrV2O7
item.description: arXiv:2611.15767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negative thermal expansion (NTE) in framework materials arises from complex lattice dynamics that are challenging to capture using conventional theoretical approaches. Here, we establish a hierarchical computational strategy for investigating NTE in ZrV2O7, integrating the quasiharmonic approximation (QHA), temperature-dependent effective potentials (TDEP), and machine-learning-accelerated ab initio molecular dynamics (ML-MD). Quasi-harmonic lattice-dynamical calculations identify low-frequency phonon modes with negative Gr\"uneisen parameters as inexpensive screening descriptors, while TDEP incorporates finite-temperature anharmonicity and ML-MD further reveals temperature-dependent structural distortions that drive the lattice contraction. The observations are further corroborated with X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements. The concurrent increase in transverse displacement (uT) provides microscopic evidence for a quasi-rigid-unit-mode (QRUM) mechanism underlying the NTE behaviour at elevated temperatures. This is consistent with previous reports on other framework materials, including ZrW2O7, where collective polyhedral rotations and transverse atomic motions have been linked to NTE. Overall, our results demonstrate how relatively inexpensive lattice-dynamical descriptors can identify potential NTE materials, while higher-level anharmonic simulations can then resolve the underlying structural mechanisms at the atomic scale.

item.title: U(1)-Symmetric Spin SYK Models: Ordering, Chaos, and Transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.15896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) model provides an analytically controlled setting for strongly interacting quantum dynamics and holography, but its fermionic formulation leads to nonlocal encoding overheads on qubit-based quantum processors. We study a U(1)-symmetric spin analogue of the complex SYK model, constructed from random charge-conserving $q$-spin interactions that are native to a qubit Hilbert space. In the large-$N$, large-$q$ limit, the model reproduces the leading saddle-point structure of complex fermionic SYK under the identification of chemical potential with magnetic field and charge density with magnetization. We investigate the finite-$N$, finite-$q$ regime using exact diagonalization. A U(1)-invariant ordering susceptibility increases with system size for $q = 2, 4$ but decreases for $q = 6$, while bulk-spectrum level statistics are consistent with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble at half filling and the Gaussian unitary ensemble in the adjacent magnetization sector. We further construct coupled-cluster chains and obtain domain-wall dynamics consistent with diffusive magnetization transport in a small-cluster regime accessible to matrix-product-state simulations. These results establish analytical benchmarks and finite-size signatures of ordering, quantum chaos, and magnetization transport in U(1)-symmetric spin-SYK models, and they motivate quantum simulation of the low-temperature, large-system regime, which remains difficult for classical methods.

item.title: ORCHID-SAGE: Fully Reproducible CALPHAD Assessment from Evidence to Phase Diagram
item.description: arXiv:2611.16308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge of phase stability is the first requirement for materials design, and predicting the conditions under which new materials can be synthesized has become a key capability of self-driving laboratories (SDLs). For inorganic materials, notably alloys, these predictions come from thermodynamic databases built with the CALPHAD method. Building a database, however, requires expert judgment at many steps, and because these decisions are rarely recorded, others can use a database but cannot regenerate or update it. Machines can already collect the data, build a first model with machine-learned interatomic potentials and refine it against experiments. The assessment itself, the sequence of judgments that turns these parts into a reliable database, is still carried out by human experts. We argue that it can be automated reproducibly only if the expert knowledge behind an assessment is encoded in formal protocols, so that an assessment delivers a record of its construction and not only its parameters. We introduce ORCHID-SAGE, a standard that organizes this record into reproducible and automatable protocols. In this first attempt, applied to Cr-Ni, the database was regenerated from its record by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent working only through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and by a refit from public sources only, with the same predictions. Recorded in this way, a database need no longer be fixed at publication but can be updated by AI agents as SDLs and other sources provide new evidence, while the judgment remains with people and on the record.

item.title: Edge-scaling softening of a universal machine-learned potential: point-defect formation energies in a coronene graphene quantum dot
item.description: arXiv:2611.16528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are increasingly used as computationally efficient surrogates for density functional theory (DFT) in high-throughput nanomaterials screening. Systematic softening has been reported for several universal MLIPs when high-energy and far-from-equilibrium configurations are underrepresented in training data. We examine how this behavior appears at under-coordinated edge sites in graphene quantum dots (GQDs), where a vacancy can have pronounced molecular-radical character. Using coronene (C$_{24}$H$_{12}$), a hexagonal GQD with $D_{6h}$ symmetry and three carbon classes, we benchmark SevenNet (7net-omni-i12) against spin-polarized PBE DFT (GPAW) for monovacancy, divacancy, and Stone-Wales defects. Beyond the full site- and bond-resolved landscapes, we perform a controlled matched-reconstruction comparison in which 28 vacancy and divacancy configurations are scored by both engines using self-consistent chemical-potential reservoirs. In this dataset, SevenNet underestimates all 28 vacancy and divacancy formation energies, and the mean deficit increases with under-coordination within each defect family: 0.30-0.74 eV for monovacancies and 0.65-1.11 eV for divacancies as the number of broken edge C-H bonds increases. By contrast, the mean Stone-Wales energies differ by only 0.013 eV. SevenNet also preserves the ordering of three hydrogen-dependent reconstruction basins and reproduces $D_{6h}$-equivalent sites to within a few meV. The within-class symmetry spread therefore provides a practical diagnostic of basin-sensitive relaxations. Within the present coronene benchmark, these results support MLIP-based structure screening and preliminary ranking, while absolute vacancy energies and multi-basin edge configurations still require DFT validation.

item.title: Systematic Evaluation of Training Data Generation Strategies for Machine Learning-Based Molecular and Materials Property Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.16792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning (ML) models for molecular and materials property prediction are often trained on large datasets curated through arbitrary or generic sampling strategies. Such approaches can lead to the over- or under-representation of regions of chemical and materials space that are most relevant to the prediction task. An important challenge is therefore how to efficiently curate training data to maximize predictive performance while minimising the number of labelled examples required. Here, we systematically compare training data acquisition strategies for molecular and materials property prediction, ranging from random sampling to various active learning approaches. We evaluate their performance across different model classes, representations, datasets, and target properties. Our results show that the effectiveness of data acquisition strategies depend strongly on the interplay between the model, dataset, and prediction task, although uncertainty-based sampling generally outperforms alternative strategies. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines for selecting data acquisition strategies under a given labelling budget.

item.title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.14948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

item.title: Atomistic simulations of electrochemical systems with machine learning potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.15939v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern machine learning potentials (MLPs) enable large-scale atomistic simulations at unprecedented accuracy. The incorporation of explicit physical interactions such as long-range electrostatics has continuously broadened their applicability to increasingly complex systems in chemistry and materials science. Extending MLPs to electrochemistry and electrocatalysis, however, is still challenging as it requires the consideration of electrode potentials and electric fields in the atomic interactions. Such approaches have emerged only recently, and although the field is evolving rapidly, further conceptual advances are still needed for carrying out reliable simulations at finite temperature under applied potential. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview about recent progress in the atomistic simulation of electrified interfaces using MLPs. Current developments fall into three different categories. The first comprises linear response models that describe polarisation, polarisability, and Born effective charges, extending conventional MLPs to finite electric fields. The second includes methods that directly learn a field-dependent potential energy surface. The third consists of a series of hybrid approaches combining classical models with machine learning. Although still under active development, these methods represent a major step toward more realistic simulations approaching the quality of electronic structure calculations. Finally, we discuss open challenges and possible future directions for advancing MLP-based simulations aiming for a bottom-up understanding of atomistic processes at electrified interfaces.

item.title: Dynamical mean-field theory of latching Potts networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spontaneous transitions between memories, as observed in internally generated cognition such as mind-wandering and free association, require neural dynamics capable of destabilizing one attractive memory state and moving towards another. We ask what minimal representational structure is required for such transitions to emerge in random associative networks. To address this question, we study Potts associative networks with $S$ active states per unit and slow adaptive thresholds. The $S=1$ case can model a standard Hopfield-like network of binary units. We employ dynamical mean-field theory in the extensive-load regime, where the number of stored patterns scales linearly with network size and connectivity, and we focus on transitions between two condensed memories, which are singled out in the connectivity matrix. In the finite-load regime, we show that transitions are governed by an effective drive term, whose sign and temporal evolution distinguish high-latching (structured), low-latching (random), and non-latching regimes. The resulting phase diagram shows that adaptation alone is not sufficient: transitions only occur within certain ranges of the overlap between the two memories. In the binary case $S=1$, in particular, no unit can be active in both memories but in different Potts states, thus strongly supressing the high-latching, structured transitions that exist for $S>1$. In the extensive-load regime, non-condensed memories generate colored fluctuations and retarded self-interactions through an effective memory kernel. We find that latching trajectories change the effective timescale of this kernel, a dynamical signature of transitions in the extensive-load regime. These results indicate that multi-state Potts-like representations are essential for structured memory-to-memory transitions, a hallmark of spontaneous thought.

item.title: peapods: A Rust-Accelerated Monte Carlo Package for Ising and XY Spin Systems
item.description: arXiv:2602.19045v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present peapods, an open-source Python package for Monte Carlo simulation of classical spin models with arbitrary couplings, whose sampling loop runs in Rust. It samples Ising models on periodic Bravais lattices given by user-specified neighbor offsets, optionally with open or antiperiodic boundaries, and XY models with signed couplings and site dilution on hypercubic lattices. Besides Metropolis and heat-bath sweeps, Swendsen-Wang and Wolff cluster updates and parallel tempering, it provides a family of replica cluster moves for spin glasses: the Houdayer, J\"org and Chayes-Machta-Redner moves, multi-pair variants of the first two, replica-permutation moves and a gauged form of them, and Swendsen-Wang replica Monte Carlo across temperatures. The same-temperature moves share one construction, a symmetry of the replicas' joint energy applied on clusters, and one-step stationarity tests from exact Boltzmann samples on small lattices check each family of moves that satisfies detailed balance. The package measures overlap distributions, spin-glass correlation lengths, autocorrelation times, equilibration and tempering-flow diagnostics, and jackknife errors over disorder samples. It reproduces the exact critical temperatures of the square and triangular Ising lattices, and its Binder curves for simple-cubic, BCC and FCC lattices agree at the literature critical temperatures. For the three-dimensional $\pm J$ spin glass, the crossings of $\xi_{\mathrm{SG}}/L$ for $L \le 12$ extrapolate, with the Janus correction exponent held fixed, to $T_c = 1.085(42)$, consistent with the Janus value $1.1019(29)$. For the two-dimensional XY model, the helicity modulus, correlation length and structure factor agree with high-precision reference data within $1.9$ standard errors. This article describes version 0.3.0.

item.title: Scaling limit of the Random Language Model
item.description: arXiv:2606.28105v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a quantitative theory of the Random Language Model (RLM), an ensemble of stochastic context-free grammars, in a scaling limit where the number of hidden symbols $N \to \infty$ while the grammar temperature $\tilde\epsilon_d \to 0$ at fixed $x = \tilde\epsilon_d \log N$. In this limit, the model admits a controlled description based on a large-deviation principle over rule-usage patterns. A semi-annealed approximation maps the problem to a class of Random Energy Models with nontrivial combinatorics. We show that the RLM exhibits a freezing transition at a critical value $x_c=1/8$, below which rule usage condenses on a subset of preferred rules and language statistics acquire a nontrivial dependence on corpus length. A second characteristic scale at $x=1/2$, associated with the breakdown of Gaussian fluctuations, separates transition and babbling regimes. Across regimes, we derive explicit scaling laws for the number of distinct rules, entropy, and energy, identifying distinct frozen and critical regimes controlled by the interplay of grammar size, corpus length, and temperature. The theory resolves previous ambiguities regarding the existence of a thermodynamic transition and explains the slow approach to the large-$N$ limit as a consequence of the dependence on $\log N$. It further provides a unified framework in which universal statistical properties of language emerge from typical realizations of generative grammars, with implications for both natural language statistics and the behavior of large language models. Heaps' law and Zipf's law are both derived, and the dependence of predictive entropy on context length is rationalized. Comparison with empirical measurements of Heaps' and Zipf's laws yields parameter estimates for real languages.

item.title: Coupled Electronic Structure and Phonon Transport Driven by Bonding Reconstruction in Ba-B-C Clathrates
item.description: arXiv:2609.32894v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Composition-driven changes in electron count, structural symmetry and bonding environment can couple the electronic and thermal responses in a material. Here, with density-functional theory and machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), we compare cubic BaB3C3 with its B-C substituted tetragonal counterpart, BaB2C4. The additional valence electron and accompanying change in crystal symmetry drive a transition from metallic BaB3C3 to semiconducting BaB2C4 and the formation of short/strong C-C bonds. The reconstructed bonding network hardens the phonon spectrum, with the maximum frequency increasing from 800 to 900. At room temperature, the in-plane lattice thermal conductivity increases from 7.6 to 18.7 W/mK, while the thermal transport alters from isotropic to anisotropic for BaB2C4. This enhancement is associated with the strengthened bonding network, higher phonon frequencies/group velocities, longer lifetimes and larger mean free paths. Machine learning potentials accurately reproduced the DFT-level energies and forces with negligible errors, and the harmonic and anharmonic features are benchmarked against explicit first-principles calculations. Our findings demonstrate that minimal B-C substitution provides a viable strategy to link composition- and structure-associated bonding reconstruction with correlated electronic and phononic alterations.

item.title: Probing chiral topological order of the Kitaev honeycomb on a trapped ion processor
item.description: arXiv:2507.08939v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Kitaev's honeycomb model is a paradigmatic exactly solvable system hosting a quantum spin liquid with non-Abelian anyons and topologically protected edge modes, offering a platform for fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, real candidate Kitaev materials invariably include complex secondary interactions that obscure the realization of spin-liquid behavior and demand novel quantum computational approaches for efficient simulation. Here we report quantum simulations of a 22-site Kitaev honeycomb lattice on a trapped-ion quantum processor, without and with non-integrable Heisenberg interactions that are present in real materials. We develop efficient quantum circuits for ground-state preparation, achieving high accuracy with energy errors equivalent to an effective temperature $\approx 0.2$ (in units of the Kitaev interactions), consistent with the experimentally relevant spin-liquid regime. Starting from these states, we apply controlled perturbations and measure time-dependent spin correlations along the system's edge. In the non-Abelian phase, we observe chiral edge dynamics consistent with a non-zero Chern number, a hallmark of chiral topological order, which vanishes upon transition to the Abelian toric code phase. Extending to the non-integrable Kitaev-Heisenberg model, we find that weak Heisenberg interactions preserve chiral edge dynamics, while stronger couplings suppress them, signaling the breakdown of topological protection. These simulations establish edge-mode dynamical simulations on quantum computers as a staple technique to understand the topological and chiral phases of matter in Hamiltonians beyond integrability.

item.title: From Accurate Quantum Chemistry to Converged Thermodynamics for Ion Pairing in Solution
item.description: arXiv:2603.06800v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantitative prediction of thermodynamic properties in solution is essential for translating atomistic simulations into reliable chemical insight. As an exemplar system, the behaviour of CaCO$_3$ in water has been widely studied to understand its mineralization in seawater, with potential implications for carbon-capture strategies. However, making accurate computational predictions has been a long-standing challenge, requiring both highly accurate electronic structure methods and extensive statistical sampling. Here, we combine advances in machine learning and electronic structure theory to fully resolve the ion pairing free energy of CaCO$_3$ with explicit solvation. We show that achieving quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond density functional theory up to the ''gold-standard'' coupled cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We generate a set of systematically improvable models, enabling reliable insights into the initial association mechanism of Ca and CO$_3$ ions prior to nucleation while fully quantifying enthalpic and entropic effects. These quantitatively accurate models further resolve a long-standing lack of consensus surrounding the hydration mechanism of the calcium ion in solution. Our results demonstrate that CCSD(T)-level thermodynamic predictions of complex aqueous systems can now be routinely achieved.

item.title: An Asymptotic Theory of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning
item.description: arXiv:2606.03217v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a widely used mechanism for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models by generating intermediate reasoning steps at inference time. Yet the scaling behavior of generalization with CoT depth remains poorly understood. To address this question, we study a theoretically solvable model of CoT for in-context weight prediction in linear regression, where test-time reasoning is represented as an iterative refinement of the weight-parameter estimate. Using tools from random matrix theory under high-dimensional asymptotics, we derive an exact formula for the generalization error as a function of reasoning depth, pretraining data amount, and context length. Our analysis reveals a sharp phase transition separating exponential and polynomial improvement, saturation, and overthinking, and characterizes how the optimal reasoning depth scales. We further show that deeper reasoning is most effective with sufficiently rich pretraining and in-context information, whereas limited pretraining or context makes longer reasoning prone to error amplification or saturation. We also validate these predictions through experiments on fully learned linear attention and softmax attention models. Our results provide a unified theoretical account of how test-time CoT depth affects generalization.

item.title: TheoPhysEval: Assessing AI agents at autonomous theoretical physics problem solving
item.description: arXiv:2610.16733v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. On average, agents show only small changes in accuracy when denied web search and access to background research papers, suggesting significant memorization of the literature. These results suggest that state-of-the-art agents can accurately perform concrete calculations required across theoretical physics research. We comment on the broader implications of these findings and discuss possible explanations for the current lack of agent-led breakthroughs in theoretical physics despite their outstanding problem-solving abilities.

item.title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.03767v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: General-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rival domain-specific pipelines on scientific prediction, but their performance under distribution shift is untested. Across six alloy and crystal-structure datasets, we benchmark LLMs against traditional, BERT-based, TabPFN, and text-regression baselines under random cross-validation and six out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols shifting input and target distributions, with severity quantified via a standardized Wasserstein distance. We isolate the LLM's advantage over k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) retrieval: it beats k-NN on all eight tasks at a fixed 5% reference budget, on seven of eight when independently optimized, and in 72.5% of 120 OOD task--protocol configurations against an optimized baseline. No model family is uniformly best; the LLM is often strongest under severe shift, and error increases with target-space but not representation-space severity. Self-reported LLM confidence tracks both shift and error, more consistently than a density-only control from the same retrieved samples, and a matched-cohort check finds no substantial evidence of memorization.

item.title: Quantitative Assessment of Crystal Structure Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.10380v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) aims to predict a material's 3D structure from its chemical composition, with applications from energy storage to biomedical devices. Despite its importance, existing evaluation frameworks suffer from key limitations: they rely on threshold-sensitive or incomparable metrics, focus predominantly on geometric performance while overlooking physical plausibility, and fail to account for polymorphism, where a chemical composition can crystallize into multiple stable structures. In parallel, recent Symmetry-Informed CSP (SICSP) methods often report results alongside standard CSP baselines while receiving crystallographic templates at inference, which constrain the search space and make SICSP a fundamentally different task. To address these limitations, we introduce an Orientation-invariant, Polymorph-Aware, Large Benchmark (OPAL-Bench) that evaluates CSP and SICSP as separate tasks. We evaluate 7 CSP and 2 SICSP methods under OPAL-Bench across 4 datasets using threshold-free geometric and physical distance metrics. Our results show that no method dominates across all metrics, and that geometric performance is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility. We also release OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline for the CSP track that performs competitively on geometric metrics and ranks among the best on physical ones. By unifying geometric and physical metrics under a polymorph-aware protocol, OPAL-Bench enables a more comprehensive assessment of generative quality in CSP.

item.title: Linear-time Shape Alignment with ROSHAMBO3
item.description: Three-dimensional (shape) similarity is a useful primitive for virtual screening and molecular machine learning, but current open implementations are limited in performance by a quadratic inner loop across pairs of query-and databasemolecule atoms. ROSHAMBO3 achieves a 78–154× speedup over the previous open SOTA ROSHAMBO2 by using query-amortized Gaussian fields that make the inner loop linear combined with system-scale optimization at the algorithmic, GPU, and host layers, screening up to 55M query–conformer pairs/s on NVIDIA GPUs, with secondary CPU (x86, ARM) and Apple Metal backends. We further describe the human expert–AI interaction loop that guided the exploration and implementation of ROSHAMBO3 and discuss implications for the scientific software commons. ROSHAMBO3 is open source at https://github.com/kimiatx-oss/roshambo3.

item.title: Zeolite ionic conduction genome
item.description: Zeolites combine diverse framework topologies, tunable compositions and exchangeable charge-compensating cations, offering a broad platform for solid-electrolyte discovery. However, how framework topology and composition jointly govern Li-ion transport remains poorly understood. Here we use machine-learning force fields to perform more than 40,000 molecular-dynamics simulations of nearly 2,900 zeolite topology–composition models spanning 263 zeolite framework types and a range of Si/Al ratios and establish a database of Nernst–Einstein ionic conductivity estimates for zeolites. We identify planar five- and six-membered rings as topological bottlenecks that impede Li-ion transport, linking local hopping barriers to long-range transport across diverse topologies. Within a given topological framework, the Si/Al ratio determines the Li content required for charge compensation and shapes the local electrostatic environment for Li-ion migration. In some frameworks, the competition between increasing Li-ion concentration and decreasing diffusivity leads to conductivity maxima at intermediate Si/Al ratios. Taking THO as an example, lowering the Si/Al ratio from 3 to 1 doubles the Li content per framework tetrahedral site but reduces ionic conductivity at 300 K by approximately 21%, showing that higher Li loading does not necessarily improve conductivity. Together, the database and mechanistic insights provide a foundation for co-optimizing topology and composition in zeolites for solid-electrolyte applications.

item.title: Generative diffusion model with inverse renormalization group flows
item.description: Natural data contain structure across multiple length scales, yet exploiting these correlations for efficient generation remains challenging. Masuki and Ashida introduce a diffusion model that uses renormalization group theory to systematically design a coarse-to-fine generation process. Applications to protein structure prediction and image generation demonstrate improved sample quality or sampling speed over denoising diffusion probabilistic model baselines with the same network architectures, highlighting how physical principles can guide the design of efficient generative models.

item.title: Enhancing the energy storage performance of ferroelectric-based composite ceramics via functional-unit-engineered interfacial heterogeneity
item.description: Ferroelectric-based composite ceramics incorporating linear dielectrics as functional units have emerged as promising candidates for high energy storage applications, owing to their synergistic advantages of robust polarization response and high electrical insulation. However, the underlying mechanism governing how local interfacial heterogeneity induced by functional units modulates the energy storage performance remains unclear. Here, high-throughput phase-field simulations are employed to systematically investigate the influence of functional-unit-engineered interfacial heterogeneity on recoding the polarization domain and altering breakdown evolution across over 150 different composite ceramics. As demonstrated in the BiFeO3–Al2O3 composite, constructing an interconnected and densely stacked functional unit network can change local electric field redistribution and form vortex-like domain configurations, thereby achieving the synergistic optimization of polarization response and breakdown resistance. Compared with pristine BiFeO3, the optimized composite exhibits theoretical improvements of 188%, 466%, and 170% in breakdown strength, energy density, and efficiency, respectively. Overall, the present work establishes a structure–property relationship between functional unit configurations and energy storage performance, offering new perspectives for designing high-performance composite ceramics through interfacial heterogeneity engineering.

item.title: FlaN-a method for calculating morphologies of molecular crystals using a flat nucleus approach
item.description: We present FlaN, a Python program for predicting crystal morphologies from two-dimensional nucleation theory. FlaN constructs polygonal flat nuclei from step-edge energies calculated directly from intermolecular interactions and introduces an edge-density correction factor, K, to account for anisotropic molecular packing. Analysis of over 200 molecular crystal structures shows that inclusion of K reduces sensitivity to user-defined parameters and improves morphology predictions for systems where edge-site densities differ substantially between crystal faces. Calculated morphologies are in good agreement with experimentally observed habits for a range of single-component and multi-component crystals, including the three known polymorphs of 7-fluoroisatin and a number of other systems. FlaN provides a computationally efficient framework for exploring morphology and supersaturation-dependent shape evolution of molecular crystals.

item.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery from Code to Clinic
item.description: Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are revolutionizing drug discovery, transforming an inefficient system of trial and error into one based on predictive modeling and data analysis. This comprehensive review on the growing role of computational techniques and tools considers every stage of the traditional drug development pipeline. This paper discusses how novel frameworks, high-throughput data analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations advance the discovery process, from target identification and molecular screening to pharmacokinetic profiling and candidate prioritization for clinical trials. By analyzing a wide range of recent studies, this review demonstrates that these approaches significantly reduce the time required to generate new chemical entities. This paper focuses on the relation between curating data, designing models, and validating experimental results, which together determine the reproducibility and usability of computational outputs. Even though computational methods have yielded many successes, their application is limited by several challenges. Only when paired with high-quality experimental data and interdisciplinary expertise can these methods substantially reduce the time, cost, and uncertainty associated with drug discovery and development. Limitations, including poor data quality, inconsistent data reporting, and limited diversity in chemical and biological databases, continue to constrain accuracy. The lack of interpretability in the results of computational systems complicates regulatory evaluation and broader acceptance within the scientific community. Addressing these challenges involves data standardization, clear benchmarking, and integrating experimental feedback into models. All in all, the findings demonstrate that computational drug discovery is moving from its exploratory phase to a more important role in pharmaceutical research, and future discovery pipelines will increasingly depend on computational frameworks.

item.title: Cost-Bounded Evolving Guardrails for Chemistry Protocol Screening via Event-Pair Evidence Retrieval
item.description: Translating a published synthesis paragraph into a machine-actionable protocol is now routine, but judging whether the resulting steps are chemically safe on a given bench is not: frontier models recognise equipment at near-perfect accuracy yet fall to 0.28 accuracy on laboratory safety questions, and whole-text screening of a multi-step paragraph cannot point to which condition–effect pair justifies its verdict. We argue that risk lives at the level of event pairs, not paragraphs, and propose UHG, a cost-bounded evolving guardrail for screening heterogeneous chemistry protocols via event-pair evidence retrieval. UHG compiles text, tabular procedures, and figure captions into one event-pair space, retrieves condition–effect pairs as auditable evidence, distils a teacher’s evidence selection into a lightweight reranker, and evolves per-lab decision boundaries under a hard annotation and inference budget. On 50 catalyst-synthesis protocols with step-level risk labels, UHG reaches unsafe F1 of 0.72 at 0.13 of the cost of whole-text GPT-4o screening, outperforming Claude-3.5-Sonnet whole-text screening

item.title: What should AI agents know? Explicit knowledge for trustworthy, sustainable materials research
item.description: Artificial intelligence can propose materials, interpret measurements and increasingly coordinate experiments. Yet reliable scientific autonomy requires more than capable models: research systems must preserve what is known, where evidence came from and which actions are justified. We argue that machine-actionable scientific knowledge is essential for trustworthy autonomous research, and that ontologygrounded knowledge graphs are a particularly powerful way of achieving it when scientific meaning must be shared across disciplines, systems and scales. Using The World Avatar (TWA) as a case study, we examine how ontologies, dynamic knowledge graphs and software agents connect models, literature, experiments and laboratory assets, and how ontology-derived tools can constrain large language model (LLM) actions. A reported design-to-synthesis study of a new metal–organic polyhedron demonstrates the integration of previously separate tasks, but not yet an environmental benefit or fully autonomous discovery. A material-passport example further shows how shared semantics can support industrial circularity assessment. We distinguish structural validation from scientific verification, and circularity indicators from demonstrated environmental benefits. The priority is not to create a universal platform but to build evidence-preserving research infrastructure whose scientific and sustainability benefits can be tested.

item.title: Machine Learning-Driven High-Throughput Discovery of Energetic Materials Based on Regioisomeric Pyrazole Scaffolds
item.description: The energy-safety trade-off remains the central challenge in energetic materials design. This study constructs a virtual library of 25,417 derivatives based on two regioisomeric pyrazole scaffolds and trains predictive models using Density Functional Theory (DFT) data from 413 molecules. Unlike conventional approaches, we systematically benchmarked three descriptor families and identified RDKit global physicochemical descriptors as superior to Morgan fingerprints, revealing that global molecular properties govern detonation performance in this regioisomeric system. Among six evaluated machine learning algorithms, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was identified as the optimal base model. Building on this, we developed a multi-task XGBoost framework that jointly trains four physically coupled properties, further improving average R2 from 0.891 to 0.927. Critically, SHAP analysis reveals that the amino group (fr_NH2) exerts a negative net contribution to detonation velocity—direct evidence of the energy-safety trade-off—and enables regioisomer-specific design rules. Screening the remaining 25,004 molecules and validating the top 20 candidates by blind DFT calculations yield mean relative errors of 3.02% for D and 5.76% for P, with the best candidate below 2%. This interpretable, multi-task screening paradigm offers a generalizable platform for accelerated energetic materials discovery.

item.title: Walk-on-Spheres Solution to Heterogeneous Transport Phenomena

Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) is a particle-based technique used to describe physical phenomena as diverse as electrostatics, heat conduction, rendering, ion transport, and chemical reactions. It is fast, scalable, meshless, and applicable to geometrically complex domains, as long as the governing equations…

Polymeric nitrogen frameworks are of interest for high-energy-density materials because their conversion to molecular ${\mathrm{N}}_{2}$ is associated with substantial energy release, while their experimental synthesis remains challenging. Here we combine particle-swarm structure prediction, first-p…

item.title: Local Chemistry of Na-Site Substitution in P2−NaxMn0.66Ni0.33O2 Cathodes for Na-ion Batteries. A First-Principles Study of Structural Fluctuations, Ion Mobility, and Charge Redistribution
item.description: Layered oxides emerge as promising materials as cathode in sodium ion batteries due to the possibility to avoid critical metals and the direct industrial transferability in lithium-ion battery factories. A key point is that the layered structure can host a wide range of cations, enabling the substitution as a strategy to improve key factors such as structural stability, electronic conductivity, ion mobility, etc. For that, it important to determine how the different substituents can affect these factors, to then mitigate side reactions and improve the desired mechanisms. In the present work, the effect of the interlayer substituent ions on the open circuit voltage, cation mobility, local structural fluctuations, and electronic structure has been investigated for P2 − NaxMn0.66Ni0.33O2 ( with x = 0.66 and 0.083) cathodes through Density Functional Theory. Calculated open-circuit voltages show that the dopants do not significantly alter the overall desodiation potential, while the local voltage response depends on the substituent identity and the sodium content. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations reveal that all dopants maintain the layered topology while inducing distinct local dynamical responses, with Mg and Zn producing the most rigid local environments and K the highest lattice flexibility. CI-NEB calculations and Arrhenius-based estimation of diffusion rates show that K facilitates the Na-ion hopping, and Ca maintains Na-ion migration barriers comparable to those of the pristine material, whereas Mg and Zn significantly increase the activation energy for Na inter site-hopping. Electronic structure analysis reveals a markedly different behavior between isovalent and aliovalent substitutions: at high Na content, divalent dopants locally promote Mn3+-like electronic configurations, while at low Na content the charge is primarily accommodated by the oxygen sublattice; in both regimes, divalent dopants enhance oxygen participation in charge compensation. These results provide atomistic insight into how Na-site chemistry governs the balance between ionic transport, electronic structure, and structural stability, offering practical guidelines for the local chemistry of high-performance layered sodium-ion cathodes.

item.title: Spectator Cations Regulate Li+ Solvation in Ionic Liquid Electrolytes
item.description: Organic cations are integral to the ionic network of ionic liquid electrolytes for lithium-ion batteries, yet their participation in lithium-ion solvation offers a design variable beyond salt concentration and anion chemistry. Here, we show that relocating the ether oxygen in the side chain of pyrrolidinium cations changes lithium-anion association and ion transport at a fixed lithium-salt mole fraction. Spectroscopy and theoretical calculations support reduced participation of N-ethoxymethyl-N-methylpyrrolidinium in the coordination network, termed a “spectator cation”. The ionic liquid electrolyte featuring a spectator cation exhibits a higher fraction of lithium-coordinated bis(fluorosulfonyl)amide anions, lower viscosity, and faster lithium-ion self-diffusion compared with electrolytes containing alkyl-substituted or alternative ether-functionalized cations. These changes accompany an increased anion-derived contribution to the solid electrolyte interphase and improved lithium plating/stripping efficiency. Related improvements in sodium electrolytes extend the cation comparison to a second alkali metal. The results identify the ether-oxygen position as a molecular design variable for adjusting local coordination and bulk transport together in solvent-free ionic liquid electrolytes.

item.title: Streamlining Lateral Flow Assay (LFA) Data Analysis: A MATLAB® Live Script for Integrated Batch Image Processing and Limit of Detection Determination
item.description: Manual quantitative lateral flow assay (LFA) analysis can span at least three software environments: image-analysis software such as ImageJ, spreadsheets such as Excel, and coding tools using MATLAB, Python or R. Repeatedly defining Test, Control and background regions of interest (ROIs) for individual strips, transferring measurements and performing separate statistical and calibration analyses makes data analysis for standard-curve experiments laborious and introduces opportunities for manual handling errors. We present a one-stop MATLAB Live Script framework for single-image and batch LFA image analysis and data analysis. For batch calibration, researchers supply a folder of cropped LFA images with concentration and replicate information encoded in filenames, select the analysis settings and click MATLAB’s Run button once. The automated workflow then extracts line signals, combines replicate measurements, generates the calibration curve and determines the limit of detection (LoD), without manual intermediate measurements or data transfers. The framework supports sandwich and competitive assays with colorimetric or fluorescent/chemiluminescent readouts for strips containing one Test and one Control line. Quantification uses baseline-corrected peak areas or peak prominences, with optional Test/Control normalization. Algorithm-defined measurement regions avoid the variability of manually redrawn ROIs, enabling reproducible image quantification when the same images and analysis settings are reanalyzed. Calibration options include four-parameter logistic, five-parameter logistic, Hill, Langmuir, linear and two-term exponential models, with two direction-aware, blank-based methods for LoD determination. Diagnostic visualizations, input validation and analysis checks help reduce signal-extraction and calculation errors and make remaining failures visible for easier rectification, while model coefficients and goodness-of-fit statistics support interpretation. By automating the intermediate steps within one analysis environment, this framework streamlines LFA quantification and reduces opportunities for errors arising from repeated manual measurements and data handling in laboratory research and assay development. This document provides a detailed user guide to use the two MATLAB Live Scripts – for single strip and batch analysis.

item.title: SmartReact: An Open-Source Python Package for Scalable Forward Synthesis Enumeration Built on Interpretable SMARTS Templates
item.description: Predicting which products can be made from a set of building blocks underpins library design, analogue generation, and synthesis-constrained generative modelling. Reaction templates encoded as SMARTS patterns are the standard tool for this forward synthesis enumeration task. However, existing approaches force a trade-off between chemical coverage, specificity, and the computational cost of applying large template sets at scale. We present SmartReact, an open-source Python library that resolves this trade-off through a template set built on SMARTS-RX, a hierarchical functional group ontology. SmartReact's templates are a combinatorial expansions over the functional group ontology of 406 patterns based on which functional groups interact in which reaction, so the library exposes only a few hundred distinct reactant-side patterns no matter how many templates it holds, and one classification per molecule resolves thousands of templates at once. Every prediction of SmartReact is traceable to a named reaction and an explicit set of functional group requirements, making results directly interpretable by chemists and straightforward to audit. New reaction types can be incorporated by specifying a SMARTS pattern and its functional group requirements, making the library easy to extend. A case study enumerating 536 001 unique products from 1 000 building blocks in 14.1 s demonstrates real-world utility at scale.Scientific Contribution: SmartReact contributes a large, expert-refined SMARTS reaction template library together with an open-source Python package designed to use it efficiently. The library's 9 770 templates spanning 37 medicinal chemistry reaction types are generated by combinatorial expansion over the SMARTS-RX functional group ontology, which gives them a chemical specificity and non-redundancy that auto-extracted libraries lack and, at the same time, a bounded reactant-side pattern space that makes them cheap to pre-filter.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Networks Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling end-to-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. For a feed-forward neural network (FNN) using extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs), embedding the EoS reduces the average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 8.67% to 5.57%. Replacing the FNN and ECFP representation with a graph neural network (GNN) using cyclic polymer graphs further reduces the average MAPE to 2.58%. Pre-training the models on PC-SAFT parameters for small molecules, followed by fine-tuning on polymer PVT data, yields additional improvements, reducing the average MAPE to 5.06% for the FNN and 2.15% for the GNN. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining an embedded EoS with geometric deep learning, and transfer learning for accurate polymer PVT predictions.

item.title: On-the-fly Neural Network based Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations of NH3-SCR over Cu-CHA
item.description: Copper exchanged chabazite (Cu-CHA) is the preferred choice for abatement of NOx from lean burn engines. The low-temperature activity depends critically on the presence of paired [Cu(NH3)2]2 + complexes, which are required for O2 adsorption. The pairing of [Cu(NH3)2]2 + complexes has so far been studied by ab initio molecular dynamics or more recently molecular dynamics using machine learning force-fields. An alternative to molecular dynamics is kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) simulations, which enable simulations over longer time scales. In this study, an on-the-fly kMC model is developed where the rates for [Cu(NH3)2]2 + diffusion are evaluated on the fly using a machine learning force field (ML-FF). We find that the fraction of paired complexes depends sensitively on the zeolite composition and the aluminum distribution. The results reveal a large distribution of Cu pair stabilities and that only few Cu ions are paired, demonstrating the heterogeneous nature of Cu-CHA. A mean field model based on the fraction of paired complexes is used to explore how changes in zeolite composition affect the catalytic activity. The methodology of combining kMC and ML-FF to account for dynamic changes in catalyst structure during reaction conditions is general and provide a possibility to go beyond the often used static approximation when evaluating reaction rates.

item.title: alchemy: bounded enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks
item.description: Automated construction of chemical reaction networks is limited by the combinatorial growth of possible molecules, intermediates, and formal transformations. We present alchemy, an open-source Python workflow for systematic enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks. Within an explicitly bounded graph space, alchemy generates connected, neutral C/N/H molecular graphs with single, double, or triple bonds and specified radical counts; RDKit sanitisation and canonicalisation then remove graph-invalid and duplicate records. Formal reaction candidates are constructed without learned reaction templates by combining bond-dissociation records into rearrangement and transfer stoichiometries. Parallel generation, persistent disk-backed storage, and Kuzu graph representation make the resulting formal network searchable. An independent brute-force control recovers exactly the same 416 neutral molecular graphs as alchemy in a three-heavy-atom C/N/H space. In a trimethylamine case study limited to at most five heavy atoms and one unpaired electron per reaction side, the workflow generated 41,735 unique molecular graphs and a seed-0 bounded sample of 60,035 first-generation reaction records. The reaction construction is not complete because high-frequency shared fragments are handled by a documented deterministic sampling cap. An optional PaiNN molecular-energy model is distributed with the software, but its closed-shell QM9 benchmark does not validate the open-shell species considered here and its output is not used to rank, filter, or interpret the case-study records. alchemy therefore provides a reproducible route to bounded reaction-space construction and downstream graph inspection.

item.title: Dopant-induced impurity states enable surface electronic responsiveness in kaolinite nanoclay
item.description: Natural nanoclay minerals offer abundant layered platforms, yet their low symmetry and complex defect chemistry make controllable electronic modulation challenging. Herein, kaolinite is used as a representative 2D nanoclay to establish a dopant-engineering strategy for electronic activation by combining structure-aware machine learning with first-principles calculations, covering 29 transition-metal dopants across multiple concentrations. The electronic properties of kaolinite are affected more strongly by dopant identity than by dopant concentration. Favorable combinations of structural stability and electronic tunability are achieved by several transition-metal dopants, among which Mn-doped kaolinite is selected as a representative case. Mn substitution alters the local Mn-O coordination environment and introduces impurity states near the band edges, effectively weakening the intrinsic insulating character of kaolinite. Adsorption of representative volatile organic compounds further induces the redistribution of the density of states, interfacial charge transfer, and work function shifts, confirming that bulk electronic modulation can be efficiently translated into surface responsiveness. These findings establish transition-metal doping as a viable route to convert inert natural minerals into tunable electronic interfaces for sensing applications.

item.title: Machine learning-assisted design of zero magnetic temperature-control chips for on-chip quantum sensors
item.description: Alkali-vapor atom-based quantum sensors are urgently needed in the cutting-edge frontier of extremely weak field measurements. However, the generation and control of atomic vapor currently heavily rely on the flexible heater and the discrete temperature sensor, which severely hinder practical application. Herein, we report on-chip, high-performance temperature-control chips with very low residual magnetic flux density, enabled by the multipole-field suppression microstructure designed by particle swarm optimization algorithms, achieving two to three orders of magnitude reduction compared with conventional structures. The unique structure is formed by multiturn parallel winding arrangement, resulting in a synergistic cancelation of the stray magnetic field. A one-step manufacturing process based on oxygen plasma treatment and metal lift-off facilitated tough adhesion is developed for high-efficiency fabrication. As a result, a low magnetic field coefficient of ∼4.3 pT/mA, a high heating power of ∼1 W, and an exceptional temperature fluctuation of ±10 mK are reached, which represents significant improvement in comprehensive performance compared to previous reports. Furthermore, we configure a chip-scale quantum magnetometer with the optimal sensitivity of 10 fT/Hz1/2. Benefiting from its high-performance capabilities, integrated functionality, and the straightforward microfabrication process, the methods reported here are, in principle, generalizable to all thermal alkali-atom-based quantum sensors, including atomic magnetometers, atomic clocks, atomic gyroscopes, and beyond.

item.title: Neuroevolution potentials uncover concentration-dependent Li + transport mechanisms in PEO–LiTFSI electrolytes
item.description: Ion transport in solid polymer electrolytes depends on local coordination, polymer segmental relaxation and collective ionic motion. Modelling ion transport across salt concentrations remains challenging because the local coordination must be accurately described while slow polymer relaxation and ionic motion are adequately sampled. Here, we combine uncertainty-guided active learning with neuroevolution potential (NEP) simulations to investigate poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO)–LiTFSI electrolytes over a broad range of salt concentrations. Trained on density functional theory reference data, the NEP reproduces local coordination, density and glass-transition-temperature trends. On the test set, the NEP achieves energy and force root mean square errors of 3.91 meV atom−1 and 132.5 meV Å−1, respectively. Increasing the salt concentration promotes anion-rich coordination around Li+ and extended ionic networks, while slowing PEO relaxation and the motion of both Li+ and TFSI−. Over the sampled timescales, slower Li+ and TFSI− motion in the high-salt range lowers the conductivity estimated from individual-ion displacements, i.e. the Nernst–Einstein estimate, and the collective conductivity estimate with the negative correlations between like ions. These findings show how anion-associated local activity weakens collective charge transport, providing a molecular interpretation of the conductivity decline at high salt concentrations.

item.title: Field-tunable Schottky-to-ohmic contact transition and visible-light absorption enhancement in a newly predicted 2D B 3 S/graphene van der Waals heterostructure
item.description: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors with tunable interfacial and optical properties are vital for advanced nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices. Using global structure prediction and first-principles calculations, we identify a previously unknown low-energy 2D B3S phase with a distinctive S–B–B–S layered configuration. The B3S monolayer is dynamically and thermally stable (up to 2000 K under ab initio molecular dynamics) and exhibits an indirect wide bandgap of 4.21 eV (HSE06) and strong intrinsic ultraviolet absorption. A B3S/graphene van der Waals heterostructure forms an n-type Schottky contact at equilibrium. Under a perpendicular electric field, the interface shows a reversible Schottky-to-Ohmic transition, achieving field-tunable carrier polarity and barrier control through charge redistribution and built-in electric fields. Moreover, visible-light absorption is significantly enhanced and spectrally tunable owing to interlayer electronic hybridization. These findings introduce a novel 2D B3S semiconductor and demonstrate a feasible strategy for designing field-responsive, broadband optoelectronic heterostructures with reconfigurable transport and photoresponse properties.
