item.title: Physics-constrained machine learning for powder x-ray diffraction
item.description: Powder x-ray diffraction is the workhorse of crystalline materials characterization, yet its interpretation still relies heavily on expert judgment. Machine learning offers a route to automate this process, with progress over the past decade revealing a clear trend toward increasingly reliable models as more physical knowledge is incorporated. Early neural networks treated diffraction patterns as generic one-dimensional signals and often failed to generalize from simulated to experimental data. Performance improved as diffraction physics was incorporated first into the data and then into the models used to interpret them. In this Perspective, we trace this progression and argue that the next step is to constrain inference using computational priors. Machine-learned interatomic potentials now make it inexpensive to predict quantities such as phase stability, thermal expansion, and defect behavior, which can constrain which phases are likely to form and how their diffraction patterns evolve with changing experimental conditions. Incorporating these priors directly into the inference objective could improve the reliability of both ex situ analysis and in situ or operando measurements, and we discuss the opportunities and challenges involved.

item.title: Advanced High-Throughput Characterization of Nanoporous Materials using Pore Graphs
item.description: Nanoporous materials databases now contain millions of structures, yet the tools for characterizing their void spaces have not kept pace. Standard descriptors such as largest cavity diameter and pore limiting diameter are global quantities that conflate local pore geometry with inter-pore connectivity, and can hide distinct pores and network topology behind a single number. We present Mofography, an open-source Python/Rust library that recasts pore characterization as a three-dimensional image-processing problem. It segments the void space into non-overlapping pore regions, connects them at shared windows, and constructs a pore graph that decouples local properties (size, shape, chemistry) from global topology (percolation, connectivity). Global textural properties are obtained as queries on this graph and agree with those from Zeo++ and Pore-Blazer across a diverse set of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), while remaining traceable to individual pores and windows. The same representation supports pore-resolved pore size distributions, multi-modal pore-type clustering, window detection across periodic boundaries, and percolation and accessibility analysis. To demonstrate its utility for material discovery, we develop a workflow integrated with Mofography to screen favorable pores in MOFs for xylene isomer separations and validate selected candidates with grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations. The results reveal how accessibility and competing pore environments influence whether local preferences translate into material performance. By linking global textural properties to local pore environments and their connectivity, Mofography provides a unique platform for interpreting structure–property relationships and accelerating nanoporous materials discovery.

item.title: Predicting Active and Inactive Targets of Small Molecules from ChEMBL Data Using the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4
item.description: Drug-like molecules often interact with multiple biological targets, which must be identified during drug development. Various models spanning classical machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence, predict active targets of a query molecule based on its structural similarity to target annotated molecules from drug-target interaction databases such as ChEMBL. Herein we report on the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4, a deep neural network trained on ChEMBL35. In contrast to its predecessor PPB3 and related tools which only return lists of probably active targets, PPB4 also lists probably inactive targets, as well as targets that are probably both active and inactive if the query molecule is similar to both active and inactive compounds for that target. Two prospective case studies illustrate the use of PPB4, which returns every predicted target together with the list of nearest neighbor molecules marked as active on that target in the training data. PPB4 is freely available at https://ppb4.gdb.tools.

item.title: Training of Neural Network Machine Learning Potentials for Activation Barrier Calculations in Predicting Growth Modes of Deposited Metals
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are opening many new opportunities to extend the capabilities of computational materials science. MLIPs deliver increased throughput and simulations at time and length scales beyond first principles density functional theory (DFT), while maintaining near-DFT accuracy, thus allowing unravelling of chemical processes not accessible with DFT. In this work, we present an approach to training a neural network MLIP using DeepMD-kit software that delivers both accurate energies and forces, suitable for determining activation energies via nudged elastic band calculations. We use the deposition of metals on substrates, in particular Ru and Cu on TaN for semiconductor device interconnects, as the example system, for which activation barriers of metal atom migration at the metal-substrate interface and on the metal deposit are important in understanding the evolution of the film morphology during deposition. The structure of the metal-substrate interface directly affects the performance of devices, from catalysts and sensors, to interconnects and contacts in nanoelectronics. The activation barrier energies from our MLIP for all sizes of metal atom deposits reproduce the DFT activation energies to within an average error of 0.08 eV (6%) for Cu and 0.23 eV (19%) for Ru. The trends of the DFT barriers are preserved by the MLIP and the computing time is reduced from days using high performance computing to minutes on a personal laptop. This allows us to assess the activation energies for complex processes such as the transition of a 2-layer metal cluster to a 3-layer cluster-a key step in metal island growth. Morphology evolution occurs on multiple scales, from initial nucleation, to layer growth and cluster ripening. By demonstrating that MLIPs can be used to accurately and rapidly deliver activation energies for the relevant atomic scale processes, a multi-scale predictive atomistic model of metal deposition and growth chemistry becomes feasible.

item.title: Mechanosensitive ion transport in hexagonal boron nitride nanopores
item.description: In biological systems, mechanical strain can trigger strong changes in ion conductance and signaling, yet in synthetic nanopores, achieving similar mechanosensitive behavior has been a significant challenge. Here, we demonstrate that subtle mechanical strain can induce strong modulation of ionic current in small hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) nanopores. Using hydrostatic pressure to apply small lateral strain to free-standing single-layer h-BN membranes featuring triangular sub-1-nm nanopores, we observed ion conductance modulation exceeding 1 30% under 0.5% strain. We attribute this response to the strain-dependent interplay of ionpore and ion-water interactions within the nanopore. The measured mechanosensitivity values also agreed strongly with those obtained from modeling of strain-tunable transport in ensembles of h-BN nanopores. These findings establish a framework for developing strain-responsive membranes for applications in molecular separations and sensing.

item.title: Goggles On, Bagels Out: A Randomized Hazard Hunt in a Browser Replica of a Real Teaching Laboratory
item.description: Students are usually introduced to the layout of a teaching laboratory, and to where its eyewash, shower, extinguisher and waste containers are, during a safety lecture on the first day of lab, a session that also covers the syllabus and the first experiment. I built a walkable, browser-based replica of the actual laboratory my students use, from a phone scan and photographs of the room, and turned it into a safety inspection. Each time a student opens the virtual lab, five hazards drawn at random from thirty-one are hidden in the room. Every hazard is tied to a rule in the course syllabus, from a drink on a bench or a fume hood sash left wide open to a classmate without goggles or a sleeve on fire. Students find and click each hazard, read what is wrong and what to do, carry out hands-on tasks such as dropping a used needle in the sharps container or guiding a splashed classmate to the eyewash, answer an emergency question, evacuate by the posted route when a fire alarm sounds, and finish with a report of what they found and missed. The inspection sits between a safety prelab page and the graded safety quiz in the learning management system; students must score at least 70% on the quiz before they are admitted to the lab room. The replica runs in an ordinary web browser with no headset or installation, downloads in about 31 MB, and was built by one instructor with a phone, free or low-cost software and generative AI tools. This report describes how the replica was built, how the hazards were designed and how the module fits into a course. Student outcomes will be evaluated in a later study.

item.title: OSC700: A GW+BSE Dataset of 700 Organic Semiconductor (OSC) Crystals with an LLM-Assisted Data Extraction Agent
item.description: Key parameters for organic optoelectronic device applications derive from the excited-state properties of molecular crystals. Data scarcity (both experimental and theoretical) limits the ability to train machine learning (ML) models to predict these properties. We present the OSC700 dataset of excited-state properties of 700 crystalline organic semiconductors (OSCs) with up to 1168 atoms in the unit cell, calculated using state-of-the-art many-body perturbation theory within the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW+BSE). OSC700 contains crystals of compounds comprising C,H,N,O,F,S capable of forming a variety of molecular scaffolds and crystal packing motifs. OSC700 is larger and significantly more diverse than the earlier PAH101 dataset [Scientific Data 12, 679 (2025)]. The data records contain the fundamental gap, quasiparticle band structure, static dielectric constant, first singlet exciton energy (optical gap), first triplet exciton energy, full dielectric function, and optical absorption spectra for light polarized along the three lattice vectors. Because absorption experiments on molecular crystals are rare (as opposed to solution or amorphous phases), we developed an LLM-assisted data extraction agent in order to find and retrieve available optical gap data for the materials in OSC700. The agent was able to find experimental data for 16 materials, which we used to validate the results of our calculations. The OSC700 dataset can be used to train ML models to predict the excited-state properties of crystalline organic semiconductors and find promising materials for optoelectronic device applications.

item.title: Applicability Domain of Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials at Solid-State Battery Interfaces
item.description: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are trained predominantly on bulk systems, yet are increasingly applied to solid-solid interfaces. Evaluating six uMLIPs against DFT across 24 Li-metal/solid-electrolyte interfaces, we map their applicability domain (AD) and where they break down. Total energies are predicted reasonably well (MAE < 15 meV/atom), whereas interatomic forces at the interfaces are not. Most models underestimate the interfacial formation energy by 0.32 J/m2 and overestimate the work of adhesion by 0.26 J/m2, and none reproduces the stability ordering of polyanion-containing interfaces. Despite large force errors for the interfaces, Li-ion kinetics agree well across models. The errors concentrate on the interface atoms and are larger for the polyanion chemistries. Descriptor-based analysis traces the higher force errors to interfacial environments that lie outside the pretraining data. Fine-tuning can close the accuracy gap, but only with data that samples the bonding across the interface, whereas slab data alone degrades performance. All models struggle on the same chemistries irrespective of the architecture, indicating the coverage of the pretraining data as the primary limitation. Overall, pretrained uMLIPs are suitable for qualitative screening of interfaces with simple single anion electrolytes, while those containing polyanions require interface-specific data.

item.title: Machine Learning for NMR Observables Sensitive to Nuclear Quantum Effects
item.description: Nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) are essential for an accurate description of systems containing light elements. Their omission in classical simulations can lead to significant deviations between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements, particularly for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observables that are highly sensitive to quantum nuclear motion. Although NQEs can be treated rigorously by using ab initio path-integral molecular dynamics (AI-PIMD), the substantial computational cost associated with these simulations continues to limit their applicability to large systems and long timescales. To address this limitation, we developed a machine learning-driven PIMD (MLPIMD) workflow for the accurate and efficient prediction of NMR observables, in which NQEs at finite temperature are explicitly included. As a demonstration, we investigate the experimentally measured isotropic chemical shifts, δiso, of the 3He monomer (3He@C706- ) and dimer (3He2@C706- ) endohedral fullerene hexaanions. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with the experiment and reveal a pronounced influence of NQEs on the 3He chemical shifts in both systems. In particular, NQEs are found to play a key role in determining the chemical-shift difference between the monomer and dimer species. The methodology introduced here is broadly applicable and provides a general framework for investigating NMR observables sensitive to NQEs in complex molecular systems.

item.title: Accurate and Rapid Vibrational Spectra of Molecular Crystals from Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Currently, vibrational spectra of molecular crystals often require computational methods to aid in band assignment, especially in the low-frequency region where no functional group specific transitions exist. DFT methods are the gold-standard for computational spectroscopy, but their high computational cost limits simulations to systems characterized by small unit cells. Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer a much cheaper alternative, but their reliability for phonons in molecular crystals has been little explored. In this work, eleven MLIPs from the ANI, MACE or UMA families of models are tested on geometry optimizations, vibrational frequencies and normal mode character with the same computational workflow utilized by DFT. The resulting phonons are then combined with DFT-calculated IR and Raman intensities to obtain vibrational spectra through a hybrid ML/DFT approach. The method is tested on three dispersion-bound molecular crystals, BTBT, naphthalene and anthracene, and three hydrogen-bonded systems, β-glycine and the two polymorphs of the ethosuximide (ETS) drug. MACE-MH omat, UMA omat and UMA omc emerge as the best-performing models and reproduce the experimental spectra with fidelity comparable to DFT.

item.title: Active Learning for Fragment-Based Kinase Inhibitor Discovery using Docking
item.description: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of vast chemical spaces while minimizing computational cost. Fragment-based drug design offers a promising route for generating novel ligands through recombination of fragments, yet the resulting combinatorial search spaces rapidly become too large for exhaustive evaluation. Here, we present an active learning framework for navigating kinase-focused fragment recombination spaces derived from KinFragLib. Our approach combines subpocket-aware fragment recombination, structure-based docking, machine learning surrogate models, and genetic algorithm-inspired exploration through fragment additions, deletions, and substitutions around previously evaluated ligands. Rather than screening a fully enumerated recombination library, the framework iteratively generates and evaluates promising fragment modifications, enabling scalable exploration of large recombination spaces. Using protein kinase A (PKA) as a case study, we evaluate the framework on a recombination space containing approximately 210,000 ligands. Active learning identifies high-scoring candidates while evaluating only about 0.5% of the available ligands with the computationally expensive docking workflow. A greedy acquisition strategy recovers 52% of the global top-50 ligands, substantially outperforming random sampling. In addition, a diversity-aware acquisition strategy increases fragment coverage and exploration of alternative hinge-binding motifs while retaining competitive optimization performance. These results demonstrate that active learning can efficiently navigate fragment recombination spaces and substantially reduce computational screening costs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a transferable strategy for kinase-focused ligand design and can be extended to other targets when suitable fragment libraries are available.

item.title: PolyGPT: A Decoder-Only Transformer for Polymer Electrolyte Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.07438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing polymer electrolytes requires control over both material properties and chemical structure. Here, we present PolyGPT, a Transformer with 38.3 million parameters that generates polymer repeat units from optional property targets, requests to include or exclude a specified chemical feature, and an electrolyte-domain condition. Using the model selected by validation loss, we compared unconditional generation with requests for electrolyte-associated structures, a low glass-transition temperature (Tg), or both. Unconditional and electrolyte-only generation achieved structural validity of 99.46% and 99.59%, respectively. However, electrolyte conditioning increased repetition: uniqueness among valid outputs fell from 99.99% to 51.74%. At a Tg target of 246.11 K, we compared generation with and without electrolyte conditioning, and adding the electrolyte condition slightly reduced the predictor-estimated mean absolute error from 26.97 to 26.07 K, but the fraction of all attempts yielding distinct valid polymers within 50 K of the target fell from 82.35% to 32.31%. When we also required absence from the training catalog, these yields were 59.90% and 19.71%, respectively. The lower yield persisted with a tighter 25 K tolerance. Domain conditioning also weakened control of inclusion requests: the mean fraction of attempts producing valid polymers containing the requested chemical feature fell from 94.27% to 31.27%. Across nine checkpoints, earlier models sometimes produced more distinct, catalog-unseen polymers meeting the Tg target: 10,000 checkpoint model with electrolyte conditioning and 30,000 checkpoint model without it. Together, these results show why property error alone is insufficient for evaluating conditional polymer generation. It must be considered alongside repetition, training-catalog novelty, and whether combined design requests are satisfied.

item.title: Masked diffusion as random sequential adsorption: an exactly solvable model for parallel decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.07845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.

item.title: Pressure-Induced Phase Transition and Superconducting Properties of LiPdH$_2$: A First-Principles Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.07989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a detailed first-principles investigation of the superconducting hydride LiPdH$_2$, focusing on the competition between its tetragonal $P4/mmm$ and rhombohedral $R\bar{3}m$ phases. Our results reveal a pressure-induced phase transition near 220 GPa, where $R\bar{3}m$ overtakes $P4/mmm$ in thermodynamic stability. The $R\bar{3}m$ phase is predicted to be superconducting, with $T_{\rm c}$ values of up to 46 K in the harmonic approximation and 28 K at the anharmonic level. In contrast, although the $P4/mmm$ phase is stable up to 200 GPa, it maintains a more rigid electronic character with weaker hydrogen involvement, resulting in lower superconducting performance. Ionic quantum and anharmonic effects play a decisive role in stabilizing $P4/mmm$ and shaping its superconducting properties, whereas these effects diminish rapidly with pressure. These findings highlight the interplay between structural stability, hydrogen orbital activity, and quantum effect in optimizing the superconductivity of hydrogen-based superconductors.

item.title: Experimental Evidence for Type-I Superconductivity in $\mathrm{OsB_2}$
item.description: arXiv:2611.08239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since the discovery of superconductivity in $\mathrm{MgB_2}$, metal diborides have attracted significant attention. Among these, osmium diboride ($\mathrm{OsB_2}$), crystallizing in an orthorhombic structure (space group $Pmmn$) with puckered boron layers, has been classified as a low-$\kappa$ Type-II superconductor ($T_c \approx 2.1~\mathrm{K}$). Here, we report experimental evidence establishing that $\mathrm{OsB_2}$ is in fact a rare nonelemental Type-I superconductor. Our identification is supported by three primary experimental hallmarks: (i) a pronounced Differential Paramagnetic Effect (DPE) peak in AC susceptibility ($\chi_{ac}$) measurements under static DC magnetic fields, signaling the intermediate state; (ii) a field-induced crossover to a divergent first-order phase transition in specific heat ($C/T$); and (iii) pronounced magnetic hysteresis in field-ramped transitions indicative of supercooling.

item.title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2611.06953v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

item.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.07998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

item.title: Unifying Dirac Spin Liquids on Square and Shastry-Sutherland Lattices via Fermionic Deconfined Criticality
item.description: arXiv:2601.19980v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a fermionic gauge theory for deconfined quantum criticality on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice and reveal its shared low-energy field-theoretic structure with the square lattice. Starting from an SU(2) $\pi$-flux parent state, we construct a continuum theory of Dirac spinons coupled to an SU(2) gauge field and adjoint Higgs fields whose condensates drive transitions to a staggered-flux U(1) spin liquid and a gapless $Z_{2}$ Dirac spin liquid. While the Shastry-Sutherland lattice permits additional symmetry-allowed fermion bilinears compared to the square lattice, the quantum field theories are identical up to additional irrelevant terms. Consequently, the Higgs potential structure and the leading low-energy theory coincide with the square-lattice case at the quantum critical point. The SO(5) critical point is expected to realize conformal deconfined criticality: we analyze it in a large-flavor expansion, calculate its critical exponents, and identify the Yukawa coupling between the fermions and Higgs fields as the relevant perturbation that destabilizes it, consistent with pseudocritical behavior observed in recent Monte Carlo studies. We show that the emergent SO(5) order parameter acquires a large anomalous dimension at the critical point, leading to strongly enhanced N\'eel and VBS susceptibilities-a hallmark of fermionic deconfined quantum criticality consistent with numerical studies. Our results place recent numerical evidence for a gapless $Z_{2}$ Dirac spin liquid on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice within a controlled field-theoretic framework and demonstrate that fermionic deconfined criticality on the square lattice-including critical exponents and stability-extends to frustrated lattices with reduced symmetry.

item.title: Hereditary Effective Atom Theory for Large-Scale Atomic Structure Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.28996v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting the atomic structure of large systems requires simultaneous exploration of atomic positions, species, and, generally, the number of atoms. The combinatorial growth of possible arrangements can make this search difficult even for standard global optimization methods. We introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), which integrates Effective Atom Theory (EAT) into a genetic algorithm. HEAT combines EAT's continuous relaxation of atomic positions, species, and population with the global search capabilities of genetic algorithms. Central to the method is a crossover scheme that directly superimposes two parent structures and relaxes the combined structure. HEAT outperforms conventional genetic-algorithm baselines in recovering a missing 240-atom H sublattice, predicting a 364-atom edge-dislocation core, and reconstructing a 1150-atom interior region of twisted-bilayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ from experimental ptychographic constraints. These results demonstrate how continuous effective-atom relaxation improves the exploration of large combinatorial structure spaces.

item.title: Dissipation accelerates quantum and classical simulation of open-system dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.40174v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating open quantum systems reveals how environmental coupling shapes relaxation, excitation transport, and the dynamics of quantum correlations. On quantum hardware, dissipative channels add operations and might seem to increase cost. However, we show that a broad class of Pauli noise, including depolarization, can ease quantum and classical simulation by exponentially suppressing high-weight components of Heisenberg-evolved observables. For bounded-degree Lindblad dynamics, this permits system-size-independent Trotter steps when estimating local observables. Combining this compression with Richardson extrapolation, we provide classical and quantum error bounds with respect to the 2-norm of the propagated observable. These give high-probability expectation-value guarantees for random input states or random Hamiltonians acting on a fixed state and control (out-of-time-order) correlators. Concretely, we show that expectation values of local observables at time $t$ can be estimated to accuracy $\varepsilon$ using circuits of maximum depth $O\!\left(\left[1+\left(t/\gamma\right)^{3/2}\right]\log^2(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, independent of the system size $n$. Classically, we show that sparse Pauli propagation runs in time polynomial in $n$, $t$ and $1/\varepsilon$ for every fixed $\gamma>0$, with polynomial degree $O(1/\gamma)$ in the weak dissipation limit. The gap between our quantum and classical upper bounds leaves room for a substantial polynomial quantum advantage as dissipation weakens, an observation further supported by our numerical results.

item.title: Lost in Chemical Space: Local Open-Source Large Language Models Display Model-Dependent Adherence to Reference Data in Molecular Generation
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) can generate drug-like molecules and may be used locally in drug discovery projects where confidentiality and intellectual-property constraints preclude the use of external APIs. Weight quantization enables deployment of large open-source LLMs on limited hardware, but its impact on molecular generation and on the ability of models to follow reference chemical spaces remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral-Small-4-119B, and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B at the BF16 (original precision), Q8, Q6, and Q4 quantization levels in two molecular generation tasks. The models were prompted either to generate small molecules without constraints or to generate drug-like molecules conditioned on 69 reference kinase inhibitors provided in-context. Quantization increased inference throughput in a model-dependent manner, with the largest gains, up to 24-fold increase in performance, occurring for Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B. In the task of unconstrained generation, model quantization did not affect molecular validity, uniqueness, drug-likeness, diversity and synthesizability. In the task of reference-guided generation, however, the models displayed markedly different levels of adherence to the provided chemical space. Gemma-4-31B was the only model that consistently generated small molecules similar to the reference compounds at all precision levels. Mistral-Small-4-119B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B failed to generate small molecules according to the reference chemical space. GPT-OSS-120B showed adherence to the reference molecules at BF16, Q8, and Q6, but lost the capacity to generate molecules in the desired chemical space at the Q4 quantization level. These results show that quantization can substantially improve the performance of local LLMs for molecular generation without compromising output quality, although model selection and validation is essential for guided exploration of the chemical space.

item.title: AI Agents as supporting infrastructure for all-solid-state battery development
item.description: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.

item.title: Self-Derived Metal/Oxide Interface Engineering via Active Nitrogen Mediation
item.description: Self-derived phase engineering of metal oxides offers a powerful route to create interfaces without introducing foreign metallic elements, yet achieving systematic control over phase transition remains challenging. Here, active nitrogen-mediated phase engineering was demonstrated across various metal oxides (SnO2, ZnO, and TiO2). As a model biphasic material, Sn/SnO2 was investigated where urea thermolysis enabled the progressive formation of metallic Sn while largely preserving the host structure, allowing the Sn0 fraction to be systematically controlled. Temperature-programmed experiments using mass spectrometry and FT-IR revealed the involvement of nitrogen-containing intermediates during urea decomposition and supported their central role in driving phase engineering of SnO2. Density functional theory (DFT) based calculations on a Sn/SnO2 model constructed using a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) revealed electron transfer from metallic Sn to SnO2 and the resulting redistribution of surface electron density. The resulting self-derived Sn/SnO2 biphasic material yields favorable surface chemistry by altered surface oxygen behavior and reactivity translating directly into two applications: enhanced chemoresistive formaldehyde gas sensing under humid conditions with ppb-level detection, as well as improved formate production in electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). Our results identify active nitrogen as a chemical handle for regulating oxide partial reduction and provide a general framework for the systematic engineering of metal/oxide interfaces.

item.title: Accelerating the Design of Cu(I) Complexes with Near-Infrared Absorption by Interpretable Machine Learning Approaches
item.description: Metal coordination complexes have emerged as promising molecules because of its interesting optical properties and among them the Cu(I) complexes are one of the most fascinating ones, because it’s combination of optical properties and sustainability at the same time. In this work we show for the first time a combination of quantum chemical and cheminformatics approaches to study the wavelength and oscillator strength as photoluminescence properties in a data set of Cu(I) complexes. As a result, machine learning-based Quantitative Structure-Property Relationship (ML/QSPR) model based on machine learning that can reliably predict the absorption wavelength and oscillator strength of Cu(I) complexes was successfully developed, laying the groundwork for high-throughput virtual screening of Cu(I) complexes optical properties. To explain the differences in absorption wavelengths and oscillator strength across structurally diverse individual Cu(I) complexes, the relation between the models and molecular descriptors was analyzed with patterns revealed positive contributing to the properties like polarizability effects, aliphatic chains connected to heteroatoms, and other with negative influence corresponding to symmetry factors, and molecular size and branching. The squared correlation coefficient values for training and validation were 0.82 and 0.85, respectively. In addition, the applicability domain demonstrated the reliability of the prediction of the obtained models. This combined quantum-chemical and cheminformatics strategy has great potential for rational design of novel Cu(I) complexes with desired optical properties. Furthermore, the described procedures might be applied to a wide variety of copper transition-metal complexes.

item.title: DNA Directed Chemistry: Scalable Programmed DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis for More Chemically Diverse and Drug-Like Libraries
item.description: DNA-Encoded Libraries (DELs) are indispensable high-throughput platforms in drug discovery, but the widely adopted split-and-pool synthesis method is fundamentally limited: the DNA merely records, rather than directs, the steps of chemistry. This lack of programmatic control imposes mandatory downstream chemistry congruency, restricts structural diversity, and inevitably generates a combinatorial explosion of un-drug-like molecules, hindering both hit-finding and the acquisition of structurally informative data required for machine learning (ML) models. To resolve these core constraints, we developed Programmed DEL Synthesis (PDS), a robust, industrially applicable platform for non-combinatorial DEL construction in which the DNA actively directs the synthesis. PDS is built upon a sort-and-pool mechanism expanded by three key innovations: sequence-specific installation of first building blocks using charged carrier codons, a multinomial encoding strategy that enables libraries exceeding 20 billion unique encodings in three chemical steps, and non-combinatorial germline assembly that allows for the programmatic omission of undesirable building block combinations. We demonstrate the platform with Library i01, a three-step, threepathway library employing 137 trifunctional scaffolds. The design successfully programmed the systematic merging and un-merging of three mutually incompatible reaction pathways: Acid→Aldehyde→Amine, Amine→Aldehyde→Acid, and Aldehyde→Acid→Amine within a single synthesis. Pilot affinity selections against Carbonic Anhydrase (BCA-II) validated the high fidelity of DNA encoding and efficient building block installation across all steps and pathways, confirming the platform's robust utility for selection. PDS transforms chemical congruency and drug-likeness into programmable properties, offering a precise, efficient solution that improves library quality without sacrificing chemical space. Crucially, PDS enables the construction of structurally tailored 2nd Generation DELs needed to provide the high-resolution data required for productive ML-driven active learning cycles, establishing a critical operational link for modern drug development.

item.title: Where machine learning for enantioselectivity on polysaccharide chiral stationary phases actually fails: a leave-one-paper-out reappraisal of 10,525 enantiomer pairs
item.description: Machine-learning models for enantioselectivity on polysaccharide chiral stationary phases increasingly report high accuracy, but almost always under random data splits. We re-examined this problem on CMRT, the largest public chiral chromatography dataset, curating it into 10,525 enantiomer pairs covering 530 DOI groupsand25columns.Underatrueleave-one-paper-outprotocol,elution-orderaccuracyfallsfrom 66.1 % under a random split to 52.9 %, indistinguishable from a within-paper permutation null (52.3 % ± 0.6). Between-paper variance accounts for 38.5 % of the total variance, but it cannot be predicted from compositional features, so domain adaptation is ineffective. The molecular signal is real within a single paper (median per-paper correlation r = +0.185) but falls to r = +0.0009 for an unseen paper, and adding trainingpapersdoesnothelp.Avariancedecompositionofasingle-laboratorygridshowsthatonly 23.05 % of the variance is attributable to additive main effects of molecule and condition, the remaining 76.95 % being an unidentifiable molecule × condition interaction and noise. We therefore argue that the bottleneck liesnotinmodelcapacityordescriptorqualitybutinthedatastructure:adding condition metadata,buildingsystematicmolecule×conditiongrids,introducingreplicatemeasurementsand recording failed separations are the prerequisites for improving transferability.

item.title: X-Ray Diffraction Model for Spiral-Growth-Driven Defects in Layered Thin Films
item.description: Out-of-phase boundary (OPB) defects are a hallmark of spiral-driven growth in Aurivillius phase thin films, often arising from screw dislocation-mediated layer propagation. These boundaries are associated with localised strain gradients and modify polarisation and diffraction responses. Existing analytical XRD models that treat OPBs as planar or parallel features have limitations in capturing the vertical gradient in lattice displacement and the angular asymmetry observed in spiral-grown films. In this work, we introduce a generalised model that represents OPBs as stacked pyramidal defects along the film thickness, as observed in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) cross sections. The model incorporates a three dimensional structure factor formalism that accounts for atomic positions, fractional lattice displacements, the inclination of the OPB boundaries and other parameters. Simulated X-ray diffraction patterns based on this model reproduce the asymmetric peak broadening and splitting observed in Bi4Ti3O12 thin films with high fidelity and enable a non-destructive estimation of OPB density, and a more realistic description of defect geometry than planar models allow. This work establishes a three-dimensional, predictive framework for spiralmediated OPB defects in layered ferroelectric oxides, offering a basis for defect engineering and materials optimisation in future memory and neuromorphic applications.

item.title: Computational Modeling of Electrolytes and the Solid–Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in Li-Ion Batteries: A 30-Year Odyssey from DFT/MD/MC to AI–A Comprehensive Review
item.description: The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI)—the passivating nanometric film that forms on anode surfaces in lithium-ion batteries—remains one of the most critical yet least understood components in electrochemical energy storage. Unraveling its formation, structure, and evolution has proven to be a formidable odyssey, spanning decades of relentless effort and confronting researchers with challenges as daunting as those faced by the ancient voyagers. This review provides a comprehensive, 30-year perspective on this arduous journey, tracing the evolution of computational methods for modeling electrolytes and SEI from early density functional theory (DFT) calculations of isolated molecules to modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) frameworks that promise to accelerate materials discovery. We organize the methodological development into five generations, each representing a milestone in this ongoing voyage: static DFT (1995–2005) establishing thermodynamic foundations; ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) for interfacial dynamics (2005–2010); AIMD integrated with free energy calculations to elucidate electron transfer and rare events (2011–2015); quantitative design rules, space charge effects, and mechanical properties (2016–2020); and advanced DFT techniques combined with MLIPs, generative models, large language models, and self-driving laboratories (2021–2026). We critically assess classical MD, reactive force fields (ReaxFF, eReaxFF), hybrid HAIR methods, kinetic Monte Carlo, and Monte Carlo approaches, demonstrating how each method bridges the chasm between electronic structure and mesoscale phenomena. The review further examines ML applications—from property prediction and spectroscopic signature forecasting to MLIPs achieving first-principles accuracy at classical force-field speeds, generative molecular design, high-throughput screening, active learning, and integration with autonomous experimentation. We identify persistent challenges that continue to test the field’s resolve: long-range electrostatics, transferability across chemical space, time-scale bridging, uncertainty quantification, and data standardization. Practical recommendations for method selection are provided, accompanied by a comprehensive comparative table. This review establishes that the integration of DFT, AIMD, MD, ReaxFF, kMC, MLIPs, and AI has created a powerful multiscale modeling ecosystem, transforming battery research from trial-and-error to rational, data-driven design.

item.title: Physics-Guided Learning with Calibrated Uncertainty for Molecular Thermodynamics Beyond Observed Chemical Space
item.description: Scientific machine learning seeks to explore vast, high-dimensional design spaces, but experimental data are typically sparse and unevenly distributed, limiting generalization beyond observed systems. Molecular thermodynamic property prediction is a prime example. We develop a Physics-guided PC-SAFT neural NETwork, P-SANET, within a reliability-oriented framework integrating physical models, physics-guided target formulation, chemically informed out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation and monotonic error calibration. P-SANET learns the temperature-dependent charging free energy and maps it through PC-SAFT to molecular interaction parameters. This thermodynamically structured target improves prediction accuracy for scaffold-disjoint and structurally novel molecules. A matched-size open-data benchmark further shows that chemically informative coverage, rather than nominal dataset size, is a key determinant of OOD reliability. A monotonic calibrator combining temperature, ensemble uncertainty and embedding novelty provides quantitative error estimates. P-SANET achieves competitive vapor-pressure accuracy against published models and transfers without property-specific retraining to enthalpy of vaporization, liquid density and critical properties.

item.title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of $\kappa$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films
item.description: arXiv:2611.05647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The thermal conductivities of (001) $\kappa$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films deposited on $c$-plane sapphire substrates were measured with frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). The thermal conductivity increases from 1.83 $^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$ W/m$\cdot$K to 2.26 $^{+0.35}_{-0.40}$ W/m$\cdot$K as the thicknesses increase from 159 nm to 689 nm. This weak thickness dependence indicates that the majority of the intrinsic phonon mean free paths are smaller than the range of investigated film thicknesses. First-principles-based calculations that include phonon-phonon and phonon-boundary scattering capture this size-dependent behavior and support our experimental observation. Temperature-dependent measurements of a 689 nm film from 293 to 400 K show a decrease in thermal conductivity with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon-phonon scattering. A weaker temperature dependence is observed in a 159 nm film where phonon-boundary scattering becomes more prominent. At comparable film thicknesses, our measured $\kappa$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit lower values of cross-plane thermal conductivity than the other experimentally measured Ga$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs. Our experimental observations are supported by prior predictions, which suggest that the low thermal conductivity of $\kappa$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ results from its complex crystal structure, which leads to increased anharmonicity and lower phonon group velocities relative to other polymorphs. Thermal management strategies, such as integration with high-thermal-conductivity substrates, may thus be required to mitigate self-heating for $\kappa$-Ga$_2$O$_3$-based electronic devices.

item.title: DefectSkills: Guiding AI agents through first-principles calculations for point defects in semiconductors and insulators
item.description: arXiv:2611.05654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-principles defect calculations can now be performed autonomously by AI agents, enabled by established computational methods and open-source Python toolkits. However, reliable and repeatable defect calculations require clear scientific and technical guidance that helps agents resolve ambiguities and avoid errors in calculation setup, execution, postprocessing, and analysis. Here, we present DefectSkills, a set of structured prompts that provides human-in-the-loop guidance to AI agents performing first-principles calculations of point defects in semiconductors and insulators using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The prompts encode human expertise and guide agents through unit-cell relaxation, electronic-structure and dielectric calculations, phase-stability and chemical-potential analysis, charged-defect supercell generation and calculations, finite-size corrections, formation-energy calculations and thermodynamic analysis, and data backup. By packaging this expertise as reusable agent skills, DefectSkills supports consistent workflow execution across agentic AI systems and reproducible defect calculations.

item.title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.05946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP), particularly the foundational models for materials chemistry, such as MACE, has significantly strengthened our capabilities in studying the complex dynamics of materials through statistical sampling. Here, by performing molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE model, that are further combined with essential dynamics analysis, a tool that is commonly applied in (bio)molecular simulations, we examine the temperature-dependent ion dynamics in a prototypical inorganic solid superionic conductor, namely argyrodite Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl. Our analyses show clear localised phonon-like dynamics for Li$^+$ ions below 500 K with trajectories lying in a low-dimensional manifold that is highly nonlinear, which is opposite to the case in the high-temperature ($\sim$800 K) end. Between 500-700 K, the system exhibit strong competition in the dynamics between the Li$^+$ and framework ions, that are reflected in both the eigenspectrum and the projected low-dimensional embeddings characterising these dynamics not showing a simple monotonic dependency upon rising temperatures, and is further supported by investigations employing Langevin dynamics that systematically examine how damping the framework motions affects the dynamics of the Li$^+$ ions, thanks to the computational efficiency provided by MLIP. This work thus contributes towards the broader theoretical and data-driven framework for studying the lattice dynamics of solids.

item.title: Hydrogen sublattice in LaH$_{12}$: structural stability and possible ordering motifs
item.description: arXiv:2611.06424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lanthanum polyhydrides, synthesized under extreme pressure, exhibit near-room-temperature superconductivity. Finding a precise arrangement of the hydrogen sublattice that is critical for understanding the strong electron-phonon coupling remains experimentally unresolved due to the small X-ray scattering form factor of hydrogen atoms. In this work, we attempt to computationally reconstruct hydrogen sublattices of the LaH$_{12}$ at 100-200 GPa combining unconstrained evolutionary searches and structure generation with fixed lanthanum sublattice. By implementing a similarity metric, we screen the computationally generated configurations against experimental powder X-ray diffraction data. We specifically identify the trigonal $R\bar{3}$-LaH$_{12}$ and pseudo-hexagonal $C222_1$-La$_2$H$_{24}$ phases, which demonstrate close agreement with the experimental X-ray diffraction data. First-principles calculations confirm the metallic and superconducting nature of these hydrides. Crucially, our lattice dynamics analysis using the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) indicates that these structures are dynamically stable. We reveal the presence of molecular H$_2$ units and soft phonon modes in the trigonal LaH$_{12}$ that suppresses superconductivity ($T_c \ge 30$ K), while the hydrogen clathrate network in the $C222_1$ phase drives strong electron-phonon interactions, yielding the coupling parameters of $\lambda\approx 1.83$, $\omega_{\log} \approx 87.5$ meV and transition temperature of $T_c\approx 150$ K at 150 GPa.

item.title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.06811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structure property prediction is a classical task in machine learning, ranging from molecular activity and materials properties to local functional responses measured in microscopy. For image-based regression, two choices define the information available to the predictor: the size of the image neighborhood and the spatial resolution retained within it. A small neighborhood can omit relevant surrounding structure, whereas a large, finely sampled neighborhood can introduce redundant or irrelevant information. Here, we develop a framework for constructing spatial descriptors for prediction of local spectra and hysteresis loops. We benchmark regression models, use SHAP maps to examine their spatial attribution, and explore the effect of the patch size and compression to establish the relationship between predictive accuracy and descriptor dimensionality. We then use a genetic algorithm to optimize spatial partitions and the assignment of mean, minimum, and maximum pooling operations. Each retained region contributes an explicit measurement of the image, allowing the search to balance prediction error against the number of descriptor values. Cartesian and polar constructions provide complementary ways to organize this information. The resulting descriptors make it possible to examine where spatial detail is needed, where regional summaries are sufficient, and how these choices depend on the predictor and the measured response. The same approach can be used for molecules and solids once the genetic algorithm rules for these are established.

item.title: Phonons under confinement: Finite Hilbert space, coarse-grained $U(1)$ charge and a new transport mechanism
item.description: arXiv:2607.14232v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An important feature of solid-state or cold atom systems in low dimensions is the restricted oscillations of ionic/atomic degrees of freedom in the confining directions, for which the conventional phonon from canonical quantization is not an ideal description. In this work we propose a general recipe to introduce this feature to otherwise unrestricted systems by mapping displacement fields to spin degrees of freedom, dubbed "soft-corization". In the strong-confinement limit $S=1/2$, we demonstrate the validity of the approach with a harmonic chain; the results lead to a gapped fermionic model showing the absence of acoustic modes as a signature of the confinement of the entire chain. Despite the non-conserved total particle number in the presence of nearest-neighbor parings, the model holds a coarse-grained $U(1)$ symmetry with conserved "polarization charge" in the absence of nearest-neighbor hopping. This enables a new transport mechanism via "dimer-tumbling" instead of single-particle hopping. We then introduce a short-range interaction via anharmonicity; for energy scales slightly above the gap, it leads to a (quantum) phase transition to a nonreciprocal state carrying dimer current and heat current with spontaneous time reversal symmetry breaking of the type $\hat{T}^2=+1$. The non-reciprocity can be probed by measuring the change of inductance due to gauge fields in and out of the ordered phase.

item.title: Why Ammoniated Lithium Borohydrides Liquefy and Resolidify?
item.description: arXiv:2608.01266v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ammonia (NH$_3$) absorption drives LiBH$_4\cdot x$NH$_3$ through a re-entrant ``solid--liquid--solid'' transition: LiBH$_4\cdot$NH$_3$ is a well-defined solid ammoniate, compositions near LiBH$_4\cdot 2$NH$_3$ are liquid-like or partially liquefied, whereas LiBH$_4\cdot 3$NH$_3$ returns to a more rigid non-liquid ammoniate state. However, the microscopic origin of this unintuitive response remains a long-lasting mystery. Here, we uncover its mechanism. Cross-database analysis identifies borohydrides as a particularly state-diverse and composition-responsive material family. Structure prediction and ab initio molecular simulations reveal that increasing NH$_3$ loading increases the direct Li--N coordination number while progressively decreasing BH$_4^-$-associated contacts in the local Li environment. Near $x \approx 2$, these contributions are most balanced among the simulated compositions, and the sampled Li--N/N$\cdots$B coordination landscape is broadest. Further ammoniation produces Li--N-dominant coordination and slower BH$_4^-$/NH$_3$ contact renewal, accompanying recovery of a more rigid ammoniate state. Pressure--composition isotherm, $^1$H and $^{11}$B nuclear magnetic resonance, and Raman measurements support this non-monotonic state evolution and associated BH$_4^-$/NH$_3$ reorganization. These findings transform ammonia-induced liquefaction from an empirical phase anomaly into a competition between native-network disruption, mixed-coordination frustration, and ligand-built network reconstruction, providing a framework for chemically switching between transport-favouring fluidity and stability-favouring rigidity in hydrogen-rich materials.

item.title: Machine-Learning-Accelerated Metallene Stabilization from High-Throughput Sandwich Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2608.01779v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Metallenes have appealing properties, but stabilizing them in a monolayer phase poses synthesis challenges. A recent experiment showed that the van der Waals squeezing method can stabilize certain metallenes in a MoS2 sandwich. This pioneering work motivates systematic studies, but such studies are experimentally impractical, while first-principles modeling remains prohibitive. Here, using universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, we constructed 1620 metallene sandwich heterostructures containing 6 different sandwich layers and 45 metals. We performed phonon calculations, which revealed 1208 dynamically stable structures and narrowed them to 331 after structural filtering. We found that Se-based transition-metal dichalcogenides stabilize metallenes effectively. Specifically, hexagonal and buckled hexagonal crystal lattices exhibit the greatest stability. We further evaluated the thermal stability of selected heterostructures with density-functional theory molecular dynamics simulations at room temperature. By uncovering the physical and chemical factors that govern metallenes stabilization, our results provide systematic insights to guide and accelerate synthesis for future applications.

item.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na$_3$PS$_4$
item.description: arXiv:2611.04547v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described by mobile cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder enhances transport remains unresolved at the mesoscale, inaccessible to ensemble-averaged probes. We use Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy to measure nanoscale structural dynamics of a single ball-milled Na$_3$PS$_4$ particle. We find that the cubic phase behaves as a strain glass: a frustrated configuration of three degenerate tetragonal variants with short-range order. Its domain-wall motion is stress-driven, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing as residual milling stress is depleted. Rearrangements follow scale-free avalanche statistics, matching ferroelastic martensites but without external driving. The tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics occur on timescales comparable to estimated ionic diffusion across the particle, indicating the host structure cannot be assumed static on transport-relevant timescales.

item.title: Vortices in a two-dimensional fermionic superfluid
item.description: arXiv:2611.05017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantized vortices are a hallmark of superfluidity. They have proven to be an indispensable probe for systems ranging from superfluid helium to type-II superconductors. In ultracold two-dimensional (2D) Fermi gases, where phase fluctuations are enhanced and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) mechanism governs the superfluid transition, their observation has remained elusive. Here, we report on the controlled creation of quantized vortices in a homogeneous 2D gas in the BEC--BCS crossover. By continuously tuning the velocity of two moving obstacles, we observe quantized steps in the absolute vortex charge. Matter-wave interferometry reveals the characteristic phase winding, quantized in units of $2\pi$. Measurements on 2D and 3D gases show a striking difference: only in 2D does the vortex number grow with temperature, reflecting thermal activation of BKT vortex pairs. Our approach provides evidence of fermionic superfluidity in 2D and offers a means to study BKT physics, vortex-controlled transport and resistance, as well as to detect unconventional superfluidity in spin-imbalanced 2D gases.

item.title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights
item.description: arXiv:2605.10795v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models excel at factual recall, yet the fundamental limits of storing input--output associations with neural networks remain unclear. We study these limits in a minimal setting: a linear associative memory that maps $p$ input embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to their $d$-dimensional targets via a linear layer, requiring each mapped input to score its own target above all other outputs. Since all inputs compete for the same outputs, these constraints are strongly correlated, which makes the storage capacity $p_c$ --- the largest number of associations that can be stored --- hard to characterise. We address this in three steps. First, we introduce a decoupled model, in which each input competes with its own independent set of outputs, and provide numerical and analytical evidence that it is equivalent to the original model, both in capacity and in the structure of the learnt solution. Second, using tools from statistical physics, we show that the decoupled model has capacity $p_c \log p_c / d^2 = 1/2$, extend this computation to linear two-layer networks, and go beyond the capacity by predicting the spectrum of the learnt weights and the storage mechanism. The latter explains how the optimal solution outperforms a na\"ive Hebbian rule: rather than boosting input--output alignments with broad fluctuations, it raises the correct scores just above the extreme-value threshold set by the competing outputs. Third, we prove the decoupled model's capacity thresholds rigorously, including in the non-convex two-layer case; combined with a recent proof for the original model, this shows that both models have the same capacity for full-rank weights. These findings give a sharp characterisation of factual storage in linear networks, and suggest decoupling as a general tool for memorisation and learning problems in which each input must be matched to one of an extensive number of outputs.

item.title: Neural networks become centroid classifiers when trained on heavily corrupted inputs
item.description: arXiv:2606.11319v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning from imperfect data is a central theme in machine learning, connecting practical questions of robustness to fundamental questions of learnability. Here we examine attribute noise: learning from corrupted inputs while keeping the labels intact, a setting that has received considerably less analytical attention than its label-noise counterpart. We consider two types of corruption models: additive noise and replacement noise. Through experiments with multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on corrupted classification datasets, we find that neural networks remain robust, maintaining well-above-chance accuracy even when inputs are >90% corrupted -- far beyond human recognition. To understand this robustness, we analyze infinite-width networks in the heavy-corruption regime using a mean-field-inspired approach and derive a leading-order decision rule for the classification outcome: the network implements a prototype rule, the nearest-class-mean, assigning each test point to the class whose training-set average it most closely resembles. This leading-order decision rule is universal across a broad range of MLP architectures, holding for any depth, as well as a wide class of activation functions and noise distributions. The same centroid mechanism closely matches finite-width network behavior in our experiments and provides an interpretable and analytically tractable account of why learning can succeed even when individual training examples carry almost no signal.

item.title: Reading and steering representations of materials-science mechanisms in an open-weight language model
item.description: Large language models can answer scientific questions, yet a correct output does not reveal whether the model represents or uses the governing physics. Here, using three open-weight Gemma 4 instruction-tuned models (google/gemma-4-E4B-it, google/gemma-4-12B-it, and google/gemma-4-31B-it) we identify three experimentally separable signatures of materials-science mechanism information: selective concept readability, relational encoding of qualitative constitutive orientation, and causal, context-dependent control of constrained engineering answers. Across 50 held-out descriptions, three independently fitted Jacobian lenses produced nearly identical concept ranks, but 36 prompts recovered no declared term within the top 100 and the family-level advantage over direct unembedding was not significant. Target-free words from both readouts nevertheless enabled blinded automated identification of 9 of 10 mechanism families. A separate 72-prompt benchmark formed mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods, but an exact graph audit showed that numerical comparison explained the same organization; absolute state geometry therefore did not uniquely identify physics. In a matched 60-law benchmark, state changes caused solely by reversing a physical input ordered direct, physically neutral and inverse relations ( ) and correctly oriented 39 of 40 directional laws. Removing the equation and prescribed reasoning scaffold preserved correct orientation for 38 of 40 laws at 4B and all 40 laws at both 12B and 31B. A prospectively frozen grain-size direction steered all 12 refinement and coarsening cases toward the correct answer. In a disjoint 24-law cohort, neutralizing, reversing and restoring a development-fitted relational coordinate selectively altered answer evidence across all three scales, while activation-matched controls remained near zero. Qualitative physical relationships are therefore revealed more clearly by controlled changes in representation than by absolute state alone, and selected relational representations can causally influence scientific decisions.

item.title: Engineering a borate-rich interphase for highly stable all-solid-state sodium batteries
item.description: All-solid-state sodium batteries (ASSBs) offer high energy density and safety, but conventional solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers suffer from low efficiency and severe side reactions. This work proposes a novel strategy based on a borate-enriched SEI that effectively suppresses side reactions and enables dendrite-free Na plating/stripping, providing valuable mechanistic insights and a feasible pathway toward high-performance ASSBs.

item.title: A Machine Learning Approach to logBB Prediction Combining Molecular Docking and Quantum-Chemical Descriptors
item.description: Blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability is a major challenge in the development of drugs targeting the central nervous system (CNS). Computational prediction methods can help prioritize candidate compounds and reduce the experimental workload during early drug discovery. In this study, machine learning models were developed to predict the blood-to-brain concentration ratio expressed as its decimal logarithm (logBB). The objective was to investigate whether molecular docking scores obtained with AutoDock Vina for P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), together with quantum-chemical descriptors, could provide additional information for logBB prediction. The dataset comprised 685 compounds. A linear regression analysis identified eight factors associated with logBB: hydrogen bond donors, gas-phase electronic energy, electronic energy difference between water and hexane, number of heavy atoms, LogP, gas-phase geometry optimization time, number of aromatic rings, and fraction of sp3-hybridized carbon atoms. Notably, the electronic energy difference between water and hexane showed a stronger association with logBB than the corresponding Gibbs free energy difference, suggesting that electronic energy descriptors may provide complementary information. Higher-level quantum-chemical calculations will be required to investigate this finding further. Twenty-one machine learning models were evaluated. The selected support vector regression model using a radial basis function kernel (SVR-RBF; C = 0.869, ε = 0.135, γ = 0.165) was trained on 585 compounds and evaluated on a held-out validation set of 100 compounds, achieving an R2 of 0.605, an MAE of 0.368, and an RMSE of 0.459. Finally, the computational time analysis showed that descriptor generation was strongly dependent on molecular weight, with quantum-chemical calculations and molecular docking accounting for most of the computational cost. Overall, this work highlights the potential of combining physicochemical, molecular docking, and quantum-chemical descriptors for machine learning-based logBB prediction.

item.title: Nanocorrugated Conducting Polymer–Based Electrochemical Transistors with Enhanced Ionic-Electronic Transduction for Ultrasensitive Biomolecular Detection
item.description: Electrolyte-gated organic transistor (EGOT) biosensors enable label-free volumetric biosensing, yet their performance in physiological environments remains constrained by polymer microstructure and inefficient ion–channel coupling. Here, we demonstrate that substrate-induced nanocorrugation reconfigures mixed ionic–electronic transport in poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) channels. The corrugated SiO2/Si substrates alter the structural and electrochemical response of conformally deposited PEDOT:PSS channels. Structural and electrochemical measurements show changes in molecular ordering, crystalline orientation, local structural heterogeneity, and mixed ionic-electronic transport in the nanocorrugated films. Compared with flat counterparts, the nanocorrugated devices exhibit enhanced molecular ordering, improved ion accessibility, and stronger gate–channel coupling. The proposed platform enables ultrasensitive nucleic-acid detection and label-free sensing of stroke-related protein biomarkers in buffer, serum, and whole blood. For DNA sensing in buffer, the mean response exceeded the detection threshold at 20 aM, the regression-derived threshold concentration was ~15.4 aM, and statistically significant separation from the negative control began at 200 aM. IL-6 produces a concentration-dependent response down to the lowest tested concentration of 1 fM. Overall, nanoscale corrugation enables a route to tune ion transport, reconfigure the polymer network, and enhance volumetric transduction in conducting polymer EGOTs, thereby facilitating robust biosensing under physiologically relevant environments.

item.title: Self-Evolving Laboratories Through Persistent Digital and Physical Adaptation
item.description: Turning a scientific idea into an experiment often requires researchers to build, configure and repeatedly adapt the labo- ratory around it. This work demands resources and specialized expertise that can place ambitious experiments beyond reach. Here we introduce a framework for self-evolving laboratories (SEL), connecting computation, physical experiments and AI models through persistent cycles of observation and revision. GPT Astra uses camera observations and physical feedback to adapt robotic actions, digital twins and CAD designs. These changes are retained as reusable skills and infrastructure, allowing the laboratory to develop alongside its scientific tasks. In our fume-hood SEL prototype, GPT Astra identified the need for a beaker holder and storage stand and generated successive designs for on-demand 3D printing. Four holder generations and two stand generations culminated in parts integrated into the robotic workflow with operator assistance. A photoresist campaign proposed by Raven, an agentic AI platform for materials discovery, connects this platform to materials fabrication. Exposure to a 405 nm continuous-wave laser in the two-photon polymerization setup produced circular features that survived development; optical microscopy and reduced acrylate-band absorbance in ATR–FTIR support polymerization and qualitative double-bond conversion. The scientific workflow connects experimental outcomes and retained capabilities to the resources needed to establish and extend them. By making laboratory capabilities reusable and adaptable, SEL offer a path towards broader participation in experimental science, empowering researchers to build and extend the tools their ideas require. Project website: https://ai4ssi.github.io/self-evolving-superintelligence-lab/.

item.title: Machine learning–driven inverse design of nanofiltration membranes for selective Mg2+/Na+ separation
item.description: Desalination brine, a byproduct of seawater desalination, contains valuable resources, including magnesium. Recovering magnesium requires selectively retaining Mg2+ while allowing the dominant monovalent cation, Na+, to permeate. Nanofiltration (NF) membranes fabricated by interfacial polymerization are promising for this Mg2+/Na+ separation, but their performance depends on coupled formulation and processing variables that are inefficient to optimize through trial and error. Here, we demonstrate a workflow integrating dataset curation, forward prediction, and inverse design of thin-film composite NF membranes. A dataset of 1,253 entries, comprising literature and in-house records, was cleaned, imputed, and augmented through chemically constrained permutation of interchangeable polymer, solvent, and salt variables in the training split only. Optimized extremely randomized tree regressors predicted pure water permeability, solute rejection, and intermediate membrane properties, achieving test-set coefficients of determination above 0.79. Shapley analysis indicated that permeability was governed primarily by formulation and processing variables, whereas rejection depended mainly on solute identity and charge, as well as membrane tightness. Using Bayesian optimization with a scalarized objective, two membrane recipes with favorable Mg2+/Na+ selectivity were identified and experimentally validated. The inversely designed membranes exhibited the required Mg2+/Na+ selectivity, demonstrating the capability of this workflow to design Mg2+-selective NF membranes for resource recovery from desalination brine.
