item.title: How to Discover New Electrolyte Additives for Lithium Batteries: A Computational Roadmap
item.description: Electrolyte additives, present at a few weight percent or less, decide whether a lithium battery forms a stable solidelectrolyte interphase, survives high-voltage operation, tolerates trace water and HF, or resists fire. For three decades most additives were found by trial and error, and the few design rules that emerged, most famously “a lower LUMO than the solvent”, were known to fail almost as soon as they were formulated. Here we organize the computational literature on additive discovery, from the first quantum-chemical studies of vinylene carbonate (2002) to self-driving laboratories, chemical foundation models and LLM agents (2026), into a step-by-step roadmap: define the function the additive must perform; choose a descriptor that is actually predictive for that function; define and enumerate the chemical space; screen it with tiered quantum-chemical funnels; establish the decomposition mechanism; accelerate with machine learning; generate candidates beyond existing libraries; simulate the interphase the additive builds; and close the loop with automated experiments. For each step we summarize what has been established, what has only been correlated, and what has failed. We show that the hierarchy of redox descriptors (frontier orbitals → vertical and adiabatic electron affinities and ionization potentials → thermodynamic cycles → Li+-and anion-containing clusters → explicit-interface dynamics) is now quantitatively documented, that solvation-and product-level descriptors are emerging as the missing axes, and that the decisive bottleneck has shifted from candidate generation to reliable, fast, function-specific experimental labels. We close with a table of what each class of method can and cannot predict and with a realistic outline of a closed-loop additive-discovery framework.

item.title: Closed-loop formulation–process optimization under unknown feasibility for extended-release pellets
item.description: Pharmaceutical formulation development frequently encounters formulation–process conditions that fail before a viable product is produced, leaving downstream performance unobservable and experimental feasibility unknown a priori. Here, we demonstrate a closed-loop formulation-development workflow that jointly optimizes formulation and process variables while learning experimental feasibility from physical outcomes. Using caffeine-loaded extended-release pellets produced by wet granulation and extrusion-spheronization, ANDROMEDA 1 selected formulation compositions and processing conditions within a large mixed categorical and numerical design space. Across 51 experiments performed in 13 sequential batches, 29 conditions produced pellets suitable for downstream characterization and 22 (43%) were infeasible. Failed experiments were retained as feasibility observations without assigning artificial drug release scores. Among feasible formulations, the best observed deviation from a predefined four-hour zero-order release target decreased from 1.63 to 0.17 fraction-hours. Release performance, pellet morphology and drug loading followed distinct trajectories, with an empirical trade-off between release deviation and median pellet aspect ratio. Retrospective Gaussian-process modelling showed that replacing an excipient-slot encoding with slot-independent material mass fractions increased leave-one-out cross validated R2 for release prediction from 0.39 to 0.60. Adding four derived wet-mass descriptors reduced release prediction R2 to 0.38 but yielded the highest morphology prediction R2 (0.64). Neither alternative representation improved forward-in-time release prediction. Together, these results show that unknown feasibility, competing product attributes and formulation representation can be incorporated within a single adaptive formulation-process workflow. Analyses further identify design space coverage and representation choice as important considerations for machine learning-guided pharmaceutical development.

item.title: EnGOAT: An Energy–Geometry Analysis Toolkit for Free-Energy Surfaces of Mobile Species in Crystalline Materials
item.description: The free-energy surface (FES) of a mobile species in a crystalline host governs its behavior within the material, including properties such as adsorption and transport, but reducing it to quantitative descriptors remains challenging. We present the Energy–GeOmetry Analysis Toolkit (EnGOAT), an open-source framework for the energetic, geometric, and topological analysis of volumetric FES data. Building on the TuTraSt algorithm, EnGOAT partitions the FES into basins and transition states, quantifies their volumes, surface areas, and energy–volume histograms, represents their connectivity as periodic graphs from which minimum-energy pathways and merge trees are obtained, and computes directional self-diffusion coefficients by kinetic Monte Carlo. Because accessibility is defined from energy isosurfaces of the FES rather than from van der Waals radii, the extracted descriptors are probe-specific and reflect the energy landscape actually experienced by the mobile species. Results are stored in a JSON/NumPy data model suited for high-throughput screening and can be explored with a dedicated visualization tool. We demonstrate EnGOAT for CH4 adsorption in a zeolite and for Li+ ion transport in a ceramic electrolyte.

item.title: Physics‐Informed Machine Learning for Solid Oxide Cell Materials and Microstructures Under Operando Constraints
item.description: Advanced Energy Materials, Volume 16, Issue 41, 4 November 2026.

item.title: When do machine-learning potentials need a configuration-dependent kernel? Learning long-range interactions with Fourier neural operators
item.description: arXiv:2611.03678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-range interactions in machine-learning interatomic potentials are commonly treated by coupling learned sources through either a prescribed electrostatic kernel or a learned but configuration-independent one. Whether such a kernel suffices depends on the underlying screened interaction. We address this question by using Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to learn how latent source fields, built from the descriptors of a local backbone (here MACE), interact across the simulation cell. For a synthetic ionic system with tunable screening, a prescribed Coulomb kernel underestimates the long-wavelength charge fluctuations by 43% under strong screening, whereas the FNO reproduces them within 3% and recovers 95-99% of the variance of the residual left by the local backbone. A linear FNO, which learns a configuration-independent kernel, performs equally well in the homogeneous case. Under inhomogeneous screening, rearranging the remote medium modulates the coupling between distant ions, a dependence that no configuration-independent kernel can represent. Among the models tested, only the nonlinear FNO responds to this modulation, and its force errors are 27-41% lower than those of configuration-independent models. In first-principles benchmarks of liquid water, lithium lanthanum zirconate, and Au2/MgO(001), MACE-FNO is comparable to a prescribed-kernel model for the bulk systems and more accurate for the interface. It further captures the reversal of the Au2 wetting preference induced by remote Al dopants, with deviations below 5 meV per cell from density functional theory. These results indicate that a configuration-dependent kernel, as learned by FNOs, becomes necessary once the screening medium varies, even though the energy remains quadratic in the charges for a fixed medium.

item.title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials
item.description: arXiv:2611.03795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatially programmed functional materials, from functionally graded alloys and metamaterials to quantum superlattices, use their spatial structure to tailor physical properties. However, translating a desired spatial structure into a practical fabrication recipe remains challenging due to the complex relationship between processing conditions and resulting material structures. Here we show that a large language model (LLM) agent can inverse-design such fabrication recipes by using a physics-based simulator of ion-matter interactions as a tool. Given an arbitrary depth profile of implanted ions or vacancies, the agent selects the ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers; writes, runs, and interprets simulations; and iteratively refines the recipe until the simulated profile matches the target, with minimal human input. Our work demonstrates physics-guided agentic inverse design as a practical approach to making the spatial structure of materials a programmable variable, opening new opportunities to explore emergent physical phenomena and functional phases of matter.

item.title: Dynamical Phonon Anharmonicity Drives Charge-Density-Wave Softening and Electronic Quasiparticle Decoherence in Monolayer 1H-NbSe2
item.description: arXiv:2611.04038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Charge-density-wave (CDW) instabilities in two-dimensional materials are governed by strongly anharmonic soft phonons, whose dynamical behavior remains poorly understood beyond the statically renormalized vibrations. Here, using monolayer 1H-NbSe2, we investigate how frequency-dependent three- and four-phonon interactions reshape phonon spectral functions and influence electronic excitations. We find that three-phonon interactions induce substantial dynamical softening of CDW modes, increasing the estimated transition temperature relative to static self-consistent phonon theory. Four-phonon interactions further promote such dynamical softening and enhance spectral broadening, producing non-Lorentzian lineshapes that challenge the quasiparticle picture. Incorporating dynamically renormalized phonon frequencies and electron-phonon coupling into Fan-Migdal electron self-energy calculations reveals enhanced electronic kinks, satellite features, and momentum-dependent quasiparticle decoherence, driven by the strong momentum dependence of the electron-phonon coupling matrix elements. These findings establish dynamical anharmonicity as a critical link between soft-mode lattice fluctuations and electronic spectral signatures, providing insights into coupled lattice-electron dynamics in two-dimensional quantum materials.

item.title: Multi-Fidelity Machine Learning for Predicting Startup Stress Growth and Strain Hardening in Wormlike Micellar Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.04115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wormlike micellar solutions exhibit formulation-dependent nonlinear startup responses, including stress overshoot, undershoot, and strain hardening, making prediction across compositions and shear rates challenging. We developed a multi-fidelity machine-learning framework to predict stress-growth curves in cetylpyridinium chloride (CPyCl)-based wormlike micelles from sparse experimental measurements. The framework combines a low-fidelity analytical model describing the overall startup response with high-fidelity experimental data capturing formulation-specific nonlinear features. This approach addresses the limited and uneven coverage of salt chemistry, concentration, and shear rate without relying solely on data-intensive neural-network training. The trained model predicts complete stress-growth responses at untested shear rates and enables extraction of strain-hardening characteristics from interpolated curves. By augmenting sparse rheological measurements, the framework provides a basis for exploring relationships among formulation variables, linear viscoelastic properties, and nonlinear startup behavior, while supporting more efficient characterization of wormlike micellar solutions.

item.title: greenWTE: Frequency-domain solver for the phonon Wigner Transport Equation with arbitrary heating using Green's functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.04156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heat transport in solids is usually described in a phenomenological way via Fourier's law. However, at small time and length scales in low thermal conductivity materials, a microscopic description is needed. This is traditionally done by invoking the phonon Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE), which has been successful in describing transport in high thermal conductivity materials. Recently, a generalization of the BTE, the Wigner Transport Equation, was developed to be able to microscopically describe transport in low thermal conductivity materials by taking into account not only phonon scattering processes but also phonon tunneling processes, so-called coherences. We present a Python package that solves the Wigner Transport Equation (WTE) in spatial and temporal Fourier space for arbitrary source terms, thereby enabling the study of heat transport at small space and time scales. This allows one to compute both static and dynamic thermal conductivities from bulk to nanoscale. Beyond that, it can be used to study the response of phonon systems in materials to arbitrary heat sources.

item.title: LaQX: A JAX Toolkit for Neural Quantum State Simulations of Lattice Quantum Many-Body Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.04333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural quantum states provide accurate variational representations for interacting lattice fermions and spins. Turning a new ansatz into a reproducible calculation, however, requires coordinated implementations of the Hamiltonian, sampling, optimization, observables, and accelerator parallelism. We present LaQX (Lattice Quantum simulation based on jaX), an open-source neural quantum state library based on JAX that organizes these components through common functional interfaces. Beyond ground-state variational Monte Carlo, LaQX supports excited-state calculations, Green's Function Monte Carlo refinement, adiabatic evolution, and real-time evolution with time-dependent variational Monte Carlo. It consolidates methods developed in recent high-accuracy neural quantum state studies of the Hubbard model and frustrated magnets, and the package has been used to investigate the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model. We document these capabilities with reproducible calculations for Hubbard, $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg, altermagnetic Hubbard, and interacting Hofstadter models. Function-oriented modules separate the scientific components and limit the source context needed for extensions by human developers and large language models. Source code, documentation, and executable examples are available at https://github.com/bytedance/laqx.

item.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na$_3$PS$_4$
item.description: arXiv:2611.04547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described by mobile cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder enhances transport remains unresolved at the mesoscale, inaccessible to ensemble-averaged probes. We use Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy to measure nanoscale structural dynamics of a single ball-milled Na$_3$PS$_4$ particle. We find that the cubic phase behaves as a strain glass: a frustrated configuration of three degenerate tetragonal variants with short-range order. Its domain-wall motion is stress-driven, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing as residual milling stress is depleted. Rearrangements follow scale-free avalanche statistics, matching ferroelastic martensites but without external driving. The tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics occur on timescales comparable to estimated ionic diffusion across the particle, indicating the host structure cannot be assumed static on transport-relevant timescales.

item.title: Bayesian optimization enhanced magnetic field gradient detection based on spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensates
item.description: arXiv:2611.04719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic field detection is of great significance in modern fields such as medical diagnostics, geological exploration, inertial navigation, and space physics. We have previously investigated the expansion dynamics of a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. Building on these results, here we propose a scheme for magnetic-field-gradient detection by establishing a quantitative relationship between the condensate's rotational deflection angle and the magnetic-field gradient. In this work, we present the parameter dependence of this scheme and perform a systematic optimization. We introduce a Bayesian optimization algorithm to automatically and efficiently search for the optimal combination of key parameters, thereby significantly enhancing the sensitivity of the magnetic field gradient measurement. The results show that the optimized gradiometer improves the sensitivity by a factor of five. This work not only provides a new approach for magnetic field gradient measurement but also serves as a reference for machine learning-empowered quantum precision measurement.

item.title: Critical amplitudes of the Baxter-Wu model from MCPA and Wolff simulations: free-exponent and fixed-exponent fits
item.description: arXiv:2611.04733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The two-dimensional Baxter-Wu model belongs to the universality class of the four-state Potts model. Exact expressions are available for its energy, specific heat, magnetization, and polarization amplitudes. We use these results as a benchmark for evaluating two simulation algorithms and two approaches to extracting critical amplitudes. Microcanonical population annealing (MCPA) and the sublattice-freezing Wolff algorithm yield highly consistent estimates for the energy and order parameters when applied to lattices of comparable size. According to the exact Joyce series, the local effective exponent does not stabilize at a constant value but instead undergoes a monotonic drift. This behaviour stems from corrections to scaling, which can be expressed as a series in the cube root of the reduced temperature. As a result, these corrections decay relatively slowly, with the leading term being of relative order $|t|^{2/3}$. When performing a fit with a free exponent on an automatically identified plateau, this drift gets incorporated into the estimated exponent, introducing a substantial bias in the derived amplitudes. In contrast, a fit that fixes the exponent to its exact value and explicitly accounts for the analytic correction series delivers a close match to the known exact amplitudes. Using this refined fitting approach, we obtain estimates for the susceptibility amplitudes and the universal amplitude ratios. These values are in good agreement with predictions from form-factor calculations. Additionally, we numerically determine the leading correction coefficient for the polarization.

item.title: Vortices in a two-dimensional fermionic superfluid
item.description: arXiv:2611.05017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantized vortices are a hallmark of superfluidity. They have proven to be an indispensable probe for systems ranging from superfluid helium to type-II superconductors. In ultracold two-dimensional (2D) Fermi gases, where phase fluctuations are enhanced and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) mechanism governs the superfluid transition, their observation has remained elusive. Here, we report on the controlled creation of quantized vortices in a homogeneous 2D gas in the BEC--BCS crossover. By continuously tuning the velocity of two moving obstacles, we observe quantized steps in the absolute vortex charge. Matter-wave interferometry reveals the characteristic phase winding, quantized in units of $2\pi$. Measurements on 2D and 3D gases show a striking difference: only in 2D does the vortex number grow with temperature, reflecting thermal activation of BKT vortex pairs. Our approach provides evidence of fermionic superfluidity in 2D and offers a means to study BKT physics, vortex-controlled transport and resistance, as well as to detect unconventional superfluidity in spin-imbalanced 2D gases.

item.title: Ferron polariton Hall effect: Deflecting optically rectified polarization with magnetic fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.05025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ferrons are elementary excitations of ferroelectric order that can propagate and transport polarization when excited with light. Here, we show theoretically that ferron polaritons exhibit a Hall effect: an applied magnetic field generates polarization transport perpendicular to the propagation direction of a ferron polariton excited by an incident terahertz pulse. We demonstrate this effect for the example of ferroelectric SnTe using first-principles calculations and a microscopic theory of the phonon-polariton current. The direction and magnitude of the transverse polarization transport can be controlled by the polarization of the terahertz pulse and the applied magnetic field. Our results establish a route toward light-controlled directional transport of electric polarization in ferroelectrics.

item.title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.03767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

item.title: Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Reveals Grotthuss Transport in Concentrated Electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2611.04558v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Proton transfer is responsible for the anomalous high conductivity in acidic or basic aqueous solutions. Yet, the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the conductivity of concentrated aqueous solutions is unknown. In this work, we compute the transport properties of KOH(aq) systems with different concentrations, using Molecular Dynamics simulations with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MLIP), which includes proton transfer. We quantify the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the diffusivities of hydroxide ions and water molecules, and the ionic conductivity and transport numbers of the electrolytes. The contribution is substantial at lower concentrations, but diminishes at very high concentrations.

item.title: Benchmarking and advancing machine-learning interatomic potentials for 3C-SiC across equilibrium and extreme conditions
item.description: arXiv:2510.06966v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Several machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have been developed for cubic silicon carbide (3C-SiC). Here, we benchmark seven existing MLIPs against a common set of structural, thermal, defect, radiation-damage, disordered-phase, and computational-performance tests. We also introduce two complementary MLIPs trained on DFT-labeled crystalline, liquid, amorphous, and defective configurations. TGAP, a Gaussian approximation potential based on the \verb|soap_turbo| descriptor, provides consistently high accuracy across the sampled configurational space. MTP, a custom moment tensor potential, retains good accuracy across these regimes while offering substantially lower computational cost, GPU acceleration, and access to multi-million-atom simulations. As an application-level test, both potentials remain stable in displacement cascades spanning short-range repulsion, transient disorder, and recrystallization. Overall, MTP emerges as a particularly strong accuracy--cost compromise for large-scale and strongly non-equilibrium simulations of 3C-SiC.

item.title: Physics-Informed and Knowledge-Driven Generative AI for Autonomous Discovery of Porous Oxide Energy Materials: Opportunities and Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2608.02858v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The discovery of next-generation energy-storage materials is increasingly limited by the complexity of the underlying design problem rather than by computational capability alone. Porous transition-metal oxides represent a particularly challenging class of battery materials because their performance emerges from coupled interactions among crystal chemistry, pore architecture, ion transport, electrochemistry, electro-chemo-mechanics, synthesis, manufacturing, and battery-system operation. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities for generating chemically plausible crystal structures. However, current approaches remain largely focused on crystallographic validity and thermodynamic stability. This perspective presents a roadmap for advancing generative AI beyond crystal generation toward physics-informed, application-aware, and synthesis-aware inverse design. Using porous oxide electrodes as a representative materials platform, we propose a seven-tier physics-informed inverse-design framework integrating chemistry, thermodynamics, transport, electrochemistry, durability, cell compatibility, and manufacturability. We further identify the "Missing Data Problem" as a fundamental bottleneck limiting application-aware AI and introduce an autonomous knowledge-generation framework supported by a Porous Oxide Energy Materials Ontology and a continuously evolving "Knowledge Base". Together, these concepts establish the foundation for Synthesis-Aware, Closed-Loop Autonomous Discovery, providing a general framework for AI-enabled autonomous materials discovery across energy-storage materials and other functional materials.

item.title: Estimating the expected output of wide random MLPs more efficiently than sampling
item.description: arXiv:2605.05179v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: By far the most common way to estimate an expected loss in machine learning is to draw samples, compute the loss on each one, and take the empirical average. However, sampling is not necessarily optimal. Given an MLP at initialization, we show how to estimate its expected output over Gaussian inputs without running samples through the network at all. Instead, we produce approximate representations of the distributions of activations at each layer, leveraging tools such as cumulants and Hermite expansions. We show both theoretically and empirically that for sufficiently wide networks, our estimator achieves a target mean squared error using substantially fewer FLOPs than Monte Carlo sampling. We find moreover that our methods perform particularly well at estimating the probabilities of rare events, and additionally demonstrate how they can be used for model training. Together, these findings suggest a path to producing models with a greatly reduced probability of catastrophic tail risks.

item.title: Predicting battery stability from electron-ion transport mismatch
item.description: A battery stability prediction model covering LIBs, SIBs, and ZIBs has been proposed. The electron-ion transport mismatch is identified as a key determinant of battery stability. A linear correlation between the battery stability and the electron-ion transport mismatch has been revealed: the closer the transport rates of electrons and ions, the more stable the battery. The battery stability could be predicted rapidly from the electron-ion mismatch, with no need for time-consuming long-term cycling.

item.title: How Chemical Evidence Shapes Mechanistic Reasoning and Prediction by Large Language Models: Fine-Grained Inference in Nucleoside-Derived Supramolecular Gelation
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) offer a distinctive capability for chemical problem solving by integrating chemical knowledge and experimental evidence through reasoning expressed in language. Yet how chemical evidence reshapes their predictions and expressed rationales is not self-evident and has received limited examination, particularly for challenging chemical problems. Here, using nucleoside-derived supramolecular gelation as a testbed, we systematically varied the evidence provided to LLMs and quantitatively evaluated their predictions and the mechanistic alignment of generated rationales. Without additional evidence, correct predictions were associated with greater alignment to literature-supported mechanisms than incorrect ones, suggesting that LLMs can draw on intrinsic chemical knowledge despite rationales remain largely general. Structurally similar gelation precedents, thought improved prediction accuracy significantly, reduced this distinction by anchoring rationales to insufficiently discriminative structural features, indicating that similarity-based evidence does not necessarily improve chemical reasoning and that prediction accuracy alone is insufficient to assess LLM performance in chemical tasks. In contrast, condition-constrained references and mechanistic information more consistently directed rationales toward chemically discriminative features, even when prediction accuracy did not improve in tandem. Together, our study highlights the importance of task-specific evidence design and quantitative rationale evaluation for reliable chemical problem solving by LLMs.

item.title: Automated Static and Dynamic Contact-Angle Analysis with Machine Learning
item.description: We present an autonomous machine-learning model, Conan-MLII, for fast, reproducible contact-angle measurement. The model was trained on >32 million synthetic images generated from Young–Laplace solutions spanning θ = 20◦–180◦, including the effects of gravity, multiple image scales and surface perturbations (roughness, reflection) as well as including sampling offsets to provide contact-point invariance. An improved contact-point identification (CPID) routine is integrated to enable autonomous processing of real images. The model produced results comparable to Young–Laplace (mean systematic underprediction ∼ 2◦) when tested on 172 experimental images drawn from multiple groups, and was much better at predicting asymmetric and low-angle cases where Young-Laplace fitting commonly misconverges. The total analysis time per image for the machine learning approach was three times faster than Young-Laplace fitting, the current best-practice approach. The model is extended to measurement of advancing and receding contact angles, showing excellent agreement with commercial tensiometers over the range 30◦ − 160◦. The model is provided as open-source for use and further development of contact angle measurement.

item.title: DolphinQCT: The Light-Weighted, Python Based Quasi-Classical Trajectory Setup Tool for ORCA
The CPOSS Database of Computed Crystal Structures
item.description: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) has radically evolved over the last two decades from a niche research topic to a tool for solid form prediction and derisking. The Control and Prediction of the Organic Solid State (CPOSS) project led by Professor Sarah (Sally) Price has developed CSP over more than two decades of research, generating a large number of deeply researched landscapes, populated by alternative crystal packings for a given chemical system, including structures and systems that have not been observed experimentally. Here we present the CPOSS Database of Computed Crystal Structures, a public collection of CSP landscapes developed within the CPOSS project. This public inventory contains 310 documented searches for 234 molecular systems, comprising 190 single-component and 44 multicomponent systems, with 517,594 archived structure files across 508 energy-model archives. Structures are accompanied by search and computational-method descriptions, tabulated properties, and connections to experimental structures and the original literature where available. The collection’s principal contribution is its depth of candidate packing arrangements for individual systems, together with the provenance needed to interpret successive searches and energy refinements. We describe the construction, coverage, access routes, and limitations of the public release, and discuss its use in physical chemistry, crystal structure prediction, and atomistic model development. The database is released together with an interactive CSP Landscape Navigator under CC0 1.0.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Model Implementation for UC Irvine Dataset 322
item.description: The dataset, sourced from the UCI repository, underscores the value of open-source resources in advancing sensor research. In this study, raw sensor data were compressed using polynomial fitting (polyfit), achieving nearly a 100-fold reduction, and subsequently analyzed with the Isolation Forest algorithm to detect anomalies. Python libraries, including scikit-learn, were deployed in an isolated environment to ensure reproducibility and scalability. The workflow was further integrated into Microsoft Copilot, enabling natural language interaction with the AI agent for streamlined big data modeling.

item.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Disentangles Pore Confinement Across Multiple Zr-MOF CO2 Capture Targets
item.description: Pore confinement in zirconium-based metal–organic frameworks (Zr-MOFs) is often described using the cage–window ratio (ΓCW), the largest cavity diameter divided by the pore-limiting diameter (Df), yet whether this composite coordinate carries information beyond Df alone remains unclear. We modeled CO2 uptake, heat of adsorption (HoA), and CO2/N2 selectivity for 239 Zr-containing MOFs at two pressures relevant to vacuum-swing adsorption using structure-grouped machine learning with SHAP interpretation, reaching test R2 values of 0.77–0.88. Although ΓCW correlated positively with all three targets, controlling for Df weakened these associations and reversed their sign, while the reciprocal analysis left the Df associations largely unchanged and a difference-based formulation produced no significant association. Df played different roles across the three targets, indicating that the apparent confinement effect mainly reflects the limiting aperture rather than relative cage–window architecture.

item.title: Attribution Fingerprinting by Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Category‐Specific Additive Design Rules for Zinc Anodes
item.description: Advanced Materials, EarlyView.

item.title: In the age of big data and AI: do we still need chemical bonds?
item.description: arXiv:2611.00228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemical bonding is the language through which chemistry rationalizes materials structure, stability, properties, and reactivity. Meanwhile, modern deep-learning models achieve remarkable predictive performance using representations based largely on compositional and structural information, raising the question of whether explicit bonding concepts remain necessary. In this work, we argue that artificial intelligence does not render chemical bonding obsolete but provides a new framework for evaluating and refining bonding concepts. We show that, through linear probing, Allegro and MACE embeddings recover bonding descriptors with (R^2 > 0.95), indicating that bonding emerges naturally from Allegro's and MACE's latent spaces. We also show that bonding descriptors provide information beyond bond distance in our electronic-structure-featurized MEGNet (ESF-MEGNet) model, reducing prediction error for properties including bulk and shear moduli by 15%. We discuss implications for interpretable machine learning, synthesizability prediction, and generative materials design, and suggest joint-embedding approaches for learning more general bonding representations. More broadly, we propose that chemical bonding can be understood as a learnable representation of electronic structure. From this perspective, different bonding models represent alternative compressions of the underlying electronic information and can be evaluated through their predictive power, dimensionality, and complexity. The age of machine learning shifts the focus from whether a bonding model is physically motivated to whether it captures the information required to explain and predict materials behavior. If a materials genome exists, it should be encodable through a representation of chemical bonding. If no bonding representation can capture this information, our understanding of the chemical bond may require revision.

item.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.00274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $\mu$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

item.title: The Agentic AI Kerr Lab: LLM Agents for Kerr Microscopy Experiments with Magnetic Skyrmions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are topological spin textures that can be observed directly by magnetic microscopy and driven by fields and currents, which makes them a model system for fundamental physics and candidates for spintronic devices. Magneto-optical Kerr microscopy is a method to image them in real time; however, most experiments use an inefficient cycle of consecutive imaging, analysis and excitation in which every step requires the judgement of the experimentalist operating the setup. Here we present the Agentic AI Kerr Lab (AgentKerr), in which an agent based on a large language model operates this cycle automatically and efficiently on a Kerr microscope. Rather than relying on pattern detection by a language model, a convolutional neural network trained on Kerr images turns live images into skyrmion observables such as position, size and shape, on which the agent bases its decisions. The architecture lets agents operate the instruments safely, as every hardware action is checked deterministically against an action policy, independently of the agent that issues it. With no procedure given, the agent determines by itself how to create, tune and move skyrmions, and writes its own analyses. The approach can be transferred to other spin textures and points towards magnetic imaging experiments in which the researcher poses the question and the agent finds the way to realize the experiments that yield the answer.

item.title: Machine Learning Aided Computational Discovery of Boride Substrates for Borophene Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2611.00533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Borophene, a monolayer of boron, is distinctive among two-dimensional materials owing to its unique properties, including polymorphism and potential applications in quantum technologies and energy conversion and storage. Nevertheless, its applications are hindered by the strong binding of borophene to metal substrates, which impedes the realization of freestanding borophene. Alternative substrates with tunable binding to borophene are therefore highly desirable. Since boride layers arise during borophene synthesis on metals, borides provide potential alternative substrates for borophene synthesis. In this work, we investigate the binding energies and interactions between borophene and 1356 boride surfaces for two borophene phases (v1/6 and v1/9), using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML). Importantly, incorporating ML-predicted charge transfer as an input feature to a subsequent ML model enables physics-informed predictions of binding energies. Additional DFT calculations on four representative cases were performed to validate the ML predictions. SHAP analysis reveals that the majority of key descriptors are associated with delocalized electrons, highlighting the role of electronic properties in governing binding strength. Combined DFT and ML screening identifies 65 and 73 promising boride surfaces for the v1/6 and v1/9 phases, respectively. Al- and Ag-based borides, including AlB2 and AgB2, emerge as predominant candidates for both phases. The computationally predicted candidate substrates and the deduced design guidelines provide a charge-transfer-informed ML strategy for substrate selection and represent promising steps toward the experimental realization of freestanding borophene.

item.title: Beyond Synthesis Conditions: Linking In-situ Growth Dynamics to Carbon Nanotube Forest Properties through Multimodal Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.00739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning for chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has largely mapped static synthesis conditions to final properties, implicitly treating these conditions as a complete description of growth. Here, we test this assumption by integrating gas-flow conditions with in-situ time-resolve growth profiles (growth curves) of vertically aligned CNT forests. We introduce an observation-window analysis, in which prediction is evaluated as a function of observation time by providing models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, to determine not only whether a property can be predicted, but when the necessary information becomes available during synthesis. Clustering of normalized growth curves revealed distinct growth patterns independent of final forest height. The gas conditions alone could predict the initial growth rate but not the growth lifetime and failed to capture the variation in yield (R^2<0). Adding the growth curve improved yield prediction (R^2~0.4-0.5), with the relevant information emerging during the intermediate and later stages of growth rather than at its onset. In contrast, density and G/D ratio, which forest height does not record, showed no consistent improvement. The maximum height and lifetime could be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-min growth. Permutation feature importance identified water vapor and H_2, both linked to catalyst activity, as the most informative gas variables. These results indicate that variation unexplained by synthesis conditions is not merely noise but reflects an evolving catalyst state, and they establish mid-growth decision points for autonomous synthesis, enabling early termination of unpromising batches and, ultimately, in-batch adjustment of growth conditions.

item.title: IRIS: an agentic eye on symmetry-derived paths and energy landscapes of structural phase transitions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural phase transitions underpin ferroelectric and multiferroic functionality, but constructing interpretable energy landscapes remains dependent on specialist expertise. Predicting this behaviour rests on Landau free energies expanded in symmetry-adapted order parameters: their coefficients classify a transition, expose the couplings between distortions, set switching paths and barriers, and parametrize phase-field and effective-Hamiltonian models at larger scales. Obtaining these coefficients from first principles means sampling the Born--Oppenheimer energy surface along symmetry-derived structural paths, which requires crystallographic analysis, reliable structure generation and extensive computation, especially for coupled multidimensional order parameters. Here we introduce IRIS, an agentic workflow that converts plain-language requests and crystal structures into symmetry-adapted energy landscapes and fitted Landau energy models. Deterministic gates govern acceptance of structures, calculations and fits, while language models interpret requests and select constrained recovery actions. Applications across six compounds include a six-dimensional BiFeO$_3$ landscape that separates competition between polar and tilt amplitudes from directional locking and ranks homogeneous switching pathways. Controlled replays detected all 53 injected faults; disabling gates allowed 14 silent errors. Four prospective BaTiO$_3$ runs produced fitted landscapes from 96 density-functional calculations in 34 minutes total without intervening human decisions. IRIS makes physical model construction a reusable computational capability and provides a framework for scientific automation grounded in explicit verification.

item.title: FLAKE: Friction and Lattice Analysis of Kinetics and Energetics of rigid 2D clusters on crystalline substrates
item.description: arXiv:2611.01805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a small solid island slides across a crystalline surface, the outcome (smooth flow or stick-slip, free rotation or angular locking) is controlled almost entirely by the geometric relationship between the island and the surface: their relative orientation, size and lattice symmetry. These phenomena are central to nanoscale friction, to the interpretation of colloidal monolayer experiments and to structural superlubricity. FLAKE (Friction and Lattice Analysis of Kinetics and Energetics) is a Python package for simulating the statics and Langevin dynamics of a rigid 2D cluster sliding over a periodic or quasiperiodic substrate potential. It enables fast, systematic exploration of how geometry and substrate symmetry control the energy landscape and friction, studies that are prohibitively expensive with fully atomistic simulations. FLAKE has been the primary simulation tool for three published studies on structural superlubricity and colloidal friction.

item.title: Temperature-Dependent Raman Signatures of Local Symmetry Breaking in Vacancy Double Perovskite Cs$_2$SnI$_6$
item.description: arXiv:2611.01830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and controlling the optical, thermal and mechanical properties of K$_2$PtCl$_6$-type double perovskites is essential for the design of lead-free, high-performance thermoelectric and optoelectronic materials. In this study, we investigate Cs$_2$SnI$_6$ using temperature-dependent near-resonance Raman scattering, complemented by density functional theory-based phonon calculations. The appearance of Raman-forbidden phonon modes in the Raman response at cryogenic temperatures provides strong evidence for local symmetry breaking that does not develop into a global structural phase transition. Through detailed analysis of phonon intensities, energies, and spectral lineshapes, we characterize the temperature evolution of the symmetry-broken structural response of Cs$_2$SnI$_6$. Below 200 K, multi-phonon scattering is strongly enhanced, and symmetry-forbidden Raman modes emerge. The temperature dependence of phonon intensities follows a phenomenological Arrhenius behavior, revealing an activation energy of 15-20 meV. These results establish temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of local structural distortions and anharmonic structural dynamics in Cs$_2$SnI$_6$, providing a robust experimental basis for discussing the microscopic origins of symmetry breaking and electron-phonon coupling in halide double perovskites.

item.title: Data-driven candidate structure ensemble generation beyond the convex hull with crystALL approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.02584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real materials consist of multiple stable or metastable states under real-world conditions, existing as statistical ergodic ensembles of configurations rather than ideal crystals. Yet, data-driven computational materials discovery increasingly biases itself toward finding "new stable structures" from ground-state DFT calculations alone. This limits our long-term ability to discover materials whose properties emerge from metastable phases, to explain experimental observations, or to model thermodynamic behavior comprehensively. Predicting ergodic sets of atomic configurations of known and hypothetical solids is a fundamental challenge in theoretical crystallography, approached via many complementary methods. We discuss this conceptually and introduce crystALL, a pragmatic and powerful data-driven approach to discovering ensembles beyond the convex hull, embracing structural diversity over stability alone, enabling robust experiment matching in cases evading traditional methods. crystALL leverages 5 million relaxed structures from OPTIMADE and MPDD to rapidly generate a comprehensive candidate set by: (1) species substitutions; (2) ML feature-space analysis with pySIPFENN; (3) representative structure selection via clustering and energy-minimization or property matching; and (4) construction of the final candidate ensemble for experimental or ab initio validation. We also uniquely address the common challenge of experimental composition uncertainties spanning many integer stoichiometries by new efficient searches across anonymized compositional ranges rather than fixed formulas. Overall, crystALL's ensemble-focused philosophy provides critical advantages over the prevailing convex-hull-searching paradigm, which often fails to account for key experimental observations and increases AI/ML discovery bias over time - akin to model collapse in LLMs retrained on iteratively generated content.

item.title: Collective dipole effects amplify field-driven ion transport in amorphous Li$_3$PO$_4$
item.description: arXiv:2611.02617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Amorphous solid electrolytes often outperform their crystalline counterparts, but how disorder shapes ionic transport under strong electric fields is poorly understood. We use molecular dynamics with a machine-learned interatomic potential and a machine-learned Born-effective-charge model to measure Li mobility in amorphous Li$_3$PO$_4$ and in a crystal with Li vacancies, from the linear to the strongly nonlinear regime. The amorphous phase shows a much stronger field enhancement, and we trace this to a collective dipole effect. The migrating ion carries the same charge in both phases. Alone it would not make the amorphous phase respond more strongly. What makes the difference is the environment. In the amorphous network the surrounding atoms move with the hop. Their motion makes the work the field performs vary widely between hops. Since hopping rates grow exponentially with the work, the most strongly assisted hops can dominate the drift. Disorder thus enhances field-driven transport through the environment rather than the carrier itself, a mechanism that may operate in disordered ion conductors in general.

item.title: Anion Engineering Enables Concurrent Optimization of Phonon and Carrier Transport in AMg$_2$X$_2$ Zintl Thermoelectrics
item.description: arXiv:2611.02961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The simultaneous suppression of lattice heat transport and enhancement of carrier transport is central to the development of high-performance thermoelectric materials. Here, we investigate the microscopic mechanisms governing phonon and carrier transport in CaAl$_2$Si$_2$-type AMg$_2$X$_2$ (A = Ca, Sr, Ba; X = P, As, Sb, Bi) Zintl compounds using first-principles calculations, machine-learning interatomic potentials, and Boltzmann transport theory. As X changes from P to Bi, the widening phonon band gap restricts three-phonon scattering channels and increases the relative importance of four-phonon processes. In CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$ and BaMg$_2$Bi$_2$, four-phonon scattering dominates the relaxation of low-frequency heat-carrying modes at 900 K. The Bi-based series also exhibits an anomalous increase in lattice thermal conductivity from Ca to Ba despite the increasing cation mass. Mode-resolved analysis links the lower thermal conductivity of CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$ to reduced low-frequency group velocities and stronger anharmonic scattering, with Ca-related mid-frequency vibrations providing additional four-phonon scattering channels. Including both particle-like and coherent contributions, its lattice thermal conductivity reaches 0.23 W$\cdot$m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ at 900 K. Meanwhile, the increasing covalent character of the vertical Mg-X bonds is accompanied by enhanced band-edge dispersion and reduced carrier effective masses. These electronic changes, together with conduction-band convergence, favor n-type transport and yield a predicted peak $ZT$ of 3.68 at 900 K in CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$. These results elucidate the interplay of phonon spectral structure and higher-order anharmonicity in thermal transport, alongside the distinct electronic response to anion substitution.

item.title: Internal friction and frequency-dependent conductivity in the bivariate site energy model for the mixed alkali effect in glasses
item.description: arXiv:2611.03591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mixed alkali effect is fundamental to understanding ion transport in glasses. It manifests itself in strong changes of various ionic transport properties when one type of ion is successively replaced by another type. Recently, we have developed a new theory of thermally activated hopping in bivariate random site energy landscapes that takes into account site occupation statistics according to generalized Fermi distributions and mixture kinetics in accordance with linear irreversible thermodynamics. The theory was successfully applied to predict the behavior of partial conductivities and their activation energies at low frequencies corresponding to the dc limit. Here we show that the theory is capable to capture the salient features of the mixed alkali effect observed in ac ion conductivities and in the peculiar behavior of the internal friction.

item.title: InformedXRD: Reproducible Benchmarks and Physics-Informed Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Symmetry Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.01525v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning for powder diffraction (PXRD) symmetry classification is being trained at scale, yet the field lacks a common evaluation standard: papers report results on different subsets of experimental archives, with different target taxonomies, preprocessing, and metrics, and published models are rarely released in a form that permits rescoring. We present InformedXRD, an evaluation framework with three parts: (i) a machine-readable mapping from 230 space groups to 99 extinction groups, the finest classes powder diffraction can identify from systematic absences alone; (ii) a benchmark-construction method whose inclusion rules are specified as code and reproduce from a frozen snapshot, instantiated as RRUFF-473, RRUFF-325, and, as a small example, opXRD-98; (iii) a reporting protocol with prior-only frequency baselines, a label-permutation test, a hierarchy-aware error metric on the condensed translationengleiche subgroup graph, and stratified evaluation. We build on the mapping, RRUFF benchmarks, subgroup graph, and four ViT checkpoints released in our earlier work (Baggett et al., 2026). Using these checkpoints, a 1D residual CNN, and six architectures trained under the XRDBench recipe (Cao et al., 2025), we show that evaluation design changes what conclusions are justified: paired tests point in different directions at Top-1 and Top-5; paired Top-k tests do not separate the three leading XRDBench models, while hierarchy-aware analysis describes error distance and direction across all six; an input-blind frequency predictor matches the models on aggregate Top-k, yet a label-permutation test still detects pattern-specific evidence; and stratified analysis exposes a label-entropy confound that aggregate accuracy hides. All mapping tables, benchmark code, scripts, and checkpoints are released as shared infrastructure for PXRD-ML evaluation.

item.title: Organizational Learning in Materials Discovery Campaigns: Which Databases, Calculations, and Agent Teams Pay Off
item.description: arXiv:2611.02571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: More databases can make a materials campaign worse. Through an organizational lens, we trace each source's contribution. One band-gap campaign ranks seven anion families from archived measured gaps, one vote per source. In the first half of its budget, all seven pooled rank worse (rank agreement 0.737; 1 = measured order) than the best pool of three (0.851). As a stability check, choosing the pool on half the runs and testing on the rest kept the gap. Splitting Materials Project afterwards points to its transition-metal oxides and fluorides. Two databases from one pipeline add nothing over one, but pooling gives their shared ordering two votes. New calculations repay their cost early only when two or three campaigns reuse them. Flat language-model agent teams trailed a random-pick baseline (mean 0.876, sd 0.096, 20 searches). An adaptive Al-Mg-Si team, mostly interatomic potentials, was scored on unseen HSE06 calculations. In its first quarter of compute it found 49% of the ten lowest-formation-energy compounds, against at most 40% for fixed teams and 73% for MACE-MP-0 alone. Merging members whose orderings agreed carried most of its gain. This suggests pooling a few sources that fit the measurements, counting each pipeline once and charging for computation.

item.title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.02906v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.

item.title: Emergent stigmergy and pheromone-guided decisions in a foraging collective
item.description: arXiv:2611.02997v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ants in a colony forage and recruit other nest-mates for cooperative transport of food through stigmergy. Traditional approach to capture the foraging dynamics relies on fine-tuning phenomenological rules for pheromone deposition, chemotaxis, evaporation, and behavioral switching after reaching the food source. Here, we show that stigmergy emerges from an infinite-horizon stochastic optimal control problem involving outbound foragers traveling from the nest to the food source and returning agents traveling from the food source to the nest. Pheromone dynamics along a trail emerge from the forward propagating Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, with the Bellman discount rate setting the rate of pheromone evaporation. Using this mapping, we identify the conditions under which trail feedback suppresses exploration or leads to the exploitation of established trails. For ants exploring multiple trails, we also find flux-potential relations, analogous to Ohm's law, with ant flux and inverse of squared value field playing the roles of current and resistance on the network. Our model captures collective behavior observed in the classic double-bridge experiments: trail selection on identical routes through a symmetry-breaking instability, selection of the shorter bridge, and bistability in the trail-length ratio that can leave ants transiently committed to the longer route. Our formulation places collective foraging in the broader framework of stochastic optimal control, while simultaneously providing an unifying picture on their emergent behavior consistent with experimental observations.

item.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
item.description: arXiv:2611.03154v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

item.title: Storage and Learning phase transitions in the Random-Features Hopfield Model
item.description: arXiv:2303.16880v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Hopfield model is a paradigmatic model of neural networks that has been analyzed for many decades in the statistical physics, neuroscience, and machine learning communities. Inspired by the manifold hypothesis in machine learning, we propose and investigate a generalization of the standard setting that we name Random-Features Hopfield Model. Here $P$ binary patterns of length $N$ are generated by applying to Gaussian vectors sampled in a latent space of dimension $D$ a random projection followed by a non-linearity. Using the replica method from statistical physics, we derive the phase diagram of the model in the limit $P,N,D\to\infty$ with fixed ratios $\alpha=P/N$ and $\alpha_D=D/N$. Besides the usual retrieval phase, where the patterns can be dynamically recovered from some initial corruption, we uncover a new phase where the features characterizing the projection can be recovered instead. We call this phenomena the learning phase transition, as the features are not explicitly given to the model but rather are inferred from the patterns in an unsupervised fashion.

item.title: Unified Learning of Interatomic Potentials and Electronic Hamiltonians, with Applications in 2D Materials
item.description: arXiv:2510.16605v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce UnIPH, an equivariant graph neural network designed to jointly predict both interatomic potentials and tight-binding (TB) Hamiltonians for an atomic structure. UnIPH is trained using density functional theory (DFT) calculations followed by Wannier projection to predict energies and forces as node-level targets and Wannier-projected TB Hamiltonians as edge-level targets. This enables physically consistent modeling of coupled mechanical-electronic responses with near-DFT-level accuracy. After separately training two UnIPH models on DFT data for bilayer graphene and monolayer MoS2, respectively, we find that these models capture key deformation-electronic effects: in twisted bilayer graphene, the trained UnIPH reveals how interlayer spacing, in-plane strain, and out-of-plane corrugation drive isolated flat-band formation, and further shows that modulating substrate interaction strength can generate flat bands even away from the magic angle (approximately 1.1 degrees). For monolayer MoS2, UnIPH accurately reproduces phonon dispersions and strain-dependent band-gap evolution, and further predicts how a non-uniform substrate creates localized strain pockets that spatially modulate the conduction- and valence-band edges.

item.title: INTERFACE Force Field for Alumina with Validated Bulk Phases and a pH-Resolved Surface Model Database for Aqueous, Electrolyte, and Molecular Interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2601.12570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Alumina and aluminum oxyhydroxides underpin numerous chemical engineering technologies in heterogeneous catalysis, corrosion protection, functional coatings, energy storage devices, and biomedical components. Yet molecular models that predictively connect phase structure, pH dependent surface chemistry, electrolyte organization, and adsorption across operating conditions remain limited. Here we introduce the INTERFACE Force Field (IFF) together with a curated, ready-to-use pH-resolved surface model database for an accurate and transferable atomistic description of major alumina phases according to experimental benchmarks available. The framework covers alpha-Al2O3, gamma-Al2O3, boehmite, diaspore, and gibbsite using a single parameter set compatible with CHARMM, AMBER, OPLS-AA, CVFF, and PCFF. Simulations reproduce experimental reference data across structural, thermodynamic, mechanical, and interfacial benchmarks with deviations of few percent relative to experiment, exceeding existing force fields and density-functional approaches. We introduce a transferable treatment of surface ionization and charge regulation across alumina phases over a broad pH range, enabling simulations of realistic solid-electrolyte interfaces without phase-specific reparameterization. Quantitative reliability is demonstrated by reproducing zeta-potential trends and pH-dependent adsorption of an organic corrosion inhibitor at alumina-water interfaces. Predicted adsorption free energies and surface contact times correlate with experiments across an order of magnitude, enabling process-relevant screening and explaining limitations of earlier adsorption models. The approach is 10,000 to 100,000 times faster than DFT-machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and supports the design of alumina-containing catalysts, corrosion-resistant coatings, energy storage and biomaterials under realistic process conditions.

item.title: Pathway to lowest-energy structures and stress relaxation for the surface triple junction of copper
item.description: arXiv:2603.01920v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The behavior of surface triple junctions (STJ) at emergent grain boundaries on free surfaces is critical to the microstructure evolution, and therefore to the stability of next generation interconnects. Yet, despite this significant importance, its lowest-energy structure and local stress have remained persistently unknown. Here, we fill this critical gap through high-resolution experimental mapping of the local surface deformation at STJs of a symmetrical tilt grain boundaries with [111] rotation axis and misorientation angles 13.17{\deg}, the analysis of the local core-shifted structure and stress relaxation, and ergodic searching metastable structures accordingly with the molecular-statics (MS) calculation. The computation clearly shows the zipped Y-shaped notch as the lowest-energy structures for this group of STJs, the line profile of which is consistent with the experimental observation. This energetic preference was well explained by the stress delocalization mechanism and was tested for a wide range of boundaries with even deeper core-shift depth using machine learning methods based on the data obtained from MS calculation. By revealing the elusive thermodynamics of STJs, our findings advance the research field by redefining the energetic framework for capillary driven structure evolution and providing foundation for understanding kinetically diffusive deformation and for engineering thin-film interconnects and related materials.

item.title: Application and Performance Assessment of Annealing Methods for Electrostatic-Energy-Based Configuration Search in Mixed Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2605.24557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In first-principles design of solid solutions and disordered materials, exhaustive evaluation of all possible substitutional configurations is often impractical because the number of site occupations increases exponentially. Here, we develop a framework for pre-screening mixed-crystal configurations using annealing methods, where the Ewald electrostatic energy is used as the objective function. Substitutional occupations are represented by binary variables, allowing the Ewald energy to be mapped onto an Ising-type Hamiltonian and the search for low-energy configurations to be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem. We implement this formulation using simulated annealing (SA) and quantum annealing (QA), and benchmark their performance against exhaustive search. For the small-scale system CaYAlO$_4$, SA achieved a speed-up of about 30 times, while QA achieved a speed-up of more than 100 times; both methods identified all lowest-energy configurations. For the medium-scale system $\beta$-KSbF$_4$ and the large-scale Ba-doped SiAlON system, SA achieved speed-ups of about 200--300 times while stably identifying the lowest-energy structures. In contrast, QA showed limited speed-up for the medium-scale $\beta$-KSbF$_4$ system and missed some low-energy configurations, likely due to chain breaks. These results indicate that, among the approaches examined here, SA showed comparatively robust performance for Ewald-energy-based configuration search in mixed crystals. The proposed formulation can be implemented using publicly available libraries and provides a practical route for accelerating candidate-structure generation before first-principles calculations.

item.title: A Cross-Entropy Audit (CEA) for Consciousness Tests Moved from Brain to Large Language Model
item.description: arXiv:2609.22300v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Brain tests of consciousness are often applied to large language models (LLMs). Here consciousness means access: whether information, such as a heard sound, becomes available for report and use. A brain recording is in microvolts and an LLM's internal activations are arbitrary numbers, so the two share no common measurement unit. A brain test of this kind compares competing statistical models of how responses vary over repeated trials. The test's decision names the best-fitting model. The decision is wrong when the test names two states for responses that vary smoothly, or the reverse. No method we reviewed measures how often a transferred test is wrong. We call such a method a transfer audit and propose one, the cross-entropy audit (CEA). First, our audit holds back part of the trials and fits each model to the remaining trials. It then scores how well each fitted model predicts the held-back responses. Comparing two models gives a score difference in nats per trial. That difference does not depend on whether the recording is in microvolts or in activations, so brain and machine are scored on one scale. Second, the audit writes down five choices that such tests make for brain data: the competing models, their fitting, what counts as one independent sample, what the uncertainty interval describes, and the decision rule. Each may need to change on a machine. Third, the audit runs the test on simulated data built to follow one model, so the right decision is known, and counts wrong decisions. In our example, the two models of a two-state test, carried over unchanged to an LLM, found two states in 989 of 12,000 smoothly varying simulated datasets. The audited version of the test found two states in none of them. It detected 599 of 600 two-state datasets. The audited version's uncertainty interval, however, was too narrow at six of the twelve smoothly varying settings and is being repaired.

item.title: MSP-LLM: A Structured Large Language Model Framework for Inorganic Material Synthesis Planning
item.description: arXiv:2602.07543v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Material synthesis planning (MSP) remains a fundamental and underexplored bottleneck in AI-driven materials discovery, as it requires not only identifying suitable precursor materials but also designing coherent sequences of synthesis operations to realize a target material. Although several AI-based approaches have been proposed to address isolated subtasks of MSP, a methodology for solving the entire MSP task has yet to be established. We propose MSP-LLM, a structured LLM-based framework that formulates MSP as a two-stage process composed of two constituent subproblems: precursor prediction (PP) and synthesis operation prediction (SOP). Our approach introduces a discrete material class as an intermediate decision variable that organizes both tasks into a chemically consistent decision chain. For SOP, we further incorporate hierarchical precursor types as synthesis-relevant inductive biases and employ precursor constraint factorization that preserves precursor-related information in the autoregressive decoding state. Extensive experiments show that MSP-LLM consistently outperforms existing methods on both PP and SOP, as well as on the MSP task, demonstrating an effective and scalable framework with practical potential for autonomous MSP.

item.title: Entanglement in quantum spin chains is strictly finite at any temperature
item.description: arXiv:2602.13386v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Entanglement is the hallmark of quantum physics, yet its characterization in interacting many-body systems at thermal equilibrium remains one of the most important challenges in quantum statistical physics. We prove that the Gibbs state of any quantum spin chain can be exactly decomposed into a mixture of matrix product states with a bond dimension that is independent of the system size, at any nonzero temperature. As a consequence, the Schmidt number, arguably the most stringent measure of bipartite entanglement, is strictly finite for thermal states, even in the thermodynamic limit. Our decomposition is explicit and is accompanied by an efficient classical algorithm to sample the resulting matrix product states.

item.description:
Nature Communications, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78923-w

Zhao and Ji present L-STAR, a framework that uses a large language model to identify and combine high-performing methods for mapping patterns of gene activity within tissues, improving the accuracy, robustness and interpretability of the analysis.

item.title: Using ChatGPT to evaluate the integration status of wetland conservation in local plans
item.description: Applied sciences; Artificial intelligence

item.title: Entropy-driven phase regulation for efficient and stable indoor photovoltaics based on Dion-Jacobson 2D materials
item.description: This work proposes a configurational-entropy strategy to optimize the phase distribution of Dion-Jacobson 2D perovskite indoor photovoltaics. Mixing alkyldiammonium spacers (2C–6C) suppresses intermediate n-value phase nucleation and promotes vertical crystal growth, while enhanced hydrogen bonding passivates defects and blocks ion migration. The optimized device achieves a 35.06% efficiency under 1,000 lux LED, and T90 stability exceeds 1,800 h.

item.title: A critical audit and methodological roadmap for machine learning in perovskite solar cells
item.description: Muppana et al. audit 80 machine-learning studies on perovskite solar cells and find that most never check prediction error in the rare high-efficiency region that matters for commercialization. They propose an imbalance-aware evaluation workflow, a fabrication data schema, and a reporting checklist to make such models reproducible.
