item.title: Inverse magneto-ionics enhances oxygen evolution reaction
item.description: Applying magnetic fields to electrodes has been reported to enhance electrochemical reactions, leading to numerous studies and the hypothesis that externally applied magnetic fields manipulate direct spin exchange at the electrode–electrolyte interface to control reaction kinetics. However, a closer analysis suggests that this mechanism is unlikely to play a significant role, whereas the influence of magnetic gradient forces on ion migration is well established. Here, we provide experimental evidence supporting the latter mechanism for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) on nickel. Moderate magnetic fields increase the electrochemical current density by up to 20%. For pristine samples, the enhancement is both field-and time-dependent. We demonstrate that the magnetic field effect does not arise from direct spin alignment at the electrode surface or from the magnetic domain structure of the underlying ferromagnetic film. Instead, the external magnetic field indirectly enhances the electrochemical performance through magnetic gradient forces that promote the growth of the electrocatalytically active nickel oxyhydroxide surface layer by driving the exsolution of paramagnetic Ni species during the OER. With the structure of the passivation layer of Ni and its evolution being common in similar d-metal (alloy) electrode materials, the magnetic field effect by ion migration is likely to be generally valid.

item.title: PyFMO: A Python Framework for Fragment Molecular Orbital Calculations
item.description: The fragment molecular orbital (FMO) method enables quantum chemical calculations on large biomolecular systems and provides interaction energies between their fragments. Its further development and wider adoption would benefit from software in which new methods can be prototyped rapidly, every stage of a calculation can be inspected, and both developers and users can contribute to extending the method. Here we present PyFMO, a Python framework for FMO calculations that uses PySCF as its electronic-structure backend. An FMO calculation is expressed as a pipeline of interchangeable steps that share a common context, and all results are collected in a serializable container that can be analyzed independently of the calculation. PyFMO supports Hartree–Fock, density functional theory, and correlated methods at the FMO1–FMO3 levels, as well as continuum solvation and pair interaction energy decomposition analysis (PIEDA), including directional charge-transfer and three-body terms. Proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, and glycoproteins are fragmented automatically using rule-based substructure matching. For production calculations, density fitting accelerates both the fragment calculations and the evaluation of electrostatic couplings, while node-level shared memory and cost-model-based load balancing are designed for execution on platforms ranging from laptops to high-performance computing clusters. Benchmarks and an application to a theophylline-binding RNA aptamer, where PIEDA provides a detailed picture of the ligand recognition, demonstrate these capabilities. By combining the flexibility of Python with the performance required for large systems, PyFMO makes the development, testing, and application of new FMO methods for biomolecular problems accessible to a broad community.

item.title: Incorporating Polarization into ML/MM Endpoint Calculations for Protein–Ligand Affinity Ranking
item.description: Endpoint free-energy calculations combine low computational cost with reasonable accuracy and are widely used to rank protein–ligand affinities, yet describing charge polarization in these calculations remains a challenge. Here we introduce a machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) framework that incorporates polarizationcorrected mechanical embedding (PCME) and electrostatic embedding (EE) into endpoint calculations, using binding-state-and conformation-dependent ML charges in both the gas-phase energy and polar solvation terms. On a benchmark of 15 targets from the JACS and Merck sets, the PCME and EE routes of ML/MM-PBSA rank affinities better than classical MM-PBSA, raising the median Spearman ρ from 0.216 to 0.343 and 0.329, respectively, at an acceptable computational cost. A charge-source control and the analysis of a representative PTP1B complex show how conformationdependent ML charges resolve asymmetric local electrostatic environments and contribute to the improved ranking of ML/MM-PBSA(PCME) over MM-PBSA. By incorporating charge redistribution into both interaction and solvation energies, this work provides a practical ML/MM endpoint framework for protein–ligand affinity ranking and analysis of the underlying electrostatic contributions.

item.title: Revealing the role of Li content on the structural stability of textured LiCoO2 battery electrodes along fast diffusing <11x> directions
item.description: Facile ion transport in layered battery cathode systems require (11x) terminating facets. However, the facets that provide accelerated transport also amplify deleterious phase transitions and chemical reactions. The coupling between initial intercalant ion content (nominal lithium-ion stoichiometry), ionic mobility and phase transformations along the fastest diffusing facets remain understudied. Here, the coupling is elucidated using electrodeposited highly textured <11x>||(sample normal direction, ND) LiCoO2 (LCO) electrodes with controlled texture, facet presentation, and initial lithium content. Contrary to powdered systems with untextured particles, here we show that minute variations in lithium content drive distinct interphase formation at (110) terminating facets and impact ion diffusivity in cathodes possessing identical <110>IIND texture, indicating the unique importance of control of lithium content in highly oriented systems. While Lithium-poor <110>IIND LCO cathodes provide initial good ion diffusivity, they exhibit accelerated interfacially originated degradation along <110> directions via rapid rocksalt formation. Lithium-rich <110>IIND LCO electrodes exhibit elevated interfacial degradation due to the poorly conducting Li2CO3 on the surface. Lithium-balanced textured LCO electrodes suppress kinetically driven degradation pathways, even at (110) terminating facets, and provide both good ion diffusivity and structural stability. The dual control of lithium content and crystallographic orientation along the fastest diffusing directions provided by the textured electrodeposited cathodes enables deterministic design of energy-dense cathodes with good ion transport kinetics and low surface reactivity, both in thin and thick electrode formats, a combination which is difficult to achieve in untextured slurry systems presenting a range of surface facets.

item.title: Integrating Generative AI and Data Science into General Chemistry Laboratories
item.description: The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

item.title: vibe-qc: expert-directed agentic engineering for scientific software development
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can implement scientific software, but useful development also requires executable comparisons, inspectable results and a record of scientific decisions. This case study examines the tooling that enables semi-autonomous electronic-structure software development under expert direction. VIBE-QC supplies molecular and periodic calculations; vibe-scheduler queues and manages calculations across clusters and a fleet of workstations; vibe-viewer and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) connect numerical outputs to portable inspection and reproducible figures. Retained development records illustrate how these tools preserve failed attempts, distinguish changes in physical conventions from implementation errors, and separate measured differences from expert-selected acceptance criteria. Publication-specific calculations were run with VIBE-QC 0.18.x and use formaldehyde to connect controlled numerical comparisons with visual inspection; diamond and lithium hydride provide periodic Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) examples with explicit convergence checks. The expert sets the physical problem, selects diagnostic controls and interprets the evidence; AI agents implement and execute those tasks. The resulting account identifies practical requirements for sustained AI-assisted scientific development. It establishes a traceable process within one project, without claiming autonomous scientific judgment or a measured productivity advantage.

item.title: Construction of a Curated Literature Dataset and Machine Learning-Guided Exploration of Supported Metal Catalysts for Low- to Intermediate-Temperature Reverse Water–Gas Shift Reaction
item.description: Literature-derived results on reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) catalysts contain extensive information about catalyst design, yet their fragmentation makes systematic, data-driven exploration difficult. Here, we establish a framework that connects a curated RWGS literature dataset to interpretable machine-learning (ML) models and a flexible catalyst-search algorithm. We compiled 607 experimental records from 42 publications on supported metal and metal oxide catalysts evaluated at 300–450 °C, integrating catalyst compositions, preparation and reaction conditions, and CO yields. By systematically comparing nine regression algorithms and nine input representations, we obtained mean cross-validated test R2 values of 0.80, 0.73, and 0.58 for models optimized for the full, 300 °C, and 400 °C datasets, respectively. SHAP analysis identified compositional and experimental features contributing to model predictions, while leave-one-out validation exposed substantial prediction errors in some literature records. In offline sequential-search simulations repeated 100 times, ML-guided search identified high-yield literature entries more efficiently than random selection. Importantly, our newly developed Local-search algorithm jointly explored elemental combinations, loadings, support materials, and experimental conditions without exhaustive enumeration, generating candidates beyond the compositions represented in the training data. The 300 °C search favored Pt–Na/ZrO2-containing candidates, whereas Pd–Na/CeO2-containing candidates predominated at 400 °C. Although these predictions await experimental validation and some violate RWGS equilibrium constraints, this integrated framework provides a reusable data resource and a practical route from accumulated literature knowledge to testable catalyst-design hypotheses.

item.title: Surfactant-Toolkit and SurfBench-200: an open computation toolkit and a benchmark of tool-augmented language-model reasoning in surfactant science
item.description: Language models are increasingly used as research assistants in chemistry, but their quantitative work insurfactantscience hasnotbeen measured.We introduce Surfactant-Toolkit, an MIT-licensed Python library and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with 123 validated tools for micellization, mixed micelles, adsorption, emulsions, micelle structure and transport,andSurfBench-200,200graduate-levelquestionswhosereferenceanswersare computed by the toolkit and graded field by field by deterministic scripts. Without tools, five frontier models passed 52.5% to 66.0% of the questions; with the toolkit, the four models run in both conditions passed 92.0% to 98.5% (exact McNemar p < 0.0001 for each), and the open-weightDeepSeek (92.0%) outscored every modelwithouttools.Remaining failures shifted from wrong magnitudes tochoices ofmodelorconvention:toolslargely remove calculation errors, not errors of judgement. Asked the same questions again, every model changed some answers and at least once stated something the data did not support. Used for new findings, the toolkit and two augmented models produced five results on seven research problems that we could not find in the literature. Used for error finding, it showed that five recent papers each contain a value or conclusion that does not follow from their own printed data, from a reversed interaction-parameter sign to a physically impossible molecular area; two frontier models given the same values recomputed nearly all of these without tools but called an undetermined result contradicted. All questions, transcripts, graders and code are released, with SurfactantKit-Studio, a local application for researchers. 1. item.title: Formation Energy is All You Need
item.description: A Pourbaix diagram maps which species of an element (metal, ion, oxide or hydroxide) is thermodynamically stable in water as a function of potential and pH, at fixed temperature, pressure and composition. Constructing one requires the Gibbs energies of formation of the participating phases and species. Obtaining reliable values, however, remains difficult: competing phases and species can differ by only a few kilojoules per mole, while published compilations may disagree and are not always freely reusable. Density functional theory (DFT) offers an alternative, but its errors can exceed the energy differences that determine phase stability. We introduce pourbase, an open, source-linked thermodynamic database with a Python package and desktop application for constructing Pourbaix diagrams. Individual reported values, their provenance and a configurable selection policy are accessible and configurable to users even while the database expands as agent-guided literature searches collect new data. We show that replacing a single formation energy can substantially change a predicted stability region and that established thermodynamic compilations can yield conflicting oxide stability boundaries. By making thermodynamic data accessible, traceable, and revisable, pourbase enables reproducible Pourbaix diagrams built directly from experimental evidence, as well as a platform for benchmarking computed values, as we demonstrate for the Materials Project, against experimental values. Ultimately, accurate phase stability predictions need not depend on increasingly complex models, but on getting the formation energies right.

item.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
item.description: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Å; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

item.title: Air pollution sensing to urban air quality insight: review of spatially interpolated data products from sensor networks
item.description: Air pollution adversely impacts health globally, disproportionately affecting urban populations. Regulatory monitoring is often too spatially coarse to capture true intra-urban variability, needed to prioritize and guide localized interventions and policies. High-density lower-cost sensor (LCS) networks, mobile monitoring, satellite-derived products, and advanced interpolation techniques are emerging to support higher spatial resolution characterization. However, results from related studies are varied, disconnected across different fields, and as yet with no defined standards or guidance. This review examines the literature from 2005-2025 to systematically compare data collection and modeling pipelines for accuracy and application to the intra-urban challenge. 166 studies from regional to neighborhood scale were analyzed quantitatively on monitoring network characteristics (geographic location, spatial density, target pollutants, study duration) and interpolation modeling approaches (algorithms, predictive covariates, performance metrics). Studies from Europe, Asia, and North America dominated the literature, with particulate matter being the most studied pollutant. While 95% of studies had measurement density below 20,000 km2/device (metro scale), none had sufficient resolution for capturing intra-urban heterogeneity. Modeling approaches shifted over time from primarily geostatistical methods toward increasingly sophisticated machine learning and deep learning techniques incorporating diverse covariates, including meteorology, land use, traffic patterns, and satellite data products. More than measurement density or model complexity, strategic use of both static and dynamic covariates in data driven models was most consistently associated with performance improvement for interpolation of both PM2.5 and NOx. However, major gaps remain including (1) imbalance in data availability geographically, temporally, and across pollutant species, leading to major challenges in assessing and achieving transferability of models globally, (2) limited data availability at appropriate intra-urban scale for most metro areas, (3) lack of evaluation and reporting standards necessary to truly compare performance of different data-model pipelines, and (4) general lack of generating or reporting uncertainty quantification on model outputs, critically needed for interpretability and sensitivity analyses. These gaps point to an urgent need for not only interdisciplinary collaboration and innovation but also discipline-wide guidance that will enable objective assessment of model performance and state-of-the-art, including shared benchmark datasets, standardized evaluation metrics, mandatory unit reporting, and guidelines for complete model specifications.

item.title: Ensemble of ∆-ML Models for Quantum Chemistry Level of Theory Selection for Interaction Energies
item.description: Ab initio quantum chemical approaches for computing interactions between molecules are useful in a wide range of applications but can be difficult to apply effectively. In particular, variations in cost and accuracy across different levels of theory (method and basis set combinations) makes it challenging to select an appropriate level of theory for a given chemical system. In this work, we train ∆-machine learning models to predict interaction energy errors for 81 levels of theory versus a reference and simple polynomial models to quantify computational cost for a meaningful subset of these methods. We demonstrate how a large language model (LLM) can leverage these models to select appropriate levels of theory and run computations autonomously on distributed resources, significantly reducing the barrier to obtaining accurate interaction energies.

item.title: Emergence of Glass-like Thermal Transport through Anion-Engineering in Complex Silver Gallium Germanium Chalcogenides
item.description: Designing crystalline materials with ultralow thermal conductivity remains an important challenge for optimizing thermoelectric energy conversion and thermal barrier coatings. Crystalline solids exhibiting glass-like thermal transport are of special interest because they approach the minimum thermal conductivity achievable in an ordered structure. Here, we investigate the ultralow thermal conductivity of crystalline AgGaGeS8-8xSe8x and Ag2-xGa2-xGe2+xS8-8xSe8x (x = 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00). In these systems, selenium incorporation strongly suppresses crystalline thermal transport, leading to glass-like properties while preserving structural crystallinity. Across all compositions, the ultralow thermal conductivity is associated with a disordered silver substructure characterized by weak Ag–Ch interactions and pronounced anharmonicity, where selenium substitution promotes softening of the silver dynamics. Heat-capacity measurements reveal boson peaks in the endmember compounds, which for AgGaGe3Se8 is significantly more intense and shifted to lower temperature. Together, these results suggest that selenium promotes low-frequency silver vibrations that drive the emergence of glass-like thermal transport. Furthermore, selenium exhibits a pronounced preference for the chalcogen site most strongly interacting with silver, demonstrating that local anion chemistry, rather than average composition, governs the thermal transport response. This selective occupancy provides a structural basis for the emergence of glass-like thermal conductivity at remarkably low selenium contents.

item.title: Machine learning–driven inverse design of nanofiltration membranes for selective Mg2+/Na+ separation
item.description: Desalination brine, a byproduct of seawater desalination, contains valuable resources, including magnesium. Recovering magnesium requires selectively retaining Mg2+ while allowing the dominant monovalent cation, Na+, to permeate. Nanofiltration (NF) membranes fabricated by interfacial polymerization are promising for this Mg2+/Na+ separation, but their performance depends on coupled formulation and processing variables that are inefficient to optimize through trial and error. Here, we demonstrate a workflow integrating dataset curation, forward prediction, and inverse design of thin-film composite NF membranes. A dataset of 1,253 entries, comprising literature and in-house records, was cleaned, imputed, and augmented through chemically constrained permutation of interchangeable polymer, solvent, and salt variables in the training split only. Optimized extremely randomized tree regressors predicted pure water permeability, solute rejection, and intermediate membrane properties, achieving test-set coefficients of determination above 0.79. Shapley analysis indicated that permeability was governed primarily by formulation and processing variables, whereas rejection depended mainly on solute identity and charge, as well as membrane tightness. Using Bayesian optimization with a scalarized objective, two membrane recipes with favorable Mg2+/Na+ selectivity were identified and experimentally validated. The inversely designed membranes exhibited the required Mg2+/Na+ selectivity, demonstrating the capability of this workflow to design Mg2+-selective NF membranes for resource recovery from desalination brine.

item.title: SKFitter: Symmetry resolved Slater Koster tight-binding models from first principles for s, p, d and f electrons, spin orbit coupling and magnetism
item.description: arXiv:2610.40729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constructing accurate and physically interpretable tight binding (TB) Hamiltonians from first principles calculations remains challenging, particularly for materials exhibiting complex orbital hybridization, spin orbit coupling (SOC), and magnetic order. SKFitter is an open-source Python framework for constructing and optimizing symmetry resolved Slater Koster TB models directly from density functional theory (DFT) calculations performed using Quantum ESPRESSO or VASP. The framework supports s to f orbitals, incorporates on site SOC and site resolved magnetic exchange interactions, and accommodates both orthogonal and nonorthogonal basis. A central feature is the symmetry resolved parameterization of orbital manifolds, which allows independent two centre hopping integrals between symmetry allowed orbital groups and across distinct neighbour shells. SKFitter also identifies missing orbital contributions and guide systematic basis set refinement and optimizes parameters through weights. The resulting Hamiltonian can be used to evaluate anomalous (AHC) and spin Hall conductivities (SHC), and topological invariants. We demonstrate the framework using eight representative materials spanning semimetals, semiconductors, transition metals, f-electron compounds, and magnetic systems. Symmetry resolved models achieve band energy errors of 9 to 41 meV within 1 eV of the Fermi level. The fitted Hamiltonians reproduce characteristic features of the SHC response of Pt, the SOC dependence of the AHC of Fe, and the momentum dependent altermagnetic spin splitting of MnTe without any altermagnet specific interaction. For EuMn2Bi2, projection guided orbital refinement reduces the near Fermi level fitting error from 120 to 32 meV. Together, these results establish SKFitter as a flexible and reproducible framework for developing symmetry consistent, physically interpretable TB models of complex materials.

item.title: Moir\'e metals and continuum models beyond a single valley
item.description: arXiv:2610.40761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive continuum models of moir\'e materials valid over the full monolayer Brillouin zone, as required for metals whose large Fermi surfaces are not confined to a single valley. To this end, we introduce an environment-resolved two-center approximation, in which each hopping amplitude depends not only on the distance between the orbitals it connects but also on its position within the moir\'e cell. Taking the local environment to be set by the disregistry of the two layers alone, these moir\'e couplings and their full set of harmonics can be learnt from commensurate bilayers at uniform stackings, without fitting. The method shows excellent agreement with ab initio band structures on moir\'e cells containing a few hundred atoms. Applied to twisted NbSe$_2$, it yields a continuum model in which moir\'e effects concentrate at the van Hove singularities, a single-particle starting point for studying moir\'e-tuned superconducting, charge-density-wave instabilities and their competition.

item.title: Faster-than-power-law decay of order parameter correlations in the two-dimensional RP$^2$ model: a rigorous result by vibe-proving
item.description: arXiv:2610.41256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the RP$^2$ model on the two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions. It is obtained by replacing the spin in the standard classical Heisenberg model with a director, which does not distinguish two opposite directions. Unlike the standard classical Heisenberg model or the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, the RP$^2$ (and its cousin RP$^3$) model allows point vortex defects classified by $\pi_1(RP^2)= Z_2$ in two dimensions. It is tempting to expect the $Z_2$ vortices to induce a phase transition analogous to the well-established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the O(2) model (XY model) in two dimensions. Indeed, the possibilities of a critical phase or a critical point with power-law correlations of the order parameter in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models have been discussed in the literature. However, the challenging nature of the problem has prevented a definitive conclusion on the phase diagram so far. In this paper, we report a rigorous mathematical proof by Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT 6 Astra) that the absolute value of the two-point correlation function of order parameters at distance $r$ in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models on the two-dimensional square lattice is bounded above by $C_\beta \exp{(-c_\beta[\log(2+r)]^2)}$ for any finite inverse temperature $\beta\ge0$, with positive constants $C_\beta$ and $c_\beta$ depending only on $\beta$. Namely, the correlation function decays faster than any power of $r$. The proof is formalized and verified in Lean; the formalization is publicly available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23548847 . A heuristic argument based on a one-parameter effective theory ansatz at large distances combined with the rigorous correlation bound suggests (but does not prove) that the $Z_2$ vortices are always unbound at any nonzero temperature.

item.title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
item.description: arXiv:2610.41599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

item.title: Evaluating Instrument-Centered AI Agents for Table-Top Science Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.41717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable evaluation of AI agents for table-top science experiments has remained elusive because live instruments are hard to reset and share at scale, while instrument statefulness and safety constraints complicate evaluation. We introduce instrMCP and q-devBench, an evaluation stack for instrument-centered AI agents in table-top experiments. instrMCP connects coding agents to scientific instruments through the Model Context Protocol, serving as the instrument-access harness. q-devBench reconstructs 37 real experimental tasks from condensed-matter physics as virtual QCoDeS instruments covering quantum electronic transport, scanning probe imaging, and calibration workflows. q-devBench exposes reproducible failure modes in laboratory-agent systems while preserving realistic instrument-control workflows. Across a range of commercial coding-agent configurations, current systems already show substantial operational competence, satisfying 70-83% of measurement-related rubric criteria. The main bottleneck is scientific analysis, where performance falls to 28-46%. In an analysis-only ablation in which agents receive clean reference datasets without running the virtual measurement session, analysis performance improves substantially, closing roughly two thirds of the difference between the measurement and analysis scores. This suggests that much of the deficit arises from the measurement-session context, including tool-use overhead, longer context, measurement-planning decisions, and possible acquisition errors, while a residual scientific-reasoning gap remains. Together, instrMCP and q-devBench provide a practical sandbox for benchmarking, diagnosing, and improving laboratory AI harnesses, and establish a route from controlled virtual evaluation to future live-hardware validation.

item.title: Magnetic control of reflectionless states and an intrinsic-mode exceptional point in a magnon-phonon coupling system
item.description: arXiv:2610.41851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reflectionless states (RLs) and exceptional points (EPs) are hallmark singular responses of non-Hermitian systems, with potential applications in sensing, wave control, and energy manipulation. Yet, realizing and independently tuning these states in a compact integrated platform remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate two-dimensional magnetic control of RLs and EPs in an on-chip magnon-phonon system based on a FeGaB-32 degree-YX-LiNbO3 heterostructure. The magnetic-field magnitude tunes the magnon-phonon detuning, driving a low-loss reflection zero across the real-frequency axis and producing two field-tunable RLs with near-vanishing reflection. A closed contour of the experimentally measured complex S11 around the reflection-zero singularity accumulates a -2pi phase winding. Independently, rotating the magnetic field tunes the magnon-phonon coupling strength, driving the intrinsic magnon-phonon eigenmode spectrum across an exceptional point, identified by the exchange between real-part and imaginary-part eigenvalue splitting. A unified one-port input-output model connects the measured complex S11 response to the field-driven dynamics of the reflection zeros and the angle-tuned intrinsic magnon-phonon eigenmodes. These results establish a magnetically programmable non-Hermitian magnon-phonon platform for integrated wave control and compact vector magnetic sensing.

item.title: Existence of the thermodynamic limit for the Hopfield model
item.description: arXiv:2610.41938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the quenched pressure of the Hopfield model with $K\sim\alpha N$ i.i.d. symmetric Rademacher patterns has a thermodynamic limit at every load $\alpha\in(0,\infty)$, finite inverse temperature and uniform external field, with no replica-symmetry, order-parameter concentration or non-condensation hypothesis required. The limit is the supremum over $r$ of limiting pressures of mixed models with $r$ binary patterns in a Gaussian bulk. Via the Hubbard--Stratonovich representation we extract the finitely many patterns whose hidden coordinates exceed $\delta\sqrt N$; a collective interpolation replaces the other binary patterns by Gaussian ones with error $O(\delta^2)$ uniform in the volume, and convex concentration on the discrete cube controls the disorder-dependent choice of retained patterns. For the mixed models we prove a Gaussian hidden-spin truncation bound uniform in the volume and in an arbitrary Ising potential, and convergence for Gaussian bulks with finitely many site-field types, reducing to results of Ho and of Chen, Ho and Issa on non-convex vector spin glasses with compact spins. For Gaussian patterns we give an alternative proof of the existence result announced by Camilli, Contucci and Mingione, extended to a uniform field and an extra binary pattern. In both cases the pressure has exponentially small deviation probabilities and converges a.s.; internal energy and entropy converge wherever the limit is differentiable. An extra binary Mattis pattern admits a scalar variational reduction. At zero field the Rademacher pressure dominates the Gaussian one with an extra binary pattern, which dominates the pure Gaussian one. No explicit formula is given. The proofs were generated through extensive interaction with the AI models Claude (Opus~5.5) and ChatGPT (Sol~6.1), based on the problem formulation and guidance of the authors.

item.title: Proof-Carrying Materials: Falsifiable Safety Certificates for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2603.12183v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are deployed for high-throughput materials screening without formal reliability guarantees. We show that a single MLIP used as a stability filter misses 93% of density functional theory (DFT)-stable materials (recall 0.07) on a 25,000-material benchmark. Proof-Carrying Materials (PCM) closes this gap through three stages: adversarial falsification across compositional space, bootstrap envelope refinement with 95% confidence intervals, and Lean 4 formal certification. Auditing CHGNet, TensorNet and MACE reveals architecture-specific blind spots with near-zero pairwise error correlations (r <= 0.13; n = 5,000), confirmed by independent Quantum ESPRESSO validation (20/20 converged; median DFT/CHGNet force ratio 12x). A risk model trained on PCM-discovered features predicts failures on unseen materials (AUC-ROC = 0.938 +/- 0.004) and transfers across architectures (cross-MLIP AUC-ROC ~ 0.70; feature importance r = 0.877). In a thermoelectric screening case study, PCM-audited protocols discover 62 additional stable materials missed by single-MLIP screening - a 25% improvement in discovery yield.

item.title: PASS: Perturbation augmented space group structure sampling for transferable Fe-O machine learning interatomic potential
item.description: arXiv:2607.28000v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Iron (Fe) oxidation is a fundamental phenomenon that is scientifically vital and technologically significant. Despite substantial experimental efforts, accurate atomistic modelling of Fe oxidation remains elusive, which requires a reliable interatomic potential, whose development hinges on a representative first-principles training dataset. However, Fe-oxygen (O) system is known for its structural complexity, rendering the generation of high-quality first-principles dataset challenging. In this work, we propose the Perturbation Augmented Space group structure Sampling (PASS) method to generate extensive dataset for Fe-O system consisting of small-cell structures (no more than 10 atoms). Based on atomic cluster expansion (ACE) framework, we present a systematic approach to developing a transferable machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The accuracy and capability of the ACE potential are thoroughly validated across pure Fe and Fe-O systems through bulk, surface, and interface properties. The large-scale Fe oxidation simulations with the ACE potential capture key features of the oxidation process, including the formation of an FeO-like structure consistent with recent experimental observations. This work demonstrates that the PASS method yields an accurate and transferable MLIP that can capture the reactive complexity of oxide growth while remaining computationally practical for extended systems.

item.title: Emergent Skyrmion Hall Effect in $d$-wave Altermagnets at Finite Temperature
item.description: arXiv:2608.27107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Altermagnets combine compensated magnetic order with unconventional symmetry-dependent responses, offering a promising platform for spintronic applications. Here, we show that a voltage-controlled magnetic-anisotropy gradient drives altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions in a nearly rectilinear, Hall-free manner in the absence of thermal fluctuations, owing to their strongly compensated gyrotropic response. Thermal magnons qualitatively modify this behavior by increasing the longitudinal drag through magnon--skyrmion scattering and generating a transverse reaction force through handedness-dependent skew scattering. Owing to the anisotropic altermagnetic magnon band structure, the relative transport weights of the two magnon handednesses are interchanged between propagation along the $x$ and $y$ directions, resulting in transverse skyrmion drifts of opposite sign. By contrast, along the high-symmetry direction, the two magnon handednesses remain degenerate and their transverse contributions cancel, preserving Hall-free motion even at finite temperature. We thus uncover a thermally emergent anisotropic skyrmion Hall effect whose direction-dependent magnitude and sign originate from the intrinsic symmetry-dependent magnon spectrum, making it a generic finite-temperature dynamical feature of ATM skyrmions. Our results establish a low-power route toward electrically controlled and thermally tunable ATM skyrmion transport.

item.title: Resolving the structural stability of the hydrogen storage borohydride NaCa(BH4)3 via data-driven screening and first-principles lattice dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.02001v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Equimolar NaCa(BH$_4$)$_3$ offers a theoretical hydrogen capacity of 11.24 wt.% and a decomposition enthalpy expected to fall between those of NaBH$_4$ and Ca(BH$_4$)$_2$, but it has never been prepared and no crystal structure has been reported. Predictions for it have so far been built within the perovskite family that its heavier homologues adopt. Here that assumption is removed. Six candidate frameworks were assembled from three independent sources --- experimentally determined ABX$_3$ borohydrides, a distorted perovskite from data-driven structure prediction, and an unbiased search over a structural database in which all 2238 generated candidates were relaxed with none excluded --- and at fixed charge-neutral composition the cation arrangement of every framework was enumerated exhaustively, 420 decorations reducing to 118 symmetry-inequivalent configurations, screened with a machine-learning potential and settled from first principles. The most stable structure is not a perovskite. It is a monoclinic framework of space group Cm, reached only by the unrestricted search, at $-$4.185640 eV/atom, 7.67 meV/atom below the best framework available beforehand; two chemically unrelated donor prototypes converge on it to 0.076 meV/atom, and its ordered cation arrangement is the ground state of its own series. Its phonon spectrum carries no imaginary mode at any wavevector the supercell resolves exactly and its relaxed-ion elastic tensor is positive definite, whereas the orthorhombic perovskite candidate is unstable to $-$2.401 THz. That contrast supplies a physical reason for the reported failure to obtain this composition in perovskite form, and the simulated diffraction pattern reported here identifies the predicted framework by seven reflections that neither parent phase nor the competing framework produces.

item.title: Reusable Operators for Irreducible Cartesian Tensor Decomposition and Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2609.05971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Molecular and material properties, from the polarizability to the elastic constants, are described by tensors. Their behavior under rotations is made explicit when a tensor is decomposed into irreducible parts that transform independently. In Cartesian form these parts are the symmetric and traceless irreducible Cartesian tensors (ICTs), whose decomposition and coupling underlie selection rules, orientational averages, and the use of symmetry. The decomposition is a textbook result at rank two, but higher rank and the intrinsic symmetry of physical tensors make it nontrivial. What has been lacking, unlike in the well-established spherical formalism, is a general construction for a given intrinsic symmetry, together with reusable operators that extract the ICTs and rebuild the original tensor exactly. Here, we develop such a construction and obtain these operators explicitly. These operators depend on rank and symmetry alone, and therefore each need only be built once and then applied to any tensor of that class. Building on them, we further obtain the Cartesian harmonics of a vector and the operators that couple two ICTs into a third, both central to equivariant machine learning. The construction is demonstrated on the elastic tensor, in both its second-order form of rank four and its third-order form of rank six. The ICTs of the rank-4 tensor also define a rotation- and scale-invariant measure of anisotropy, which we evaluate across the first-principles elastic tensors of crystalline materials from the Materials Project. The construction is implemented in the open-source package natto, which produces the operators in both exact symbolic and numerical form.

item.title: An explainable machine-learning framework for seasonal early warning of West Nile virus using predictive climate data

item.title: Rethinking lithium content in inorganic solid-state electrolytes
item.description: Inorganic solid-state electrolytes are being developed for safer, energy-dense batteries, yet many contain nearly an order of magnitude more lithium than liquid electrolytes. This perspective proposes low-lithium-content electrolyte design and introduces a lithium-transport realization index connecting local ion motion with long-range conductivity. Evidence across existing materials shows that reduced lithium content does not necessarily sacrifice performance. The resulting design roadmap aims to preserve conductivity with less lithium, potentially easing resource, cost, and environmental burdens.

item.title: A systematic framework for constructing reactive machine learning interatomic potentials
item.description: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as an essential tool for extending the reach of atomistic simulations, offering near quantum level accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. However, constructing reactive and transferable MLIPs that describe rare events, transition states, and high energy intermediates remains a significant challenge. While the active learning (AL) protocol has proven effective for iterative MLIP refinement, its integration with enhanced sampling techniques has typically been implemented in an ad hoc and problem specific manner, which limits its reproducibility and generalizability. Here, we present a systematic methodology for automated construction of reactive MLIPs using SPARC, an open-source workflow package that integrates AL with enhanced sampling through the PLUMED library. SPARC combines (i) query-by-committee uncertainty estimations to identify configurations where the ensemble of ML models disagrees, with (ii) enhanced sampling methods to access reactive regions of the potential energy surface that are otherwise inaccessible in unbiased molecular dynamics. We demonstrate the robustness of the workflow across three chemically distinct reactive systems, showing that stable and accurate reactive MLIPs can be constructed from minimal initial training data. In all cases, the workflow discovers high-energy configurations, including transition states.

item.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
item.description: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

item.title: BigFingerprint: A Topology-aware Extended-connectivity Fingerprint for Polymers
item.description: Machine learning-driven polymer design and property prediction require molecular representations that encode not only local chemistry but also the statistically distributed monomer sequences and connectivity patterns and global topology that distinguish polymers from small molecules. Existing fingerprinting workflows often fail to capture global polymer architecture, as well as connectivity across repeat units, end groups, and linking groups. This work develops BigFingerprint, a topology-aware extended-connectivity fingerprint for polymers represented by BigSMILES. BigFingerprint consists of two components, a polymer extended-connectivity fingerprint, p-ECFP, that encodes atom-centered substructures within and across stochastic molecular fragments, and a polymer topology fingerprint, p-TFP, that encodes global architectural features such as block, statistical, graft, star, branched, and network topologies. Through representative structural examples and polymer property prediction tasks, BigFingerprint retains the chemical interpretability of circular fingerprints while extending their applicability to complex polymer architectures. As a critical component of the BigSMILES-centered ecosystem, BigFingerprint integrates local substructural information with global topological descriptors to provide a general and chemically interpretable representation for substructure analysis, similarity

item.title: Bio-derived ionic conductive Guar Gum hydrogels as distributed circuit elements for analogue signal processing: the case of Resistor-Capacitor filters
item.description: Developing functional electronic materials from renewable resources is a key challenge toward more sustainable electronics. Here, we report on a bio-derived ionic conductive hydrogel based on guar gum and demonstrate its direct integration as a functional circuit element for analogue signal processing. Ionic conductivity is introduced by incorporating sodium chloride into the polysaccharide matrix and systematically tuned through the glycerol and salt contents. Increasing glycerol loading enhances conductivity, while varying NaCl concentration produces a non-monotonic response, with maximum conductivities in the 10-2 S cm-1 range and an optimum salt-loading window. The conductive formulation is subsequently combined with pristine guar gum, used as a dielectric, to fabricate guar gum-based resistor-capacitor elements. Their integration into low-pass and high-pass filters demonstrates frequency-selective operation in the audio range, with cut-off frequencies of 658 and 576 Hz and transition slopes of −17 and +15 dB dec-1, respectively. These results demonstrate that guar gumbased ionic hydrogels can move beyond conventional roles as substrates or electrolytes and directly perform circuit-level functions, providing a simple materials platform for low-frequency analogue electronics.

item.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.
