item.title: Meta-Altermagnetism and Enhanced Spin-Splitting
item.description: arXiv:2610.37754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Altermagnets are collinear magnets with zero net magnetization and spin-split electronic bands. Here, we explore whether altermagnetism can exhibit a discontinuous jump, a phenomenon we refer to as meta-altermagnetism. We show that meta-altermagnetism can emerge in 2D systems when magnetic-order-induced band reconstruction drives spin-split van Hove singularities (vHSs) across the Fermi level. Using mean-field theory for an extended $t$-$J$ model on a two-sublattice square lattice including anisotropic hopping integral, we find that a first-order meta-altermagnetic transition produces an intermediate altermagnetic regime with reduced staggered magnetization but strongly enhanced magnetic octupole and time-reversal-odd spin-splitter conductivity. We further show that the first-order transition line terminates at a quantum critical endpoint, giving rise to a rich phase diagram as the chemical potential and anisotropic hopping strength are varied. Our results identify the spin split vHSs as a route to enhancing spin-splitter effect for spintronic applications.

item.title: Planar energetics do not determine twin persistence in nanocrystalline aluminium
item.description: arXiv:2610.37925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planar energetics are the standard descriptors of twinnability in face-centred cubic metals and the usual validation targets for interatomic potentials. Here we show that they do not determine whether deformation twins persist in nanocrystalline aluminium. Two machine-learned potentials reproducing the same zero-load slip curves and closely spaced layered energy surfaces predict, from a common separated-fault precursor under identical loading, retained twin coverage of 64\% and 14\%. The divergence traces to forces within distorted partial cores acting along the trailing translation that would remove an outer fault. Planar energetics do set the margin: an outer fault more than halves the incremental barrier for middle-plane shear, yet twin completion and fault removal remain separated by only 10--21 mJ m\textsuperscript{-2}. Whether an assembled twin persists is decided instead by the orientation of local traction relative to the full-slip bisector and by the arrival order of partial-slip fronts from the grain-boundary network.

item.title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.38195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale crystal databases have transformed materials discovery by making millions of structures and thermodynamic properties accessible to materials informatics. Yet dynamical stability remains sparsely characterized at a comparable scale because its evaluation is substantially more computationally demanding than conventional structure and energy calculations. This mismatch creates a critical gap between the rapidly expanding crystal-structure space and the physical information available for materials research and machine learning. Here we introduce Crystoria, a large-scale crystal dataset designed to bring dynamical stability to the scale of modern materials data. We construct Crystoria by systematically curating low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals, standardizing their structural identities, and combining machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation with phonon-based dynamical screening. The resulting dataset contains 2,649,640 crystal structures, spanning 89 elements, 219 of the 230 space groups, and primitive cells containing 1-48 atoms. Among them, 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable, revealing substantial variation in dynamical stability across chemical and crystallographic space. By bringing dynamical stability to the scale of millions of crystal structures, Crystoria provides a physically grounded foundation for materials artificial intelligence (AI) and enables systematic exploration of the dynamical crystal landscape.

item.title: Strain-Induced BCC-to-FCC Transformation in Tungsten Uncovered by Molecular Dynamics Simulations with Machine Learning Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.38477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polymorphic transformations occur in a minority of metals. Tungsten is not one of them. This observation does not rule out its intrinsic phase transition possibility, but may be due to inaccessible thermodynamic and mechanical conditions in conventional experiments. Herein, we investigate the body centered cubic (BCC) to face centered cubic (FCC) transformation in tungsten via a rigorously validated machine learning potential (MLP) molecular dynamics (MD) approach. Our simulations demonstrate that strain induced BCC to FCC transformation indeed occurs in tungsten. The FCC phase exceeds 20 at.% at low temperature and in the presence of dislocations. In the perfect crystal moderate temperatures favor phase transformation kinetics. Structural analysis confirms the transformation following the Bain and Nishiyama Wassermann orientation relationship. These results establish the viability of strain induced polymorphic transformation in tungsten and provide a critical guideline for the experimental production of duplex tungsten with enhanced ductility addressing a longstanding challenge in tungsten material engineering for high-temperature structural applications.

item.title: Learning Between the Lines: Interaction Interpolation in a Multi Element Machine Learning Interatomic Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.38876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The continuous development of machine learning inter-atomic potentials (MLIAPs)has greatly accelerated materials research in recent years. However, the need to con- struct custom MLIAPs for each unique problem remains a bottleneck which raises the question of the transferability of MLIAPs. While foundation MLIAPs can achieve transferability due to the broad coverage of chemical space represented in their training sets, their size and computational cost limits their routine use. We address this gap by developing a lightweight general-purpose MLIAP for metal alloys spanning twelve elements (Al, Sc, Ti, V, Cu, Zn, Zr, Nb, Mo, Hf, Ta, W). Here, we utilize a step-wise active learning (AL) approach to develop a compact yet diverse dataset and model that generalizes well by interpolating from previously seen interactions. The resulting potentials transfer effectively to unseen, higher body-order alloys systems, requiring only unary and binary training data to capture ternary and quaternary systems. The model also transfers well to new elements via an alchemical extrapolation within the network, requiring only unary data for the new element and its alloys. These findings suggest that MLIAPs trained on targeted, diversity-driven datasets provide transferability at a relatively low computational cost, offering a practical path toward general-purpose, resource-efficient MLIAPs for materials modeling.

item.title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load
item.description: arXiv:2610.38937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Friction and wear of diamond are controlled by its surface chemistry, which determines whether covalent bonds form across the sliding interface. First-principles simulations have explored the role of surface orientation and passivation, but are limited to a few hundred atoms and tens of picoseconds. To bridge this gap, we develop a reactive machine learning interatomic potential for the C/H/N/O/Si chemical space, covering diamond, silicon nitride, silicon oxide, their surfaces, interfaces, and environmental molecules. The potential is trained on a large dataset of diverse structures and is tested on multiple physical properties, including ab initio reaction barriers on diamond surfaces, and structural/mechanical properties of amorphous Si$_3$N$_4$ and SiO$_2$. We then simulate sliding of diamond-Si$_3$N$_4$ interfaces with four surface orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated terminations, and normal loads from 0.1 to 23 GPa. We identify two different regimes: one where sliding is localized at the interface, and shear stress is proportional to the interfacial bond density, and another where shear is distributed inside the softer material, and adhesion due to full interfacial bonding dominates. These results show how passivation, surface orientation and load together determine interfacial bonding and friction, with implications for the environmental sensitivity of diamond wear. More broadly, the potential enables reactive simulations of diamond, silicon nitride and silica with near-ab initio accuracy at length and time scales beyond first-principles methods, providing a useful tool for future studies of wear at plowing asperities, chemical-mechanical polishing, and properties of amorphous ceramic films.

item.title: Lone-Pair Stereoactivity Overrides Mass Scaling of Thermal Expansion and Heat Conduction in Non-vander Waals Layered Bismuth Oxychalcogenides
item.description: arXiv:2610.39213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heavier chalcogens are generally expected to soften isostructural semiconductor lattices, raising thermal expansion and lowering thermal conductivity. Layered bismuth oxychalcogenides, Bi2O2X (X = S, Se, Te), are mixed-anion crystals whose covalent slabs and ionic sheets are bound electrostatically rather than by van der Waals forces and whose Bi3+ 6s^2 lone pairs can become stereochemically active. Despite the rapid development of Bi2O2Se for fin and gate-all-around transistors, its fundamental thermal expansion and heat transport mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that lone-pair stereoactivity, not chalcogen mass, governs both properties. Path-integral molecular dynamics shows that the volumetric thermal expansion coefficient at 300 K decreases from 8.14 x 10^-5 K^-1 in Bi2O2S to 6.72 x 10^-5 and 6.61 x 10^-5 K^-1 in Bi2O2Se and Bi2O2Te, respectively, despite a 13% larger unit cell in the telluride, whereas substituting the S mass into Bi2O2Se changes its value by only 0.6%. Lone-pair-driven Bi off-centering in orthorhombic Bi2O2S makes b-axis expansion 1.63 times a-axis expansion yet leaves in-plane thermal conduction isotropic within 3%. Phonon transport calculations including four-phonon scattering and Wigner coherence predict a thermal conductivity maximum in Bi2O2Se (1.83 and 0.95 W m^-1 K^-1 in the in-plane and cross-plane directions, respectively, at 300 K) because Bi2O2S is limited by anharmonic scattering and Bi2O2Te by slow cross-plane phonons. Thermoreflectance measurements from 300 to 500 K and in situ X-ray diffraction on Bi2O2Se single crystals agree with these predictions within 6.4%. Phonon Boltzmann transport simulations of 12-nm-wide fins, which run hotter than Fourier diffusion predicts, show that Bi2O2Se minimizes the hotspot temperature and the thermal-mismatch strain at the gate dielectric.

item.title: Hidden Phase Transition in Single-Polymer Stretching under Elongational Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.39575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using machine learning, we identify a second transition in polymer chain stretching driven by planar elongational flow, beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition. We achieve this by developing a conditional extension of Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics (UIDD) that jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As the flow strength increases, the evolving landscape exhibits the expected coil-stretch transition, and then a previously unrecognized dynamical transition. In the latter, the stretched states persist, but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. Large-deviation analysis of a simplified analytical chain model reproduces both transitions and shows that they are phase transitions in the long-chain limit. Single-molecule DNA experiments provide qualitative support for the dynamical transition through the predicted reversal of the folding response.

item.title: Light-Cone Friedel Oscillations: a Window into van Hove Superconductivity
item.description: arXiv:2610.40648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Van Hove (vH) singularities can enhance superconductivity by generating a large pairing susceptibility. Yet, it remains challenging to experimentally establish whether pairing really occurs near these points. We show that the saddle-point dispersion near a vH point gives rise to a `light-cone' vH-selective behavior of Friedel oscillations, which is drastically different from the familiar concentric circles. Each vH point maps onto its own real-space light-cone sector, allowing STM around a single impurity to measure whether---and how strongly---that saddle-point quasiparticle sector is gapped. A superconducting gap near vH points suppresses the oscillations in the directions corresponding to peaks in the gap function angular dependence, a behavior that provides a signature of vH-related pairing at STM-accessible length scales. This STM protocol, targeting vH superconductivity, is capable of determining whether superconducting pairing emerges near the vH points or elsewhere on the Fermi surface.

item.title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
item.description: arXiv:2610.39513v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

item.title: Computing with Coupled Oscillator Networks: Optimization, Memory, and Modern AI Primitives
item.description: arXiv:2610.39703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.

item.title: Going deep, reaching further: What can Boltzmann machines efficiently represent?
item.description: arXiv:2610.39731v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While universal approximation theorems theoretically underpin the representation capabilities of machine learning models, they have two shortcomings: They do not focus on efficient representations and they tend to be insensitive to depth and other heuristically important properties. In this work we show that these two shortcomings are intertwined. We prove that machine learning models which are deeper or have higher-order interactions can efficiently represent a larger set of functions, i.e. have larger efficient reach. It follows that deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) sub-maximal, and k-body generalizations of RBMs form a hierarchy between the two, even though all are universal. More generally, (i) we provide a full characterization of machine learning models with maximal efficient reach; (ii) we derive separations between deep and shallow models for three representation tasks; and (iii) we prove that the efficient reach of shallow models constitutes an infinite hierarchy indexed by the interaction order. The proofs draw on different methodologies, namely on (i) a recent characterization of universal spin models; (ii) computational complexity bounds for spin models; and (iii) communication complexity bounds applied to shallow models. This work shows that universal machine learning models can strongly differ in their efficient representation capabilities, and provides a theoretical foundation for heuristic observations.

item.title: Does System Size Matter in Uncertainty Quantification for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials?
item.description: arXiv:2610.40126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) commonly use uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations and select structures for active learning. A key question is whether the resulting structure-level uncertainty scores remain comparable across different system sizes. A common practice is to aggregate per-atom uncertainties by their mean or maximum and compare the resulting score against a fixed threshold, implicitly assuming such comparability. We test this assumption across several in-distribution (ID)/OOD pairs by characterizing both aggregations as a function of atom count. The two aggregations exhibit distinct size dependencies. Mean aggregation remains size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells. In contrast, maximum aggregation grows with system size for ID systems while remaining approximately flat for defect-containing systems, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in a manner consistent with extreme-value statistics. Although highly uncertain atoms in large structures may indicate novel local environments, retraining on these structures yields little improvement, in contrast to retraining on OOD structures constructed to lie outside the training distribution. Our results reveal a practical limitation of size-unaware uncertainty criteria and motivate size-aware calibration for more reliable OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.

item.title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.40443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Theoretical predictions of novel materials rely on a variety of techniques, from data-mining-based ion substitution methods to fully de novo generative models. Each approach imposes specific constraints and encounters unique challenges when extrapolating beyond the distribution of known materials to discover new ones. The foremost goal of materials generation is to produce stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) structures. Predicted structures that meet these criteria, however, typically result from novel chemical compositions mapped onto known structural prototypes or frameworks. We leverage this heuristic insight to present a new generative paradigm for the de novo prediction of inorganic crystalline materials constrained by their structural framework---i.e., the unit cell shapes and respective particle positions. Our method, termed OMatG-FC (Open Materials Framework-Conditional Generation), learns via a combination of discrete flow matching on the atomic species and stochastic interpolants for the volume scaling of the unit cell lattice, while fixing in-place the fractional coordinates and the unit-volume lattice vectors, dramatically reducing the dimensionality of the problem compared to unconstrained (framework-free) generation. Our method is more flexible than existing prototype-constrained methods, demonstrating capability for discovery of unseen, stable prototypes derived from known structural frameworks. We also investigate the number of unique frameworks in the MP-20 dataset, demonstrating the propensity of duplicate frameworks within the dataset and providing a framework-split version. We benchmark the performance of our model using the LeMat-GenBench suite using three ML interatomic potentials and achieve state-of-the-art S.U.N. rate below the convex hull, eschewing the need to learn atomic packings for materials discovery.

item.title: ML-COHP: predicting bond descriptors using latent space of a universal interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.40445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) is the standard measure of bond strength in a DFT calculation, but every structure needs its own DFT single point and LOBSTER projection, which takes days for a cell of a hundred atoms, such as a grain boundary or a catalytic nanoparticle. We predict ICOHP from the frozen descriptors of a MACE foundation model. A symmetric pair head reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the element embeddings of the same model. We tested the model on the high-entropy diboride (Hf,Zr,Ti,Nb,Ta)B$_2$, Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed O$_2$. The error on bonds stronger than 0.5 eV is 1.6-4.1%, about half that of the Gaussian-process model of Ferreira et al. trained on the same data. Trained only on high-temperature HEB$_2$ snapshots, the model reproduces the LOBSTER ICOHP of relaxed grain boundary cells to 0.06 eV in about a second, against 5-51 hours of LOBSTER. The vector channels halve the error compared to the scalar ones, and the baseline keeps the model usable with two training structures. With geometries from a fine-tuned MACE potential, the model gives the bonding of Pt/Pd particles over a continuous O$_2$ coverage, and DFT on these particles shows that O$_2$ costs a Pt-rich shell several times more metal--metal bonding than a Pd shell.

item.title: On Zeros and Algorithms for Disordered Systems II: The Antiferromagnetic Ising Model up to Kesten-Stigum
item.description: arXiv:2610.40598v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give the first polynomial-time algorithm to estimate the partition function of the antiferromagnetic Ising model on the uniformly random $d$-regular graph to arbitrarily high accuracy for all inverse temperatures up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold. This is the entire regime in which the model is "replica symmetric," and is conjectured to be optimal for polynomial-time counting and sampling. To achieve our algorithmic result, we establish the absence of Fisher zeros for the partition function in a constant-width strip around the interval from $0$ up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold, with high probability over the randomness of the input graph. AI Disclosure: The overarching vision and proof architecture were developed solely by the authors without AI input. GPT 5.5 Pro was used, with extensive guidance from the authors, for only a few minor technical aspects of the proof. The authors independently verified correctness and wrote everything by hand. We take full responsibility for its contents. A more detailed statement can be found in Section 1.2.

item.title: LightPFP: A Lightweight Route to Ab Initio Accuracy at Scale
item.description: arXiv:2510.23064v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) bridge the gap between quantum-mechanical accuracy and scalable molecular simulations. However, a fundamental trade-off persists: universal MLIPs (u-MLIPs) offer broad transferability but are computationally expensive, whereas task-specific MLIPs (ts-MLIPs) achieve high efficiency at the expense of costly DFT training data. Here we introduce LightPFP, a data-efficient knowledge distillation framework. Instead of relying on expensive DFT calculations, LightPFP constructs a distilled ts-MLIP by using a u-MLIP to generate high-quality, material-specific training data, while employing a pre-trained lightweight model to further improve data efficiency. Across diverse material systems, LightPFP reduces model development time by approximately three orders of magnitude compared with DFT-based workflows, while maintaining DFT-level accuracy. Combined with a LAMMPS/Kokkos inference backend, LightPFP achieves more than three orders of magnitude higher inference efficiency than u-MLIP baselines while enabling simulations of systems thousands of times larger. When the teacher exhibits systematic bias, LightPFP supports few-shot precision correction using as few as 10 high-accuracy DFT configurations, as demonstrated by reproducing MgO's experimental melting point. This u-MLIP-driven distillation establishes a scalable route to high-fidelity, data-efficient MLIPs, accelerating the pace of materials discovery and design.

item.title: Meta-generalized gradient approximation made in the Hartree gauge
item.description: arXiv:2603.11517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In density functional theory (DFT), exact constraints, fundamental mathematical properties of the exchange-correlation (XC) energy and its underlying XC hole, along with paradigm systems such as the uniform electron gas and the hydrogen atom have been instrumental in developing exchange- correlation (XC) density functional approximations (DFAs). However, since the spatial XC energy density is not uniquely defined, its exact constraints can only be formulated within a chosen gauge and are therefore seldom utilized in DFA construction. Here, we propose a meta-generalized gradient approximation for the exchange energy, explicitly constructed within the Hartree gauge, using the hydrogen atom's exchange energy density for gauge alignment in core and asymptotic regions. By formulating DFAs at the XC energy density level, this approach expands reference datasets for machine learning and establishes a foundation for more accurate nonlocal density functionals requiring gauge alignment.

item.title: Dynamic Behaviors of Materials Under Angle-Resolved Experiments: A Matrix Framework for Nonlinear Physics
item.description: arXiv:2604.13752v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Matter and external stimuli interact dynamically almost everywhere in nature. Under an applied field, a material seldom stays in the state in which it was characterized, and its properties change with time. Angle-resolved experiments are the standard way to resolve direction-dependent properties, however, current theoretical tools for data analysis are built for static states, leaving dynamic behaviors largely neglected. Here, we develop a generalized ``input-coefficient-output'' (ICO) approach that constructs spatial operation matrices and symmetry-reduced coefficient matrices across diverse physical systems, as we verify for nonlinear optics, elasticity, electrostriction and magnetostriction, and a Python program is released for convenient application. Using angle-resolved polarized second-harmonic generation (SHG) as an example, we focus on the dynamic modeling of material properties under angle-dependent stimuli, construct dynamic matrix equations that capture the time-dependent evolution of material responses, and propose three dynamic models and a point-to-point data fitting method. For the SHG experiments performed on $T_d-$WTe$_2$, the discrete dynamic model captures the asymmetric characteristics of the measured polar pattern with a significantly improved coefficient of determination ($R^2$ increasing from 0.567 to 0.773), whereas conventional static models are constrained to a symmetric curve. The evolution operator extracted from the dynamic model connects the macroscopic measurement to microscopic intermediate states during their interaction with stimuli. This work provides a practical matrix framework for dynamic modeling of material properties, paving the way for exploring complex nonlinear physics under realistic experimental conditions.

item.title: A first-principles approach for predicting infrared optical properties of solids
item.description: arXiv:2606.13143v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a simplified formalism for predicting infrared optical constants from first-principles calculations. Addressing limitations of the widely used four-parameter semi-quantum Lorentz model, the proposed approach bridges the gap between the harmonic three-parameter model and full self-energy-based methods. By incorporating essential anharmonic effects including four-phonon scattering and phonon renormalisation, the model provides an efficient and accurate alternative while maintaining low computational cost. The frequency-dependent refractive indices of MgO and rutile TiO$_2$ are computed and compared with experimental data, demonstrating good quantitative agreement. The framework offers a practical approach for predicting optical properties of materials across a wide range of materials.

item.title: Efficient Large-Scale STEM-EELS Simulations With Torched-TACAW
item.description: arXiv:2607.02236v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The time auto-correlation of auxiliary wave functions (TACAW) method enables efficient simulations of ultra-low-loss electron energy loss spectra (EELS) arising from vibrational and magnon excitations. In practical applications to realistic materials systems, however, TACAW calculations become challenging due to the large system sizes required for models containing defects, interfaces, impurities, or grain boundaries, as well as the substantial computational cost and data throughput associated with molecular dynamics and multislice calculations. Here we discuss a practical methodology for large-scale TACAW simulations and present torched-TACAW, a freely available implementation of the TACAW part of the described workflow for efficient STEM-EELS simulations. The overall approach combines molecular dynamics based on foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials, partitioning of elongated supercells, and on-the-fly processing of multislice outputs in order to enable near ab initio quality simulations with tractable memory use and data flow. Using rutile TiO2 as a model system, we analyze important numerical aspects of the method, including windowing and supercell partitioning, and demonstrate atomic-resolution STEM-EELS simulations for thick samples.

item.title: Time-Reversal-Invariant Altermagnetic Acoustic Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2608.08827v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Altermagnets have emerged as a new class of magnetic materials that combine spin-split electronic bands with zero net magnetization. Extending this paradigm to classical-wave systems has, however, been fundamentally challenging because conventional realizations require broken time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Here, we overcome this limitation by introducing a pseudospin degree of freedom and constructing a pseudo-time-reversal operator that faithfully reproduces the action of its physical counterpart while preserving actual TRS. Building on this framework, we theoretically propose and experimentally realize the first time-reversal-invariant altermagnetic acoustic crystal. Acoustic measurements directly reveal pseudospin-dependent band splitting--a defining hallmark of altermagnetism--under strictly TRS-preserving conditions. Moreover, the altermagnetic acoustic crystal exhibits sublattice-pseudospin locking, enabling flexible control over acoustic pseudospin splitting and filtering. Our work establishes acoustic crystals as a versatile platform for exploring altermagnetic physics and opens new avenues for spin-inspired wave manipulation in nonmagnetic devices.

item.title: Machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals for molecules, solids, and reactive surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2608.21525v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The application of density functional theory to heterogeneous catalysis is hindered by the shortcomings of conventional density functional approximations. We combine machine learning with explicitly non-local physically informed descriptors and introduce an exchange-correlation functional (CIDER26SS) framework regularized for wide transferability. CIDER26SS is size-extensive, highly efficient, provides a balanced and accurate description of both molecular and solid-state systems, and is specifically well-optimized for transition metal surface chemistry. Surpassing existing conventional functionals, CIDER26SS resolves the CO/Pt puzzle, identifying the correct binding site for CO adsorption on the Pt(111) surface, along with an accurate adsorption energy, Pt lattice constant, and surface energy. Predictions agree well with the experimental values, even when all bulk and surface data for Pt are excluded from the training set. Remarkably, CIDER26SS exceeds the accuracy of semilocal approximations even for systems far outside the training domain.

item.title: Benchmarking Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Temperature-Dependent Elasticity of Binary and High-Entropy Refractory Carbides
item.description: arXiv:2610.11878v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate predictions of temperature-dependent stiffness are essential for assessing the high-temperature performance of refractory carbides, yet the cost of ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) limits systematic exploration across compositions and temperatures. Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) offer a computationally efficient alternative, but their reliability for finite-temperature elasticity remains insufficiently established. Here, we benchmark nine uMLIPs against consistent AIMD reference data for five binary and two high-entropy (HE) carbides between 300 and 1200 K. Elastic constants and the corresponding bulk, shear, and Young's moduli are obtained using stress-strain molecular dynamics, explicitly sampling thermal atomic motion and anharmonic effects beyond thermal expansion alone. We assess absolute elastic properties and normalized thermal softening separately. MACE-MH-1 achieves the lowest overall mean absolute percentage error (5.7%). MACE-MH-1 and DPA4-Mini reproduce thermal softening most accurately, with mean deviations of 2.5 and 2.3 percentage points, respectively. All models generally underestimate stiffness, with larger equilibrium volumes relative to the AIMD reference likely contributing to this trend for most models. C12 exhibits the largest model-dependent errors. The HE carbides are described with accuracy comparable to that of the binary carbides, indicating no apparent accuracy penalty from chemical complexity. Accuracy instead varies with transition-metal composition, with group-V carbides, particularly TaC, presenting the greatest challenge. These results identify promising pretrained models for finite-temperature elasticity in carbides and show why accurate absolute stiffness and thermal softening must be assessed independently.

item.title: Symmetry-Guided Machine Learning of Spin-Dependent Nonlinear Hall Response
item.description: arXiv:2610.28529v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A Berry-curvature dipole can generate a current perpendicular to an applied electric field even when the linear Hall response is zero. This work examines how lattice symmetry, magnetic orientation, and carrier occupation control this nonlinear response in an anisotropic honeycomb model. Unequal hopping permits one dipole component without magnetism. Rotating the local moments can activate the second component and change the sign and magnitude of both. Reversing all moments leaves the dipole unchanged but reverses the intrinsic linear Hall conductivity. Equal populations of reversed domains can therefore retain the dipole contribution when their local electric fields are the same. A symmetry-constrained polynomial machine-learning model describes the calculated dipoles for 1024 spin configurations. At the reference chemical potential, both components have $R^2>0.9995$ for 256 configurations excluded from training. Keeping the carrier density fixed shifts the chemical potential as the moments rotate and gives slightly larger prediction errors. Separate fits across a chemical-potential sweep show a stronger loss of accuracy for $D_y$ at higher energies. Within weak-field semiclassical transport with a constant relaxation time, the predicted dipole determines the angular dependence, rectification, and second harmonic of the current. The results connect magnetic control of the nonlinear Hall response to the balance of Berry-curvature contributions near the Fermi level.

item.title: Mechanistic discovery in grain boundary structure and deformation driven by agentic AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.28629v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending these capabilities to domain-intensive mechanistic studies remains challenging. General grain boundaries (GBs) exemplify this challenge, as their structural complexity complicates experimental characterization and atomistic modeling. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general GBs, which are common in real polycrystals yet remain understudied. By integrating large language models into a modular architecture, GBClaw effectively combines systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis through iterative workflow refinement and dynamic replanning. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, the framework characterized interfacial defect structures and deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. It established a general approach to identify previously unobserved, widely spaced secondary GB misfit dislocations (SGBMDs) alongside closely spaced primary GB misfit dislocations (PGBMDs) in simulated atomic configurations and experimental images. Comparisons of GB sliding with and without SGBMDs revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of misfit-dislocation hierarchies in sliding resistance. Researcher-guided follow-up calculations further elucidated the structural origins of shear asymmetry and an anomalous shear response. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening and deep mechanistic discovery at complex material interfaces.

item.title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Microgel Glasses via Particle Stiffness
item.description: arXiv:2610.29389v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, particle stiffness governs deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, and thereby dictates the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses, and establish Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.

item.title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.31924v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models and spatial resolution. Here we demonstrate a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model that establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit. We discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from a pinned state directly at the channel-dielectric interface of an organic transistor, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics that contradict models based on substrate patterning. This non-destructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final configuration opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.

item.title: Strain Functionals: A Complete and Symmetry-adapted Set of Descriptors to Characterize Atomistic Configurations
item.description: arXiv:2402.04191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Extracting relevant information from atomistic simulations relies on a complete and accurate characterization of atomistic configurations. We present a framework for characterizing atomistic configurations in terms of a complete and symmetry-adapted basis, referred to as strain functionals. In this approach a Gaussian kernel is used to map discrete atomic quantities, such as number density, velocities, and forces, to continuous fields. The local atomic configurations are then characterized using nth order central moments of the local number density. The initial Cartesian moments are recast unitarily into a Solid Harmonic Polynomial basis using SO(3) decompositions. Rotationally invariant metrics, referred to as Strain Functional Descriptors (SFDs), are constructed from the terms in the SO(3) decomposition using Clebsch-Gordan coupling. A key distinction compared to related methods is that a minimal but complete set of descriptors is identified. These descriptors characterize the local geometries numerically in terms of shape, density, and orientation descriptors that recognize n-fold symmetry axes and net shapes such as trigonal, cubic, hexagonal, etc. They can easily distinguish between most different crystal symmetries using n = 4, identify defects (such as dislocations and stacking faults), measure local deformation, and can be used in conjunction with machine learning techniques for in situ analysis of finite temperature atomistic simulation data and quantification of defect dynamics.

item.title: Online Surrogate Repair: Decoupling High-Fidelity Feedback from Search Length in Closed-Loop Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2609.07655v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Closed-loop AI scientists can generate candidate designs at low marginal computational cost, whereas reliable feedback may require wet-lab synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity computation. Addressing this imbalance through custom laboratory automation remains infrastructure-intensive and costly, while replacing new experiments with a fixed surrogate leaves persistent model errors that can be amplified by optimization. We propose \emph{online surrogate repair} (OSR), a closed-loop algorithm that uses sparse high-fidelity evaluations to update the surrogate throughout a longer agent search conducted primarily with inexpensive surrogate feedback. An acquisition rule selects which designs from the agent's accumulated proposals receive high-fidelity evaluation, and the resulting labels update the surrogate used in subsequent episodes. Across controlled synthetic environments, we demonstrate that improving global surrogate fit does not necessarily reduce maximum regret, whereas Q90-UCB and expected improvement (EI) substantially reduce regret by directing evaluations toward regions that determine the optimizer's decisions. \osradded{Across LLM and Chemeleon workflows, Online EI reduces the amount of oracle queries required by 84.3--90.3\% for matching discovery counts and by 77.9--81.6\% for matching the quality of the best material found.} Online surrogate repair introduces a third feedback regime between fixed-surrogate operation and high-fidelity feedback after every episode, separating the frequency of high-fidelity evaluation from the duration of the agent's search.

item.title: Open Ontology of Polymer Chemistry: Accumulation and Self-Improving Memory Mechanisms for Polymer Research
item.description: Memory systems for AI agents are a valuable component of long-running workflows. They are also a strong form of lock-in for model providers, because the memory system that makes a model better with use may be inaccesible to users. An ideal memory system would accumulate both factual knowledge and the relationships of that knowledge to recurring tasks performed by the researcher. People accumulate particular and general knowledge through experience, the latter often through periodic reflection on what is working and isn’t working at a higher level of abstraction. Here, we introduce an open-source harness for polymer research meant to heuristically mimic (i) knowledge accumulation across research tasks, (ii) the review of new knowledge against existing knowledge, and (iii) performing periodic updates to task-knowledge relationships through reflection. The system, which we call the Open Ontology of Polymer Chemistry (OOPC, pronounced ‘oopsie’), is initialized with a knowledge base consisting of an open-source wikipedia with entries for most known polymers. From this starting point, the knowledge base was enriched by running a 1,092 task campaign across different areas of polymer chemistry, producing 8,899 distinct findings extracted from 1,679 sources on 157 different polymers. GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 comparisons were run with and without the accumulated memory from this campaign on 60 held-out tasks with varying overlap in terms of polymer and properties being researched. The performance improvements tracked with research topic similarity to prior work researched from the harness, with token reductions of up to 19% and 48% and web search reductions of up to 80% and 72% (10.3 to 2.1 and 7.6 to 2.1 per answer) for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, respectively. The harness was tested through five independent restarts of 500 tasks each with reproducible performance gains. An independent review of the performance caught rare contradictory claims and occasionally unsubstantiated claims depending on the underlying model (up to a few percent of all claims by claude on withheld tasks, none by codex). The reflection heuristic was tested as an update to the knowledge ontology after the accumulation period. These updates mainly consisted of extended lists of property names with marginal improvements to finding recall. The roles of review and ontology updates require further study as after knowledge accumulation these tests had little room to show appreciable gains given the consistently strong evidentiary basis for findings within the harness. Looking forward, domain-specific memory systems are likely to be valuable and ideally transferable research artifacts that can be shared at the group, community, and organizational levels.

item.title: Comparative Analysis of Basic Machine Learning and Rigorous Free-Energy Calculation on Benchmarking Datasets of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity
item.description: Rigorous free-energy methods based on molecular dynamics simulations like free-energy perturbation (FEP) are nowadays widely applied in lead optimization in pharmaceutical companies. Due to sampling restrictions and potential force-field deficiencies, it is common practice to first validate the applicability of FEP to a target/chemical series using a small number of known compounds, before applying it prospectively. As rigorous methods require significant computational resources, we want to explore how basic machine learning (ML) methods perform under the same conditions, i.e., training on a small number of known compounds and estimating the affinity of novel variants in the same chemical series. We apply classical ML models using 2D and 3D molecular descriptors, alongside two implementations of 3D quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, and integrate the predictions through meta-learning. For many of the standard benchmarking datasets, we find that one of the ML models matches or exceeds the performance of FEP. Interestingly, ML-based predictions generally exhibit flatter slopes in parity plots, but without substantial effect on the relative rank ordering of compounds. Given their lower computational cost and ease of deployment, basic ML methods, particularly the meta-learner, emerge as a powerful complement to rigorous free-energy methods for estimating binding affinities within chemical series.

item.title: Transfer learning on universal interatomic potential embeddings improves generalization in structure-property defect models
item.description: Oxygen vacancy formation energies govern the performance of metal oxides across energy conversion, catalysis, and electronics, yet predicting them accurately without density functional theory calculations for novel chemical systems remains challenging. Here, we show that frozen 256-dimensional embeddings extracted from a pretrained MACE universal machine-learning interatomic potential encode information sufficient to predict vacancy formation energies obtained from density functional theory without requiring supercell construction, vacancy creation, or geometry optimization. A lightweight multilayer perceptron trained on these embeddings (MACE-dGNN) achieves an element-wise cross-validation mean absolute error of 0.38 eV, halving the error of a baseline graph neural network trained from scratch (0.72 eV) and offering a modest advantage over direct MACE relaxation calculations (0.51 eV). Because the embedding approach decouples representation from the prediction task and generalizes well with limited data, it will (1) extend naturally to fine-tuning and prediction of properties (e.g., charged defects) that are inaccessible to generic energy-and force-output interatomic potentials and (2) be trainable on necessarily small datasets, potentially enabling the use of more expensive but accurate tools for generating training data (e.g., hybrid functional calculations) for which training or fine-tuning of interatomic potentials will be difficult. We demonstrate practical impact by revisiting a prior screening of thermochemical water-splitting materials, where improved generalization alters ∼45 % of candidate classifications.

item.title: Machine Learning for NMR Observables Sensitive to Nuclear Quantum Effects
item.description: Nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) are essential for an accurate description of systems containing light elements. Their omission in classical simulations can lead to significant deviations between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements, particularly for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observables that are highly sensitive to quantum nuclear motion. Although NQEs can be treated rigorously by using ab initio path-integral molecular dynamics (AI-PIMD), the substantial computational cost associated with these simulations continues to limit their applicability to large systems and long timescales. To address this limitation, we developed a machine learning-driven PIMD (MLPIMD) workflow for the accurate and efficient prediction of NMR observables, in which NQEs at finite temperature are explicitly included. As a demonstration, we investigate the experimentally measured isotropic chemical shifts, δiso, of the 3He monomer (3He@C706- ) and dimer (3He2@C706- ) endohedral fullerene hexaanions. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with the experiment and reveal a pronounced influence of NQEs on the 3He chemical shifts in both systems. In particular, NQEs are found to play a key role in determining the chemical-shift difference between the monomer and dimer species. The methodology introduced here is broadly applicable and provides a general framework for investigating NMR observables sensitive to NQEs in complex molecular systems.

item.title: Computer-Guided In-situ Screening of Poly(acetylene)s for Gene Delivery
item.description: We report a new methodology for the discovery of polymer-based gene vectors that enables the simultaneous optimization of polymer composition and polyplex formulation, while bypassing the need to prepare, isolate, and characterise new candidates using conventional polymer synthesis. At the core of this approach is the combination of computer-aided experimental design, in situ screening of polymer composition and polyplex formulation, and machine learning, which allows us to treat polymer synthesis and formulation as a single optimizable problem. Central to this methodology is a new reactive and water-soluble poly(acetylene), poly(N-(propargyl)-2-(aminooxy)-acetamide), which can be functionalized in aqueous conditions with readily available aldehydes. This provides candidate polymers under biologically compatible conditions, which are then directly complexed with nucleic acids and evaluated within the same workflow. Iterative modelling then correlates inputs readily controlled by the operator—such as reagent concentrations and ratios—with the key performance metric, transfection efficiency, guiding subsequent rounds of candidate generation. In doing so, we move beyond post hoc correlations of physicochemical properties to establish an iterative, data-driven methodology for materials discovery. Ultimately, this methodology has unlocked the potential of poly(acetylene)s, a polymer family not previously explored in this context, to move beyond compositional mimicry and capture the dynamic helicity that underpins nucleic acid complexation and delivery in natural systems.

item.title: Adaptive Hydration-Shell ML/MM Simulations Recover Full ML Accuracy in Biomolecular Conformational Description
item.description: Residue-specific backbone conformational preferences govern the conformational ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, yet their accurate description using classical force fields is limited by prescribed functional forms that cannot fully represent environment-dependent many-body interactions. Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) learn complex atomic interactions directly from quantum-mechanical reference data, providing a systematic alternative to classical parameterisations. Here, we employ a pretrained MLFF to simulate nine cationic Gly-x-Gly tripeptides in water and compare the resulting conformational ensembles against experimental NMR scalar J-couplings. To improve computational efficiency, we develop and assess hybrid Machine Learning/Molecular Mechanics (ML/MM) protocols as computationally tractable alternatives to full ML simulation. Mechanical-embedding ML/MM is found insufficient for accurate conformational sampling, as the classical treatment of peptide–solvent interactions fails to adequately represent solvation effects on backbone conformational preferences. We therefore implement an adaptive ML/MM scheme that incorporates the immediate solvation environment into the ML description and recovers near-full-ML accuracy at a reduced computational cost.

item.title: SandCat: OpenMM Framework for Prospective Cryptic Pocket Discovery
item.description: Proteins are dynamic biomolecules, yet often in drug discovery they are treated as static entities. A relevant example of this are cryptic pockets, which are pockets that are not present in the apo structure but reveal themselves upon binding to a particular ligand. Methods based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can dynamically probe the protein structure and have been validated on known cryptic pocket sites. SWISH-X is one of the most prominent methods in this field. Previously, it was only available with GROMACS and PLUMED, which limited its speed. Here, we present SandCat, an OpenMM-based toolkit that implements this enhanced sampling method for cryptic pocket discovery. SandCat reproduces previous results from SWISH-X with twice the computational speed. Furthermore, SandCat provides standardised protocols for prospective use on targets where cryptic pockets are not known. We tested the SandCat pipeline on challenging targets, and recovered every characterised cryptic site within the top six candidate sites, with no sites detected for a negative control. We believe that the increased speed and the implementation of a prospective toolkit will enable SandCat to be used at scale to unlock previously undruggable targets.

item.title: A Pharmacophore-Based Virtual Screening Approach for the Discovery of Novel P2Y12 Receptor Ligands
item.description: Microglia play key roles in neuroinflammation, which is a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease and Multiple Sclerosis. To strengthen our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of these disorders, we need to understand the complex dynamics in microglial states. Developing new positron emission tomography (PET) tracers is exceptionally useful for this purpose, as they enable the assessment of microglia dynamics and function in the living human brain. The purinergic receptor P2Y12 (P2Y12R) is highly expressed in the homeostatic microglial states, and thus makes for a promising biomarker. In particular, P2Y12R PET tracers could complement translocator protein (TSPO) and P2X7 receptor tracers, which image microglial density or target the pro-inflammatory state, respectively. Unfortunately, current high-affinity P2Y12R ligands do not enter the brain because they are charged in vivo or because they are substrates for efflux transporters. Attempts to increase brain uptake by improving their physicochemical properties have not yet resulted in a successful P2Y12R PET tracer. This emphasizes the need for novel chemotypes. Herein, we applied a pharmacophore-based virtual screening strategy to a library of about three million compounds. As a result, we identified the imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazolone scaffold as a promising structural class to use as a starting point for developing P2Y12R ligands. After extensive hit expansion and structure-activity relationship studies, the two best ligands displayed excellent binding affinity for human P2Y12R (96: Ki = 9.61 ± 1.70 nM; 109: Ki = 3.10 ± 0.34 nM) and rat P2Y12R (96: Ki = 65.6 ± 25.9 nM; 109: Ki = 17.9 ± 12.8 nM) in a radioligand binding assay. Furthermore, imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazolone [18F]91 was successfully radiolabeled as a proof-of-concept in sufficient radiochemical yields. Future work will assess whether the more potent ligands can be radiolabeled and used to image the P2Y12R in the brain. Together, these results highlight the use of pharmacophore-based strategy in PET tracer development and provide a robust basis for further hit exploration.

item.title: Foundation interatomic potentials learn the practical chemistry they were never taught
item.description: Chemists understand molecular reactivity through simplified concepts such as substituent effects, acidity, and aromaticity, which are compact descriptors of the potential energy surface and of the electronic structure that shapes it. Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming applied computational chemistry by learning the same surface from atomic structures, energies, and forces, making atomistic simulations of complex systems practical. Like chemists, MLIPs build compact internal representations of that surface, yet these are usually treated as a means to faster, larger-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Here we show that they also contain directly recoverable chemical information: simple models applied to the invariant per-atom embeddings of pretrained universal MLIPs recover Hammett substituent constants, Brønsted and Lewis acidity, and ring aromaticity with Spearman ρ = 0.8–0.99. The same representations predict the yield of a four-component palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling at ρ = 0.96, matching models built from curated descriptors, while pinpointing the aryl halide as the reaction’s key substrate and ranking isoxazole additives by catalyst-poisoning strength. Universal MLIPs are therefore not only fast engines for energies and forces but also chemically meaningful representations of molecular reactivity, opening a route to extracting chemical insights directly from the learned potentials themselves.

item.title: Correcting the Liquid Densities of Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Using Local-Number-Density Repulsion
item.description: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) such as UMA, trained on reference data from meta-generalized gradient approximation or hybrid functionals that incorporate dispersion interactions, often overestimate molecular-liquid densities, thereby placing every property computed at constant pressure at the wrong state point. This study proposes a correction that adds to the MLIP a repulsive energy quadratic in the local number density of each atom, with two coefficients fitted only to the equations of state of water and ethanol; the forces and stresses follow analytically, so neither electronic-structure calculations nor retraining is required. For UMA, the correction reduces the density mean absolute error (MAE) of 22 liquids from 10.8% to 2.5%, lowering the error for every liquid and bringing 20 of them within ±5% of experiment, while improving the bulk modulus (MAE from 71.6% to 22.1%), heat of vaporization, and second hydration shell of water, none of which was calibrated. Applied to SevenNet-Omni without

item.title: SKIER: A Scientific Skills Framework for Evidence-Grounded AI Reasoning
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to interpret experiments and propose mechanisms, but its mechanistic claims often lack traceable evidence. Here we introduce SKIER (Skills for Evidence-grounded AI Reasoning), a scientific skills AI framework that combines AI orchestration, researcher-defined analytical procedures, deterministic calculations, and versioned records. Using 49 records from a published methanol-oxidation case study, the framework recovered an m/z 48 signal exceeding 60% of the combined m/z 44, 46, and 48 signals in the H218O experiment, which was assigned to C18O18O. This observation supported the previously reported C–O cleavage pathway. AI then used the processed data to propose three competing mechanisms and design CH318OH-labelling, oxygen-exchange, and residence-time experiments to distinguish them. Those follow-up experiments further refined the published mechanism by locating C–O cleavage before formic acid formation. With shared skills, all 11 AI configurations completed data processing, compared with none without them. In the 100 expert-designed questions evaluating mechanism inference and validation-experiment design, GPT-5.6-sol achieved 100% accuracy. Together, these results demonstrate how a scientific skills framework connects reproducible data analysis with experimentally testable mechanistic reasoning across AI models.

item.title: Benchmarking thermoelectric property extraction from scientific text
item.description: We compare five methods for extracting thermoelectric property records from paragraphs of the literature (regular expressions, the ChemDataExtractor thermoelectric parsers, MaterialsBERT named-entity recognition with rule-based linking, a single-prompt large language model (LLM) and an LLM agent) on one corpus of 311 papers with one scoring rule, with all methods frozen before the 200-paragraph test sample was annotated. A record counts as correct only if property, value, temperature and material all match the gold standard. On the 160 in-scope test paragraphs (241 core records), the single-prompt LLM reached F1 = 0.79 (95% CI 0.71–0.87) and the agent 0.73 (0.64–0.83), against 0.22 for the regular-expression baseline and 0.06 for the ChemDataExtractor and NER pipelines; both LLM methods recover property, value and temperature with F1 above 0.94, and most of their remaining errors concern the material. We found no evidence of an accuracy improvement from the tested agent configuration, and we release the protocol, code, gold standard and all method outputs.

item.title: Electronic Descriptors Lower Oxygen-Vacancy Formation-Energy Error Relative to Crystal Structure Alone in Non-Magnetic Oxides
item.description: Oxygen vacancies control conduction, catalysis and ion transport in oxides, and an error of 0.3 eV in their neutral formation energy changes their concentration at 1000 K thirty-fold. Graph networks predict this energy from structure alone, but whether electronic descriptors of the pristine host from density-functional theory help is untested at matched training oxides. We compared a structure-only network (S) with one also given 22 such descriptors (D) on 1726 vacancy sites in 818 non-magnetic oxides of the Kumagai database, testing on unseen formulas. S reached 0.297 eV, the published accuracy. With 654 training oxides and equal tuning, D lowered the site error by 0.033 [0.021, 0.045] eV (95% interval), inside a 0.05 eV tolerance (1.8-fold in concentration). Tuned alone in a wider search, D* gained 0.069 [0.060, 0.078] eV, above it, but 0.039 [0.030, 0.048] eV over default-initialised S. The descriptors remove 11 to 23% of the error of S, depending on tuning. Within oxides the gain is concentrated in hosts whose cations have an empty valence s shell: empty-shell post-transition hosts gain 0.075 [0.050, 0.102] eV more than lone-pair hosts. Descriptors predicted from structure never surpass S, so the gain requires computed descriptors; where these are unavailable, S suffices for neutral vacancies.

item.title: Foldability Is an Intrinsic Property of Protein Sequences: A Lattice Model Study with Information-Theoretic Approach and Unsupervised Machine Learning
item.description: Protein structure prediction has been largely solved, but why a given sequence is foldable has not. We address this question for 27-, 48- and 64-residue lattice heteropolymers with statistical thermodynamics, the informationtheoretic approach (ITA) and a variational autoencoder (VAE). Native populations, folding probabilities and freeenergy surfaces are reproducible and independent of the initial denatured ensemble, so foldability is an intrinsic property of the sequence at a given temperature and solvent. We then ask where the observed regularities come from. Stability is governed by an information balance: the information content (self-information) of the native energy relative to the maximum-entropy description of compact alternatives, ℐtail, must exceed their Shannon entropy, 𝑆c = ln𝛺c. This is the random-energy-model condition for a folding transition, and ℐtail/𝑆c fixes the ratio of folding to glass temperatures, recasting minimal frustration in information units. Foldable sequences have smooth funnels, minimal Shannon entropy and minimal Fisher information in the native state, and a single sharp maximum of Fisher information at melting (cooperativity). Mutual and conditional information show that stability is an approximately sufficient statistic for kinetic accessibility of compact 27-mers. No hierarchical folding order is found. Variational autoencoders trained without labels distinguish sequences by their folding ensembles, supply a six-variable reaction coordinate that retains 91% of the kinetic information in the full native-contact map, and rediscover the native energy gap from the density of compact states.

item.title: Reference Conventions and Structure Types, Rather Than 4f Occupancy, Shape Lanthanide Errors in Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Compounds that pair a lanthanide with a d-block metal and a p-block anion sit behind permanent magnets, catalysts and energy-storage materials, yet large parts of this chemical space have not been computed. Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials now make it possible to screen such spaces for stability at a small fraction of the cost of density functional theory, and they are increasingly used to decide which candidates are worth calculating properly. Their training data, however, hold few lanthanide compounds, describe the same element with different pseudopotentials from one database to the next, and carry empirical energy corrections fitted on compound sets from which lanthanides were excluded, so their reliability for felectron chemistry has not been established. Here we benchmark five universal potentials against density functional theory computed with Materials Project settings on 82 lanthanide–d-block–anion ternaries covering the lanthanide series (excluding Pm) and seven anions. Apparent accuracy turns out to be set mainly by the energy convention of the reference: judged against the quantity each model was trained to predict, all five reach mean absolute errors of 0.07 to 0.10 eV per atom, while the wrong convention inflates the error by more than a factor of three. Error does not follow 4f occupancy or the 4f pseudopotential treatment assigned to each element. It is larger for intermetallic than for ionic compounds and concentrates in two structure types, the CeNiC2-type carbides and the PbFCl-type phosphides, which most models miss even though these compounds have Materials Project entries. For ytterbium, every model follows the divalent convention of the older Materials Project data rather than the trivalent one now in use, a singleelement inconsistency of roughly 0.2 to 0.3 eV per atom. These results indicate where lanthanide chemical space can be screened with current potentials and where explicit DFT validation is still required, and they point to structural and data-provenance diagnostics, rather than elemental ones, for the next generation of models.
