item.title: Limits of geometric packing descriptors in molecular crystal energy ranking
item.description: Simple packing descriptors do not consistently reproduce molecular crystal energy rankings across chemically distinct compounds. A retrospective benchmark of 98 deposited crystal structure prediction candidates from seven molecules was assembled from published relative r²SCAN-D3 electronic energies. Forty entries from four earlier systems were combined with 58 entries for indomethacin, nicotinamide and aspirin. Density, heavy-atom proximity, N–H···O/N geometry and planar-ring proximity were evaluated individually and through an equal-weight rank composite, without fitting feature weights. An implementation audit identified incomplete periodic-image enumeration affecting at least one descriptor in 23 structures. Recalculation with geometry-dependent complete image bounds changed 3.5 Å contact counts in 13 structures. On the three additional molecular systems, the corrected four-feature composite gave a macro-averaged Spearman correlation of 0.187, compared with 0.501 for density and −0.004 for 3.5 Å contacts. The composite improved on density for indomethacin but underperformed for nicotinamide and aspirin. Fifty-four of 813 within-molecule pairs had reference energy differences below 0.2 kJ mol⁻¹. This retrospective threshold does not provide calibrated predictive uncertainty or a prospective abstention rule. Metadata-verified energy joins, exact input hashes, representative invariance tests and reproducible numerical outputs accompany the analysis. The results document representation and implementation sensitivities and heterogeneous transfer between molecules. Neither superiority over established energy-ranking approaches nor prediction of experimental thermodynamic stability is demonstrated.

item.title: Compliance Mismatch Drives Mechanochemical Reactivity in Diels-Alder Reactions
item.description: Mechanical forces can alter chemical reactivity by reshaping the potential energy surface landscape, but the relationships between force direction, molecular structure, and barrier structure remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a compliance-based framework for understanding primary mechanochemical activation by means of the compliance matrix and test it across a systematically designed chemical space of cyclopentadiene-based Diels-Alder reactions. Under the harmonic approximation, the force-induced change in a barrier height is determined by the difference in the compliances along the direction of force between the reactant complex and the transition state. We then evaluate this model across 233 Diels-Alder reactions, generating 1,271 reaction profiles and performing over 284,448 force-modified critical point calculations enabled by frontier machine-learned interatomic potentials. When deformation is restricted to a single coordinate, where the compliance matrix is effectively diagonal, the mechanochemical response depends strongly on the selected distortion, with dihedral motions providing a particularly effective mode of activation. However, upon optimizing in the presence of force, including the off-diagonal elements of the compliance matrix, the barrier-lowering behavior becomes widespread and is substantially less sensitive to the initial force direction. This behavior arises from the finding that reactant complexes are generally more compliant than their corresponding transition states. We show that a global reactant compliance descriptor captures this trend and identifies substituent-dependent differences in mechanochemical susceptibility, including candidate reactions for observing changes in stereoselectivity. These results show that mechanochemical activation for this reaction class does not require the force to be aligned with the traditional reaction coordinate. Instead, differential distortability across the reactant and transition states provides a general physical principle for understanding and potentially designing force-sensitive reactions. Finally, by extending this model to understand reactions under hydrostatic pressure conditions, this work provides insight into primary mechanochemistry across all distortion modes of molecular systems.

item.title: IMPLICIT LEARNING: REACTION OUTCOME PREDICTION FROM POSITIVE-ONLY DATA
item.description: Machine learning models for reaction product prediction have largely been trained and evaluated on datasets of successful reactions. While this setting allows reaching high accuracy scores, these models generally struggle to discriminate between successful and unsuccessful transformations due to the lack of negative training data. This critically limits their practical use, as reliably recognizing unproductive substrate combinations in silico is required to accelerate experimental campaigns and save resources in the laboratory. While the availability of negative reaction data remains limited to date, we show that even purely positive datasets implicitly contain a significant amount of information about cases in which no reaction occurs. To exploit this, we introduce TACIT (TAckling Chemistry through ImpliciT negative learning). While trained on positive-only data, TACIT learns to distinguish between productive and unproductive transformations. On two published high-throughput experimentation datasets, it outperforms all evaluated reaction outcome prediction models in separating successful from failed reactions. Crucially, TACIT’s accuracy on the popular USPTO-MIT benchmark remains competitive, despite its added ability to predict negative reaction outcomes.

item.title: ePC-SAFT: an electrolyte equation-of-state engine with exact derivatives for phase and reaction equilibrium and parameter estimation
item.description: Electrolyte parameter estimation and equation-oriented process models require properties of a solved phase and reaction equilibrium and their responses to temperature, pressure, feed and molecular parameters. The ePC-SAFT package supplies these calculations in native C++ through a Python interface. Published hard-chain, dispersion, association, polar and electrolyte contributions define a selected Helmholtz energy; association and pressure closure, constrained equilibrium and exact derivatives share its mathematical implementation. One equilibrium driver handles declared neutral, charged and reacting phase specifications, while explicit tangent-plane searches test additional phases. Implicit derivatives of the defining equations supply observation Jacobians, least-squares and guarded minimax parameter estimation, and first and second derivatives for process models. Comparisons span pure-fluid saturation, neutral and associating mixtures, aqueous and mixed electrolytes, solvent transfer, liquid splits and reacting systems, with calibration, withheld prediction and published-model reproduction identified separately. With fixed published parameters, propane saturation pressures and liquid densities deviate from measurements by 2.70 % and 0.305 % on average; on 19 temperatures withheld from a threetemperature refit, the refit gives 1.00 % and 0.180 %, against 1.07 % and 0.228 % for the published parameters. The comparisons also expose failed mixed-salt transfer, large reactive-amine pressure discrepancies and unresolved source conventions. Numerical verification gives liquidliquid mole fractions within 4.62 × 10−9 of an independent matched electrolyte implementation and selected solved-state derivatives within 3.40 × 10−10 relative. Settler and hydrogen-mixture examples show how the same calculations enter engineering models, with physical accuracy bounded by the stated parameter domains and data.

item.title: Correcting the Liquid Densities of Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Using Local-Number-Density Repulsion
item.description: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) such as UMA, trained on reference data from meta-generalized gradient approximation or hybrid functionals that incorporate dispersion interactions, often overestimate molecular-liquid densities, thereby placing every property computed at constant pressure at the wrong state point. This study proposes a correction that adds to the MLIP a repulsive energy quadratic in the local number density of each atom, with two coefficients fitted only to the equations of state of water and ethanol; the forces and stresses follow analytically, so neither electronic-structure calculations nor retraining is required. For UMA, the correction reduces the density mean absolute error (MAE) of 22 liquids from 10.8% to 2.5%, lowering the error for every liquid and bringing 20 of them within ±5% of experiment, while improving the bulk modulus (MAE from 71.6% to 22.1%), heat of vaporization, and second hydration shell of water, none of which was calibrated. Applied to SevenNet-Omni without recalibration, the same coefficients reduce the density MAE from 8.2% to 1.8%, with 21 of 22 liquids within ±5% of experiment.

item.title: Hybrid Joining Technologies for Composites: Mechanisms, Performance, Challenges, and Perspectives
item.description: Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites are increasingly used in aircraft structures with their high specific strength, stiffness, corrosion resistance, and lightweight nature. However, reliably joining FRP components is challenging because mechanical joining can create stress concentrations, fiber damage, and delamination, while adhesive bonding can cause peel stress, environmental degradation, and inspection challenges. This review systematically covers hybrid joining approaches for FRPs, emphasizing joint designs, load-sharing mechanisms, mechanical performance, surface treatment, interlayer engineering, aerospace applications, certification concerns, and emerging technologies. This systematic literature review focused on bolted-bonded, riveted-bonded, welded-bonded, and friction-based hybrid connections. The review analyzed the evaluated research for static strength, fatigue behavior, impact resistance, failure mechanisms, joint design parameters, surface modification, interlayer engineering, aerospace implementation, inspection, repair, and certification. Other emerging themes included structural health monitoring, thermoplastic composites, automated joining, and bio-inspired interfaces. Based on the literature, this study shows that hybrid joining provides load-transfer mechanisms and progressive failure behavior comparable to those of single-joining approaches. Reported impact testing suggests that hybrid joints absorb roughly 45% more energy than adhesive joints. Moreover, surface treatments such as abrasion, plasma treatment, laser ablation, and chemical etching, as well as toughening interlayers, can further improve interfacial performance and damage tolerance. Aircraft applications include thermoplastic control surface components, wing-box joints, and fuselage splices. The performance of hybrid FRP joints depends heavily on controlled load sharing between the adhesive and mechanical or friction-based joints. Therefore, adhesive layer thickness, fastener torque, edge distance, overlap length, and fastener spacing are important in reducing stress concentrations and progressive failure. Tailored interlayers and surface activation may further improve fracture resistance and adhesion. However, the following are restricted: certification, non-destructive assessment, long-term durability, repair techniques, and uniformity of repair procedures. Future work should develop new solutions for monitoring, automation, production efficiency, and damage tolerance by combining embedded sensors, machine learning, thermoplastic welding, robotic joining, and bio-inspired interfaces. Hybrid joining methods provide an integrated approach to enhancing the structural performance of FRP composite connections, including damage tolerance, fatigue endurance, and reliability, particularly in aerospace applications. This is achieved through complementary joining techniques that enable gradual load transfer and maintain load-carrying capacity after local damage. Future research should also focus on standardized qualification procedures, standardized processes for reliable non-destructive inspection, environmental durability, automated process control, intelligent health monitoring, and scalable certification procedures to enable the wider application of hybrid composite joining technologies in next-generation aerospace structures.

item.title: A training-free, domain-extensible LLM-based approach for automated extraction of standardized preparation procedures
item.description:
Nature Communications, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78605-7

item.title: Turning time series into algebraic equations: Symbolic machine learning for interpretable modeling of chaotic time series
item.description: Chaotic time series are notoriously difficult to forecast: small uncertainties in initial conditions amplify rapidly, while strong nonlinearities and regime-dependent variability constrain predictability. Although modern deep learning often delivers strong short-horizon accuracy, its black-box nature limits scientific insight and practical trust in settings where understanding the underlying dynamics matters. To address this gap, we propose two complementary symbolic forecasters that learn explicit, interpretable algebraic equations from chaotic time series data. Symbolic neural forecaster adapts a neural network-based equation learning architecture to the forecasting setting, enabling end-to-end differentiable discovery of compact and interpretable algebraic relations. The symbolic tree forecaster builds on evolutionary symbolic regression to search directly over equation structures under a principled accuracy–complexity trade-off. We evaluate both approaches in a rolling-window one-step-ahead forecast setting using several accuracy metrics and compare against a broad suite of baselines spanning classical statistical models, tree ensembles, and state-of-the-art deep learning architectures. Numerical experiments cover a benchmark of 132 low-dimensional chaotic attractors and two real-world chaotic time series (weekly dengue incidence in San Juan and the Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperature index). Across datasets, symbolic forecasters achieve competitive one-step-ahead accuracy while providing transparent analytical equations that reveal salient aspects of the underlying dynamics.

item.title: Atomistic islet amyloid polypeptide fibril simulations reveal interplay of amyloid kinetic and mechanical stability

item.title: From Processing to Programmable Properties: A Review of Artificial Intelligence in Metal Additive Manufacturing
item.description: Machine learning has accelerated process–structure–property (PSP) prediction in metal additive manufacturing (AM), but a predicted optimum is useful only if it can be realized through processing and verified experimentally. This review examines that transition by connecting physics-based simulation, data curation, microstructure representation and reconstruction, and inverse design. We assess the information each stage retains, the assumptions it introduces, and the uncertainty it passes to subsequent decisions. Three tests organize the synthesis: structural fidelity, independently evaluated property performance, and accessibility through a specified processing route. Using these tests, we compare forward and inverse methods in terms of their data requirements, physical constraints, and validation evidence, distinguishing metal-AM demonstrations from transferable approaches developed in adjacent fields. Recurring limitations include simulation–experiment mismatch, incomplete dataset provenance, representation-dependent ambiguity, and insufficient testing outside the training domain. We outline benchmarks and reporting practices that make these limitations visible and connect them to priorities in physics-informed, multifidelity, interpretable, and multimodal learning. The resulting roadmap places experimental feedback at the center of the design workflow and identifies the evidence needed to translate rapid predictions into reproducible control of microstructure and properties.

item.title: Neural quantum states for non-Markovian open quantum dynamics in bosonic environments
item.description: Condensed-phase quantum dynamics are strongly shaped by vibrational, solvent, and protein environments, yet their nonperturbative, non-Markovian description requires a rapidly growing high-dimensional representation as environmental complexity increases. Here, we extend neural quantum states (NQS) to the dissipaton-embedded quantum master equation (DQME) for bosonic environments using a complex-valued restricted Boltzmann machine adapted to nonbinary bosonic occupations. An explicit filtering scheme further concentrates the neural representation on dynamically relevant dissipaton configurations. The resulting NQS-DQME approach reproduces representative quantum dissipative dynamics while effectively compressing the reduced density tensor (RDT). For an anharmonic model of condensed-phase hydrogen transfer, the method also reproduces weak-coupling tunneling dynamics. At stronger system-bath coupling, however, errors become localized in a small subset of RDT elements, showing that a small global variational residual does not necessarily ensure accurate chemically relevant observables. This limitation identifies observable-level error control as a key challenge for reliable long-time NQS propagation.

item.title: Mobilis: an open-source toolkit for charge transport in organic semiconductors, from crystal structures to temperaturedependent mobilities with dynamic disorder and active learning
item.description: Computing a charge mobility for an organic semiconductor involves a chain of steps: monomer site energies, intermolecular couplings, the thermal fluctuation of those couplings, and a transport model whose validity depends on the ratio of coupling to reorganization energy. These steps are usually carried out with separate scripts and different quantum-chemistry codes, which makes results hard to reproduce and models hard to compare. Mobilis is an open-source Python package (GPL-3.0) with a graphical interface and a command-line interface that runs the whole chain from a CIF file or an MD morphology. It prepares and reads Gaussian and ADF calculations (and xtb from the command line), and contains its own extended-Hückel and ZINDO couplings, a polarizable site-energy model, Marcus–Jortner hopping with kinetic Monte Carlo, and transient localization theory. For dynamic disorder it builds coupling surfaces over the six rigidbody intermolecular coordinates and samples them by full-crystal rigid-body molecular dynamics. A Gaussian-process active-learning loop chooses the DFT dimer calculations needed for these surfaces and stops when the posterior uncertainty of the coupling fluctuation σV falls below a target. For pentacene, 24–40 DFT dimers per pair reproduce σV within 4%, against 273 points for a quadratic fit. Chiral molecules in centrosymmetric crystals, such as mer-Alq3 and Ir(III) emitters, are treated by mirror-image fragments. The code is tested by 34 automated test scripts, including an exact-solution check of the kinetic Monte Carlo, and is archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23593488).

item.title: Agentic Swarms Discover Enhanchment of Fractional Chern Insulator Gaps Beyond Ideal Quantum Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.35934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can artificial intelligence (AI) move beyond solving well-defined problems to contribute to open-ended discovery in fundamental physics? Could AI propose what to explore, identify unexpected phenomena, and uncover their mechanisms? We address this using MOSAIC (Multi-agent Open-ended Scientific Analysis and Investigation through Collaboration), a collaborative swarm of AI agents (Claude Opus 5.5), to tackle a longstanding bottleneck: the small energy gaps limiting the robustness of fractional topological order and the study of anyons at higher temperatures. Rather than prescribing a model, we ask frontier models (GPT-6 Astra) to propose a theoretical framework, which MOSAIC explores through diverse strategies and rapid exchange of ideas. This reveals a striking finding: although ideal quantum geometry is considered favorable for fractional states, departing from this limit can dramatically enhance their robustness, with many-body gaps more than an order of magnitude larger than in the ideal case. Without centralized coordination, the agents explored autonomously, combined findings across agents, and formed insights from individual runs, outperforming isolated agents with the same tools. AI-assisted theoretical analysis further develops simplified models with an analytical gap enhancement factor that is unbounded within the single-band approximation. Remarkably, AI identifies the real-space quantum metric, rather than the momentum-space one, as the key quantity governing the many-body gap, revealing how flat-band wavefunctions shape two-electron interactions and yielding an index computable from single-particle wavefunctions without many-body ED to guide gap optimization. Our study demonstrates how collaborative AI agents can integrate exploration, discovery of unexpected physics, and theoretical understanding, opening new possibilities for AI-driven research in fundamental physics.

item.title: Machine learning enabled design of sustainable alloys considering real world constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.35946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing sustainable alloys must reconcile high performance with real-world constraints, including feedstock scarcity and variability, processing and energy requirements, regulatory thresholds, and economic limitations. Addressing these constraints reaches far beyond today's conventional performance-focused frameworks. It needs to consider not only complex property-processing-performance trade-offs but also sustainable production pathways. Here, we propose a physics-informed ensemble (PIE) learning framework that integrates fundamental structure-property relationships with processing routes and sustainability criteria for mechanism-based alloy design. It predicts properties from composition-microstructure relationships and infers processing routes under sustainability constraints, establishing an interdisciplinary approach to identifying sustainable alloy solutions. We validate the approach for Mg alloys, a lightweight yet energy-intensive metallic material class, considering performance, cost, and carbon emissions. Trained on a benchmark dataset, the PIE model systematically explores plausible alloy compositions and microstructures to construct a digital library of millions of candidate alloys. From this space, we identify two sustainable Mg alloy solutions that overcome the conventional performance-cost-emission trade-off: a rare-earth-containing alloy increases yield and tensile strength by 72.8 percent and 61.1 percent, respectively, over alloys from the same family at comparable cost and emissions; and a rare-earth-free alloy reduces cost and carbon emissions by 40.4 percent and 88.9 percent, respectively, relative to its primary-feedstock counterpart, without compromising mechanical performance. This work introduces a general, physics-informed, and quantifiable framework for designing sustainable alloys under real-world constraints.

item.title: Mesons, Confinement, and Complexity: A Krylov Space Perspective on the Long-Range Ising Chain
item.description: arXiv:2610.36054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the interplay between confinement and Krylov complexity in the long-range transverse-field Ising chain, where power-law interactions $\sim 1/r^{\alpha}$ generate an effective confining potential between domain walls without an explicit symmetry-breaking field. Using the time-averaged Krylov state complexity after a quench as a diagnostic, we find that the complexity is strongly suppressed and only weakly system size-dependent at small $\alpha$ and small transverse field $h_x$, where confinement is strongest, and crosses over to rapid growth at larger $\alpha$, where it increases with system size. Within the confined regime, the oscillation frequencies of the complexity agree with the meson masses of an effective two-kink model, with the dominant frequency growing linearly with the lightest meson mass and the time-averaged complexity decreasing approximately as its inverse square. We further study operator Krylov complexity at finite temperature using the Wightman inner product. At low temperature, it exhibits bounded oscillations that directly encode the meson spectrum, whereas this structure is progressively washed out as the temperature increases. These results identify Krylov complexity as a spectroscopic probe of interaction-induced confinement and reproduce, in a microscopic lattice model, the hallmarks of Krylov complexity identified in confining field theories.

item.title: Learning the Chronology of Materials Discovery for Synthesizability Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.36193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-throughput computational and generative approaches are proposing candidate materials far faster than they can be synthesized, making it increasingly important to identify which hypothetical materials are likely to be experimentally realizable. Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning has emerged as a representative framework for synthesizability prediction, yet existing approaches treat experimentally reported materials as a static collection, overlooking the historical trajectory of materials discovery and the diverse practical factors that have driven its progress. Here we introduce ChronoSyn, a chronology-aware machine learning model that jointly learns synthesizability and the relative reporting order of known materials through a shared composition representation. Incorporating discovery chronology provides additional supervision beyond conventional synthesizability labels, improving prediction performance and enabling ChronoSyn to identify experimentally realizable compositions more effectively than baseline models. Applied to approximately 50 million hypothetical compositions, ChronoSyn identifies chemically coherent high-scoring families that include experimentally reported compositions unseen during training. These results highlight the chronology of materials discovery as an informative learning signal and suggest that the path along which known materials were discovered can point the way to those that will be discovered in the future.

item.title: Comprehensive QM/ML Study of Dislocation Loop Line Segments in {\alpha}-Zr Part I: <a> Loop Core Geometries, Solute Binding, and Transition Barriers
item.description: arXiv:2610.36619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zr cladding alloys in nuclear reactors are exposed to high neutron fluxes, making irradiation-induced defects and solute segregation central to understanding their in-service behaviour. Dislocation cores involve short-range chemistry and long-range elastic fields, which are difficult to describe simultaneously using conventional atomistic methods. Using a hybrid quantum mechanics/machine learning (QM/ML) framework, this part of work examines prismatic <a> loops in hcp {\alpha}-Zr. All three loop variants are considered, including faulted and perfect, interstitial- and vacancy-type, and first- and second-order prismatic configurations. Nine possible dislocation line segments are characterised in terms of core geometry, solute binding, glide barriers and faulted-to-perfect transition pathways using QM/ML and newly implemented QM/ML-NEB calculations. Shockley and half-Shockley partials, together with basal and prismatic fault ribbons, are found to govern core stabilisation. Fe and H preferentially bind to faulted segments, whereas Sn and Nb favour perfect segments. Solutes can also drive partial motion, recombination and local unfaulting. These results establish a comprehensive picture of <a> loop microstructure, solute trapping and transition mechanisms in {\alpha}-Zr.

item.title: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding
item.description: arXiv:2610.36673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.

item.title: Robustness of Anyonic Time-Domain Interference Against Dephasing
item.description: arXiv:2610.36686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent anyon-collider experiments have identified time-domain braiding (TDB) as a new route to probing anyonic statistics. However, how such time-domain interference responds to environmental noise remains an open question. Here we show that TDB interference is intrinsically more robust than its spatial counterpart. In conventional spatial interference, environmental noise induces phase fluctuations that accumulate throughout all paths, leading to exponential suppression of the interference as the dephasing rate increases. In TDB, by contrast, the interfering temporal paths experience largely overlapping environmental fluctuations, whose contributions cancel out in the relative phase, so that only a small nonoverlapping temporal window contributes to dephasing. As a result, TDB interference decays only algebraically with the dephasing rate, providing a new experimental hallmark for its identification. We propose a Fabry-Perot fractional quantum Hall setup in which both types of interference coexist and experience the same environmental noise, enabling a direct comparison of their dephasing behaviors. Our results establish robustness against dephasing as a fundamental advantage of TDB and suggest new opportunities for exploiting anyonic interference in noisy mesoscopic systems.

item.title: Magnon Super-Bloch Oscillations and Switchable Transport in Driven Magnonic Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2610.36721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Super-Bloch oscillations (SBOs) offer a powerful route to control wave packet propagation in driven lattices, yet their realization in magnonic systems has remained elusive. Here, we predict SBOs of magnon wave packets in periodic magnonic crystals driven by static and ac gradients of magnetic anisotropy field. A static gradient alone induces magnon Bloch oscillation (BO) with a constant carrier frequency. Remarkably, adding a near-resonant MHz-scale ac driving gives rise to a slow large-amplitude envelope oscillation, the hallmark of SBO. At exact resonance, the ac driving enables phase-controlled directional transport with a carrier-frequency shift up to GHz scale. Consequently, the same structure can be switched among three distinct regimes: conventional BO, SBO, and directed transport. Analytical expressions for the oscillation amplitudes, superperiod, drift velocity, and frequency evolution are validated by micromagnetic simulations. Extending to antiferromagnet magnonic crystals, we further demonstrate that these effects drive opposite motions of two oppositely polarized magnon modes in THz range. Our work establishes magnon SBOs as a versatile platform, opening a new avenue for reconfigurable magnonic devices.

item.title: Cu intercalation and field-driven filament formation in vertically aligned MoS$_2$ memristors
item.description: arXiv:2610.37152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vertically-aligned MoS$_2$ films paired with a Cu top electrode have been used as electrochemical metallization cell memristor devices. The memristive switching has been attributed to the formation of conductive filaments, yet their exact structure has remained elusive. Here we carry out a multi-scale computational study of Cu intercalation, clustering, and field-driven dynamics to eventually model the filament formation under operating conditions. We use density-functional theory results to fine-tune a machine learning force field, and the most important physical phenomena are further distilled into multi-particle kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. By exhaustive enumeration of Cu intercalated structures, we find the most stable structure at MoS$_2$Cu$_{0.11}$ composition, with Cu atoms forming a dice lattice between the MoS$_2$ layers. These structures are shown to exhibit metallic character and can thus form conductive filaments under memristor operation. The simulated switching speed and threshold voltage agree well with the available experimental data. Our results give fundamental insights on the device operation mechanism and guidelines for maximizing switching speed and endurance.

item.title: The Acridine Polymorph Landscape: Characterization and Selective Control by Additives
item.description: arXiv:2610.37597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polymorphism in molecular crystals presents a major challenge for controlling crystallization. Here, we combine experiment and theory to characterize the polymorph landscape of acridine and investigate its selective control by additives. Melt crystallization experiments resolve the previously unknown structure of form VIII, while topological crystal structure prediction recovers all seven known unsolvated polymorphs with determined crystal structures. Combining a fine-tuned machine-learned interatomic potential with anharmonic free energy calculations reproduces the experimentally observed stability relationships and reveals a shallow free energy landscape. Finally, experimentally observed additive-induced polymorph preferences correlate with mixed-crystal substitutional defect energies and topological similarities between additive and acridine crystal structures. Together, these results provide a comprehensive picture of acridine polymorphism, linking crystal structure, thermodynamic stability, and additive-controlled crystallization.

item.title: ODAT-SE: A modular and parallel framework for simulation-based inverse problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.36746v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open Data Analysis Tool for Science and Engineering (ODAT-SE) is an open-source Python framework for inverse problems that are solved by repeated forward simulations. It succeeds 2DMAT, which was developed for surface-structure analysis with quantum-beam diffraction and has since been applied to other fields. In version 3, the search algorithms were separated from the application-specific solvers, which became independent packages, and the software was renamed; this paper describes the current version 4.0. The framework connects optimization and sampling algorithms to solvers through a common interface for parameter mapping, constraints, and objective evaluation, so that an existing simulation code can be used with any of the algorithms. Relative to the previously published 2DMAT, it provides two-level MPI parallelism, which distributes candidate evaluations over processes and each evaluation over a parallel solver, checkpoint and continuation facilities, random search, global optimizers from SciPy, tensor-train optimization, and a Bayesian workflow that estimates partition-function ratios, model evidence, effective noise levels, and marginal posterior distributions. We validate the Bayesian workflow against closed-form results for a linear regression, benchmark tensor-train optimization on continuous, binary, and mixed-integer problems, and verify the two-level parallelization by the same optimum for all process decompositions. Taking up the positron-diffraction example of the 2DMAT paper, the workflow identifies the correlated structural solutions and an effective noise scale close to the imposed perturbation, while exposing incomplete convergence of symmetry-related mode weights. Solver packages, templates, and a gallery of examples support the use of the framework as a general platform for inverse-problem analysis.

item.title: Prospector: learning a compact graph traversal policy for scientific reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.37121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scientific reasoning in specialized engineering fields depends on knowledge scattered across the literature, often proprietary and absent from frontier LLM training data. In such domains, frontier models tend to give generic answers. Knowledge graphs (KGs) can ground LLM reasoning. Because a graph is too large to provide in full, typical LLM+KG systems preselect a portion, deciding relevance before reasoning begins. Here we train a compact model, Prospector, to reason over a domain knowledge graph by traversing it step by step, seeking evidence in light of what it has already found. Prospector calls a small set of tools one at a time to progressively build its context, and answers with a chain of evidence that can be checked edge by edge against what its tools retrieved from the graph. On a knowledge graph built from the semiconductor-manufacturing literature, Prospector approaches the strongest off-the-shelf models given the same graph and tools, and it far exceeds off-the-shelf models answering closed-book or from a pre-selected portion of the graph. Although trained only on the semiconductor graph, Prospector transfers to unseen knowledge graphs from three other distinct fields: bio-inspired materials, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and materials properties. Served on a single GPU, Prospector answers faster and at a fraction of the cost of a hosted service, while keeping proprietary data on the owner's hardware. We find that the policy's latent state is indicative of its next move on both seen and unseen graphs, and modulating the latent state can steer the policy from one behavior mode to another. These results suggest a practical LLM + KG paradigm for scientific and engineering reasoning over private data, in which a compact model trained on a graph from published literature transfers its traversal to unseen graphs that stay with their owners.

item.title: Machine learning cannot decarbonise the subsurface until it can be audited
item.description: arXiv:2603.14907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Geological CO2 storage, geothermal energy and underground hydrogen storage depend on irreversible or high-cost decisions made with sparse data and incomplete physical understanding. Machine learning (ML) increasingly informs these decisions, yet methods are usually judged on predictive accuracy rather than on whether their outputs can be trusted, traced and acted upon. We argue that subsurface ML should be designed as decision infrastructure with shared systems that carry calibrated uncertainty and provenance from observation to operating decision. We propose a decision-readiness checklist, an audit-trail workflow for monitoring updates, and benchmark designs that score models by the decisions they support. We identify validation needs shared across the three technologies, and the data-access and governance steps needed for ML to support regulatory and investment decisions.

item.title: Sustainability-Aware Discovery of Dual-Atom Hydrogen Evolution Catalysts via a Unified Machine Learning Framework for Activity and Carbon Cost
item.description: arXiv:2605.29821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Catalyst discovery for green hydrogen has optimized activity alone, deferring economic and environmental costs to stages where they disqualify otherwise promising candidates. Here we introduce a unified machine learning framework that screens catalytic activity and monetized carbon cost in a single pipeline. A machine learning potential predicts hydrogen evolution activity and stability at density-functional-theory accuracy. A second model, trained on published estimates of the social cost of carbon, converts each candidate's embodied CO2 into a monetary burden. Screening 460 graphene-supported dual-atom catalysts across 23 transition metals and 20 nitrogen-coordination motifs yields 26 active, synthesizable candidates. The two axes then conflict. The most active candidates span Mn-, Fe-, Zr-, Cr-, Cu-, Ni-, Ti-, Nb-, V-, Pd-, Au-, and Rh-based catalysts, indistinguishable in adsorption energy yet spanning a 58,000-fold range in carbon cost. Joint optimization selects Mn2@2Nf and Zr2@2Nc, matching the best precious-metal activity at tens-of-thousands-fold lower carbon cost, independent of catalyst loading.

item.title: Detailed balance in large language model-driven agents
item.description: arXiv:2512.10047v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agents are emerging as a powerful new paradigm for solving complex problems. Despite the empirical success of these practices, a theoretical framework to understand and unify their macroscopic dynamics remains lacking. This paper proposes a method based on the least action principle to estimate the underlying generative directionality of LLMs embedded within agents. By experimentally measuring the transition probabilities between LLM-generated states, we report evidence consistent with a tendency toward detailed balance in LLM-generated transitions, indicating that LLM generation may not be achieved by generally learning rule sets and strategies, but rather by implicitly learning a class of underlying potential functions that may transcend different LLM architectures and prompt templates. To our knowledge, this provides an effective macroscopic description of LLM generative dynamics that does not depend on specific model details. This work is an attempt to establish a macroscopic dynamics theory of complex AI systems, aiming to elevate the study of AI agents from a collection of engineering practices to a science built on effective measurements that are predictable and quantifiable.

item.title: Discovering quantum phenomena with Interpretable Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.16015v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpretable machine learning techniques are becoming essential tools for extracting physical insights from complex quantum data. We build on recent advances in variational autoencoders to demonstrate that such models can learn physically meaningful and interpretable representations from a broad class of unlabeled quantum datasets. From raw measurement data alone, the learned representation reveals rich information about the underlying structure of quantum phase diagrams. We further augment the learning pipeline with symbolic methods, enabling the discovery of compact analytical descriptors that serve as order parameters for the distinct regimes emerging in the learned representations. We demonstrate the framework on experimental Rydberg-atom snapshots, classical shadows of the cluster Ising model, and hybrid discrete-continuous fermionic data, revealing previously unreported phenomena such as a corner-ordering pattern in the Rydberg arrays. These results establish a general framework, which constitutes an important step toward the autonomous discovery of physical descriptors from diverse quantum datasets. All methods are available through qdisc, an open-source Python library designed to make these tools accessible to the broader community.

item.title: An Asymptotic Theory of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning
item.description: arXiv:2606.03217v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a widely used mechanism for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models by generating intermediate reasoning steps at inference time. Yet the scaling behavior of generalization with CoT depth remains poorly understood. To address this question, we study a theoretically solvable model of CoT for in-context weight prediction in linear regression, where test-time reasoning is represented as an iterative refinement of the weight-parameter estimate. Using tools from random matrix theory under high-dimensional asymptotics, we derive an exact formula for the generalization error as a function of reasoning depth, pretraining data amount, and context length. Our analysis reveals a sharp phase transition separating exponential and polynomial improvement, saturation, and overthinking, and characterizes how the optimal reasoning depth scales. We further show that deeper reasoning is most effective with sufficiently rich pretraining and in-context information, whereas limited pretraining or context makes longer reasoning prone to error amplification or saturation. We also validate these predictions through experiments on fully learned linear attention and softmax attention models. Our results provide a unified theoretical account of how test-time CoT depth affects generalization.

item.title: sft-wick: A formalism and package for Feynman-diagram expansion and evaluation in stochastic field theories
item.description: arXiv:2606.19480v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When stochastic field dynamics are cast into a path-integral formulation, perturbation theory becomes systematic but the resulting expansion quickly grows combinatorially large. The setting targeted here includes fields with several components and several dimensions, matrix propagators, tensor-valued couplings, and non-Gaussian driving noise specified by arbitrary n-point cumulants. Wick pairings grow factorially, and component indices must be routed through the tensor-valued vertices. The useful output is not a raw contraction list, but a diagram table: one entry per topology, with multiplicities, coupling sums, signs, and causal constraints resolved. We present sft-wick, an open-source Python package that constructs these diagram tables and computes their integrals numerically. Given an action and an observable, it enumerates topologically distinct Feynman diagrams, derives their algebraic coefficients, and evaluates the resulting diagram integrals from user-supplied response and cumulant functions. The core algorithm enumerates spatial topologies before routing component indices, avoiding contraction-by-contraction Wick expansion. Response-field constraints, including vanishing response-response contractions, the Ito prescription, and the absence of causal response loops, are enforced during enumeration. Predictions are validated against direct Langevin simulations in two worked examples, with Gaussian and with non-Gaussian driving noise, and agree with the simulations within stated error budgets.

item.title: Boundary-Canceled Score-Hamiltonian Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2609.05904v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion sampling is related to imaginary-time quantum annealing through a forward/backward Schr\"odinger equation pair and its one-sided counterdiabatic connection. For a smooth, gapped Score-Hamiltonian path, the exact connection transports the target density at any evolution time. We apply quantum-annealing performance analysis to residuals from approximating this connection with a trained score. If the first $r$ terminal schedule derivatives vanish, the squared Hellinger error scales as $T^{-2r-2}$, with a prefactor determined by the terminal learning residual and inverse gaps. Direct two-dimensional imaginary-time evolution with one fixed neural score reproduces these powers and prefactors. Terminal schedule design thus suppresses the distributional effect of imperfect score learning without retraining the network.

item.title: On the uniqueness of translation-invariant ground states of the $S=1$ Heisenberg and $J$--$D$ antiferromagnetic chains
item.description: arXiv:2610.34330v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using the analytic machinery and numerical inputs of OpenAI's proofs of the Haldane gap, we prove uniqueness of the translation-invariant ground state of the infinite $S=1$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain and of the $J$-$D$ model for sufficiently small $|D|$. Uniqueness is among all translation-invariant ground states in the operator-algebraic sense, without assuming a gap or spin-rotation symmetry for a competing state. The proof combines concentration of the spatial transfer spectrum, an exponentially small low-temperature free-energy correction, and a Golden--Thompson comparison for separated local observables. The unique translation-invariant state is pure, locally unique and gapped, and continuous in $D$. The ground states of even periodic chains and odd open chains with equal positive endpoint fields converge to this state along their full sequences, uniformly in $D$, with a stretched-exponential local rate. Every choice of ground states of open chains without endpoint magnetic fields has the same local limit. These conclusions do not establish uniqueness among arbitrary nontranslation-invariant ground states of the infinite chain. The author formulated the problems and proposed the core strategies. ChatGPT Astra made substantial contributions to developing the proofs and preparing the manuscript.
