item.title: Calcium Poly(heptazine imide): Reproducible Synthesis for Structural Analysis, Mechanism of CO2 Uptake, and Evaluation of Photocatalytic CO2- to-CO Conversion
item.description: The framework material, calcium poly(heptazine imide) or CaPHI, is reportedly capable for CO2 absorption, although harsh conditions from literature synthesis method result in low and unpredictable yield that hinders evaluation of its applicability for CO2 capture and conversion (CCC). This work presents a synthesis procedure for CaPHI with cross-laboratory reproducibility and scalable to 100s mg by employing a CaCl2-based eutectic as synthesis medium. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the PHI structure, with Ca2+ residing in the structural porosity having ionic conductivity of 10-10–10-11 S cm-1 as estimated by electrochemical measurements. In addition to the literature’s physisorption mechanism for dry CO2, we demonstrated these Ca2+ to participate in direct air capture of humid CO2, which chemisorbs as CaCO3 from structural analyses. For photocatalytic CO2-to-CO conversion, CaPHI outperforms its K+-bearing counterpart, which we speculatively attributed to strong Ca2+–CO2 interactions that concentrate this reactant near the active sites. In establishing a reliable synthesis and demonstrating its ability for CO2 capture and photoreduction, further optimization of CaPHI’s structure, morphology and compositing with co-catalyst could reveal its potential for CCC, while incorporation of mobile Ca2+ may represent a broad design principle warranting future research for material development for improving the efficiency of carbon capture & utilization.

item.title: Wigner Momentum Estimation and Sampling with Local Modes: A Second-Moment Approximation to High-Frequency Momentum Marginals
item.description: Instantaneous local Gaussian approximations assign nuclear momentum widths from the curvature of the potential at each sampled configuration. Strongly compressed bonds can consequently acquire large momentum widths even when their positions are drawn from an anharmonic path-integral ensemble. We estimate momentum covariances from pathintegral coordinates and forces in local modes that follow molecular deformations. These covariances define Gaussian approximations to high-frequency Wigner momentum marginals without evaluating a Hessian at each configuration. The resulting sampling recovers the Maxwell momentum distribution in the classical limit. A rotating bond model with harmonic stretching and periodic torsion agrees with an independent quantum reference within statistical uncertainty. For trans-azobenzene at 300 K with 32 beads, the most compressed C–H bond receives a mass-weighted momentum variance of 36.53 kJ mol−1 from LGA and 19.55 kJ mol−1 from the local covariance along the same physical stretch direction. Temporal holdout errors in C–H second moments are 7.2–7.6%, compared with 2.2–5.1% for LGA relative to the finite-bead reference; the demonstrated benefit concerns the suppression of local width spikes. The largest collective C–H width remains sensitive to estimator noise. These results support the method as an approximation to high-frequency momentum widths without a frequency cap. Position-conditioned quantum correlations, non-Gaussian tails, and the continuum-bead molecular limit remain outside the demonstrated accuracy.

item.title: Explainable Graph Neural Networks Reveal Molecular Features Associated with Umami Taste
item.description: Umami is one of the five basic tastes, and understanding the relationship between molecular structure and umami perception is important for food science. Although machine learning models have been developed to predict umami taste, the molecular features underlying their predictions remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we developed a graph neural network (GNN) model for umami taste prediction and investigated the structural features contributing to its predictions using Integrated Gradients (IG). Three datasets were constructed from ChemTastesDB, comprising 74 umami compounds and different sets of non-umami compounds. Under five-fold Murcko scaffold-disjoint cross-validation, the model achieved mean receiver operating characteristic areas under the curve of 0.935, 0.950, and 0.910 for the strict, full primary, and physicochemically matched datasets, respectively. Atom-level IG analysis revealed that functional-group prevalence did not necessarily correspond to positive attribution toward umami prediction. Notably, carboxylic acids occurred at similar frequencies in umami and non-umami compounds but showed significantly greater positive attribution in umami compounds. Furthermore, analysis of 31 structurally similar umami–nonumami molecular pairs demonstrated that regions specific to umami compounds generally received greater positive attribution than the corresponding regions in non-umami compounds. These findings suggest that the GNN captures molecular features associated with umami taste in a manner that depends on their surrounding structural context. Combining scaffold-disjoint prediction with atom-level attribution analysis provides an approach for investigating structure–taste relationships and identifying molecular features potentially relevant to umami perception.

item.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Synthetic Conditions and H2 Uptake Capacity in Oxidatively Activated Turbostratic Carbons through Machine Learning
item.description: The relationship between synthesis parameters, porosity, and H2 uptake in activated carbons is a field of significant investigation and discussion. Conclusions about these relationships are typically drawn from limited datasets of carbons produced for a given publication, and are not able to consider the interplay between various synthesis parameters and properties of the resultant turbostratic carbons. We present the first attempt at understanding the relationship between synthesis parameters and H2 uptake capacity in turbostratic carbons, using the single point pore volume as a proxy due to the dearth of available high pressure H2 isotherms. The methods used herein have exploited a dataset of 237 samples to determine the most important synthesis parameters in determining the porosity of the product and thus their suitability for high pressure H2 storage applications.

item.title: Spontaneous defect formation as the origin of superionic transitions in antifluorite-type structures
item.description: Solid-state electrolytes offer the possibility of safer and higher energy density batteries, yet only a limited number of materials achieve ionic conductivities suitable for practical applications. Type-II superionic conductors, which undergo continuous temperature-driven transitions between low and high ionic conductivity regimes are strong candidates for high-performance solid state electrolytes, but the transition mechanism is not sufficiently understood. In this study, we investigate the archetypical superionic conductors Li2O and Li2S with the antifluorite structure using long-time-scale molecular dynamics simulations with an Allegro machine-learning force field (MLFF) trained on density functional theory data selected using an on-the-fly active learning procedure. To this end, superionic transitions are identified around 1450 K for Li2O and around 1100 K for Li2S through continuous peaks in the heat capacity. Diffusion coefficients and concentration of Frenkel defects are found to exhibit strong non-Arrhenius behavior coinciding with the superionic transition where both diffusion activation energy and defect formation energy decrease significantly across the transition. This suggests a self-enhanced spontaneous defect formation mechanism, which drives the superionic transition and promotes increased ionic diffusion. These results identifies the microscopic origin of type-II superionic behavior as a result of correlated defect formation and support the design of improved solid-state electrolytes.

item.title: Factorised Cartesian Atomic Cluster Expansion for Low-Cost Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials can reach the accuracy of density functional theory at a fraction of its cost, but the most accurate equivariant models remain expensive, mainly because of the tensor operations they perform for every pair of neighbouring atoms. We present FACE, a factorised Cartesian atomic cluster expansion that removes this bottleneck. Each neighbour contributes only a small set of radial functions and messages, and all mixing of feature channels is done once per atom, so the cost per neighbour no longer grows with the size of the model. Custom GPU kernels evaluate the remaining steps, and long-range electrostatics, dispersion and short-range repulsion attach through a single interface. We show that the training divergences we encountered originate in how the network weights are scaled, and we introduce a distillation scheme in which an ensemble generates additional, uncertainty-checked training data. On five rMD17 molecules, with identical training budgets and hardware, FACE is about as accurate as a 64-channel MACE model (over three seeds: better on one molecule, within the seed spread on two, 7–14% higher force errors on two), while it is 5.7 times faster at inference (4.9 times at the same cutoff) and needs 3.5–3.9 times less GPU memory. Training costs about the same per step. Distillation lowers the energy and force errors of a single aspirin model by 20% at fixed width, to 2.26 meV and 6.74 meV/Å, close to the published MACE values (2.2 and 6.6), and the distilled model runs stably in molecular dynamics.

item.title: Reactive Machine-Learned Potentials Improve Predictions of Water Diffusion Behaviour in Defective Industrial Zeolite HY
item.description: Dealuminated HY (USY) zeolites are of major industrial catalytic importance, and the defects they contain, such as extraframework aluminum (EFAL) and silanol groups, strongly influence the behaviour of adsorbed species. Here, we show that reactive neural network-based machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) provide a substantial improvement in the simulation of water diffusion in these catalysts. They yield markedly improved agreement with quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) measurements of mobility for models of intact framework regions, refined further once EFAL and silanol defects are included explicitly, capturing the additional hindrance these sites impose on water motion. The ability of MLIPs to generate and stabilise realistic defect structures constitutes a step change in the molecular level and nanoscale modelling of industrial zeolites. This combined capability enables the quantitative investigation of defect-specific effects on nanoscale diffusion and provides a new approach for accurately modelling transport in industrially relevant zeolite catalysts.

item.title: The Nuclear Landscape: A Five-Variable 3D-Printed Representation of the Nuclides
item.description: Traditional charts of the nuclides convey proton number, neutron number, and one other property (e.g. half-life or decay mode). We describe the design and fabrication of a modular three-dimensional model of the nuclides that encodes five nuclear properties. Proton number and neutron number determine planar position, half-life is represented by column height using a quantile-logarithmic transformation, decay mode is represented by colour, and year of discovery is represented by the area of the top of the column. The model provides a tactile and visual representation of >3400 nuclides with the stable nuclides forming the spine of the model. The digital models were made by an iterative human-artificial intelligence (AI) co-design workflow in which generative AI helped translate educational objectives and geometric constraints into 3D printable stereolithography (STL) files. Feedback from visitors to the completed piece was uniformly positive when describing their interaction and learning experience. Complete datasets, STL files, and representative design prompts are provided to facilitate reproduction and adaptation for educational use.

item.title: Adsorption Free Energy of a Mobile Physisorbed Molecular Catalyst from Well-Tempered Metadynamics and from the Harmonic Approximation
item.description: The adsorption free energy of a molecular catalyst is usually calculated with harmonic frequency analysis of the optimized adsorbed structure, and errors are often blamed on anharmonicity. Here, using fac-Re(bpy)(CO)3Cl on graphene, we show that the main source of error is different. Harmonic analysis treats the complex as vibrating around a single minimum, but at 298 K, the complex can move across the surface, rotate around the surface normal, and rock. In this work, we use multiple-walker well-tempered metadynamics to sample the desorption coordinate and then convert the free-energy profile to a standard-state value, with the gas at 1 bar and the adsorbate at the standard surface concentration as recommended by Campbell et al. The result is ΔG°ads(298 K) = −64.1 ± 2.1 kJ mol−1 at PBE-D3(BJ), while the harmonic approximation gives −26.3 kJ mol−1. Of the 37.8 kJ mol−1 difference, only 1.7 kJ mol−1 comes from the anharmonic shape of the binding well along the surface normal; 36.3 kJ mol−1 is due to the frustrated translations and rotations of the bound complex, which the harmonic model treats as small vibrations around a single minimum. The two exceed the total by the 0.2 kJ mol−1 quantum-to-classical step, which acts in the opposite direction. Insertion-based estimators, which work well for small adsorbates in pores, do not apply here because the ensembles with and without the adsorbate–surface interaction are separated by 34 kBT and do not overlap. The missing entropy cancels out when comparing similar poses of the same adsorbate, but not when referencing the gas phase.

item.title: Toward Interpretable Graph-Based Machine Learning for Combustion Kinetic Model Generation
item.description: This work presents an atom-conserving and interpretable graph neural network (GNN) for combustion kinetic model generation, where atoms are represented as nodes, covalent bonds are represented as edges, and reactions are represented as bond-rearrangement operations. Its artificial-intelligence (AI) contribution is a reaction generator that extends a standard Graph Isomorphism Network with Edges (GINE) architecture through reaction-context embeddings, reaction branching & third-body reaction inputs, Arrhenius-rate-parameter prediction, pairwise decoding, and stochastic inference over evolving reactant pools. Trained on the Li–Dryer hydrogen combustion kinetic model (8 species and 21 reactions), the GNN reproduces trained chemistry and generates element-balanced new reactions and intermediate species outside the training dataset, many of which have experimental analogues. When trained on a subset of the Li–Dryer dataset, the model recovered most held-out reactions and revealed relationships between samples (reactions) in the model’s latent space. The results suggest that the model learns transferable local reaction structures and generates valid species and reactions. As with any reaction generators, the generated reaction models require thermochemical and kinetic verification; the intended engineering application is low-cost reaction-pathway exploration for new fuels and prioritization of experiments and first-principles calculations to develop new combustion kinetic models.

item.title: Charge Density Waves and In-Gap States in Coupled Chains and Moir\'e Superlattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.30281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Charge density waves (CDWs) arise from the interplay between electrons and lattice distortions and are a hallmark of low-dimensional systems. Here we study coupled Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains, both lattice-matched ladders and lattice-mismatched moir\'e superlattices, and find a rich set of CDW phases together with symmetry-protected bound states. In lattice-matched chains, the competition between electron-phonon coupling and interchain tunneling drives a sequence of CDW phases, including staggered dimers, trimers, and incommensurate states. These phases are generally gapped and host bound states protected by crystalline symmetries rather than chiral symmetry, and are therefore not pinned to zero energy. Lattice mismatch further reconstructs these phases into long-period supermoir\'e CDWs, with an ordered array of defects, pinned to the moir\'e length scale, that host localized electronic states. Interchain tunneling and lattice mismatch thus emerge as natural control parameters for CDW order and bound states in one-dimensional chains.

item.title: Decoding Composition-Structure-Performance Relations in Sodium Layered Oxide Positive Electrode Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.30591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layered sodium transition-metal (TM) oxides, Na$_x$TMO$_2$, are among the most promising sodium-ion positive electrode materials, yet their Na/vacancy orderings, layer stacking sequences, and cooperative Jahn--Teller distortions are known only for a few single-TM compounds. We compile the Na/vacancy orderings reported in earlier studies into a single library of 41 unique orderings and apply this uniformly to five single-TM and all ten Na$_x$TM$_{0.5}$TM$'_{0.5}$O$_2$ oxides (TM = Ti, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni), screening more than 120,000 structures with machine-learning interatomic potentials prior to 1,025 accurate first-principles calculations. The phase diagrams explain the observed O3/P3/O1 sequences and voltages, and the O3-to-P3 competition hinges on ordering energies of a few meV per atom that scalar descriptors, such as the cationic potential and the interlayer-slab distance, miss. Our extensive analysis reveals that the redox couples form a nearly partner-independent ladder, Ti$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Mn$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Co$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Ni$^{2+/3+}$ $<$ Fe$^{3+/4+}$, explaining pristine charge transfer and the oxidation sequence. Van Vleck analysis of every TMO$_6$ octahedron reveals that TM mixing suppresses the cooperative Jahn--Teller distortions of Mn$^{3+}$ and Ni$^{3+}$ through charge transfer to Jahn--Teller-inactive states or dilution of Jahn--Teller-active centers. We formulate an energy-density-versus-strain map that yields a design rule: a high-voltage couple without Jahn--Teller strain, which Mn$^{4+}$/Ni$^{2+}$ charge transfer realizes in Na$_x$Mn$_{0.5}$Ni$_{0.5}$O$_2$, the most practical composition. We release the ordering-resolved dataset as a training set for subsequent training of accurate machine-learning interatomic potentials.

item.title: How good are universal MLIPs for alloys? A benchmark is only as trustworthy as its controls
item.description: arXiv:2610.30641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are ranked by their formation-energy error against a DFT database, as if that database were ground truth, but independent DFT databases disagree. We benchmark fourteen uMLIPs on 1.45 million ordered intermetallics against AFLOW, which none trained on, and compare every energy and stability error with that disagreement. For half the structures, AFLOW, Alexandria, and OQMD differ by less than 6-8 meV/atom, but a minority differ by far more, raising the average to 16-30. That disagreement sets a floor on any model's measurable error. Re-referenced, the best uMLIP agrees with AFLOW as closely as Alexandria does, and the next four sit 2-7 meV/atom above the floor. Once broken elemental references are screened, the energy and stability rankings agree almost everywhere. Three apparent model failures shrink or vanish under the right control: poorly correlated shear moduli, thousands of "bad" DFT references, and the leader's inflated lead.

item.title: From phase analysis to phase tracking: a robust approach to atomic-scale strain mapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.30665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomic-scale strain governs the electronic, ferroic and mechanical properties of materials, and atomic-resolution microscopy measures it most directly. Geometric phase analysis (GPA) is the standard tool, but it fails when a Bragg reflection moves outside its fixed Fourier aperture under large strain or rotation, or in misoriented grains. Here we introduce geometric phase tracking analysis (GPTA), whose Fourier aperture tracks the Bragg reflection at each pixel in real space. A narrow aperture can therefore reject noise without losing a displaced reflection. On 13,795 simulated and experimental atomic-resolution images under various imaging conditions, GPTA reduces GPA's failure rate from 27% to 11.5% with up to 335 times better accuracy. It also gives strain and dislocation maps across grains, resistance to dynamical-scattering extinction, and a confidence map, capabilities that GPA lacks. Tracking the aperture combines reciprocal-space dose efficiency with real-space spatial resolution and extends atomic-scale strain metrology to beam-sensitive materials and challenging imaging conditions.

item.title: Thermal expansion mechanisms, heat transport, and band-gap renormalization in strongly anharmonic Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ from machine-learned interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.30918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ are structurally complex materials whose thermal expansion has been interpreted, on the basis of high-temperature x-ray diffraction, in terms of specific polyhedral rearrangements. We study their lattice dynamics and its consequences for thermal and electronic properties using molecular dynamics with actively learned moment tensor potentials trained on density-functional theory data. The anharmonicity measure $\sigma^A$ (compares the anharmonic contribution to the interatomic forces with the total forces acting on atoms) reaches $\approx$0.3-0.5 for $\beta$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ and $\approx$0.75 for orientationally disordered $\alpha$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, and the imaginary harmonic modes of Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ and $\alpha$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$ are stabilized at finite temperature. The simulations reproduce the measured thermal expansion and support the mechanisms proposed from diffraction: expansion along $c$ in $\beta$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$ arises from both elongation and straightening of corrugated Rb chains, BO$_3$ reorientation accompanies the anisotropic expansion of Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$, and bending of polyhedral linkages limits expansion along the weakly expanding directions and in cubic Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$. Green-Kubo lattice thermal conductivities differ by more than an order of magnitude between compounds with comparable $\sigma^A$, showing that the anharmonicity measure alone does not determine heat transport. Phonon-induced band-gap renormalization, including lattice thermal expansion, reaches 2.7 and 1.7 eV at 1250 K in Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ and 1.4 eV at 650 K in $\beta$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, with zero-point renormalizations of 0.64, 0.70, and 0.31 eV for $\beta$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$, respectively.

item.title: Anomalous polar chains in halide perovskites
item.description: arXiv:2610.31184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local polar distortions, their collective ordering, and their field-driven reversal have been studied extensively in ferroelectric perovskites for decades. Here we identify an unusual behavior in the ferroelectric halide perovskite CsGeBr3 using large-scale molecular dynamics with first-principles-trained interatomic potentials. In its nominally cubic phase the Ge off-centering forms one-dimensional polar chains that extend over at least tens of nanometers and relax on nanosecond timescales, four orders of magnitude slower than in BaTiO3 and PbTiO3, with CsSnBr3 in between. The cubic CsGeBr3 phase is a dynamically disordered state in which oppositely polarized chains flip throughout the crystal, and a long-lived one-dimensional local polarization coexists with zero net polarization. A simple three-dimensional perovskite thus hosts long-ranged one-dimensional polar correlations with remarkably slow dynamics. In the ferroelectric phase the same chains set a one-dimensional switching mechanism, in which the polarization reverses chain by chain.

item.title: Dynamical Nonrelativistic Spin Splitting via THz Nonlinear Phononics
item.description: arXiv:2607.10091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) in collinear antiferromagnets, including altermagnets and compensated ferrimagnets, offers a route to high-frequency spintronics immune to stray fields, but its dynamic control has remained elusive. We demonstrate, using density functional theory (DFT) and nonlinear phononics, that THz laser pulses can achieve ultrafast, reversible control of NRSS on picosecond timescales in antiferromagnets. We derive two mode-selection criteria, accounting for phonon and magnetic wavevector compatibility and inversion parity, to identify which phonon modes can activate NRSS. Our calculations illustrate the creation of NRSS in spin-degenerate NiO and the enhancement of existing splitting in LaFeO$_3$. While practical implementation depends on excitation conditions, lattice dynamics, and mode coupling, these results establish design principles for identifying materials with stronger and more accessible responses. Limitations imposed by driving fields, phonon damping, and anharmonic detuning motivate further materials screening based on accessible excitation strengths, lattice stability, resonance frequency matching, and favorable anharmonic coupling.

item.title: Extended strange metal and superconductivity in partially filled moir\'e Hubbard bands
item.description: arXiv:2610.22307v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Moir\'e semiconductors provide a physical realization of the Hubbard model. Bandwidth-tuned Mott transitions and complex phase diagrams mimicking those of high-temperature superconductors have been demonstrated near a weak Mott insulating state at half-band-filling. The platform also provides an opportunity to explore the physics of a partially filled Hubbard band at doping densities far away from the Mott insulator, a regime that has remained largely unexplored. Here we report the emergence of an extended strange metal (ESM), in both doping density and twist angle, in a partially filled Hubbard band of twisted bilayer WSe2. The ESM is in the clean limit, persists down to about 50mK, and spans over multiple symmetry-breaking ground states; it also appears only at small twist angles, where electronic correlations are strong. These observations distinguish the state from the reported strange metals associated with quantum criticality and favor the viewpoint that it is an intrinsic state of matter. We also report the observation of a new superconducting dome being developed from the ESM but far away from both the Mott insulating state and the van Hove singularity of the material. Our work opens the door to exploring the new regime of partially filled Hubbard bands in the clean limit.

item.title: Origins of Faceted Anomalous Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2610.26356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fluctuating interfaces are typically characterized by their global, spectral, and local roughness exponents. Faceted anomalous scaling, characterized by $\alpha_s>1$, $\alpha_s\neq\alpha$, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}=1$, owes its name to the tendency of such interfaces to develop long, nearly linear segments called facets. Its statistical origin, and whether facets are required, have remained unclear. We show that this exponent structure is determined by the spatial statistics of the slope field. Slope increments split into typical fluctuations and rare, larger jumps. This anomalous scaling arises either when the typical slope increment displays genuine system-size-dependent anomalous scaling or when the rare jumps dominate the second moment. The two contributions can coexist, and their competition leads to bifractal scaling of the slopes. We establish this framework analytically in the generalized anharmonic Larkin model and the columnar Kardar--Parisi--Zhang equation, and we derive exactly the global, spectral, and local roughness exponents in both cases. The Larkin model realizes both mechanisms and produces anomalous interfaces with or without facets, whereas columnar KPZ belongs to the jump-dominated case and yields $\alpha_s=3/2$.

item.title: Meta-learning of Gibbs states for many-body Hamiltonians with applications to Quantum Boltzmann Machines
item.description: arXiv:2507.16373v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The preparation of quantum Gibbs states is a fundamental challenge in quantum computing, essential for applications ranging from modeling open quantum systems to quantum machine learning. Building on the Meta-Variational Quantum Eigensolver framework proposed by Cervera-Lierta et al. and a problem-driven ansatz design, we introduce two meta-learning algorithms: Meta-Variational Quantum Thermalizer (Meta-VQT) and Neural Network Meta-VQT (NN-Meta VQT) for efficient thermal state preparation of parametrized Hamiltonians on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Meta-VQT utilizes a fully quantum ansatz, while NN Meta-VQT integrates a quantum--classical hybrid architecture. Both use collective optimization over a finite set of training parameter values to prepare approximate Gibbs states at held-out parameter values within the sampled parameter domain. We validate our methods on Transverse Field Ising Models (TFIM) with up to eight qubits and on a two-qubit Heisenberg model with all field terms. Within these finite-size benchmarks, the trained models accurately prepare thermal states at test points inside the training interval. For the six and eight qubit cases of TFIM, meta-learned parameters when combined with appropriately designed ansatz serve as warm-start initializations, significantly outperforming random initializations in the optimization tasks. Furthermore, a 3 qubit Kitaev ring example showcases our algorithm's effectiveness across finite-temperature crossover regimes. Finally, we apply our algorithms to train a Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM) on a 2-qubit Heisenberg model with all field terms, achieving enhanced training efficiency, improved Gibbs state accuracy, and a 30-fold runtime speedup over existing techniques such as variational quantum imaginary time (VarQITE)-based QBM highlighting the practicality of meta-algorithm-based QBMs.

item.title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.27762v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

item.title: Structural basis of bile acid lateral diffusion facilitated by the OSTα/β transporter
item.description:

item.title: Using NMR to predict molecular reactivity
item.description: NMR chemical shifts are plainly transformed into machine learning features that have rational and intuitive chemical meaning. A small number of these features are used to predict molecular reactivity (via the HOMO-LUMO energy gap), resulting in a model that is not reliant on a priori knowledge of chemical structure or charge.

item.title: Charge-Transfer-State Descriptors from Donor–Acceptor Interfaces Enable Improved Prediction of Indoor Organic Photovoltaic Efficiency
item.description: Organic photovoltaic (OPV) devices have attracted significant attention as lightweight, flexible, and solution-processable alternatives to conventional solar cells. In this work, a novel computational workflow was developed to generate donor–acceptor interfacial adducts for non-fullerene acceptor (NFA)-based indoor OPV systems and to investigate their charge-transfer (CT) characteristics using density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT calculations. Molecular docking followed by excited-state analysis enabled identification of important CT descriptors, including excitation energies, electron–hole separation, participation ratios, and charge-transfer characteristics. A dataset containing 30 donor–acceptor pairs were subsequently constructed by combining these CT descriptors with molecular fingerprints and frontier molecular orbital (FMO) parameters. Machine learning (ML) models based on ElasticNet and XGBoost algorithms were then trained to predict OPV power conversion efficiency (PCE). Our results demonstrate that incorporating physically meaningful CT descriptors derived from donor–acceptor interfaces significantly improve the ML-based prediction of OPV efficiencies from a small dataset.

item.title: PerMix: Algorithmic Pathway Planning for Multicomponent Halide Perovskite Synthesis
item.description: The reproducible growth of multicomponent halide perovskite single crystals depends critically on the stoichiometry of the precursor solution: even small deviations introduced during weighing or dissolution can change phase purity, defect density, and the lattice parameters of the resulting crystals. Today, recipes for such systems are still planned largely by hand in spreadsheets, which are error-prone, difficult to audit, and impractical for the compositional spaces of multicomponent solid solutions. We present PerMix, an open-source Python framework that formalizes precursor planning as a constrained mass-balance problem and solves it transparently. The stoichiometric model, the combinatorial enumeration of precursor pathways based on a rigid/flexible partition of cations, tolerance-based validation, deduplication of identical salt formulations, deterministic ranking of pathways, geometric stability indicators (Goldschmidt tolerance and octahedral factors), and the SQLite reference database are described in full, with every governing equation stated explicitly. The tool was used to grow nine (MA1−xCsx)Pb(Br1−zYz)3 (Y = Cl, I) single crystals by antisolvent vapor-assisted crystallization; X-ray diffraction shows the systematic lattice expansion and contraction expected from the nominal substitutions. We also discuss the limits of the approach explicitly: precursor stoichiometry does not account for ion segregation, and quantitative composition analysis as well as homogeneity profiling are identified as future work.

item.title: VHH-Bench: A Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating Nanobody–Antigen Complex Predictions Across CDR3 Conformations
item.description: Accurate prediction of nanobody–antigen complex structures is critical for the development of diagnostic, therapeutic and biosensing applications. However, progress in this area have been constrained by the limited availability of experimentally determined nanobody–antigen complex structures. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled highly accurate prediction of protein structures and protein-protein complexes, yet accurate modelling of nanobody–antigen interactions remains challenging due to the diverse binding modes exhibited by nanobodies. Here, we present VHH‑Bench, a benchmarking workflow for the systematic evaluation of nanobody–antigen complex structure prediction methods. We curated a non-redundant dataset of experimentally resolved nanobody–antigen complexes and evaluated six state-of-the-art models: AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Chai-1, ESMFold2, HelixFold3 and Protenix-v2. Complexes were stratified according to CDR3 conformation, enabling separate assessment of kinked and extended nanobody classes. Prediction performance varied substantially between models and conformational classes. Protenix-v2 achieved the highest overall docking accuracy, success rate and proportion of high-quality predictions, with its advantage most pronounced for nanobodies with extended CDR3 conformations. In contrast, all evaluated models showed reduced accuracy and higher failure rates for complexes containing kinked nanobodies. While increased stochastic sampling provided slight improvements in some cases, its overall impact was limited and did not substantially affect the relative performance ranking of the evaluated models. VHH-Bench provides an extensible and reproducible benchmarking workflow for standardised dataset curation, nanobody classification, model evaluation and confidence analysis, facilitating the rigorous assessment and future development of nanobody–antigen complex prediction methods. The VHH-Bench framework is available at https://github.com/haiboyugroup/VHH-Bench.

item.title: UNDERSTANDING THE ROLE OF AROMATICITY IN TAUTOMERIC EQUILIBRIA
item.description: Tautomerism, the interconversion of small molecules via proton and π-electron shifts, poses a fundamental challenge in drug discovery, as different tautomers can exhibit distinct physicochemical properties and receptor-binding profiles, while computational approaches have been widely applied to predict tautomeric equilibria, most methods often overlook electronic properties such as aromaticity, which are critical to molecular stability. Here, we explore the role of aromaticity in tautomeric equilibria using a computational framework that integrates density functional theory (DFT) calculations with interpretable machine learning (ML) models. Aromaticity, which is challenging to measure experimentally, is quantified via Harmonics Oscillator Model of Aromaticity (HOMA) values and incorporated as a molecular descriptor. To enhance interpretability, we employ shallow ML models and assess feature contributions both intrinsically and using post-hoc explainability techniques. Our results demonstrate that both intrinsic and post hoc feature importance approaches capture similar trends associated with aromaticity. This highlights the complex influence of aromaticity on tautomeric equilibria and suggest that ML models, when combined with quantum-mechanics-based descriptors and explainable feature analyses, could be applied more broadly to capture important trends in other physicochemical properties beyond tautomer stability.

item.title: GVIM 2.0: A Multi-Agent Research System for Chemistry and Materials Science
item.description: Large language models are increasingly used as natural-language interfaces for chemistry and materials research, but their utility in scientific workflows depends on their ability to connect user requests with executable tools, structured data handling, and verifiable outputs. Here, we present GVIM 2.0, a multi-agent research system designed to support computational and informatics workflows in chemistry and materials science. GVIM 2.0 integrates language-model-based task planning with domain-specific Skills, packagebacked computational tools, sandboxed execution, and artifact generation. On a 400-question public benchmark suite spanning ChemBench, MaScQA, and ChemLLMBench, the complete GVIM 2.0 workflow answered 325/400 questions correctly, achieving an accuracy of 81.25%, compared with 285/400 questions and 71.25% accuracy for a same-base API-only baseline. We further evaluated GVIM 2.0 on task-native workflows covering molecular solubility prediction, steel yield-strength prediction, reaction-table extraction, MS/MS spectral retrieval, chemical entity extraction, retrospective BACE inhibitor prioritization, Matbench experimental band-gap modelling, and temporal external validation of BACE1 activity prediction. These workflows generated inspectable outputs, including prediction files, metrics, figures, and reports. The results show that GVIM 2.0 can organize reproducible data-to-result workflows for selected chemistry and materials informatics tasks, providing a practical framework for tool-augmented scientific research assistance.

item.title: Wigner Momentum Estimation and Sampling with Local Modes: A Second-Moment Approximation to High-Frequency Momentum Marginals
item.description: Instantaneous local Gaussian approximations assign nuclear momentum widths from the curvature of the potential at each sampled configuration. Strongly compressed bonds can consequently acquire large momentum widths even when their positions are drawn from an anharmonic path-integral ensemble. We estimate momentum covariances from pathintegral coordinates and forces in local modes that follow molecular deformations. These covariances define Gaussian approximations to high-frequency Wigner momentum marginals without evaluating a Hessian at each configuration. The resulting sampling recovers the Maxwell momentum distribution in the classical limit. A rotating bond model with harmonic stretching and periodic torsion agrees with an independent quantum reference within statistical uncertainty. For trans-azobenzene at 300 K with 32 beads, the most compressed C–H bond receives a mass-weighted momentum variance of 36.53 kJ mol−1 from LGA and 19.55 kJ mol−1 from the local covariance along the same physical stretch direction. Temporal holdout errors in C–H second moments are 7.2–7.6%, compared with 2.2–5.1% for LGA relative to the finite-bead reference; the demonstrated benefit concerns the suppression of local width spikes. The largest collective C–H width remains sensitive to estimator noise. These results support the method as an approximation to high-frequency momentum widths without a frequency cap. Position-conditioned quantum correlations, non-Gaussian tails, and the continuum-bead molecular limit remain outside the demonstrated accuracy.

item.title: Interstitial Oxygen and a Two-Dimensional Migration Pathway in Mo-Substituted Palmierite Ba3V2−xMoxO8+x/2
item.description: Palmierite oxides are promising oxide-ion conductors, with conductivities exceeding those of related hexagonal perovskite derivatives. However, aliovalent Mo6+ substitution in Ba3V2O8 has previously been demonstrated only at high substitution levels. Here, the Ba3V2-xMoxO8+x/2 series (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.3) was investigated using X-ray and neutron powder diffraction, 51V and 17O solid-state NMR spectroscopy combined with density functional theory (DFT), and bond-valence site-energy (BVSE) calculations. Combined Rietveld refinement reveals that Mo6+ substitution introduces a charge-compensating interstitial oxygen site (O3) at x = 0.3, transforming isolated (V, Mo)O4 tetrahedra into corner-sharing polyhedra with mixed coordination. DFT-supported 17O NMR identifies additional oxygen environments associated with Mo in four- and five-fold coordination, suggesting oxygen bridges between adjacent MoO5 polyhedra. 51V NMR confirms predominantly tetrahedral vanadium coordination, alongside a minority V environment , distorted by occupation of a nearby O3 site. BVSE calculations indicate that O3 bridges neighboring polyhedra in the abplane, enabling a low-barrier, two-dimensional oxide-ion migration pathway involving apical O1 and interstitial O3 sites. These findings establish interstitial oxygen incorporation as the key structural mechanism facilitating low-barrier two-dimensional oxide-ion transport at low Mo substitution levels in the palmierite family, with broader implications for hexagonal perovskite ionic conductors.

item.title: ChemEidos: Synthesis-Aware Multimodal Foundation Models for Domain-Specific Generative Design
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence models for de novo drug discovery often suffer synthetic tractability issues and lack fidelity in underrepresented chemical domains. This white paper highlights ChemEidos, a novel multimodal generative design platform that utilizes the underlying patterns, forms, and organizing principles of chemical space (eidos) by incorporating expert domain knowledge in focused training sets and at inference time.

item.title: Universality of Lithium Metal and Solid Electrolyte Interphase Descriptors of Coulombic Efficiency Governed by Lithium Connectivity
item.description: Coulombic efficiency (CE) is a key metric governing the cyclability of lithium metal anodes, motivating efforts to identify physicochemical descriptors that correlate with CE. Diverse descriptors spanning electrolyte thermodynamics and interphase properties have been proposed, but their interrelationships and underlying physical origins remain unclear. Here we show that, when evaluated across a consistent electrolyte set, these descriptors exhibit a common hockey-stick relationship with CE that can be unified through the mesoscale connectivity of lithium deposits. A percolation-like transition from isolated deposits to interconnected networks sharply suppresses inactive Li0 formation during stripping, which underlies the common CE transition across descriptors. Tuning plating current density reproduces this transition within individual electrolytes, demonstrating that connectivity is not uniquely determined by electrolyte chemistry. These findings establish lithium connectivity as a common mechanistic basis for diverse CE correlations and provide a framework for interpreting these correlations across distinct capacity-loss regimes.

item.title: Tunable Emission from Quasi-2D Perovskites via Electrospinning
item.description: Quasi-2D Ruddlesden-Popper halide perovskites are promising materials for light-emitting applications. They comprise corner-sharing metal-halide octahedra separated by bulky, insulating organic spacers and exhibit tunable bandgaps by varying the number of octahedral layers, n. Isolating a single n-phase within a film remains challenging, with spin-coated films generally containing a broad distribution of n phases. Their emission is dominated by the largest n-number present due to energy funneling towards narrow bandgap phases. Here, we electrospin phenylethylammonium (PEA+)/methylammonium (MA+) lead bromide quasi-2D perovskites into 140 - 400 nm nanofibers to restrict molecular diffusion. We observe progressive redshifts in absorption and photoluminescence from blue (410 nm) to cyan (470 nm) to green (530 nm) with decreasing PEA+:MA+ molar ratio. In contrast, spin-coated films with the same PEA+:MA+ ratios exhibit green emission (524 - 532 nm) across all MA+ containing compositions. Transient absorption spectroscopy reveals energy transfer within 80 ps from low n phases to MAPbBr3 domains in spin-coated films, which are absent in electrospun fibers. Electrospun fibers are also highly emissive compared to spin-coated films, with average photoluminescence quantum yields up to 77±1%. These results suggest that electrospinning limits organic cation diffusion to selectively stabilize intermediate n phases, providing a scalable route to achieve tunable solid-state emission.

item.title: Accelerating Mechanistic Understanding and Prediction of Chemical Selectivity with Foundation Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Selectivity in chemical reactions is often dictated by small energetic differences between competing transition states of less than 2 kcal mol-1. Computational predictions of selectivity for organic and organometallic reactions must reach these levels of quantitative accuracy, while simultaneously navigating the mechanistic and conformational complexity involved. Here, we assess the suitability of foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for this task. We introduce the SELECT50 dataset, a chemically diverse collection of paired selectivity-determining transition state structures, evaluated at the ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD//ωB97X-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVP level of theory, spanning representative cases of kinetically-controlled stereo-, chemo- and regioselectivities, along with competing mechanistic pathways. We compare the performance of four MLIPs, alongside semiempirical and low-cost quantum chemical approaches, in determining transition state geometries, energetic discrimination, and pathway ordering. The Universal Model for Atoms MLIPs UMA-M-1.1 and UMA-S-1.2 predict relative transition state energies with sub-kcal mol-1 accuracy and mean absolute errors of 0.36 and 0.44 kcal mol-1, providing saddle points that closely reproduce triple-ζ DFT geometries. DFT single-point refinement further reduced the mean absolute error (MAE) to 0.25 kcal mol-1, supporting DFT//MLIP as a practical strategy for selectivity prediction. The major reaction pathway was correctly assigned in up to 98% of cases. Beyond individual transition structures, MLIPs reproduce complete organic and organometallic reaction landscapes and enable full-system treatment of selectivity-determining assemblies containing up to 211 atoms. Finally, MLIP-derived transition state energetics strongly track experimental selectivity across Ni- and Pd catalyzed reaction families (R2 = 0.87–0.90; ρ = 0.80), and with calibration, yield mean held-out MAEs of 0.12 and 0.63 kcal mol-1. Our results position foundation MLIPs as practical surrogates for the exploration and screening stages of DFT-based mechanistic analyses, enabling the throughput required for large-scale catalyst, substrate, and reaction screening.

item.title: FAIRaman: making clinical Raman spectroscopy data FAIR through biobanking and NeXus standards
item.description: Raman spectroscopy is increasingly applied in biomedical and diagnostic research, generating spectral datasets that could support the development of robust artificial intelligence (AI) models for disease diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment guidance. However, most clinical Raman datasets remain difficult to reuse across laboratories because spectra are often stored separately from structured metadata describing the samples, their clinical context, experimental conditions, and data governance. This limits reproducibility, external validation, multicentre integration, and the development of transferable models.Here, we introduce FAIRaman, a FAIR-by-design framework and open-source software tool for the structured organisation of clinical Raman spectroscopy data. FAIRaman combines the hierarchical logic of the Investigation–Study–Assay (ISA) model with biobanking-derived descriptors for sample, donor, and processing-event annotation, and with NeXus/NXraman-inspired metadata for Raman acquisition parameters and spectral data. The resulting structure implemented in the open HDF5 file format. The software, developed in Python, converts native Renishaw WDF files and vendor-neutral text-based spectral files into FAIRaman-compliant HDF5 files through a graphical user interface (GUI), allowing users to combine batch-level metadata with sample-specific clinical data. We demonstrate the framework using a real Raman map of breast cancer tissue, and a Raman spectrum acquired from plasma-derived extracellular vesicles. These examples show that spectral data, acquisition metadata, and clinical sample descriptors can be stored within a single structured file and that the stored information can be easily retrieved using independent, freely available software tools.

item.title: Cellulose Coating Altered the Electro-Chemo-Mechanical Evolution of Sodium Thioantimonate Electrolyte in Solid-state Sodium Batteries: An Operando Raman Study
item.description: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) attracted increasing attention due to their improved safety and energy densities; yet electrolyte decomposition and subsequent contact loss limited the interfacial stability of ASSBs. Herein, we report an operando Raman characterization that provides high voltage, time, and spatial resolutions, which enables simultaneous analysis of interfacial decomposition mechanism and morphological evolution. Using Na3SbS4 electrolyte (NSS) and its carboxymethyl-cellulose-encapsulated analogue (NSS-CMC) as exemplars, we precisely contrasted the subtle differences in the two-step reduction mechanism of the two electrolytes. In both systems, Na3SbS3 formed as an intermediate, and Na3Sb binary as one major final product; while the CMC coating altered the kinetics of Na3SbS3 formation and consumption, and extended the formation potential of Na3Sb from 1.35 V (seen in NSS) to 0.50 V (vs. Na/Na+). Oxidation of NSS and NSS-CMC both occur near 2.20 V, although CMC coating altered the crystallinity of the oxidative products. Simultaneously, we captured phenomena that are unique to solid-state electrochemical systems such as particle relocation, morphological change, and reversed reactions. We inferred CMC’s dual role as a voltage barrier and a mechanical buffer in suppressing the electro-chemo-mechanical decomposition of NSS electrolyte. The deep mechanistic insights unravel the exact modification needed for improved interfacial stability.

item.title: The Illusion of Chemical Continuity Limits Machine Learning Generalization
item.description: The central dogma of materials informatics is the "Scaling Hypothesis": the assumption that chemical space is a continuous manifold, and that, with sufficient data, deep learning models can approximate any structure-property relationship. While this strategy has achieved near-DFT accuracy for thermodynamic properties like formation energy, prediction accuracy for bandgaps suffers from a fundamental, non-converging error floor (~0.4 eV). By analyzing a comprehensive dataset of binary semiconductors and state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (including coGN and foundational embeddings), this work isolates the root cause: unlike the smooth, transferable landscape of total energy, the electronic bandgap manifold is topologically disjoint. Consequently, increasing dataset size fails to improve predictions, instead resulting in negative learning, where increasing the structural diversity of the training set (e.g., adding rocksalt data to zincblende models) degrades prediction accuracy for unseen chemistries. This can be traced back to the discrete quantization of atomic orbitals and the resulting band crossings, which create non-differentiable cusps in the property surface. This work establishes a boundary condition for the "Big Data" paradigm: simple regression on atomic coordinates cannot resolve the intrinsic discontinuities of eigenvalue phenomena. Instead, a more detailed integration of quantum mechanics is required, such as direct entrainment of Hamiltonians as descriptors.

item.title: Ionic Microenvironment Regulator Enables Enhanced Anion Trapping in Cationic Poly(Ionic Liquid) Solid Electrolyte for Low‐Temperature Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description: Advanced Functional Materials, EarlyView.

item.title: Hereditary Effective Atom Theory for Large-Scale Atomic Structure Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.28996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting the atomic structure of large systems requires simultaneous exploration of atomic positions, species, and, generally, the number of atoms. The combinatorial growth of possible arrangements can make this search difficult even for standard genetic algorithms. We introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), which integrates Effective Atom Theory into a genetic algorithm to enable efficient global search through a differentiable effective-atom representation. Central to the method is a crossover scheme that directly superimposes two parent structures and relaxes the combined structure. HEAT outperforms conventional genetic-algorithm baselines in recovering a missing 240-atom H sublattice, predicting a 364-atom edge-dislocation core, and reconstructing twisted-bilayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ containing 1150 atoms from ptychographic constraints. These results demonstrate how continuous effective-atom relaxation improves the exploration of large combinatorial structure spaces.

item.title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Glasses via Microgel Particle Stiffness
item.description: arXiv:2610.29389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, the stiffness of the constituent particles governs their deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, thereby dictating the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N'-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses and establishing Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.

item.title: Construction of highly coarse-grained molecular models for aqueous electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2610.29653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular modelling of electrochemical systems at larger than atomic scales poses particular challenges, not least the ability to represent correct thermodynamic, hydrodynamic and dielectric properties while still being computationally viable for large scale applications. In the case of aqueous electrolytes such as those used in vanadium-based batteries with oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions, both a background medium that can respond to localised electric fields due to high-valence ions and control over ion transport properties are crucial to embed consistently in the model. To this end, we propose the use of Dissipative Particle Dynamics (DPD) combined with a newly-devised highly coarse-grained polarisable water model with pairwise interactions designed to produce realistic thermodynamic behaviour as the basis for the aqueous electrolytes found in vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB). We consider how the core water model can be modified to incorporate the ionic species found in VRFB catholytes and anolytes, as well as how the DPD pairwise thermostat forces can be parameterised to attain realistic diffusivities for those species.

item.title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.29895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

item.title: Hierarchical Response Theory of Electronegativity from Atomic Mean Inner Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.29765v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electronegativity, introduced by Pauling nearly a century ago, remains chemistry's most widely used yet conceptually ambiguous quantity: is it a fixed atomic constant, or does it depend on chemical environment? We resolve this debate by recasting electronegativity as a continuous response function rooted in the Atomic Mean Inner Potential (AMIP), a quantum-mechanical observable accessible through first-principles calculation and, ultimately, electron holography. Expanding the AMIP with respect to fractional electron removal defines a hierarchy of physically distinct coefficients: the static electronegativity $\chi_0$, the Electrostatic Rigidity $\mathcal{R}$---whose sign indicates whether an atom hardens or softens upon oxidation---and the Electrostatic Anharmonic Modulus $\mathcal{A}$. A logarithmic-derivative decomposition links these coefficients to two competing microscopic channels, electronic screening loss and geometric volume collapse, whose balance governs the response of all 102 elements. This competition produces a systematic dichotomy between softening main-group elements and hardening d-block elements, two scaling laws within the transition series (closed-shell stiffening and principal quantum softening), and two anomalies: a pronounced exchange-driven effect at half-filled d$^{5}$ configurations and a near-perfect cancellation in Ce. It also resolves the long-standing Cs--Fr controversy, identifying Fr as a critical element whose near-boundary response is amplified fivefold by relativistic contraction of the 7s orbital. The framework reproduces the classical Allen, Pauling, and Mulliken scales as well as Lewis acidity trends, and makes three falsifiable experimental predictions. It transforms electronegativity from a lookup-table number into a predictive, hierarchically structured quantum descriptor.

item.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.30009v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

item.title: Finite-time Polytropic Steering Reveals Non-monotonic Irreversibility
item.description: arXiv:2602.13765v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How irreversibility evolves from slow to fast driving is a central question in nonequilibrium thermodynamics. While near-equilibrium theory predicts increasing irreversibility with driving speed, the corresponding crossover far from equilibrium is not generally resolved within a unified control framework. Here we introduce polytropic steering, in which a prescribed relation between the ensemble energy and a time-dependent control parameter continuously organizes finite-time processes between isothermal and adiabatic limits. A Fokker-Planck formulation makes the construction applicable to general confining potentials, and yields closed-form thermodynamic expressions for a harmonic trap. We find a non-monotonic irreversibility: the entropy generation decreases in both the quasistatic and fast-driving limits and exhibits a maximum at an intermediate protocol duration. The resulting most-irreversible timescale quantifies the competition between thermal relaxation and external driving. We verify the persistence of this behavior in an anharmonic optical-lattice potential and demonstrate how the same steering principle controls power-efficiency trade-offs in finite-time Brownian engines.

item.title: A Combined Tight Binding with Machine Learning Potential Model for Magnesium Compounds
item.description: arXiv:2606.25853v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a model for magnesium-based systems that combines density functional tight binding (DFTB) with MACE, a machine learning interatomic potential (DFTB+MACE). In this model, the conventional repulsive potential, pair potential, is replaced by a many-body MACE potential. The MACE component of the model is trained on the difference between density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces and the corresponding DFTB values, but neglecting the pair potential contribution. Using this model we performed structural relaxation of MgO-CO2 adsorption systems, molecular dynamics calculations of water clusters and phonon spectrum calculations of stable fcc-MgO and metastable bcc-MgO structures. We compare the performance of our model with a pure MACE model and with DFT. We demonstrate that the DFTB+MACE model achieves improved accuracy relative to DFTB with a pair potential, in many cases with only a moderate increase in computational cost. In addition, it can provide electronic structures that most of the machine learning potentials cannot. The training dataset, originally developed for MACE, may not fully represent all regions of the potential surface we may encounter during simulations. Expanding the dataset for a wider potential surface is expected to further enhance predictive accuracy of DFTB+MACE model. Overall, the resulting DFTB+MACE framework enables simulations at length and time scales beyond the reach of first-principles methods while retaining an explicit description of electronic structures, making it particularly attractive for studying charge-transfer in materials.

item.title: Entropy functional theory for inhomogeneous fluids
item.description: arXiv:2606.28240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an exact variational scheme for the physics of inhomogeneous classical fluids in thermal equilibrium. A joint metadensity minimization principle is proven for the one-body density and the global interparticle distance distribution. The theory bypasses the inhomogeneous two-body density and thus remains computationally simple. A universal excess entropy functional accounts for all many-body correlations in arbitrary pairwise interacting systems. The framework is relevant for neural functional machine learning, for soft matter design, and for predicting hyperobservables, structural correlation functions, and first-principles mechanisms of entropy-energy competition.

item.title: Machine Learning for High-Entropy Catalysts: Methods and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2609.19837v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit exceptional catalytic performance in various reactions due to their high configurational entropy, synergistic elemental effects, tunable electronic structures, and excellent structural stability. However, the vast compositional space of HEA catalysts makes traditional experimental and theoretical design costly and inefficient. In recent years, data-driven machine learning (ML) methods have emerged as powerful tools for studying HEAs in catalysis. Through predictive models and ML surrogates, researchers can decipher the intricate composition-structure-performance relationships of these materials. In addition, by leveraging large language models (LLMs) for knowledge extraction, hypothesis generation and validation, and as a foundation to build integrated design workflows, ML approaches can significantly accelerate the design of novel HEA catalysts. This review systematically summarizes the latest methodological advances and applications of ML methods for HEAs in catalysis, discusses the challenges, and offers insights into future research directions to support the rational design and efficient development of catalysts.

item.title: SoLiD26: A First Principles Solid-Liquid Interface Dataset for Machine-learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2609.28013v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable simulations of larger atomistic systems over longer timescales than traditional ab initio methods but require large, diverse training data. Existing datasets lack comprehensive sampling of solid-liquid interfaces, which exhibit complex phenomena such as solvent layering and surface reconstruction critical for energy and catalytic materials. Here, we present SoLiD26, a curated solid-liquid interface dataset of 15.4 million first-principles structures with up to 576 atoms and 15 chemical elements for training and evaluating MLIPs. The structures were compiled from density functional theory (DFT) calculations, with most configurations originating from ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. SoLiD26 includes aqueous coinage metal interfaces, electrode-electrolyte systems, and selected bulk reference structures, calculated with VASP using the PBE functional and D3 dispersion corrections. The application of SoLiD26 for training and evaluating MLIPs is demonstrated with a suite of MACE models on a simple training, validation and test split. This dataset provides a valuable resource for advancing MLIP development targeted at modelling solid-liquid interfaces in electrochemical and catalytic systems.

item.title: Observation of Universal Quantum Chaos at Shallow Depths
item.description: arXiv:2609.28623v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Universal statistical laws are a hallmark of quantum chaos. A natural route to probing them in quantum circuits is offered by the statistics of output probabilities, which for sufficiently deep chaotic circuits approach the Porter--Thomas distribution. Here we show, theoretically and experimentally, that the approach to this limit is itself universal, and is organized into geometry-dependent universality classes. At shallow depths, growing only logarithmically with system size, we derive universal output-probability distributions that differ markedly from Porter--Thomas statistics, and we test them on a programmable superconducting processor. Two-dimensional lattices, open one-dimensional chains, and periodic rings exhibit distinct universal forms, retaining signatures of geometry and boundary topology within the same logarithmic-depth regime. Within each class, the distributions depend on only two parameters: an effective many-body Thouless scale and the accumulated number of incoherent errors. Extracting these directly from measured bitstring frequencies provides access to scrambling, entanglement growth of the target state, and global fidelity, without reconstructing or classically simulating the implemented circuit. We also identify a noise-driven transition between output statistics retaining system-wide quantum correlations and those reproducible by independent small patches. Our results establish universality beyond Porter--Thomas statistics as a quantitative tool for characterizing noisy quantum processors.

item.title: SpectraFit-Core: a Rust-cored nonlinear curve-fitting library validated against the NIST Statistical Reference Datasets
item.description: Nonlinear least-squares fitting of parametric line shapes is routine in the analysis of spectra, and the analyst often knows relationships between the parameters before the fit starts, such as a shared width or a fixed intensity ratio. SpectraFit-Core is an open-source curve-fitting library in which this knowledge is part of the model. A model is a graph of named components, and each relationship is an expression edge on that graph, within one spectrum or across several spectra fitted jointly in one call. On a measured Fe L2,3 energy-loss spectrum, four such relationships leave the fitted values unchanged and make the edge-step amplitude 28 times more precise. Because the model is a description rather than code, the same graph can be fitted by other implementations and their parameters compared name by name. The parameters and standard errors of the library are checked against certified values: on 22 of the 27 nonlinear-regression problems of the NIST Statistical Reference Datasets, the least accurately recovered parameter agrees to more than six significant figures, and the standard errors agree nearly as well except on Lanczos1. Kernels, analytic Jacobians, and solver iteration run in compiled Rust behind a typed Python interface, which also makes the library faster than lmfit, SciPy, and JAX on its benchmark. A companion repository regenerates the results from the published release. SpectraFit-Core is released under the MIT license, distributed on PyPI and archived on Zenodo.

item.title: Toward Interpretable Graph-Based Machine Learning for Combustion Kinetic Model Generation
item.description: This work presents an atom-conserving and interpretable graph neural network (GNN) for combustion kinetic model generation, where atoms are represented as nodes, covalent bonds are represented as edges, and reactions are represented as bond-rearrangement operations. Its artificial-intelligence (AI) contribution is a reaction generator that extends a standard Graph Isomorphism Network with Edges (GINE) architecture through reaction-context embeddings, reaction branching & third-body reaction inputs, Arrhenius-rate-parameter prediction, pairwise decoding, and stochastic inference over evolving reactant pools. Trained on the Li–Dryer hydrogen combustion kinetic model (8 species and 21 reactions), the GNN reproduces trained chemistry and generates element-balanced new reactions and intermediate species outside the training dataset, many of which have experimental analogues. When trained on a subset of the Li–Dryer dataset, the model recovered most held-out reactions and revealed relationships between samples (reactions) in the model’s latent space. The results suggest that the model learns transferable local reaction structures and generates valid species and reactions. As with any reaction generators, the generated reaction models require thermochemical and kinetic verification; the intended engineering application is low-cost reaction-pathway exploration for new fuels and prioritization of experiments and first-principles calculations to develop new combustion kinetic models.

item.title: Data-efficient molecular and nanoparticle design via fine-tuned large language models
item.description: Designing molecules with prescribed properties is central to pharmaceutical and materials innovation, but vast chemical design spaces make development lengthy and costly. Generative artificial intelligence can accelerate molecular discovery, but its deployment in many real-world domains remains limited by the need for large task-specific training datasets. To enable generative design when property-labeled data are scarce, we present a data-efficient foundation-model adaptation strategy combining complementary positive and negative property prompts with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Generated molecules are then ranked by molecular graph-kernel Gaussian process regression for structure-aware prioritization. In a controlled computational setting, the platform generated candidates with novel scaffolds satisfying multiple design objectives, including predicted target binding, synthesizability, and drug-likeness. Although only a few hundred training molecules per target met all three criteria, the model generated thousands of new molecules matching the desired profiles. For prospective validation, we applied the model to nanoparticle design, a domain of high clinical potential but limited excipient diversity. Fine-tuning on only 1,521 labeled drug-excipient pairs - including just 139 nanoparticle-forming examples identified new nanoparticle-forming excipients for the anticancer drug sorafenib. The model proposed lithocholic acid and the sorafenib metabolite M6, and experiments confirmed that both form stable sorafenib nanoparticles with high encapsulation efficiency and increased in vitro potency. These findings show that foundation-model fine-tuning with complementary prompts and graph-based prioritization enables data-efficient molecular design in low-data chemical domains.
