item.title: Vegetation-Rainfall Relationship within the Caatinga Biome
item.description: With drought and extreme weather events increasing in frequency, it has become crucial to understand the relation between weather and biome responses. The semi-arid Caatinga biome of Brazil is highly sensitive to climatic variability, and particularly to changes in precipitation and drought frequency. This study explores a remote-sensing workflow to estimate green vegetation cover and assess its relationship with precipitation using satellite imagery. Monthly satellite composites were processed to distinguish green and non-green vegetation, comparing the efficacy between a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a python classification method. We match the computational measurements of green vegetation cover with monthly precipitation data from the four nearest weather stations. Green cover analysis shows a lagged positive relationship with precipitation, with wetter months generally exhibiting greater green vegetation coverage. The study demonstrates the potential of combining satellite imagery, CNN classification and climatic data for longterm remote ecosystem monitoring.

item.title: Atomistic prediction of magnetic behaviour across chemistry, structure and temperature
item.description: arXiv:2610.24407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlling magnetic phases and properties through composition and external conditions is central to the development of magnetic materials. Atomistic foundation models offer a route to predicting such behaviour across diverse materials, but magnetic materials remain challenging because their atomic structure and local moments are strongly coupled, while temperature and disorder drive magnetic moments into non-collinear states with evolving orientations and magnitudes. Broadly pretrained atomistic models still sample only limited magnetic diversity, while finite-temperature descriptions of coupled lattice and magnetic fluctuations remain largely material-specific. Here we introduce MagPT, pretrained across 48 elements on 912,492 spin-lattice configurations spanning structural, orientational and longitudinal magnetic fluctuations over 0 $\sim$ 1,000 K and 0 $\sim$ 10 GPa. By treating species, atomic positions and vector moments together, MagPT distinguishes magnetic states that share the same atomic structure but differ in spin configuration and energy. It captures magnetic behaviour across composition, temperature and length scales, from Slater-Pauling-type composition-magnetism relations in transition-metal alloys and finite-temperature phase evolution in elemental ferromagnets and magnetic shape-memory Heusler alloys, to emergent long-wavelength non-collinear spin textures in chiral magnets and local chemistry-magnetism coupling in high-entropy alloys. MagPT moves atomistic studies of magnetic materials beyond material-specific approaches, establishing a general framework for exploring and designing magnetic matter across diverse chemistries and conditions.

item.title: Reticulating Local Dynamics in Three-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description: arXiv:2610.24418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In covalent organic frameworks (COFs), the geometry of the building units predetermines the structure of the framework, yet comparable design principles relating the COF linkers to the local motions that govern guest adsorption and diffusion as well as mechanical response have remained beyond reach. Here, we combine synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function (PDF) analysis with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations accelerated by machine learning interatomic potentials to resolve and compare the local dynamics of two three-dimensional imine-linked COFs, chosen to differ in the geometry and rigidity of one of their two building units. Both are constructed from the same 4-connected square planar linker, $4,4',4'',4'''$-(pyrene-1,3,6,8-tetrayl)tetraaniline (PyTTA), reticulated with the 12-connected nanographene hexakis{[3,5-bis($p$-formylphenyl)-4,6-dimethoxyphenyl]}hexabenzocoronene to give COF-412, {[(HBC-LA$_{12}$)(PyTTA)$_3$]}$_{\mathit{imine}}$, and with the 6-connected triptycene 2,3,6,7,14,15-hexakis(4-formylphenyl)triptycene to give COF-564, {[(Trip-CHO)$_2$(PyTTA)$_3$]}$_{\mathit{imine}}$. The PDF-MD approach resolves the amplitude, the time scale, and the spatial extent of the motion of all COF linkers, separating the limited libration of the fused aromatic cores from the larger reorientational tilts of the pendant aryl rings they carry and from the translation of whole linkers within the net. The simulations further reveal that exchanging the nanographene- for the triptycene-based linker tunes the equilibrium tilt and the positional probability density of PyTTA, raising the tilt amplitude of its linker partner, and, notably, strengthens the coupling between the translations of neighbouring linkers. This approach provides a blueprint for understanding local dynamical properties in COFs, and shows them to be selectable through the choice of building unit and amenable to design.

item.title: Understanding compression-extension error asymmetry in universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.24514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials are increasingly used across diverse materials, yet their reliability under directional deformation remains unclear. We compare compression and extension along paired deformation paths from the same parent structures for eleven pretrained potentials. The benchmark comprises 1,963 Materials Project trajectory (MPtrj) parents and 1,286 experimental-source MinX-Eq parents at six strain magnitudes from 1% to 10%. Density-functional theory provides references for isotropic, uniaxial and biaxial loading in MPtrj and isotropic loading in MinX-Eq. At $\pm 10\%$, every model has a larger median force error under compression, with pooled isotropic compression-to-extension ratios of 2.12 and 3.30 for MPtrj and MinX-Eq. Decomposing error growth into DFT force-scale growth and relative-error evolution shows that relative errors decrease on both branches, faster under compression in MPtrj but slower under compression in MinX-Eq. Force-scale matching moves the error ratios toward unity, although MinX-Eq retains a compression-side excess across models. Radial and SOAP analyses place compressed structures at shorter separations and farther from public reference pools, while readout-associated model features show larger compression-side displacements. These results distinguish stronger physical responses from changes in relative predictive accuracy and provide a basis for assessing universal potentials in deformation simulations.

item.title: Signed FK percolation in Ising spin glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.24629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce signed Fortuin-Kasteleyn (FK) percolation for the +/-J random-interaction Ising model to characterize nonzero uniform magnetization density and two-replica overlap within the class of Gibbs distributions whose infinite-volume Edwards-Sokal (ES)/FK representation has at most one infinite FK cluster almost surely. The construction refines ordinary FK connectivity by retaining the parity of coupling products along open paths. Using the infinite-volume ES representation and its DLR equations, we study pairs of companion objects and the compatible spin assignments on them. In one replica, companions are defined by positive-parity FK connections. For extremal states satisfying the infinite-cluster assumption and almost-sure existence of companion densities along the chosen van Hove sequence, nonzero limiting expected magnetization density is equivalent to density distinguishability of the companions of the infinite FK cluster. For two independent replicas, companions are defined by FK connections coherent in parity. For products of extremal one-replica states satisfying the infinite-cluster assumption and almost-sure existence of the companion densities along the chosen sequence, density distinguishability of the companions is equivalent to nonzero limiting expected mutual overlap. For two independent replicas drawn from the same extremal state, this specializes to the Edwards-Anderson self-overlap.

item.title: HEXRD and HEXRDGUI: a flexible toolkit for X-ray diffraction analysis in dynamic compression experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.24989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article describes the application of HEXRD, an open-source Python library for X-ray diffraction analysis, and HEXRDGUI, its companion graphical application, to dynamic compression experiments. Built on a generic multi-detector geometric model, the toolkit supports arbitrary instrument configurations with independently positioned planar or cylindrical detector panels, arbitrary beam directions, and multiple X-ray sources. It calibrates instruments from powder rings, Laue spots or the rings of an unknown phase, fits whole patterns by Le Bail or Rietveld refinement, and imports data from the TARDIS, FIDDLE and PXRDIP platforms at the National Ignition Facility (NIF) and OMEGA EP. Although originally developed for high-energy diffraction microscopy at synchrotron sources, HEXRD has been adopted as an analysis tool for dynamic compression X-ray diffraction experiments at facilities including the NIF, the Matter in Extreme Conditions end-station at the Linac Coherent Light Source, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS) at the Advanced Photon Source, OMEGA EP at the Laboratory for Laser Energetics, and the High Energy Density (HED) instrument at the European XFEL. Calibrated from the same ring positions on a single planar detector, HEXRD and the independent code pyFAI predict the same scattering angle 2$\theta$ to numerical precision. On a dual-source dataset from the NIF, calibrating the detectors against both X-ray sources at once fits the rings of both to an RMS of 0.18{\deg} in 2$\theta$, about one image-plate pixel, whereas a fit to either source alone, with the plate tilts held at their nominal values, fits its own rings nearly as well but mispredicts the other's by about 0.6{\deg}. The software is freely available under a BSD license.

item.title: Frustration-Assisted Electrical Switching in $Co_xTaS_2$
item.description: arXiv:2610.25112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrical switching in antiferromagnets is commonly described as the action of current-induced torques on a rigid order parameter. In frustrated magnets, however, competing states can create a history-dependent energy landscape in which slow collective dynamics actively participate in electrical reconfiguration. Here, we demonstrate frustration-assisted switching in near-stoichiometric $Co_xTaS_2$, a van der Waals antiferromagnet located at the composition-sensitive boundary between Hall-active and Hall-inactive multi-Q-related magnetic regimes. Although the crystals exhibit no resolved spontaneous Hall response, they retain van Hove singularities near the Fermi level and order antiferromagnetically below $T_N \simeq 31.5 K$. Current pulses write nonvolatile anisotropic resistance states in microstructured devices, with an activation current density nearly an order of magnitude below that reported for the Hall-active lower-intercalation phase. The switching response separates into two temperature-dependent dynamical regimes rather than following a single current threshold. Independent magnetization-aging and post-field-relaxation measurements reveal slow, history-dependent magnetic dynamics, and the relaxation strength closely follows the inverse switching amplitude. These results identify magnetic frustration and glassy dynamics as central ingredients in the electrical reconfiguration of $Co_xTaS_2$, establishing a route to functional switching through a dynamically soft antiferromagnetic landscape.

item.title: NEP-kappa 2.0: A unified framework for phonon transport and nonequilibrium thermalization with machine-learning interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.25477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present NEP-kappa 2.0, a unified framework that integrates density-functional theory, material-specific machine-learning interatomic potentials, and pretrained force models for advanced phonon calculations. A common workflow enables harmonic lattice dynamics, quasi-harmonic and stochastic self-consistent phonon treatments, three- and four-phonon transport, Wigner population--coherence transport, and time-dependent phonon dynamics. Applications to 3C-SiC, BAs, and Cs$_2$AgInCl$_6$ demonstrate consistent force-model comparisons, finite-temperature renormalization, higher-order scattering, and intermode coherence. Beyond steady-state transport, mode-resolved simulations of selectively excited 3C-SiC reveal that half of the injected optical-phonon energy reaches acoustic modes within approximately 3.75 ps, primarily through one-optical--two-acoustic scattering. Acoustic branches exhibit response times differing by a factor of five, with competing scattering channels producing a transient energy overshoot. Channel-resolved entropy production and persistent nonthermal occupations distinguish interbranch energy redistribution from intrabranch thermalization. The framework connects equilibrium phonon transport with microscopic nonequilibrium energy dynamics.

item.title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
item.description: arXiv:2610.25619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.

item.title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.25775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI/ML models are useful for the prediction of materials' properties. Recently, there has been great progress in developing Neural Network models to predict the properties of solids, molecules, and crystals, avoiding expensive and time-consuming laboratory testing. This study presents a novel AI/ML-based multi-modal approach to predict material magnetic ordering using material crystal structure information as input to a Graph Neural Network model (GNN) and semantic text descriptions of the material's properties and structure as input to a Large Language Model (LLM), before performing information fusion of the GNN and LLM outputs to predict material magnetic ordering in four classes (Non-magnetic, Ferromagnetic, Antiferromagnetic, Ferrimagnetic). The model is trained, validated, and tested on a dataset which is a combination of Materials Project dataset, Magndata dataset, and a set of uranium compounds with magnetic ordering determined in laboratory testing, with an 80/10/10 (training/validation/testing) data split. The proposed GNN and LLM multi-modal approach achieves better overall accuracy than both the standalone GNN and LLM approaches with three fusion strategies.

item.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Discovery of Carbon-Related Defect Formation Mechanisms in Diamond
item.description: arXiv:2610.26301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diamond is an important host material for functional defects such as solid-state spin qubits. During the defect creation by irradiation and subsequent thermal annealing, carbon-related defects, including vacancies and interstitials, are generated and can migrate to form new defect complexes. To investigate this kinetically driven process and reveal the formation mechanisms of the di-interstitials and di-vacancies in the neutral charge state, we fine-tuned a universal machine learning interatomic potential using a small dataset generated from density functional theory calculations. We obtained a barrier of 1.84 eV for mono-interstitial migration and found that two initially separated mono-interstitials only need to overcome a lower barrier to form di-interstitial configurations. Beyond the training data, the MLIP also identified the formation pathway for an additional di-interstitial configuration and a stepwise divacancy dissociation mechanism. These results reveal migration-assisted defect complex formation mechanisms and demonstrate how targeted MLIP training can identify reaction pathways.

item.title: Origins of Faceted Anomalous Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2610.26356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluctuating interfaces are typically characterized by their global, spectral, and local roughness exponents. Faceted anomalous scaling, characterized by $\alpha_s>1$, $\alpha_s\neq\alpha$, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}=1$, owes its name to the tendency of such interfaces to develop long, nearly linear segments called facets. Its statistical origin, and whether facets are required, have remained unclear. We show that this exponent structure is determined by the spatial statistics of the slope field. Slope increments split into typical fluctuations and rare, larger jumps. This anomalous scaling arises either when the typical slope increment displays genuine system-size-dependent anomalous scaling or when the rare jumps dominate the second moment. The two contributions can coexist, and their competition leads to bifractal scaling of the slopes. We establish this framework analytically in the generalized anharmonic Larkin model and the columnar Kardar--Parisi--Zhang equation, and we derive exactly the global, spectral, and local roughness exponents in both cases. The Larkin model realizes both mechanisms and produces anomalous interfaces with or without facets, whereas columnar KPZ belongs to the jump-dominated case and yields $\alpha_s=3/2$.

item.title: Atomic-level study of dose-dependent lattice thermal conductivity degradation in irradiated tungsten
item.description: arXiv:2610.26502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plasma-facing components (PFCs) in future fusion reactors must withstand extreme environments, making tungsten (W) a prime candidate material due to its high thermal conductivity, high melting temperature, low sputtering yield, low tritium absorption. However, neutron irradiation introduces complex nanostructural defects that severely degrade these critical properties. In this work, we use Non-Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics (NEMD) simulations coupled with the Creation Relaxation Algorithm (CRA) to investigate the lattice thermal conductivity (kappa) of W across a wide range of irradiation doses. Systems treated with different doses up to 1.8 canonical displacements per atom (cdpa) were simulated to generate and study diverse defect structures, including vacancies and self-interstitial atom (SIA) clusters. By correlating spatially-resolved temperature gradients with local defect concentrations, we show that even small changes in defect type and distribution significantly affect thermal transport. We employ Machine Learning (ML) models to develop a quantitative relationship between the defect features and the resulting thermal conductivity degradation. The ML analysis identifies vacancy density as the dominant structural factor controlling thermal transport. We found a significant, nonlinear suppression of kappa with increasing defect density. Predictive multi-defect mapping built upon our ML model resolved a step-like degradation transition at a critical vacancy threshold of 0.05 at.%, beyond which phonon scattering completely saturated and capped the maximum relative lattice thermal conductivity degradation at approximately 30 at.%. This integrated simulation and ML approach provides a powerful, predictive framework for quantifying the complex relationship between structure and thermal conductivity in irradiated fusion materials.

item.title: CME-SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
item.description: arXiv:2610.24304v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are presently well assessed by expert-level mathematics and physics benchmarks which focus on theoretical, symbolic reasoning. However, we lack experimental benchmarks that evaluate data analysis in frontier research problems, a capability that future domain-specific foundation models must have. To this end, we present CME-SpectrumBench, an expert-designed benchmark consisting of 190 questions that measures how reliably frontier LLMs analyze research-level spectral scientific data in condensed matter experiments (CME). Using simulated CME spectral data, we prompt models to identify structures from 2D intensity arrays in the face of noise and limited instrumental resolution, a test of dense context reasoning. Models are scored by how accurately their numerical answers approach the ground truth. Under direct query, scores generally pale in comparison to handwritten code due to clear failure modes: models can find simple features but struggle to trace patterns or compute derived quantities, and performance typically degrades with increased data resolution and noise/convolution levels. LLM performance becomes comparable to handwritten code by allowing tool use (access to a Python interpreter) with/without ReAct prompting, in effect mapping questions onto agentic code generation problems. Our findings show that frontier models can serve as research assistants by interfacing with data through code, but still face difficulties processing information directly from large datasets - a key barrier future foundation models must overcome. The code and data are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jingene/CMESpectrumBench.

item.title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
item.description: arXiv:2610.26701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.

item.title: Numerical and theoretical studies of the Anderson transition in the chiral symmetry classes with weak topology
item.description: arXiv:2509.16555v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Combining lattice-model simulations with a renormalization group (RG) analysis of effective theories, we investigate the nature of the Anderson transition in chiral symmetry classes with one-dimensional (1D) weak topology. In the simulation study, we extend previous transfer matrix analyses to the chiral symplectic class, and study numerical Lyapunov exponents via a finite-size scaling (FSS) analysis that assumes spatially isotropic scaling. The analysis shows that, as in the other two chiral symmetry classes, the weak topology induces an intermediate quasi-localized (QL) phase between metal and Anderson insulator phases. In this QL phase, the localization length of wave functions diverges exclusively along the direction of the 1D weak topology. A comparison of the universal critical exponents across the three chiral symmetry classes indicates that the quantum criticality of the metal-to-QL transition varies, depending on the nature of the time-reversal symmetry. Motivated by this numerical observation, we revisit and extend our previous two-dimensional (2D) RG analysis to all three chiral classes, now newly incorporating a one-loop renormalization of the weak topological term in the analysis. The revised analysis reveals that a quasi-localized strong-coupling fixed point previously reported in the chiral unitary class is unstable under this new inclusion; instead, the strong-coupling phase is entirely governed by a stable fixed point with conventional localized character. Nevertheless, in the chiral unitary and chiral symplectic classes, the RG analysis still yields the hallmark of the 1D weak topology through the spatially anisotropic scaling of the Anderson transition criticality. These theoretical findings suggest that a conclusive numerical identification of the 2D QL phase requires a finite-size scaling approach that accommodates generic (anisotropic) spatial scaling.

item.title: Data-Efficient Indentation Size Effect Mitigation in Steels Using Machine Learning and a Physics-Constrained Neural Network
item.description: arXiv:2604.27775v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Shallow nanoindentation, needed for thin layers, individual phases and small volumes, gives hardness inflated by the indentation size effect (ISE). The Nix-Gao correction reduces this inflation but requires deep indentations of the same material, often impossible in such samples. We present a data-efficient workflow, trained on a few reference materials, that predicts a high-load reference hardness from a single shallow indentation. Seven models were trained on 703 indentations (5-350 mN) on three steels (2.0-6.5 GPa): Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, two feed-forward networks, and two physics-constrained neural networks (PCNNs) that apply a bounded learned correction q as H_app/sqrt(1+q). Over five seeds, models were tested on an external steel not used for training and indented at different loads, in leave-one-steel-out folds, and on fused silica, an out-of-domain material where all models failed. Random Forest and XGBoost, the best on the development set, transferred worst over all loads (MAPE 10.2 and 8.5%), whereas Ridge regression, the PCNNs and one feed-forward network reached 3.7-4.8%; with three training steels, development-set accuracy thus did not indicate accuracy on an unseen steel. From only the external steel's 3-15 mN indentations, the smooth (non-tree) models estimated the reference within 0.03-0.19 GPa on average. The PCNNs matched the linear baseline within the training hardness range and were the most accurate for a held-out steel softer than the training steels, but failed for a harder one. The workflow uses no steel-specific inputs and can be retrained for other material classes.

item.title: Bias Tunable Transport Modulation and Gas Selectivity in Layered BiOI: A DFT NEGF Study
item.description: arXiv:2608.03308v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding the interplay between adsorption energetics and charge-transport modulation is essential for the rational design of low-power and bias-tunable gas sensors. Here, we present a comprehensive first-principles study of gas selectivity in layered bismuth oxyiodide (BiOI) by integrating density functional theory with nonequilibrium Green's function transport calculations. The adsorption and bias-dependent transport responses toward NO2, NH3, CO2, and representative volatile organic compounds are systematically examined. While NH3 and NO2 exhibit strong chemisorption and localized electronic perturbations, CO2 interacts through weak physisorption, demonstrating that adsorption strength alone does not determine sensing performance. Instead, the evolution of transmission channels near the Fermi level governs the sensing response. Bias-dependent calculations reveal an electrically tunable sensitivity hierarchy, in which weakly adsorbed CO2 preserves conductive pathways and exhibits pronounced low-bias sensitivity despite minimal charge transfer. Recovery-time analysis further highlights the trade-off between transport modulation and reversibility for strongly adsorbed species. These results establish a transport-centered selectivity framework for layered BiOI and provide mechanistic insight into electric-field-controlled gas sensing under ambient conditions.

item.title: Deep Generative Crystal Structure Prediction: A Benchmark Study and a Controlled Test of Prototype Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2609.26502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep generative models are widely reported to enable de novo crystal structure prediction (CSP), but their capability has not been measured consistently against template-based methods. We evaluate 12 representative generative CSP models, spanning latent-variable, diffusion, flow-matching, autoregressive, and manifold random-walk architectures, against TCSP 2.0 on 180 test structures and a leakage-controlled subset of 46. All methods use identical structure-matching, symmetry, and consensus criteria. Template retrieval is the strongest single method, reaching 68.3% top-1 success; symmetry-aware EquiCSP (66.4%) and Uni-3DAR (62.9%) form the next tier. However, comparison with TCSP 2.0 shows that most structures correctly predicted by generative models are also correctly predicted by template substitution. Thus, the set of structures uniquely reachable by generation is small, limiting its practical advantage for discovering structures outside existing prototype libraries. To test the source of this performance, we removed entire stoichiometric prototype families from the training set and retrained the strongest generative model. Accuracy declined by 50-78% across four families, establishing that performance is substantially prototype-dependent. A small minority of structures survived removal of their prototype family, demonstrating a real but limited retrieval-independent predictive capacity. Present generative CSP models therefore function largely as implicit, softer-edged prototype libraries rather than genuinely de novo predictors. Enlarging this residual capacity, rather than aggregate match rate alone, is the central open problem.

item.title: AutoREC: A reinforcement learning platform for equivalent circuit model generation
item.description: arXiv:2604.27266v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces AutoREC, an open-source Python platform for developing, training and evaluating reinforcement learning (RL) agents that automatically generate equivalent circuit models (ECMs) from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) data. Although ECMs are widely used to interpret EIS measurements, their identification typically relies on manual trial-and-error, requiring domain expertise and limiting scalability, particularly in autonomous experimental pipelines such as self-driving laboratories. In AutoREC, ECM generation is formulated as a Markov decision process in which an RL agent sequentially modifies a circuit topology based on the current state, available actions and feedback from the resulting model. The platform supports an end-to-end workflow encompassing EIS preprocessing with selectable impedance representations, agent setup and training, ECM generation for new measurements and visualization-based evaluation and analysis of agent decision-making. AutoREC implements a configurable Double Deep Q-Network agent with prioritized experience replay and a dedicated deadloop mitigation strategy for navigating the complex circuit-generation action space efficiently. To demonstrate the platform, we trained a representative agent on 1350 synthetic spectra from five reference circuit families, evaluated it on 150 held-out synthetic spectra and applied it to 32 previously unseen experimental spectra from battery, corrosion, oxygen evolution reaction and CO2 reduction systems. These case studies illustrate the end-to-end capabilities of AutoREC while revealing challenges associated with experimental complexity and limited training-data coverage. The demonstrated agent serves as a reference implementation; AutoREC provides an extensible foundation through which users can develop and evaluate agents tailored to their specific electrochemical systems and research objectives.

item.title: The Dichotomy Between Pattern Recognition and Step-by-Step Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.09186v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We argue that pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning are two ends of a spectrum. A large language model (LLM) learns to reason step-by-step when data is structured such that the next token depends on a small amount of preceding context. Inference in LLMs resembles pattern recognition when the next token depends on a large amount of preceding context. If the next token depends on only the $c$ most recent tokens, reasoning traces are paths on a De Bruijn graph whose nodes are $c$-length contexts and edges are next-token transitions between contexts. The set of reasoning traces of a task forms a directed acyclic subgraph of the De Bruijn graph. An LLM that has learned all edges of this subgraph can compose them to solve longer, unseen tasks, i.e., it reasons step-by-step. We prove that the number of edges is vanishingly small compared to the number of reasoning traces. Empirically, the number of training samples a transformer needs is a power law in the number of edges, so learning to reason step-by-step is sample efficient. We can induce De Bruijn structure in any task by maintaining a ``state'' that makes future reasoning independent of the past. The frequency of states in the reasoning trace determines $c$. We show, by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to solve equations and answer questions about stories, that frequent states (small $c$) result in higher accuracy but greater fragility to perturbations at test time. LLMs trained with a large $c$ are only as good as models that perform pattern recognition without reasoning. A moderate density of states balances accuracy and robustness. We show that real-world data has De Bruijn structure: Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B retain over 75% of their accuracy on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond when attention is restricted to a sliding window less than 15% as long as the full reasoning trace.

item.title: Covalency-driven amorphization in dual-anion-doped Li-Zr-Cl electrolytes enables long-life all-solid-state batteries
item.description: Dual-anion regulation induces covalency-driven amorphization in Li-Zr-Cl electrolytes, promoting Li+ transport, oxidative stability, and mechanical compliance. This bond-covalency-mediated strategy enables long-life all-solid-state lithium batteries and provides a general design principle for high-performance halide solid-state electrolytes.

item.title: Superconductivity near two-dimensional Van Hove singularities: A determinant quantum Monte Carlo study
item.description:
Author(s): Gustav Romare, Daniel Shaffer, Alex Levchenko, Edwin Huang, and Ilya Esterlis

Using determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, the authors compute here the superconducting transition temperature Tc of the two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model near ordinary and higher-order Van Hove singularities. Contrary to conventional wisdom, the authors find that the maximal Tc in the model occurs away from the Van Hove singularities, when the system is in the intermediate coupling regime.


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 204506] Published Mon Oct 19, 2026

item.title: Evaluating transfer across modalities in autonomous materials systems
item.description: A power device needs a wide-gap semiconductor and a heat-treated Al–Mg–Si alloy to cool it, and both draw on sources that disagree: band gaps from several levels of density functional theory (DFT) and from measurement, alloy formation energies from DFT and interatomic potentials. Multi-fidelity methods combine such sources only through paired values on a common scale and do not state in advance whether one source’s guidance holds in another. We test whether the relative differences between candidates, which lead and by how much, are preserved across sources whose values disagree. PEGKi infers relative ratings of decision bodies (any rule that ranks candidates) from comparison outcomes within each source, and scores every donor-to-receiver route with a robustness certificate or a refusal. The evidence is 261,053 archived band-gap records from eight sources and an Al–Mg–Si pool where every query runs a DFT or molecular-dynamics calculation. Orderings alone recover the accuracy ladder of the DFT levels, and experiment spreads material classes about twice as widely as the generalised gradient approximation. Transfer follows the database of origin more than the functional, and routing learned from measured campaigns outperforms the fixed default at every query size. For the alloy, the score picks each potential’s room-temperature run as donor at heat-treatment temperatures, the best measured choice in five of six cases, and discounts the two potentials that predict Mg2Si to be unstable. Relative margins therefore transfer where values do not, so a campaign can rate whose knowledge to reuse before committing compute or instrument time.

item.title: Provenance records predict which multi-scale conclusions a foundation-potential release can change in SiGeC semiconductors
item.description: Multi-scale simulations of semiconductor alloys rest on foundation interatomic potentials (machine-learned force models trained on large density-functional databases), re-released as training data grow. A release changes defect energies and phonon stiffness and, through them, the recipes and design verdicts downstream; recomputing everything is costly, and recomputing nothing leaves conclusions that may no longer hold. Workflow records list every result downstream of a calculation, not which could change a decision. We tested whether the conclusions a release can change are predictable from a campaign’s provenance record (a record of which calculation fed which result) before any rerun and settled by recomputing only the predicted units. The chain served a SiGeC design question (germanium content, carbon content and SiC particle size for low lattice thermal conductivity), with MACE-MP-0 replaced by MACE-MPA-0 and all predictions and decision rules fixed in advance. From the record, 49 of 128 record entries were reached, 24 conclusions were classified by their margin to a decision threshold, and four recompute units were named. Recomputing those units (70 relaxations, 91 molecular-dynamics runs) settled 20 conclusions: none changed outside the predicted set (exact 95% upper bound on the miss rate 0.24), eight of nine flagged as at risk held, and one, Ge attraction to the first shell around a SiC particle, reversed by less than a millielectronvolt past its threshold, while the conclusion it served (no germanium-depleted zone forms) held. Magnitudes moved more than assumed: the energy carbon gains by precipitating as SiC grew by 0.65–0.75 eV against an assumed 0.3 eV; the recipe and the germanium saving held. Recomputation cost 3.5 CPU-task-hours and 354 GPU-hours, 2.2 times the GPU estimate scaled from the recorded runs. Decisions whose margins exceed a measured release shift can be carried across a release with a recorded check; magnitudes need recomputation, and explicit records of each result’s inputs and code would make the prediction a lookup.
