item.title: Universal link between structural relaxation and self-diffusion in simple supercooled liquids
item.description: arXiv:2610.22385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite a vigorous effort, a comprehensive and satisfactory understanding of the dynamics underlying the glass transition in finite-dimensional systems has not yet emerged. One key hallmark of supercooled liquids approaching the glass transition is the breakdown of the classical Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, manifested as the decoupling between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time, commonly described by a fractional SE relation. Whether and how the fractional SE exponents vary remains an ongoing debate, even for the simplest supercooled liquids. In this work, we numerically establish a universal relation between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time by introducing characteristic scales that are revealed under the condition of constant dynamical heterogeneity. Moreover, this universal relation could also capture literature data for supercooled water and silica. Remarkably, we find that the fractional SE exponent is invariant across various supercooled liquids studied spanning a wide range of fragility, thereby challenging the prevailing view that the fractional SE exponent is correlated with fragility. Our study demonstrates that investigating dynamical heterogeneity yields more valuable insights into understanding glassy dynamics than expected.

item.title: Visualizing surface-reaction-driven chloride migration and cascading failure in sulfide solid electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2610.22394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Moisture instability of sulfide solid electrolytes limits practical use in all-solid-state batteries. Spatially resolving gas--solid reactions during moisture exposure remains challenging. Here, cryogenic four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (cryo-4D-STEM) maps nanoscale degradation in low- and high-Cl argyrodite electrolytes, Li\(_6\)PS\(_5\)Cl and Li\(_{5.5}\)PS\(_{4.5}\)Cl\(_{1.5}\). Li\(_6\)PS\(_5\)Cl undergoes predominantly surface-localized degradation that progressively extends inward, whereas Li\(_{5.5}\)PS\(_{4.5}\)Cl\(_{1.5}\) exhibits rapid interior amorphization accompanied by outward chloride redistribution. Density functional theory calculations indicate a lower chloride-migration barrier along the modeled pathway in the higher-Cl composition, while chloride removal and vacancy formation distort the PS\(_4^{3-}\) framework and may destabilize the lattice. Surface treatment suppresses detectable large-scale chloride segregation and improves moisture tolerance, retaining 99.9% of the capacity measured at the start of 0.33 C cycling after 150 cycles. These results identify chloride redistribution as a key process in degradation propagation and suggest a route toward moisture-tolerant solid-state batteries.

item.title: Semiclassical Analysis of Wave Dynamics via Wigner Transforms: Applications to the Quantum Harmonic, Anharmonic, and Dirac Oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2610.22414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this Master's thesis, we give a pedagogical introduction to the semiclassical analysis of wave dynamics in single-band and multi-band systems. We show how the semiclassical evolutions of Wigner functions can approximate the dynamics of wave packet centers and wave packet deformations. Three systems of increasing complexity are considered: the quantum harmonic oscillator and the quantum anharmonic oscillator as single-band systems, and the Dirac oscillator as a two-band system. We explain the origins of the first-order semiclassical corrections (Moyal, Littlejohn-Flynn, and Berry) in the equations of motion and examine their effects on predictive accuracy. Another focus is set on the conditions for validity of the semiclassical analysis. For both the quantum anharmonic and the Dirac oscillators, a dimensionless parameter controlling the accuracy of the approximation is identified. In multi-band systems, the formalism applies only to states within a single adiabatic subspace, which, for the Dirac oscillator, corresponds to an energy branch. This motivates the construction of single-branch almost coherent states: approximately Gaussian wave packets formed by superpositions of states from a single energy branch. Their centers undergo oscillations with an aperiodic envelope. These states enable comparison between semiclassical Wigner function evolution and the commonly used Sundaram-Niu formalism. We show that semiclassical Wigner function evolution captures deformation-related dynamics, including the initial decay of oscillations, which the Sundaram-Niu formalism cannot describe by construction. Additionally, exact quantum evolution reveals partial relocalization of these single-branch almost coherent states, a phenomenon that cannot be captured by the semiclassical evolution.

item.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Crystal Structural Prototypes: Construction, Classification, and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.22600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crystal structural prototypes describe recurring atomic arrangements across chemically distinct materials. Prototype libraries are built through crystallographic curation, standardization, geometric matching, local-environment clustering, and periodic-graph analysis, and support chemical substitution, derivative enumeration, high-throughput screening, structure solution, crystal structure prediction (CSP), and generative design. This survey compares methods by the structural information they retain and the equivalence rules they impose, distinguishing crystallographic structure types, geometric realizations, chemistry-anonymous topologies, and chemical decorations. We review curated and automatically extracted prototype libraries (AFLOW, CSPD, LAE-ICSPD, EMFDTW, TYPIX, ICSD structure types), their source databases, and algorithms for assigning family membership. A GraphID-based analysis of samples from ICSD, the Materials Project, OQMD, and LeMat shows that the 100 most frequent families in each sample cover 30 to 67 percent of analyzed structures, while 72 to 82 percent of observed families are singletons. The GraphIDs of up to 76 percent of structures change when the neighbor tolerance is varied. In our comparison of 12 generative CSP models, template retrieval achieves the highest top-1 success rate. Removing a reduced-stoichiometry class from training introduces new failures in 50 to 78 percent of the test structures of that class, which measures sensitivity to stoichiometric coverage, not generalization to unseen prototypes. We relate these findings to earlier statistics of structure types, space groups, and periodic nets, and to protein-fold coverage studies. We propose independent-database coverage measurements, discovery-rate analyses, and family-held-out tests to assess how prototype reuse affects prediction accuracy, generalization, and novelty.

item.title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Response Tensors in Crystalline Magnets: Application to Kagome Metals
item.description: arXiv:2610.22642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The prediction of response tensors from magnetic textures is a crucial challenge in the study of noncollinear magnets. Existing methods for constructing descriptors of a given response tensor are limited to first-order multipole expansions or restricted to simple magnetic structures. In this work, we construct a complete symmetry-invariant descriptor basis for arbitrary crystal structures and magnetic textures, providing interpretable features for machine learning modeling of response tensors. We modify the standard principal component analysis framework and derive uncorrelated order parameters that are hierarchically stable: extending the order parameter space to include higher-degree spin order introduces additional order parameters that are uncorrelated to the previous ones. We apply this framework to regression and classification of the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) in a magnetic kagome lattice. In particular, in the regime where AHC is well modeled by linear regression of the symmetry-invariant order parameters, we find that the squared regression coefficients, ranked by their magnitude, obey a Zipf-like power law: $\beta_{r}^2 \propto r^{-\alpha}$. Our method provides a systematic route to construct interpretable order parameters of all spin orders that connect the symmetry of a magnetic crystal to its response tensors.

item.title: Interplay between high-entropy effects and the superionic transition in fluorite oxides: A liquid-like perspective
item.description: arXiv:2610.22850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minor actinide (MA)-bearing mixed oxide (MOX), a prominent high-entropy ceramic (HEC), is a promising candidate for advanced fast reactor fuels. Using a hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics (MC/MD) approach, we reveal that Np and Am segregation establishes a distinct short-range order (SRO) that induces severe lattice distortion. We uncover a competitive mechanism between localized high-entropy blocking effects and collective superionic dynamics, where the anionic kinetic and structural evolution within the 2000-2800 K range is partitioned and governed by the Tammann crossover temperature and superionic transition temperature. In the low-temperature regime, severe lattice distortions induced by the SRO structures create localized electrostatic and strain-coupled potential wells, which spatially confine the O-ions and lead to their sluggish diffusion. The system exhibits increased dynamical heterogeneity as thermal activation alleviates these structural constraints. Crucially, these localized traps spontaneously transform into a highly interconnected, string-like polyhedral topological network. Driven by the maximization of configurational entropy, this structural change creates low-viscosity transport pathways that trigger confinement-enhanced diffusion. Consequently, a dramatic kinetic inversion occurs, where the O-ion mobility of SRO model surpasses that of random solid solution (RSS) model via an entropy-driven compensation mechanism. Finally, through Gibbs free energy minimization and defect analysis, structural and thermodynamic origins of the superionic transition in HEC are elucidated. This study unveils how local chemical ordering regulates ion transport under extreme conditions, providing theoretical support for the design of high-performance nuclear fuels with both superior radiation tolerance and optimized mass transfer capabilities.

item.title: Pressure-Dependent hcp-to-fcc Phase Transition Path Derived from Exact Lattice Summations over Inverse Power Law Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.22855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the phase transition between hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and face-centered cubic (fcc) structures along the Burgers-Bain transformation path at pressures up to several hundred gigapascals. We consider a hierarchy of interatomic potentials, from $(n,m)$-Lennard-Jones potentials to extended Lennard-Jones two-body interactions in terms of inverse-power expansions and the Axilrod-Teller-Muto three-body term, alongside density functional theory (DFT) calculations for solid argon. For inverse-power potentials, free energies are evaluated through exact lattice sums and efficient integral representations based on generalizations of the Epstein zeta function to anisotropic interaction kernels, followed by lattice-parameter optimization. This methodology enables an accurate determination of the pressure-dependent Burgers-Bain minimum-energy path and the associated activation barrier for the phase transition. The transformation exhibits pronounced symmetry breaking connecting the Burgers and Bain paths, a feature confirmed by DFT calculations. At high pressure, the hcp-to-fcc activation barrier increases approximately linearly with pressure, owing to the dominant pressure-volume contribution. Including entropy and anharmonic effects yields excellent agreement with experimental temperature-dependent volumes up to the melting point. DFT results also highlight the increasing importance of many-body interactions under compression. Whereas two-body potentials predict that the path passes through the body-centered cubic (bcc) structure only at very high pressures, DFT generally predicts a pathway that bypasses bcc. The Axilrod-Teller-Muto term slightly reduces this discrepancy. Furthermore, DFT performs better at high pressures, where dispersion forces become less important.

item.title: topas-editor and TOPilot: tools for AI-driven analysis of diffraction and total scattering data
item.description: arXiv:2610.23512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper describes topas-editor and TOPilot, which provide a powerful interface to the TOPAS software suite and allow generative AI-driven automation of complex crystallographic tasks. topas-editor is a TOPAS-aware VS Code extension designed for the rapid creation and editing of TOPAS input files and for interacting with the software. It knows TOPAS syntax, has crystallographic-aware editing features and provides in-line user guidance via hover tips and automated links to reference manuals. TOPilot is a collection of Python routines and machine-accessible reference documents that allow AI-driven automated analysis in TOPAS. It uses a transferable topas-inp-writer skill that can be applied in all TOPAS application areas. We demonstrate the power and reliability of the approach using examples including: a complex Rietveld refinement with sample- and data-related complications; automatic analysis of multiple data sets; a pipeline from indexing through structure solution to refinement; automatic identification of the phases present in a sample; single crystal and powder diffraction analysis of incommensurate structures; and fitting PDF data. TOPilot can be used directly alongside topas-editor, via a stand-alone topilot-wizard, or via command line interfaces or desktop apps from major AI providers. TOPilot was developed and tested using Claude large language models, but can be configured to use other cloud or local models. topas-editor and TOPilot are freely available.

item.title: pymatgen: 15 years of community growth, new functionality, and future prospects
item.description: arXiv:2610.23538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a retrospective on the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) library, reflecting on 15 years of community growth and established best practices. The current version of pymatgen builds on its robust, open-source foundation, emphasising its collaborative nature. Over the past decade, pymatgen has thrived as one of the largest open-source materials science codebases. We detail how pymatgen supports advanced computational materials science workflows, how it adapts to changing demands, and the lessons learned from its growing community, providing guidance beyond pymatgen's open-source community. Pymatgen will continue to evolve in response to the current rapidly changing landscape of computational materials science and materials informatics. We discuss the challenges and potential solutions to managing the community-driven evolution of pymatgen and provide an outlook on its future development.

item.title: Linear response for machine-learned interatomic potentials: phonons at arbitrary wave vectors from the primitive cell
item.description: arXiv:2610.23545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phonon calculations with machine-learned interatomic potentials are almost exclusively performed with finite displacements in supercells, an approach that is exact only at wave vectors commensurate with the supercell and whose error depends on the range of the force constants. In message-passing networks this range grows with the number of layers, and reaches 140 angstrom for the deepest universal models. Here we show that the dynamical matrix of a message-passing potential can be obtained exactly in the primitive cell, at any wave vector, as the linear response of the forces to a displacement modulated by a Bloch phase, in the spirit of density-functional perturbation theory. The phase enters only where the features of neighboring atoms are gathered, and the trained model is used without modification. One further derivative yields group velocities and mode Gr\"uneisen parameters analytically. We apply the method to NequIP and Prophet, and reproduce the Hessians of supercells to machine precision. Using these results as a reference, we find that the supercells commonly employed in high-throughput calculations lead to errors of several tenths of a THz in the phonon frequencies, and that these errors decrease slowly with the size of the supercell, in particular for deep models. For a low-symmetry silicate, the supercell predicts a dynamical instability that the model does not have. Quantities that depend on derivatives of the dispersion, such as the group velocities and the Gr\"uneisen parameter at low temperature, are considerably more affected than the frequencies themselves. When both approaches are used to obtain the same force constants, their computational cost is comparable for crystals with symmetry.

item.title: Scalable long-range machine learning interatomic potentials with electrical response for atomistic material modeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.23643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate atomistic simulations of materials under electric fields require long-range electrostatics and electrical-response modeling at length scales beyond the reach of conventional first-principles methods. Yet these capabilities remain difficult to reconcile with the scalability of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Strictly local models enable efficient spatial parallelization but neglect long-range interactions, whereas existing electrostatic extensions introduce global dependencies that hinder distributed computation. Here, we overcome this limitation by analytically separating the long-range electrostatic forces and Born effective charges (BECs) into a global electrostatics calculation and strictly local derivatives of learned latent charges. This formulation preserves the spatial decomposability of equivariant MLIPs while enabling distributed evaluation of energies, forces, stresses, and BECs across different boundary conditions. Implemented as DPA4C-LR on the \texttt{nvalchemi} platform, the framework scales to 5.2 million atoms on four GPUs at approximately twice the computational cost of its short-range backbone. Trained on energies and forces, DPA4C-LR accurately infers BECs and reproduces the field-dependent infrared spectra of water. We further demonstrate its capabilities by recovering the characteristic slim polarization hysteresis of relaxor \ce{Pb(Mg_{1/3}Nb_{2/3})O3}, which is obscured by finite-size effects in smaller simulations; predicting a room-temperature field-driven ionic conductivity of $6.8 \pm 0.7$~mS/cm in amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}}; and modeling interfacial thermal transport across Si/diamond interfaces with slab-corrected electrostatics. By combining long-range physics, electrical-response inference, and distributed computation, this framework extends predictive atomistic modeling toward device-relevant length scales.

item.title: Limits from nonlinear loss of spin-orbit-torque control of magnon transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.23763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlling magnon currents is central to the development of magnonic devices, which exploit spin excitations for information transport without charge flow. Here, we use the spin-orbit torque (SOT) from a Pt gate to control the effective magnon damping in three-terminal devices fabricated from low-damping lithium aluminum ferrite (LAFO) thin films and identify the nonlinear damping that ultimately limits the gate response. With increasing gate current, the nonlocal magnon signal initially increases, but saturates and subsequently decreases above a critical gate current density. Brillouin light scattering microscopy reveals that this turnover coincides with the emergence of an SOT-driven auto-oscillation mode localized beneath the gate, whose frequency continuously redshifts with increasing gate current, characteristic of large-amplitude nonlinear dynamics, and with a suppression of the propagating magnon population away from the gate. Micromagnetic simulations reproduce the observed nonmonotonic gate response only when an amplitude-dependent effective damping is included, indicating that nonlinear losses, rather than saturation of spin injection, limit the degree of magnon modulation. Our results show that SOT compensation of magnon damping is ultimately limited by nonlinear damping attributed to auto-oscillations, providing a framework for understanding the limits of magnon current modulation in magnetic insulators.

item.title: Ionic switching between supermagnetic states
item.description: arXiv:2610.23829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Supermagnetic states are typically set during synthesis. Changing and retaining these states requires sustained external stimulus. Without resynthesis or continued stimulus, we show, for the first time, a reversible magneto-ionic switching between superferromagnetic (SFM) and superspin-glass (SSG) states using room-temperature Li-ion transport. We utilize the incomplete lithiation of NiO into nanoscale Ni and Li2O to switch between the states. Lithiation generates a fragmented nano-Ni network that strengthens dipolar interactions and promotes SFM order with stronger memory and higher room-temperature moments. Delithiation partially regenerates NiO and drives the system into an SSG state with higher low-temperature coercivity and sharper temperature-selective memory. The interconversion between SFM and SSG persists at all measured subsequent lithiation-delithiation cycles, creating a general framework for supermagnetic switching.

item.title: Automated end-station at the soft X-ray beamline featuring robotic air-to-ultrahigh-vacuum sample transfer, scanning probe spectroscopy, and machine learning analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.22384v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driven by the growing integration of artificial intelligence and robotics in experimental science, we redefine the execution of user experiments at synchrotron soft X-ray beamlines by developing a highly automated end-station that can be operated without on-site staff. Installed at beamline BL08U of NanoTerasu, the system comprises four chamber units and two robots that automatically transfer samples from ambient air to an ultrahigh vacuum measurement stage for spectroscopic evaluations, before returning them to their original locations post-measurement. Soft X-ray absorption spectra are automatically acquired once programmed by scanning the micro-focused beam over the designated sample area, followed by automated evaluation using machine learning techniques such as principal-component analysis, multidimensional scaling, t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding, and uniform manifold approximation and projection. The high-throughput data are systematically accumulated in the database for remote user examination. This unstaffed end-station provides efficient beamtime for users and allows beamline scientists/technicians to pursue more human and creative endeavors.

item.title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.

item.title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2610.23776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

item.title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.23779v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function's linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.

item.title: Universality classes, Thermodynamics of Group Entropies, and Black Holes
item.description: arXiv:2603.02385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional Boltzmann--Gibbs statistical mechanics successfully describes systems with weak to moderate correlations, in which the number of accessible configurations $W(N)$ grows exponentially with the number of degrees of freedom $N$. However, this framework breaks down for systems for which the effectively occupied configuration space exhibits non-exponential growth. While numerous generalized entropies have been proposed to address this limitation, a coherent link to classical thermodynamic laws has remained elusive. Here, we propose group entropies as a unifying framework, defining universality classes of entropies through the asymptotic scaling of $W(N)$, each yielding an extensive entropy. We show that this approach provides the basis for a consistent thermodynamic formulation beyond the Boltzmann--Gibbs paradigm. In particular, by expressing these entropies in terms of thermodynamic state variables, we demonstrate their consistency with classical thermodynamics, in close analogy to the emergence of the Clausius entropy from the Boltzmann--Gibbs formalism. Focusing on the zeroth thermodynamic law, we identify the empirical temperature and, by using Carath\'{e}odory's formulation of the second law, we derive the associated absolute temperature. As an application, we analyse black-hole thermodynamics using the extensive group entropy class corresponding to stretched-exponential behaviour of $W(N)$ and derive a negative heat capacity, known to be a hallmark property of black holes. This result holds for the stretched-exponential entropies associated with both the Bekenstein--Hawking and Barrow entropy scalings.

item.title: From Atomistic Impurity Landscapes to Two-Level-System Distributions and Microwave Loss: Hydrogen-Induced Losses in Nb$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$ and Ta$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$
item.description: arXiv:2603.17194v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a first-principles-guided framework for predicting statistical TLS distributions from mobile impurities in disordered materials. Machine-learned interatomic potentials, with DFT and minimum-action-path validation, connect impurity landscapes to tunnel-splitting and asymmetry distributions, TLS densities, and dielectric loss. Applied to amorphous Nb$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$ and Ta$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$, the framework implicates interstitial hydrogen as a source of microwave loss. Loss tangents match Nb-pentoxide measurements at inferred H concentrations, while weaker H uptake in Ta reproduces the Nb/Ta TLS contrast.

item.title: Negative thermal expansion, lattice dynamics, and complex magnetism in TbFeO$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2608.00469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report a temperature-dependent investigation of orthoferrite TbFeO$_3$ using x-ray diffraction, DC magnetization, and Raman scattering, complemented by room-temperature x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. X-ray diffraction reveals negative thermal expansion over 5-300 K, with a small but systematic increase in unit-cell volume upon cooling in the absence of any structural phase transition. Raman scattering measurements identify the Raman-active phonon modes and show clear deviations from the conventional Klemens anharmonic decay model, particularly in phonon frequencies, indicating the presence of spin-phonon coupling. Two modes of $A_g$ and $B_{1g}$ symmetry exhibit a crossover from Gaussian-dominated line shapes at low temperatures to mixed Gaussian-Lorentzian profiles at higher temperatures, reflecting a transition from inhomogeneous broadening to lifetime-driven dynamics. High-energy Raman spectra reveal two-magnon excitations associated with the Fe sublattice, consistent with linear spin-wave theory, whose spectral weight shows only weak temperature dependence. In addition, a broad Raman mode emerging below $\sim 175$ K exhibits an order-parameter-like temperature evolution and coincides with the onset of phonon anomalies, while no corresponding strong anomaly is observed in the two-magnon response. Taken together, these results establish TbFeO$_3$ as a system with pronounced interplay among lattice dynamics, spin correlations, and emergent local magnetic-lattice anomalies.

item.title: ZStar: A unified toolkit for polarization, Born effective charges, dielectric and piezoelectric responses, and infrared and Raman spectra
item.description: arXiv:2609.16802v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Born effective charge (BEC) tensors link atomic displacements to polarization, thereby connecting lattice vibrations with dielectric response and infrared activity. We present ZStar, an open-source Python toolkit that automates calculations of polarization, BEC, phonons, static and frequency-dependent dielectric response, and infrared and Raman spectra. ZStar supports bulk crystals, two-dimensional materials, one-dimensional structures, and molecules through an integrated workflow for input preparation, execution, and response analysis. Berry-phase polarization and real-space dipoles describe responses along periodic and open directions, respectively. Its unified, symmetry-adapted finite-displacement framework jointly determines BEC and zone-center force constants from the same calculations, improving computational efficiency while preserving numerical accuracy. Strain-response calculations further provide proper piezoelectric coefficients and their internal-relaxation contributions for bulk crystals. In the ABACUS+PYATB route, electronic Hamiltonian data are reused to obtain Raman response without additional self-consistent calculations. Native response implementations from VASP and CP2K are also integrated. Matched infrared/Raman benchmarks against the implemented separate workflows achieve speedups of up to 8.4. An accompanying agent skill provides an agent-friendly interface for workflow integration. ZStar therefore offers an efficient and automated route for exploring polarization, BEC, dielectric and piezoelectric responses, and vibrational spectra across different material dimensionalities.

item.title: Electrified Metal-Water Interfaces at Constant Potential: Data-Efficient Transfer Learning for Machine-Learning-Based Molecular Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2511.19338v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating electrified metal-water interfaces with explicit solvent under constant potential is essential for understanding electrochemical processes, yet remains prohibitively expensive with ab initio methods. We present TRECI, a data-efficient workflow for constructing machine learning force-fields (ML-FFs) that achieve ab initio-level accuracy in electronically grand-canonical molecular dynamics. By leveraging transfer learning from general-purpose and domain-specific models, TRECI enables stable and accurate simulations across a wide potential range using a reduced number of reference configurations. This efficiency allows the use of high-level meta-GGA functionals and rigorous surface-electrification schemes. Applied to Cu(111)-water, models trained on just one thousand configurations yield accurate molecular dynamics simulations, capturing bias-dependent solvent restructuring effects not previously reported. TRECI offers a general strategy for characterising diverse materials and interfacial chemistries, significantly lowering the cost of realistic constant-potential simulations and expanding access to quantitative electrochemical modelling.

item.title: Tersoff-NN: Hybrid Machine-Learned Bond-Order Extension of the Tersoff Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.15591v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate, robust, and efficient interatomic potentials are highly desirable for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Although machine-learning interatomic potentials can reproduce first-principles potential-energy surfaces with high accuracy, they typically incur higher computational costs than conventional empirical potentials and may be less reliable outside their training domains. We developed Tersoff-NN, a hybrid machine-learning potential for Si, which retains the analytical radial interactions and cutoff structure of the Tersoff potential while representing its environment-dependent bond-order factor using compact neural networks (NNs). Benchmarks for 32,768-atom systems show that Tersoff-NN is 4-12 times faster than the Behler-Parrinello-type NN potentials tested in this study. Tersoff-NN improves the short-range structure of liquid Si relative to the conventional Tersoff potential, closely reproduces the ab initio radial and angular distributions, and reproduces the equilibrium structure of diamond Si and qualitative energetic trends among several crystalline phases. Furthermore, melt-quench simulations reveal a disordered solid with predominantly four-coordinated, tetrahedral-like local environments. Additionally, characteristic reconstruction motifs are retained on Si surfaces despite their exclusion from the training dataset. A direct comparison with an alternative atom-centered bond-order NN highlights the critical role of physical constraints in ensuring dynamic stability. Despite exhibiting comparable validation errors, the selected triplet-based architecture remains stable, while an alternative model exhibits unphysical bond-order growth and atomic collapse. These results confirm that learning only the bond-order term improves the description of diverse Si environments while retaining substantial computational efficiency and enhancing dynamical stability.

item.title: Trustworthy machine learning of diffractograms to prevent silent failure of apparently accurate models
item.description:
Communications Materials, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43246-026-01354-z

Machine-learning models can accurately predict outcomes from diffractograms, but differences between images and diffractograms may introduce vulnerabilities. Here, the authors compare neural networks trained on natural images and simulated diffractograms, revealing that physics-driven pre-training enhances model robustness by focusing on relevant features, underscoring the need for domain-specific training in scientific applications.

item.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03313-7

Large language models can mimic thought and feeling with uncanny skill. But evidence from neuroscience suggests that intelligence alone is not enough for subjective experience.

item.title: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
item.description:
Nature Communications, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78785-2

Designing efficient photoreactors remains challenging due to the complex interplay of light transport phenomena, shaped by reflection, scattering and absorption processes. Here, we introduce a workflow that integrates ray-tracing digital twins with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to autonomously design photoreactors in a closed-loop manner, achieving high photon capture and uniform irradiation.

item.title: Towards understanding and monitorability of reasoning LLMs
item.description:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01333-6

Frontier LLMs are trained to solve problems in a step-by-step way, generating reasoning text in human-understandable language. However, these reasoning tokens are not accurate explanations of LLMs’ internal computations, raising challenges for monitorability.

item.title: Tunneling characteristics of twisted double bilayer graphene heterostructures
item.description: Electron tunneling between sheets of bilayer Bernal graphene twisted at different small angles was studied experimentally and theoretically. The current–voltage characteristics exhibit resonant peaks, steps, and regions of negative differential resistance, the origin of which is explained by the intersections of energy- and momentum-shifted electron dispersions of adjacent layers. A theoretical analysis of tunneling transport demonstrated that the key to understanding this phenomenon lies in the competition between two contributions: between like (conduction–conduction or valence–valence) and unlike (conduction–valence) bands of parallel bilayer graphene sheets. A systematic evolution of the tunneling current patterns with increase in the twist angle is investigated. Polarization of electron wave function across graphene sublayers caused by displacement field within bilayer graphene is shown to strongly affect the tunneling probability, thus enhancing negative differential resistance due to Van Hove singularities at the band edges.

item.title: Phase-field simulation of dendrite evolution in all-solid-state sodium batteries during cycling
item.description:
Publication date: 1 January 2027

item.title: Developing stacking models for interacting biopolymers using quantum mechanical calculations and machine learning
item.description: Using quantum mechanical calculations and machine-learning models, Brinckerhoff et al. reveal that stacking configurations—rather than the conventionally accepted double-helix structure—are energetically favored in agarose chains. These findings settle a decades-long debate over biopolymer assembly and offer key insights for designing high-performance biopolymeric systems.

item.title: A lean statistical cell-to-pack framework for sustainable battery pack capacity estimation
item.description: Traditional pack capacity estimation relies on costly, unsustainable pack-level aging tests. Ma and Zhang et al. propose a lean statistical cell-to-pack (LS-CTP) framework bypassing pack cycling, using light machine learning and minimal cell data to track pack capacity from fragmented charge data, cutting battery waste and energy costs by over 90%.

item.title: Describing the Fluxional Dynamics of Sub-nanoscale Clusters with Markov State Modeling
item.description: Fluxionality, or the population of and interconversion between multiple structures, has long been suggested to be relevant for understanding the physical and catalytic behavior of sub-nanoscale metal clusters on an oxide support. Much of this treatment has, however, been thermodynamic, neglecting direct exploration of the timescales for interconversion between di!erent isomers. Previously, we exploited machine-learned interatomic potentials, combined with automatic process exploration (MLIP-APE) to identify isomerization networks for MgO-supported Pd clusters, capturing all barriers for cluster restructuring. In the current work, we demonstrate a new analysis approach based on Markov State Modeling (MSM) which captures the complex contribution of multiple timescales on the overall fluxional dynamic behavior over a range of cluster sizes. This overall fluxional behavior can then be classified between the extremes of highly dynamic “labile” clusters, to “rigid” clusters which exhibit much less dynamic behavior. These dynamics are of particular interest when using fluxional clusters for catalysis, as these dynamics could influence the observed catalytic reactions. Ultimately, this work demonstrates a rigorous and general approach to investigate the dynamics of reaction networks of well-defined states.

item.title: TAPERSS-MoCa: A Physics-Based Monte Carlo Framework for 3D RNA Structure Prediction from Sequence
item.description: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) function is intrinsically linked to its three-dimensional architecture, yet experimental structure determination remains challenging. Here, we introduce TAPERSS-MoCa (Theoretical Analyses, Prediction, and Evaluation of RNA Structures from Sequence using a Monte-Carlo Simulator), a physics-based fragment assembly framework for predicting RNA tertiary structures directly from sequence. By utilizing a novel fragment library grounded in dinucleoside monophosphate (DNMP) energetics parameterized via Discrete Path Sampling (DPS), TAPERSS-MoCa efficiently samples low-energy conformational landscapes. Evaluated across 6-, 10-, and 12-nucleotide RNA test sets, TAPERSS-MoCa consistently recovers native-like global minima with canonical Watson–Crick base pairs adopting near-planar geometry. By combining dinucleoside fragment energetics with an angularly constrained hydrogen-bonding potential, TAPERSS-MoCa accurately captures A-form structures in 6-nucleotide linear RNAs, outperforming traditional fragment-assembly algorithms that frequently misfold these flexible sequences. Thermodynamic evaluations based on ensemble partition functions (ΔGfolding) and macrostate basin free energies (ΔFfolding) demonstrate strong predictive performance for rigid, well-stacked GNRA tetraloops. Furthermore, TAPERSS-MoCa systematically reproduces key physical stability trends predicted by empirical nearest-neighbor models. This physics-based approach provides a robust platform for structural prediction and thermodynamic profiling of short RNA motifs, supporting RNA-targeted drug discovery and functional design.

item.title: Machine Learning Identifies an Information-Sufficiency Regime for Critical-Mineral Recovery
item.description: The recovery of critical minerals from spent lithium-ion batteries is governed by coupled feedstock chemistry, solvent composition, and processing conditions, yet heterogeneous experimental reporting makes it difficult to determine which information is essential for reliable prediction across heterogeneous experimental systems. Here, using deep eutectic solvent-based recovery as a representative resource recovery platform, we curate 814 experimental observations from 38 publications and develop an interpretable machine learning framework to identify an informationsufficiency regime. Five descriptors, including temperature, electrode material type, leaching time, target metal, and hydrogen-bond donor identity, retain 98.3% of the predictive performance of the full 13-descriptor model while reducing the descriptor space by 61.5%. Reducing the representation from five to four descriptors causes a pronounced performance loss, whereas adding a sixth provides negligible additional benefit. Descriptor removal and domain ablation analyses further show that temperature and target metal identity contain the least replaceable predictive information, while material identity, solvent chemistry, and processing conditions provide complementary information. These results identify a compact, chemically structured information core for critical-mineral recovery and provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing experimental measurements, improving cross-study data consistency, and developing more transferable datadriven frameworks for battery resource recovery.

item.title: Whole-Enzyme Reactive Free-Energy Simulations with a Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potential: Catalytic Mechanism and Mutational Effects of PETase
item.description: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) have emerged as powerful tools for atomistic simulations that achieve quantum mechanical accuracy at significantly reduced computational cost. Yet, their direct application to complex enzymatic reactions remains challenging owing to the immense size of solvated enzyme systems and the scarcity of transition-state structures in training data. In this study, we demonstrate that PFP (PreFerred Potential), a pretrained uMLIP across 96 elements in nature, simulates the complete hydrolytic cycle of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) catalyzed by PETase as a single reactive domain of approximately 20,000 atoms, without multiscale partitioning or system-specific fine-tuning. Umbrella-sampling simulations revealed stepwise mechanisms for both acylation and deacylation through distinct tetrahedral intermediates. The computed rate-limiting deacylation barrier of 20.5 ± 0.3 kcal/mol is in agreement with the range of 18.0–18.7 kcal/mol inferred from experimental turnover numbers. The PFP-based simulations further capture catalytic consequences of point mutations from loss of function (D177N, M132A) to predicted activity enhancement (D157N) and reveal that simultaneous neutralization of three distal acidic residues which are located more than 10 Å from the active site raises the activation barrier due to a collective long-range electrostatic effect that emerges naturally in the partition-free treatment. These findings demonstrate that the pretrained uMLIP, PFP, can provide physically plausible free-energy profiles for enzymatic reaction mechanisms and capture mutational effects, providing a powerful platform for rational enzyme design.

item.title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations
item.description: arXiv:2610.20779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fr\"ohlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

item.title: MASON: Materials Atomistic Structure builder Operated in Natural language
item.description: arXiv:2610.21015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building reliable atomistic models is a critical and often challenging step in first-principles calculations. Although large language model agents can assist with structure generation, they lack direct capabilities for crystallographic operations and therefore struggle to construct complex structures reliably. Here we present MASON, an AI-native toolkit for atomistic structure construction that can be invoked by agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In an end-to-end example, an agent builds a CO/Pt(111) adsorption model from a natural language request. By equipping agents with dedicated structure-building tools, MASON enables reliable and efficient atomistic model construction and provides a foundation for autonomous first-principles workflows.

item.title: Theory of Dispersion and Exchange Interactions Subjected to Surface Roughness in Application to Signal Transmission through a Nanoswitch
item.description: arXiv:2610.21652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the theoretical description of a resistive nanoswitch designated for a change-over between the two operation modes by calculating the electri elastic, dispersion (van der Waals and Casimir), and also exchange repulsive forces in its configuration with an account of surface roughness. The dispersion forces are described by means of the Lifshitz theory and, at the shortest separations between the interacting bodies, where this theory is inapplicable, by the method of additive summation of the interatomic potentials corrected for the role of the effects of nonadditivity. The exchange repulsion is also found by a summation of the interatomic potentials and using the proximity force approximation. It is shown that the nanoswitch possesses the equilibrium closest separation between a cantilever tip and a ground plate calculated as a function of the actuation voltage and operates in a cyclic manner with no pull-in when this voltage is switched on and off. We have found the tunnel current between a cantilever tip and a plate and investigated distortions appearing in the signal transmitted through a nanoswitch. According to our results, the amplitude distortions arising in the low-frequency information signal can be made sufficiently small by increasing a difference between the amplitudes of the carrier and information signals. Possible applications of the obtained results are discussed.

item.title: Interlocked Vortex Order in the Frustrated $A_3$V$_9$Te$_{13}$ Lattice ($A$=Cs,Rb)
item.description: arXiv:2610.21854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently synthesized $A_3$V$_9$Te$_{13}$ ($A$ = Cs, Rb) provides a unique platform for exploring the interplay between geometric frustration, magnetism, and correlated electronic states beyond conventional kagome systems. Based on first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the frustrated V sublattice naturally stabilizes a robust vortex or anti-vortex antiferromagnetic ground state, whose total energy is substantially lower than all other configurations. In addition, the Heisenberg model analysis show strong constraints on the ground state magnetic configuration, such that fixing spin configuration of 1 triangle propagates and fixes all others. The vortex or anti-vortex phase hosts electronic structures reminiscent of kagome metals, including Dirac-like band crossings, van Hove singularities, and flat bands near the Fermi level. Owing to the noncollinear spin texture and quasi-two-dimensional magnetic character, the N\'eel temperature exhibits an extremely weak dependence on both the magnitude and direction of external magnetic fields, consistent with experimental observations. For Cs-based compound, the ground state band structure is metallic with 6 Weyl points in the BZ; while for the Rb-based compound, spin--orbit coupling opens an approximately 27-meV gap at ambient pressure due to the lifted C$_3$ symmetry. Our results establish $A_3$V$_9$Te$_{13}$ as a promising platform for studying frustration-driven chiral magnetism and its interplay with topological electronic states.

item.title: Microwave spectroscopic evidence of a moir\'e-commensurate electron crystal in monolayer graphene
item.description: arXiv:2610.21875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We probe the conductivity of the lowest Landau level of a moir\'e-aligned monolayer graphene device by broadband microwave transmission through a coplanar waveguide ($\sim$50 mK, 15.4--18 T), isolating the longitudinal channel through a low-minus-high frequency band difference $D(\nu)$. We resolve a series of minima in $D(\nu)$ that drift with field along lines of fixed carrier density rather than fixed Landau filling, the hallmark of moir\'e-commensurate electron crystals. The strongest minimum is present at every field and matches no fractional quantum Hall or integer Hofstadter state. It lies at band filling $s=1/3$, one electron for every three moir\'e cells---the generalized Wigner crystal that DaSilva, Jung, and MacDonald predict as the most favorable fixed-density ($t=0$) commensuration. The weaker minima fall near neighboring commensurate fillings.

item.title: Extended strange metal and superconductivity in partially filled moir\'e Hubbard bands
item.description: arXiv:2610.22307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Moir\'e semiconductors provide a physical realization of the Hubbard model. Bandwidth-tuned Mott transitions and complex phase diagrams mimicking those of high-temperature superconductors have been demonstrated near a weak Mott insulating state at half-band-filling. The platform also provides an opportunity to explore the physics of a partially filled Hubbard band at doping densities far away from the Mott insulator, a regime that has remained largely unexplored. Here we report the emergence of an extended strange metal (ESM), in both doping density and twist angle, in a partially filled Hubbard band of twisted bilayer WSe2. The ESM is in the clean limit, persists down to 100mK, and spans over multiple symmetry-breaking ground states; it also appears only at small twist angles, where electronic correlations are strong. These observations distinguish the state from the reported strange metals associated with quantum criticality and favor the viewpoint that it is an intrinsic state of matter. We also report the observation of a new superconducting dome being developed from the ESM but far away from both the Mott insulating state and the van Hove singularity of the material. Our work opens the door to exploring the new regime of partially filled Hubbard bands in the clean limit.

item.title: Thermodynamically Consistent Machine Learning for Fracture Prediction in Heterogeneous Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.20614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding fracture behavior is critical for assessing the structural integrity and longevity. Highly time-consuming physics-based fracture simulations motivate the development of machine-learning-based fracture evolution prediction with surrogate models. However, most existing machine-learning models for fracture prediction operate as black boxes and require large training datasets to generalize reliably. In this work, Thermodynamically Consistent Latent Dynamics Identification (tLaSDI) for parametric systems is introduced to predict fracture patterns and evolution in heterogeneous materials. The model learns the thermodynamic state variable in a lower-dimensional latent space using parametric GENERIC Formalism-Informed Neural Networks (pGFINNs) that enforce key thermodynamic principles, such as total energy conservation and entropy generation. This model embeds physics into the neural network architecture using a hard-constraint method that inherently complies with the underlying thermodynamic principles. The proposed tLaSDI-pGFINNs is further enhanced by a Geometry-Conditioned Autoencoder in learning the geometry configuration for effective geometry-guided learning. The energy and entropy evolution histories demonstrate that the model preserves the thermodynamic constraints on unseen testing samples. The results further show that tLaSDI-pGFINNs can more accurately capture both fracture patterns and the subsequent fracture evolution than the purely data-driven Autoencoder Long Short-Term Memory (AE-LSTM) model.

item.title: Dynamic Coarse-Graining of Linear and Non-Linear Systems: Mori-Zwanzig Formalism and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2307.08143v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To investigate the impact of non-linear interactions on dynamic coarse graining, we study a simplified model system, featuring a tracer particle in a complex environment. Using a projection operator formalism and computer simulations, we systematically derive generalized Langevin equations (GLEs) describing the dynamics of this particle. We compare different kinds of linear and non-linear coarse-graining procedures to understand how non-linearities enter reconstructed generalized Langevin equations and how they influence the coarse-grained dynamics. For non-linear external potentials, we show analytically and numerically that the non-Gaussian parameter and the incoherent intermediate scattering function will not be correctly reproduced by the GLE if a linear projection is applied. This, however, can be overcome by using non-linear projection operators. We also study anharmonic coupling between the tracer and the environment and demonstrate that the reconstructed memory kernel develops an additional trap-dependent contribution. Our study highlights some open challenges and possible solutions in dynamic coarse graining.

item.title: Emergent chiral Higgs mode in $\pi$-flux frustrated lattices
item.description: arXiv:2601.08925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neutral-atom quantum simulators provide a powerful platform for realizing strongly correlated phases, enabling access to dynamical signatures of quasiparticles and symmetry breaking processes. Motivated by recent observations of quantum phases in flux-frustrated ladders with non-vanishing ground state currents, we investigate interacting bosons on the dimerized BBH lattice in two dimensions-originally introduced in the context of higher-order topology. After mapping out the phase diagram, which includes vortex superfluid (V-SF), vortex Mott insulator (V-MI), and featureless Mott insulator (MI) phases, we focus on the integer filling case. There, the MI/V-SF transition simultaneously breaks the $\mathbb Z_2^{T}$ and U(1) symmetries, where $\mathbb Z_2^{T}$ corresponds to time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Using a slave-boson description, we resolve the excitation spectrum across the transition and uncover a chiral Higgs mode whose mass softens at criticality, providing a dynamical hallmark of emergent chirality that manifests via the oscillation of the loop currents in quench dynamics. Our results establish an experimentally realistic setting for probing unconventional TRS-broken phases and quasiparticles with intrinsic chirality in strongly interacting quantum matter.

item.title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.17987v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Energetic materials involve multiple interactions, making reliable machine-learning potentials (MLPs) difficult to construct without extensive datasets. Here, we enhance the ability of the neural network interatomic potential (NNAP) to describe molecular systems using sphmulti, a refined spherical-harmonic basis set that combines extra radial basis with element-specific chemical weighting in each radial channel. We further integrate hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria with knowledge-guided key events, enabling the NNAP to retain essential information for describing the material system. For 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan, the resulting NNAP is trained on only 13,680 configurations yet captures key properties, including the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior. NNAP-driven molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that pyrolysis proceeds through furazan-ring opening followed by chain reactions, whereas shock loading induces anisotropic hydrogen transfer driven by interlayer structural deformations. This work enables efficient and reliable MLPs for energetic materials.

item.title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.00636v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

item.title: Photogenerated Carrier-Mediated Ion Transport for Self-Adaptive Neuromorphic Vision
item.description:
CCS Chemistry, Ahead of Print.
DOI:10.31635/ccschem.026.202608458
Artificial vision that emulates the retina’s self-adaptation to changing illumination is critical for applications such as drones’ navigation, security surveillance, and augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR). However, current devices rely on continuous external bias, as they fail to replicate the biological opto-electro-ionic conversion mechanism. Here, we present a self-adaptive neuromorphic vision device based on a semiconductor–ionogel heterojunction that exploits photogenerated carrier-mediated ion transport. Light intensity modulated the concentration of photogenerated carriers, thereby altering the electrical double layer at the semiconductor–ionogel interface and inducing distinct ion transport behaviors. This mechanism enabled reversible switching between paired-pulse facilitation (dim light) and paired-pulse depression (bright light), faithfully emulating the retina’s bidirectional adaptation in a single device without additional stimuli. Leveraging this capability, the device achieved over 95% accuracy in handwritten digit recognition under both scotopic and photopic conditions and replicated complex visual phenomena, including negative afterimage and Troxler’s fading. This work provides an effective strategy for self-adaptive neuromorphic vision systems.

item.title: High-pressure Raman study of phonon dynamics and phase transition in ZnO nanowires
item.description: We report high-pressure Raman scattering measurements on ZnO nanowires up to ∼20 GPa, supported by density functional theory calculations. The wurtzite (B4) phase transforms to the cubic rock salt (B1) structure at ∼10 to 13 GPa, accompanied by the appearance of disorder-activated Raman modes. The pressure dependence of phonon modes in the nanowires is directly compared with theoretical predictions for both the B4 and B1 phases of bulk ZnO, providing a unified description of lattice dynamics across the phase transition and deeper insight into size- and dimensionality-related effects, a connection not systematically explored in previous studies. Upon decompression, the B1 phase persists metastable down to ∼0.8 GPa, revealing pronounced hysteresis and a substantially reduced reverse transition pressure. The recovered wurtzite phase exhibits broadened Raman features and frequency shifts, indicative of residual strain and defect accumulation. Linewidth analysis shows that most B1 modes exhibit comparable FWHM values during compression and decompression, implying similar phonon lifetimes and reversible lattice dynamics, with deviations attributed to disorder. Anomalies near ∼10 and ∼0.8 GPa are linked to lattice anharmonicity and phase reconstruction. Pressure coefficients and Grüneisen parameters agree with bulk trends, while deviations reflect size- and defect-related effects in the nanowires.

item.title: MaRs: A Universal Python Library for Steady-State and Time-Resolved EPR Simulations
item.description: MaRs is an open-source Python library for the simulation and fitting of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra. MaRs supports simulations of field-swept and frequency-swept continuous-wave EPR, accounting for various spin-sublevel polarizations. Moreover, MaRs is capable of simulating complete 2D time-resolved EPR spectra (in field-time domain). The latter can be computed in different levels of theoretical complexity. First, the time evolution can be computed either with kinetic rate equations, which describe population transfer, or in full Liouville space, which captures coherence dynamics. Second, the relaxation pathways in timeresolved simulations can be specified either through intuitive rate parameters that are automatically expanded into the Lindblad master-equation form, or derived microscopically using the Bloch-Redfield formalism. To handle physically complex relaxation scenarios, MaRs provides automatic thermal-balance enforcement and composition operations that allow multicomponent relaxation models to be assembled from simple building blocks. Built on PyTorch (popular platform for machine learning development), MaRs leverages operations on both CPU and CUDA (GPU) backends. We demonstrate MaRs time-resolved EPR capabilities as well the differences and limitations of each built-in approach to time-domain simulations on the examples of coupled triplet-doublet pairs and systems exhibiting the reverse intersystem crossing phenomenon. Separately, we validate stationary EPR simulations across diverse spin systems, including high-spin complexes, achieving excellent agreement with established packages. We also show the possibilities of parameter fitting framework, applicable to all spectrum types implemented in MaRs, that supports multiple optimization strategies and uncertainty quantification.

item.title: Predicting Glass Transition Temperature of Polyimide Homopolymers and Copolymers Using Interpretable QSPR-Based Machine Learning: The MFKit Framework
item.description: In this work, we address the problem of predicting the glass transition temperature of polyimides, a class of high-performance engineering thermoplastics, with an emphasis on both homopolymer and copolymer systems. While machine learning approaches have been widely applied to polymer property prediction, their extension to copolymers remains limited and often lacks the interpretability required for rational materials design. To overcome these limitations, we develop an interpretable QSPR-based framework (MFKit) that combines physically grounded descriptors for monomer featurization with Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). The model is trained on a dataset of polyimide homopolymers from PoLyInfo and achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches (R2 = 0.856, MAE = 20.7 °C on the test set). Causal inference and SHAP analysis reveal key structure–property relationships, identifying aromatic content, backbone flexibility and rotation, side chain volume and hydrogen bonding as dominant factors governing Tg. The framework is subsequently extended to polyimide copolymers by constructing copolymer representations through combination of monomer descriptor vectors using several aggregation schemes. The best-performing approach yields R2 = 0.832 and MAE = 23.3 °C on an external dataset compiled from the literature. Furthermore, guided by the identified structure–property relationships, polyimide copolymers are designed, synthesized, and experimentally characterized, each exhibiting increased Tg compared with the parent homopolymer. Validation against DSC measurements demonstrates strong agreement with predictions (MAE = 16.3 °C). Overall, the proposed approach provides a unified and interpretable framework for Tg prediction for both homopolymer and copolymer systems, enabling physically grounded and data-driven design of polyimide-based materials.

item.title: Gas-Conditioned Message Passing Graph Neural Network for Permeability Prediction in Polymeric Membranes
item.description: Designing polymeric membranes for diverse gas-separation applications remains a critical challenge. Machine learning (ML) models can significantly accelerate this effort by capturing complex relationships between polymer-gas pairs and enabling permeability prediction over an extended chemical space of gases and polymers. In this work, we present a novel ML framework, the gas-conditioned message passing neural network (GC-MPNN), that jointly combines gas descriptors and polymer chemistry in a fused neural network model. Polymers are represented at the monomer level and encoded as molecular graphs, where node and edge information is propagated through message-passing layers. Six gas species (He, H2, N2, O2, CH4, and CO2) are represented using multiple descriptor sets spanning thermodynamic, kinetic, and electrostatic properties, along with one-hot encodings and combined feature sets that include kinetic plus thermodynamic descriptors and the full physicochemical descriptor set. For each descriptor combination, model hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization within a leave-one-gas-out (LOGO) validation framework. Test performance is then evaluated on the gas species excluded entirely from the corresponding training fold (out-of-training set) and compared across descriptor sets. For most gas species, the model achieves strong predictive performance (R2 ∼ 0.86–0.96), while CO2 remains more challenging in terms of absolute prediction accuracy (R2 ∼ 0.44). Active learning sampling further improves model performance by adding a few labeled samples from the test gas species into the training set. Among the three strategies tested, deep ensemble-based sampling and random sampling show strong improvement, with R2 reaching approximately ∼ 0.95 for all gas species, while evidential regression shows less consistent improvement. The model is further evaluated on a smaller polymer-gas dataset containing hydrocarbon species (C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, and n-C4H10) using the GC-MPNN trained only on the six base gases, achieving moderate to strong Pearson correlations (r ∼ 0.77–0.89) for these out-of-training gases. Overall, this work presents a machine learning model that can learn transferable polymer-gas relationships from known gas species and extend them to previously unseen gases.
