item.title: On physical implementability of reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the machine learning community, the reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning process has been intensively studied since around 2025. In this article, we present a negative result on the hardware implementation of this reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning process in a physical neural network model in the presence of a reward external potential energy for a given reward. In this hardware implementation, the existence of a chain of thought in dynamics contradicts the Lyapunov stability of the system.

item.title: Benchmarking machine-learning interatomic potentials using classical force fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.14239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a rational comparison between several well-known machine-learning interatomic potentials (linear atomic cluster expansion, the Behler-Parrinello high-dimensional neural network potential, and the graph neural network-based MACE potential) by testing their performance for fitting classical potentials such as the Lennard-Jones and Stillinger-Weber potential. With this we assess their advantages and limitations regarding several aspects: varying training dataset size, robustness to noise, carbon footprint, as well as the ability to reproduce the radial distribution function as an example observable. Overall the MACE models are shown to most accurately reproduce the potential energy surface, with little sign of overfitting, but at a significant computational cost, highlighting important questions regarding the choice of models in computational materials science.

item.title: Large Out-of-plane Polarization in Two-dimensional Bi2O3 Monolayers Predicted by an AI-driven Inverse-design Workflow
item.description: arXiv:2610.14429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) polar oxides with built-in electric fields offer promising opportunities for nanoscale electronics, optoelectronics, and surface charge engineering. However, their discovery remains challenging due to the enormous structural complexity of nonlayered oxide networks. Here, we combine inverse structural design with a machine-learning interatomic potential and first-principles calculations to explore 2D oxide configurations. Using Bi2O3 as a representative system, we identify two previously unreported polar monolayers with tetragonal and orthorhombic symmetries. Both structures exhibit vertically separated Bi and O sublayers, giving rise to pronounced intrinsic polarity with Berry-phase 2D polarizations of 34.12 and 37.15 pC/m, respectively. Notably, the o-Bi2O3 monolayer exhibits one of the largest reported out-of-plane polarizations among 2D oxides. Both monolayers exhibit dynamical stability, finite-temperature structural integrity, and wide band gaps (~3.8 eV). The large polarization originates from dimensionality-induced reconstruction of the nonlayered Bi-O network, which breaks local coordination symmetry and produces out-of-plane charge redistribution, while the stereochemically active Bi 6s2 lone pair further favors asymmetric Bi-O bonding. These findings suggest dimensionality-induced local-coordination symmetry breaking as a promising design motif for high-polarization 2D oxides, and demonstrate the utility of combining inverse design with machine-learning-assisted screening to explore unconventional polar phases in nonlayered oxide networks.

item.title: Pressure-transferable universal machine-learning potentials: the WBM-MatPES benchmark and Tuga-FF
item.description: arXiv:2610.14891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials hold the promise to replace costly ab initio calculations in materials science workflows. However, the accuracy and transferability of current models are limited by the availability of training data. We release WBM-MatPES, a dataset of 182 thousand structures recomputed with consistent MatPES settings, together with two reference convex hulls of different depths and test sets at six pressures up to 150 GPa. These datasets reproduce a realistic discovery workflow and allow potentials to be ranked systematically at this level of theory, similar to the Matbench Discovery leaderboard at the Materials Project settings. In this benchmark, five published MatPES potentials agree within 12 meV/atom at 25 GPa, yet their errors increase dramatically to 0.4-5 eV/atom at 150 GPa. To address this limitation, we develop Tuga-FF, a graph transformer trained on datasets spanning ambient and high-pressure configurations alike. Tuga-FF is the most accurate model in the benchmark at ambient pressure, with an energy error of 13.6 meV/atom, and maintains an error of just 21 meV/atom at 150 GPa. We believe this benchmark will encourage the community to train higher-accuracy models and generate richer datasets, advancing machine-learned interatomic potentials as a whole.

item.title: Indirect prediction and screening of frustrated magnetic materials using machine learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic frustration is commonly quantified by the frustration index, calculated from the Curie-Weiss and Neel temperatures. Because both quantities are not simultaneously available for most materials, direct prediction of the magnetic frustration index remains challenging. Here, we propose a machine learning workflow for indirect prediction of the frustration index and consequent screening of potential frustrated magnetic compounds through independent prediction of Curie-Weiss and Neel temperatures. In our work, composition-based models implemented via the CatBoost algorithm, trained on experimental data were optimized using chemically informed dataset subdivision. The highest predictive accuracy was achieved for the rare earth-oxide model in predicting Neel and for the rare earth model in predicting Curie-Weiss. Ensemble uncertainty was incorporated through a conservative frustration index to improve the reliability of candidate selection. Screening of approximately 67000 Materials Project compounds identified 20 high-confidence frustrated magnetic candidates, including several experimentally known frustrated magnets and previously unexplored oxide systems potential for further investigation.

item.title: Field Response of the Orbital Moment Probed by Integrated Magnetic Circular Dichroism
item.description: arXiv:2610.15684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) is an optical probe of orbital time reversal symmetry breaking. Although frequency integrated MCD is related to the self-rotation contribution to orbital magnetization at zero field, its magnetic response generally differs from the thermodynamic orbital susceptibility. Here, we define the MCD susceptibility and derive general expressions for multiband systems using an electromagnetic $U(1)$ gauge invariant approach. For insulators, the response contains contributions from the non-Abelian quantum metric, Berry curvature, and field induced interband mixing. For metals, a finite temperature Green function formulation separates the smooth response into Fermi sea and Fermi surface contributions. An independent Landau level calculation confirms the expressions for the zero-field MCD moment and its linear magnetic response. In a continuum model for twisted bilayer graphene, the MCD susceptibility vanishes within the charge neutrality gap, while the thermodynamic orbital susceptibility remains markedly diamagnetic. Near the gap edges, the orbital moment term dominates the response. Features near the van Hove energies are associated with density of states enhancement. These results clarify how the two susceptibilities reflect different orbital processes even for the same electronic structure and thus establish the MCD susceptibility as a distinct probe of orbital magnetic response.

item.title: Eigenstate transitions and critical transport in 3D Aubry-Andr\'e model
item.description: arXiv:2610.15842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We numerically study spectral and wave-function properties, as well as time evolution, in finite-size commensurate approximations of the 3D Aubry-Andr\'e model. We explicitly show, through scaling analysis, the existence of two critical points. One of the critical points is a localization-delocalization transition in real-space, similar to the critical point in the 3D Anderson model. The other is a localization-delocalization transition in a dual momentum space, which does not have any analog in the 3D Anderson model. We estimate their values from spectral measures, such as the gap ratio and the spectral form factor, as well as from wave-function measures, such as the inverse participation ratio and the participation entropy. Additionally, we demonstrate that both critical points exhibit hallmarks of critical points between quantum ergodicity and localization. First, the eigenstates and the eigenspectrum at the critical point fulfill the mutual universal relation between the eigenspectrum compressibility $\chi$ and the eigenstate fractal dimension $d^{(1)}$ [S. Jiricek et al., Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. 123, e2518027123 (2026)]. Second, the dynamics of the wave packet at the critical point is governed by the critical dynamical exponent $z$, characterized by the spectral fractal dimension and the dimensionality of the lattice [M. Hopjan and L. Vidmar, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 060401 (2025)]. Thus, similarly to the 3D Anderson model, the critical dynamical exponent is sub-diffusive with the value of $z=3$.

item.title: Extreme anharmonicity determines the superionic transition in the prototypical antifluorite Li$_2$O
item.description: arXiv:2610.15986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superionic conductors are promising electrolyte candidates for all-solid-state batteries, thanks to their liquid-like ionic mobility. In the prototypical lithium-ion oxide superionic conductor with antifluorite structure, the high-temperature transition to the fast-ion regime has long been attributed to volume-driven harmonic phonon softening. However, this quasi-harmonic picture neglects the strong lattice anharmonicity inherent to the fast-ion regime, leaving the microscopic origin of the transition unresolved. Here, we apply non-perturbative lattice dynamics combined with a first-principles-accurate machine-learning interatomic potential to study the phase transition in Li$_2$O. We demonstrate that anharmonicity, rather than volume expansion alone as commonly assumed, plays the decisive role in determining the transition temperature and the underlying mechanism. Finally, we analyze the spectral properties using the time-dependent self-consistent harmonic approximation, revealing the breakdown of the quasi-particle picture in this material. The spectral function and the infrared response provide signtures of the phase transition that can be investigated experimentally using inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering and infrared spectroscopy. All these results establish the extreme anharmonicity of Li$_2$O near the superionic regime and provide a lattice-dynamic framework for understanding and engineering the fast-ion transition in this type of materials.

item.title: An empirical model for deriving information on ion dynamics from $\mu$SR data via the conventional Kubo-Toyabe function analysis
item.description:
arXiv:2610.16006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an empirical model that analytically relates the parameters of the extended Kubo-Toyabe (KT) function $G_z^{m EA}(t;\Delta,
u_{m i},Q)$, which describes muon spin relaxation ($\mu$SR) induced by jump diffusion of ions using the Edwards-Anderson parameter $Q$, to those of the conventional KT function $G_z^{m KT}(t;\Delta_{m KT},
u_{m KT})$ that serves as an approximation of $G_z^{m EA}(t)$. The proposed formulae successfully reproduce the anomalous temperature dependences of the linewidth $\Delta_{m KT}(T)$ and the fluctuation rate $
u_{m KT}(T)$ which are artifacts observed upon analyzing $\mu$SR data on ion diffusion using $G_z^{m KT}(t)$. Applying this model to $\Delta_{m KT}$ and $
u_{m KT}$ published in the literature of battery materials yields activation energy $E_{m i}$ and pre-exponential factor $
u_{m i0}$ in the Arrhenius equation for ion diffusion, $
u_{m i}(T)=
u_{m i0} e^{-E_{m i}/kT}$, that are in excellent agreement with those deduced using other techniques, transforming peculiar artifacts into a powerful diagnostic tool.

item.title: Chirally pinned flat bands, helical minibands, and bias-controlled topology of Jackiw-Rebbi states in a periodically modulated Dirac mass texture
item.description: arXiv:2610.16183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flat bands amplify interactions into correlated phases, and topological bound states are robust by principle; combining the two in a model that is both exactly analyzable and experimentally accessible is therefore especially desirable. Here we show that a square-lattice model with a slowly modulated Dirac mass texture, $m(x)=m+m_0\cos(2\pi x/L)$ with $L$ up to hundreds of sites, provides such a setting, without engineered geometries, lattice-scale textures, or long-range hoppings. Exact nesting reduces the problem, independently at each transverse momentum $k_y$, to a $1+1$ dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian with a position-dependent mass: every simple zero of $m(x)$ binds Jackiw-Rebbi zero modes, and the two walls of a period form an effective Su-Schrieffer-Heeger ring. The model interpolates between a chirally pinned flat band at large $L$, a helical miniband whose nodes are enforced by a boundary phase of the ring, and a bias-dimerized regime in which the sign of the bias sets a winding number. A central result is that the miniband bandwidth is not a single scale: a max-min measurement conflates three widths of different origin, the helical height $W_{\rm JR}$ exponential in the period, the zone-edge upturn $W_{\rm edge}\propto L^{-2/3}$ dominating at large $L$, and a bias bump exponential in $L$, so the flat band is robust against bias in the thermodynamic limit. We analyze two lattice realizations, a two-orbital model with modulated inter-orbital hybridization and a single-orbital bond-order texture sharing the nodal physics while leaving the van Hove points gapless, and propose experiments on cold-atom superlattices, Kekule-ordered graphene, STM designer lattices, and microwave arrays.

item.title: Photon echo from Maki-Thompson interference in a fluctuating s-wave superconductor
item.description: arXiv:2610.16462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study theoretically the nonlinear optical response of a fluctuating s-wave superconductor driven by two successive terahertz pulses. We show that the response exhibits a photon echo signal that arises from the quantum interference between the time-reversed electron and hole trajectories in the Maki-Thompson process. By contrast, the transport of the fluctuating Cooper pairs responsible for the Aslamazov-Larkin conductivity does not generate an echo. The photon echo signal can be readily measured using terahertz two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy, highlighting its potential to distinguish different fluctuation conductivity mechanisms.

item.title: H$_2$-Like Units and Pressure-Tunable High-$T_\mathrm{c}$ Superconductivity in NaH$_6$
item.description: arXiv:2610.17148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hydrogen-rich materials offer a route to high-temperature conventional superconductivity, but often require extreme pressures. Here we report a first-principles study of NaH$_6$, identified in our large-scale hydride search and independently predicted in a subsequent high-throughput study. Several phases compete, with $R\bar{3}m$ and $Pm\bar{3}m$ dominant over broad pressure ranges. The $R\bar{3}m$ phase remains dynamically stable down to 10 GPa, where its calculated $T_\mathrm{c}$ is 34 K, rising to 99 K at 50 GPa. Cubic $Pm\bar{3}m$ becomes thermodynamically competitive at higher pressures and reaches a calculated $T_\mathrm{c}$ of 230 K at 50 GPa, decreasing only weakly upon further compression. Molecular dynamics and phonon-renormalization calculations support structural persistence over the sampled timescale and indicate relatively small anharmonic effects. Despite their high $T_\mathrm{c}$, both phases contain elongated H$_2$-like units, often considered unfavorable for high-$T_\mathrm{c}$ hydrides. Mode-resolved electron-phonon coupling links Raman-active hydrogen vibrations to superconductivity. In $R\bar{3}m$, the linewidths of these modes increase with the pressure-induced tilt of H$_2$ units relative to the threefold axis, alongside the rise in $T_\mathrm{c}$. A minimal symmetry-based model of the vibration-induced second-moment tensor of the hydrogen sublattice shows that these trends are consistent with a significant contribution from response components perpendicular to the threefold axis. NaH$_6$ thus represents an unusual molecular-like hydride in which hydrogen-sublattice reorganization may enable high-$T_\mathrm{c}$ superconductivity at comparatively moderate pressures.

item.title: Can Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Capture Small Polarons? A Geometry-Based Benchmark in Transition-Metal Oxides
item.description: arXiv:2610.17352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small polarons, formed when excess electrons become localized through lattice distortions, play a critical role in charge transport, catalysis, and degradation processes in transition-metal (TM) oxides. Whether universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs), which lack explicit electronic degrees of freedom, can describe them remains unclear. Here, we investigate H-induced electron localization across a range of TM oxides using a geometric descriptor based on TM-O bond-length expansion (Z-score) to identify polaronic distortions. We find that uMLIPs exhibit varying degrees of electron localization, from delocalized states to metastable small polarons, with their behavior strongly dependent on the training data and treatment of electronic correlations. In particular, the absence of Hubbard U corrections for specific TM cations in the training data leads to electron delocalization, in contrast to DFT+U predictions. Although some uMLIPs reproduce polaron hopping barriers during coupled proton-polaron transfer, all of them fail to stabilize spatially separated polaron-donor configurations, instead favoring localization near the H dopant.

item.title: WannierSTM: Efficient superconducting scanning-probe spectroscopy from maximally localized Wannier functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a Python-based program that combines maximally localized Wannier functions-based first-principles electronic structure with the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism to enable efficient simulations of scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). The workflow builds upon standard density functional theory packages to construct compact transport Hamiltonians that preserve the properties of realistic materials. Superconductivity is incorporated via an effective pairing potential within the Nambu-spinor formalism, while coupling to the STM tip and substrate electrodes is treated using the wide-band limit approximation. Within this formulation, transport quantities such as current-voltage characteristics and differential conductance are evaluated in a closed analytical form. This avoids explicit numerical energy integrations and enables rapid spectroscopic calculations over broad parameter spaces. The framework provides a unified and computationally efficient approach for modeling superconducting hybrid nanostructures with spin-orbit coupling, magnetic textures, and spin polarization. Representative applications in spin chains, two-dimensional and molecular magnets on a superconductor demonstrate its robust capabilities for both simple model systems and realistic ab initio molecular structures relevant to modern STM experiments.

item.title: Direct view of exciton and carrier dynamics in twisted bilayer graphene
item.description: arXiv:2610.17984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) on H-intercalated SiC (twist angle of $9 \pm 1^{\circ}$) is studied by position\mbox{-}, time\mbox{-}, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Both graphene layers are hole doped, with a Dirac-point offset of 30~meV. Time-resolved ARPES near the van Hove singularity reveals a spectral feature within the hybridization-induced band gap, together with excited electrons in the conduction band. The in-gap feature exhibits distinct dynamics, and its binding energy and $k$-space location are consistent with the proposed non-hydrogenic ``ghost-Fano'' exciton arising from destructive interference between two nearly degenerate excitonic channels. Near the Dirac points, the twist separates the largely layer-polarized Dirac cones in momentum space, providing direct layer selectivity. We find markedly different peak electronic temperatures in the two graphene layers, even though their subsequent cooling dynamics are very similar. We attribute this to an ultrafast interlayer redistribution of electronic energy, driven by an interlayer electric field that arises from the different doping in the layers.

item.title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.17987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energetic materials involve multiple interactions, making reliable machine-learning potentials (MLPs) difficult to construct without extensive datasets. Here, we enhance the ability of the neural network interatomic potential (NNAP) to describe molecular systems using sphmulti, a refined spherical-harmonic basis set that combines extra radial basis with element-specific chemical weighting in each radial channel. We further integrate hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria with knowledge-guided key events, enabling the NNAP to retain essential information for describing the material system. For 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan, the resulting NNAP is trained on only 13,680 configurations yet captures key properties, including the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior. NNAP-driven molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that pyrolysis proceeds through furazan-ring opening followed by chain reactions, whereas shock loading induces anisotropic hydrogen transfer driven by interlayer structural deformations. This work enables efficient and reliable MLPs for energetic materials.

item.title: High-throughput screening of Heusler alloys for thermoelectrics combining machine-learned densities of states and first-principles transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.18179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermoelectrics turn waste heat into electricity, but finding new ones requires transport calculations too costly for whole databases. Searches therefore choose what to calculate from the electronic density of states (DOS), increasingly predicted by machine learning, yet such choices are rarely tested. We test them on all 106,235 Heusler structures in the DXMag database, screening 51,257 on density-functional spectra and 54,978 on neural-network predictions, and judging both by 3,625 band-structure and transport calculations. A DOS-derived Seebeck indicator ranks most compounds passing every transport and stability test within the top 1% of their population, and ten of the eleven established half-Heusler thermoelectrics calculated pass. Predicted spectra lose most band gaps, unnoticed by spectral-similarity metrics, yet still rank passing compounds near the top. The screen certifies 80 computational candidates, 61 without reported measurements. Computed or predicted, the DOS can choose what to calculate; only a band structure shows whether a gap exists.

item.title: Unexpected stabilization of a single-$q$ charge density wave in pristine 1T-TiSe$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2610.18211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past decade, studies revisiting the classical charge-density-wave system 1T-TiSe$_2$, long understood to host the $2 \times 2$ triple-$q$ order with equivalent subcomponents, have suggested that these subcomponents may not be identical, challenging a 50-year-old paradigm. Here, we demonstrate not only that these subcomponents are non-identical but also that they develop sequentially rather than simultaneously. By tracking folded-band features, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that a unidirectional $2 \times 1$ single-$q$ order stabilizes first, while the other two components emerge sequentially at lower temperatures, completing the triple-$q$ phase. Our free-energy analysis explains this hierarchy through repulsive coupling among the three subcomponents, as supported by first-principles calculations incorporating phonon anharmonicity. Consequently, the three subcomponents are inequivalent in both phase and amplitude. These results reconcile reported symmetry breaking and differing characteristic temperatures and establish a framework in which ostensibly simple, high-symmetry charge-density order emerges from temperature-dependent competition and cooperation among inequivalent subcomponents.

item.title: MINFF: A Family of Classical Force Fields for Minerals with Tunable Angle Terms
item.description: arXiv:2610.18220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomistic simulations of minerals are limited by the accuracy and transferability of the force field. We introduce MINFF, a force field family for layered and non-layered oxides and hydroxides of M being Si, Al, Fe, Mg, Ca, Ti, Li and F. MINFF has no M-O bond terms. Instead M-O distances follow from electrostatics and dispersion, while a single harmonic angle term on all M-O triplets controls coordination geometry. Metal charges are DDEC6 charges from reference mineral structures, and oxygen charges are assigned by nearest-neighbour charge smearing, covering basal, apical, hydroxyl and edge sites and sites adjacent to isomorphous substitutions. The oxygen Lennard-Jones parameters are based on the OPC3 water model and change by less than 5% when re-optimised per mineral, so compatibility with OPC3 and related ion-pair potentials is measured rather than assumed. Metal Lennard-Jones parameters were fitted to unit-cell metrics, bond distances and angles, both synchronously across more than 30 reference minerals (general, GMINFF) and for individual minerals (tailored, TMINFF), each at four angle force constants (0, 250, 500 and 1500 kJ/mol/rad^2). With angle terms, MINFF reproduces experimental unit-cells metrics to within 0.5% and atom-type distances and angles to within 0.7-1.4% and 0.1-0.4%, with Global Instability Index values as low as 0.11, below those of CLAYFF (0.34) and INTERFACE (0.21). A moderate angle constant reproduces the stiff in-plane and soft shear elastic constants of phyllosilicates and improves the Kaolinite librational bands, and in hydrated Na-Montmorillonite MINFF gives the lowest residual factor against the 2W 00l pattern of the models tested. The general and tailored sets at four angle stiffnesses give direct control over the transferability-fidelity trade-off. Topologies can be generated with the atom (MATLAB) and atomipy (Python) libraries and at www.atomipy.io.

item.title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.18317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks that predict density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonians from material structures offer a route to efficient electronic-structure calculations. However, extending localized atomic-orbital (AO) Hamiltonian learning to plane-wave (PW) calculations with hybrid functionals requires a compact AO representation that preserves the effects of nonlocal operators. Here we propose a projectability-guided construction of nonorthogonal AO Hamiltonians from a small, selected set of PW eigenstates and eigenvalues. High-projectability states are retained, and selected higher-energy states complete the AO subspace, avoiding an empirical shift and its arbitrary contribution to the learning targets. Because the construction uses PW eigenstates and eigenvalues, it incorporates nonlocal contributions present in the reference calculation without explicitly reconstructing their AO matrix elements. Benchmarks for MoS2 and sodium phases show accurate reproduction of PW bands with smaller AO bases than real-space reconstruction. The resulting PBE and HSE Hamiltonians can be learned by equivariant neural networks, connecting PW reference calculations with electronic-structure prediction. This approach broadens the range of PW DFT calculations available for AO Hamiltonian learning and enables compact, accurate training targets for developing more widely applicable electronic-structure models.

item.title: Imaging Gate-Tunable Single-Layer Molecular Kagome Lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.18539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kagome lattices provide a simple geometry for engineering electronic states that exhibit novel quantum behavior. In conventional kagome materials, however, the relevant states are often embedded in chemically complex three-dimensional crystals and are difficult to isolate or tune. Molecule-based kagome networks offer structural precision and tunability, but have largely been confined to metallic substrates incompatible with 2D devices. Here we report growth of single-layer Ni$_3$(HITP)$_2$ metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) on van der Waals substrates including graphene-based field-effect devices using metal-salt molecular beam epitaxy. Low-temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy resolves kagome-derived flat-band and van Hove singularity-based spectral features consistent with first-principles calculations. Gating hybrid 2D MOF devices allows us to energetically shift kagome spectral features, thus establishing electrostatic control of chemically programmable 2D kagome electronic lattices.

item.title: Time-Resolved Phonon Dispersions of Thermally Excited Graphite at the Nanoscale
item.description: arXiv:2610.18561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice vibrations govern the propagation of heat in materials, and investigating their dynamics through time-resolved phonon dispersion measurements would provide insight into these excitations and their interactions. However, time-resolved measurements that directly resolve the phonon dispersion at the nanoscale have not been previously demonstrated. Momentum-resolved vibrational electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) provides access to phonon energies and momenta with nanoscale spatial resolution. Here, we combine momentum-resolved vibrational EELS with pulsed laser heating and synchronised gated electron detection to observe the phonon dispersion of graphite during controlled heating and cooling on the microsecond timescale. Recording both the gain and loss spectra at defined times relative to laser excitation, we determine the temperature at each time delay and follow changes to the phonon branches as a function of temperature. The momentum-resolved spectra reveal a decrease in energy of the optical phonon branch with increasing temperature accompanied by an increase in peak width. These changes are consistent with temperature-dependent phonon renormalisation and scattering associated with anharmonic interactions. The approach is compatible with detector gating on timescales down to 50 ns, providing a route towards extending these measurements to faster dynamics. This work demonstrates time-resolved phonon dispersion spectroscopy using vibrational EELS and provides a route towards probing temperature-dependent phonon dynamics at the nanoscale with simultaneous energy and momentum resolution.

item.title: Full Lyapunov Spectra of Random Neural Networks, Part I: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.14922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

item.title: Tersoff-NN: Hybrid Machine-Learned Bond-Order Extension of the Tersoff Potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.15591v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate, robust, and efficient interatomic potentials are highly desirable for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Although machine-learning interatomic potentials can reproduce first-principles potential-energy surfaces with high accuracy, they typically incur higher computational costs than conventional empirical potentials and may be less reliable outside their training domains. We developed Tersoff-NN, a hybrid machine-learning potential for Si, which retains the analytical radial interactions and cutoff structure of the Tersoff potential while representing its environment-dependent bond-order factor using compact neural networks (NNs). Benchmarks for 32,768-atom systems show that Tersoff-NN is 4-12 times faster than the Behler-Parrinello-type NN potentials tested in this study. Tersoff-NN improves the short-range structure of liquid Si relative to the conventional Tersoff potential, closely reproduces the ab initio radial and angular distributions, and reproduces the equilibrium structure of diamond Si and qualitative energetic trends among several crystalline phases. Furthermore, melt-quench simulations reveal a disordered solid with predominantly four-coordinated, tetrahedral-like local environments. Additionally, characteristic reconstruction motifs are retained on Si surfaces despite their exclusion from the training dataset. A direct comparison with an alternative atom-centered bond-order NN highlights the critical role of physical constraints in ensuring dynamic stability. Despite exhibiting comparable validation errors, the selected triplet-based architecture remains stable, while an alternative model exhibits unphysical bond-order growth and atomic collapse. These results confirm that learning only the bond-order term improves the description of diverse Si environments while retaining substantial computational efficiency and enhancing dynamical stability.

item.title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.16161v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between generalization and memorization.

item.title: TheoPhysEval: Assessing AI agents at autonomous theoretical physics problem solving
item.description: arXiv:2610.16733v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. On average, agents show only small changes in accuracy when denied web search and access to background research papers, suggesting significant memorization of the literature. These results suggest that state-of-the-art agents can accurately perform concrete calculations required across theoretical physics research. We comment on the broader implications of these findings and discuss possible explanations for the current lack of agent-led breakthroughs in theoretical physics despite their outstanding problem-solving abilities.

item.title: Extreme Suppression of Thermal Conductivity in Monolayer Beryllene
item.description: arXiv:2409.05766v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We demonstrate an extreme suppression of thermal conductivity in monolayer beryllene through first-principles solutions of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation. While the fully converged three-phonon calculation predicts a room-temperature lattice thermal conductivity of 154.3 W/(m$\cdot$K), inclusion of four-phonon interactions suppresses it to 10.7 W/(m$\cdot$K), a reduction of more than 90\%. This exceptionally large reduction of the thermal conductivity is amongst the highest reported in two-dimensional materials. The microscopic origin of this breakdown is traced to the strong sensitivity of the low-frequency flexural ZA phonons to four-phonon scattering: mode-resolved scattering rates reveal a pronounced enhancement of ZA scattering, which substantially shortens their lifetimes and suppresses their dominant contribution to heat conduction. Moreover, the temperature dependence of the thermal conductivity changes from $\kappa\propto T^{-0.86}$ to $\kappa\propto T^{-1.38}$ upon inclusion of four-phonon processes. Our results establish $\alpha$-beryllene as an unusually strong case of four-phonon-controlled thermal transport amongst two-dimensional materials. These findings identify selective higher-order scattering of flexural phonons as a key mechanism for controlling thermal transport in strongly anharmonic low-dimensional systems.

item.title: peaks: a Python package for analysis of angle-resolved photoemission and related spectroscopies
item.description: arXiv:2508.04803v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The electronic band structure, describing the motion and interactions of electrons in materials, dictates the electrical, optical, and thermodynamic properties of solids. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) provides a direct experimental probe of such electronic band structures, and so is widely employed in the study of functional, quantum, and 2D materials. \texttt{peaks} (\textbf{P}ython \textbf{E}lectron spectroscopy \textbf{A}nalysis by \textbf{K}ing group @ \textbf{S}t Andrews) provides a Python package for advanced data analysis of ARPES and related spectroscopic data. It facilitates the fast visualisation and analysis of multi-dimensional datasets, allows for the complex data hierarchy typical to ARPES experiments, and supports lazy data loading and parallel processing, reflecting the ever-increasing data volumes used in ARPES. It is designed to be run in an interactive notebook environment, with extensive inline and pop-out GUI support for data visualisation.

item.title: Gap structure and phase diagram of twisted bilayer cuprates from a microscopic perspective
item.description: arXiv:2603.10865v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Since the prediction of a time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) $d+id^\prime$ state in twisted bilayer cuprate superconductors by Can et al. (Nat.Phys. 17,519(2021)), several experiments have attempted to detect this state, yielding conflicting results. At present, it is not clear which differences in samples or experimental conditions might explain these discrepancies. In this work, we perform a tight-binding lattice model calculation with phenomenological interlayer tunneling, examining the order parameter as a function of twist angle, interlayer tunneling, doping, and temperature. We observe the TRSB state to be correlated to the position of the Van Hove singularity in the normal state, which changes not only as a function of doping but also the tunneling strength. Two such phases are identified as nominally consistent with in-plane $d+id'$ and $d+is$ order, but with unexpected transformation properties under bilayer symmetry operations. We calculate the Josephson critical current, in particular examining the angle dependence for various tunneling strengths. Finally, we discuss the existing experiments in the context of our results.

item.title: First-Principles Investigation of Ammonia Adsorption and N-H Activation on W-B Nanoclusters
item.description: arXiv:2606.22395v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tungsten-boride nanoclusters are nanoscale systems of potential catalytic interest, but their structural stability and reactivity remain poorly understood. We combine evolutionary structure prediction with density functional theory to investigate W$_m$B$_n$ nanoclusters containing up to 43 atoms. The calculated stability descriptors reveal a strongly non-monotonic landscape, with several compositions locally favoured relative to neighbouring stoichiometries within the explored isolated-cluster model. Molecular NH$_3$ adsorption was examined at W-top and accessible B-top sites, with adsorption energies ranging from $-1.78$ to $-0.54$ eV on W sites and from $-1.54$ to $+0.62$ eV on B sites. H adsorption at W-top and B-top sites spans $-1.47$ to $+0.67$ eV, indicating pronounced composition- and site-dependence. CI-NEB calculations show that the first N-H bond-cleavage barrier is strongly pathway-dependent. These results characterize the initial activation of NH$_3$ on W-B nanoclusters and provide an atomistic basis for further investigation of the complete ammonia-decomposition mechanism.

item.title: Phonons under confinement: Coarse-grained $U(1)$ charge and a new transport mechanism
item.description: arXiv:2607.14232v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An important feature of solid-state or cold atom systems in low dimensions is the restricted oscillations of ionic/atomic degrees of freedom in the confining directions, for which the conventional phonon from canonical quantization is not an ideal description. In this work we propose a general recipe to introduce this feature to otherwise unrestricted systems by mapping displacement fields to spin degrees of freedom, dubbed soft-corization. In the strong-confinement limit $S=1/2$, we demonstrate the validity of the approach with a harmonic chain; the results lead to a gapped fermionic model showing the absence of acoustic modes as a signature of the confinement of the entire chain. Despite the non-conserved total particle number in the presence of nearest-neighbor parings, the model holds a coarse-grained $U(1)$ symmetry with conserved polarization charge in the absence of nearest-neighbor hopping. This enables a new transport mechanism via "dimer-tumbling" instead of single-particle hopping. We then introduce a short-range interaction via anharmonicity; for energy scales slightly above the gap, it leads to a (quantum) phase transition to a nonreciprocal state carrying polarization charge current and heat current with spontaneous time reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) of the type $\hat{T}^2=+1$. The non-reciprocity can be probed by measuring the change of inductance due to gauge fields in and out of the ordered phase.

item.title: ATLAS: A Foundation Neural Sampler for Amorphous Materials
item.description: arXiv:2607.19198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Amorphous materials exhibit exceptional mechanical and functional properties, yet their rugged energy landscapes are notoriously difficult to sample. Below the glass-transition temperature, conventional molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo become inefficient because equilibration relies on rare barrier-crossing events, while data-driven generative models are constrained by scarce and biased reference ensembles. Here, we introduce ATLAS, an efficient sampler that learns a diffusion process to generate Boltzmann-distributed amorphous structures directly from a target energy function. Parameterized by an equivariant graph neural network, ATLAS generalizes across system size, temperature, and composition. By exploiting the time reversal of the diffusion process, it enables efficient estimation of thermodynamic quantities and steering toward target observables. In two-dimensional Kob-Andersen systems, ATLAS reproduces parallel tempering Markov chain Monte Carlo structural distributions, free energies and entropies, achieving below 0.2% free energy error in the low-temperature glass regime with over 500-fold fewer energy evaluations. In Cu-Zr and Cr-Co-Ni metallic glasses, ATLAS recovers experimentally observed short-range-order trends and steers structures toward prescribed order parameters and optimized bulk moduli. Moreover, composition-amortized pretraining outperforms composition-specific training from scratch, reduces inverse-design costs by several hundred-fold, and enables sampling with expensive universal machine learning interatomic potentials. Coupled to a large language model agent, ATLAS searches an eight-element space for high-entropy metallic glasses balancing stiffness and ductility, identifying a converged Pareto frontier within 480 oracle evaluations. Together, these results establish ATLAS as a foundation model for sampling, steering and designing amorphous materials.

item.title: Interplay of Kekul\'e order, flat bands and electron-phonon coupling in graphene
item.description: arXiv:2609.11711v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Kekul\'{e} order in graphene is known to coexist with both an extended flat band near the van Hove singularity (VHS) and enhanced electron-phonon coupling. However, the microscopic origin of this interplay is still not fully understood. Here, this behavior is traced to the Kekul\'{e}-induced bond distortion and the resulting redistribution of electronic delocalization. In this picture, the conduction band below the VHS is observed to flatten with increasing Kekul\'{e} order, extending its intrinsically weakly dispersive region around the saddle point over a broader momentum range. In parallel, the VHS and dimensionless electron-phonon coupling exhibit approximately quadratic upward responses. The resulting enhancement of the electron-phonon coupling is found to be predominantly governed by the increasing density of states, with the effective deformation potential remaining weakly affected by the distortion. As such, the obtained results are consistent with previous theoretical and experimental studies, while also pointing toward the narrowing of the conduction band and a possible departure of the electron-phonon coupling from the conventional adiabatic regime. Altogether, they highlight the potential of controlled Kekul\'{e} ordering for engineering emergent correlated quantum phases in graphene.

item.title: GEM: An implementation of the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation for simulating interacting quantum systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.32633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present GEM (Ghost Embedding Method), an open-source software package written in Python for computing equilibrium properties of strongly correlated electronic systems within the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation method. GEM provides a computationally efficient framework for studying multi-orbital lattice models. It supports zero- and finite-temperature calculations and symmetry broken phases. It is integrated with the TRIQS ecosystem, providing tools for model construction, self-consistent solution, and evaluation of physical observables. We first detail the method's theoretical formulation, then we present the software architecture, and finally we introduce some practical workflow, which also validates the implementation against established results. In particular, we illustrate the capabilities of GEM through multiorbital and finite-temperature applications and discuss its computational cost relative to more demanding quantum embedding approaches.

item.title: Tensor-reduced atomic density representations
item.description: arXiv:2210.01705v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Density based representations of atomic environments that are invariant under Euclidean symmetries have become a widely used tool in the machine learning of interatomic potentials, broader data-driven atomistic modelling and the visualisation and analysis of materials datasets.The standard mechanism used to incorporate chemical element information is to create separate densities for each element and form tensor products between them. This leads to a steep scaling in the size of the representation as the number of elements increases. Graph neural networks, which do not explicitly use density representations, escape this scaling by mapping the chemical element information into a fixed dimensional space in a learnable way. We recast this approach as tensor factorisation by exploiting the tensor structure of standard neighbour density based descriptors. In doing so, we form compact tensor-reduced representations whose size does not depend on the number of chemical elements, but remain systematically convergeable and are therefore applicable to a wide range of data analysis and regression tasks.

item.title: Physics-Informed Graph Neural Networks to Reconstruct Local Fields Considering Finite Strain Hyperelasticity
item.description: arXiv:2507.05291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a physics-informed machine learning framework called P-DivGNN to reconstruct local stress fields at the micro-scale, in the context of multi-scale simulation given a periodic micro-structure mesh and mean, macro-scale, stress values. This method is based in representing a periodic micro-structure as a graph, combined with a message passing graph neural network. We are able to retrieve local stress field distributions, providing average stress values produced by a mean field reduced order model (ROM) or Finite Element (FE) simulation at the macro-scale. The prediction of local stress fields are of utmost importance considering fracture analysis or the definition of local fatigue criteria. Our model incorporates physical constraints during training to constraint local stress field equilibrium state and employs a periodic graph representation to enforce periodic boundary conditions. The benefits of the proposed physics-informed GNN are evaluated considering linear and non linear hyperelastic responses applied to varying geometries. In the non-linear hyperelastic case, the proposed method achieves significant computational speed-ups compared to FE simulation, making it particularly attractive for large-scale applications.

item.title: Provably scalable learning from quantum many-body data via locality
item.description: arXiv:2509.13705v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning (ML) holds great promise for extracting insights from complex quantum many-body data obtained in quantum experiments, potentially solving certain classically intractable problems. However, addressing large-scale problems still requires significant amounts of data that exceed the capabilities of near-term quantum devices. We propose a scalable ML framework, the Geometrically Local Quantum Kernel (GLQK), that efficiently learns from quantum many-body data by leveraging the exponential decay of correlations prevalent in noncritical systems. For learning an unknown polynomial of quantum expectation values, we rigorously prove that the GLQK substantially improves the sample complexity in the system size $n$ over the existing shadow kernel, by constructing a feature space from local quantum information at the correlation length scale. This improvement is particularly notable when each term of the target polynomial involves few local subsystems. Remarkably, for translationally symmetric data, the GLQK achieves constant sample complexity, independent of $n$. Numerical experiments on two quantum many-body tasks corroborate these theoretical results, demonstrating the high scalability of the GLQK. Beyond the polynomial setting, we further show that it can efficiently learn certain non-polynomial functions. Our framework establishes new avenues for utilizing experimental data to advance the understanding of quantum many-body physics.

item.title: The Information Content of Krylov Observables: A Machine Learning Approach
item.description: arXiv:2607.17346v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We employ machine learning techniques to estimate the amount of information contained in three Krylov-space observables: the spread complexity $C(t)$, the discrete Wigner negativity $N(t)$, and the normalized negativity $\chi(t)=N(t)/|S(t)|$, where $S(t)$ is the survival amplitude. We study thermofield-double evolutions on GUE, GOE and Poisson spectra, and on the integrable $SL(2,R)$ Krylov chain of a two-dimensional CFT primary, with Lanczos coefficients $b_n=\alpha\sqrt{n(n+2h-1)}$. To introduce chaos we add a GUE random matrix to the integrable chain, $H(\varepsilon)=H_{SL(2,R)}+\varepsilon R_0 W_{GUE}$, where $R_0$ is its spectral half-width. Either $C(t)$ or $N(t)$ alone determines the thermofield temperature, with $R^2\simeq0.999$. However, neither can reconstruct the fine structure of the spectral form factor. In the integrable sector all three observables carry the same information. When we turn on chaos an asymmetry appears: $\chi$ predicts $C$ better than $C$ predicts $\chi$. This gap grows from $+0.33$ to $+0.77$, while the same gap for the raw negativity decays to zero. The extra information comes from the survival amplitude, and $\chi(t)$ carries it while $C(t)$ can still be recovered from $\chi(t)$. We derive a lower bound on this gap, set by the fraction of the variance of $\chi$ that comes from $S$.

item.title: The equivalence of topological indices for $\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric quantum spin chains
item.description: arXiv:2609.34119v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases in quantum spin chains are distinguished by topological indices. Ogata's operator-algebraic indices apply to a broad range of symmetry classes without requiring continuous symmetry, whereas the elementary twist index of Tasaki requires $\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry. We prove their equivalence in the common setting of integer-spin chains with on-site $\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry and a symmetric locally-unique gapped ground state, without assuming translation invariance or a matrix product representation. A charge-fluctuation estimate yields a strong-limit construction of half-chain rotations with their phases fixed. An exact group commutator identity then identifies the Ogata index with the limit of local twist expectations and gives an explicit error bound. This provides a computable formula for the index when a lower bound on the gap and the relevant ground-state expectations are available. Combining the equivalence with a recent boundary-field gap theorem of OpenAI and our earlier twist-index calculation, we obtain a spin-rotation-invariant locally-unique gapped ground state of the infinite $S=1$ antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain with both indices equal to $-1$, without assuming infinite-volume uniqueness. The author formulated the problem and proposed the basic strategy, while ChatGPT Astra made substantial contributions to the development of the proof.

item.title: A strategic roadmap for an atomistic machine-learning ecosystem
item.description: arXiv:2609.39090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-driven machine learning (ML) techniques have become an essential tool in many domains of science. Their application to atomistic simulations of matter is particularly widespread and impactful. This success is due largely to the existence of a well-developed and established physics-based modeling framework, ranging from first-principles electronic-structure calculations to molecular dynamics and statistical sampling, into which ML was integrated naturally to reshape long-standing trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and scale. Nevertheless, this integration raises both conceptual and practical challenges, from choosing between data-centric and physics-based modeling approaches to adapting established software stacks to modern hardware accelerators and ML libraries. As the field evolves rapidly, fueled in part by widespread enthusiasm but also by tangible impact, it seems appropriate to take a moment to consider the current state of the art and open challenges, and reflect on what can be done to better coordinate efforts across the community. With this goal in mind, several members of this community met in Lausanne in January 2026 at CECAM to discuss algorithms, models, software and hardware infrastructure, and the most promising scientific applications that have become possible thanks to the use of artificial intelligence in atomic-scale simulations. This strategic roadmap paper summarizes the outcomes of these discussions, suggesting some long-term goals, and some concrete actions, to establish a healthy, sustainable and impactful atomistic ML ecosystem.

item.title: AtomWorld-Mirror: Macro-Step World Modeling of Critical Evolution Backbones for Materials Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.11527v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Atomistic simulation is a fundamental tool for studying long-term materials evolution, from diffusion and defect dynamics to interfacial reactions and fracture. Yet conventional simulators typically advance at microscopic resolution, spending substantial computation on low-impact local updates before reaching structurally consequential states, an evolutionary-resolution bottleneck that limits long-horizon simulation. We propose AtomWorld-Mirror, a time-aware macro-step world model for the critical evolution backbone of atomic systems. For Step-Wise atomistic simulation, AtomWorld-Mirror distills short micro-event segments into physically reachable transitions between key states, jointly predicting sparse structural edits and accumulated physical time through latent macro-step dynamics. Local reachability, inventory conservation, and continuous-time consistency constrain each transition. By amortizing local atomic physics into a reusable latent macro model and replacing explicit micro-event replay with macro-step inference, this formulation provides a path toward substantially faster prediction of long-term materials evolution while preserving structural validity and time semantics. Across five atomic systems, spanning Cu-rich RPV steel irradiation aging, Cu-Zr metallic glass, and Li$_3$N-based anti-perovskite solid electrolyte, macro-step inference delivers a speed up of $10^3$ to $10^4$ times over event-by-event simulation.

item.title: High-throughput screening of Heusler alloys for thermoelectrics combining machine-learned densities of states and first-principles transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.18179v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermoelectrics turn waste heat into electricity, but finding new ones requires transport calculations too costly for whole databases. Searches therefore choose what to calculate from the electronic density of states (DOS), increasingly predicted by machine learning, yet such choices are rarely tested. We test them on all 106,235 Heusler structures in the DXMag database, screening 51,257 on density-functional spectra and 54,978 on neural-network predictions, and judging both by 3,625 band-structure and transport calculations. A DOS-derived Seebeck indicator ranks most compounds passing every transport and stability test within the top 1% of their population, and ten of the eleven established half-Heusler thermoelectrics calculated pass. Predicted spectra lose most band gaps, unnoticed by spectral-similarity metrics, yet still rank passing compounds near the top. The screen certifies 80 computational candidates, 61 without reported measurements. Computed or predicted, the DOS can choose what to calculate; only a band structure shows whether a gap exists.

The transition manifests as a sharp change from underdamped oscillations to overdamped relaxation, with the Wigner function negativity serving as a hallmark of genuine quantum coherence.

item.title: pyDAC: Open-Source two-dimensional modeling of s-TVSA for direct air capture: experimental assessment and validity of one-dimensional approximations.
item.description: Open and experimentally validated process models remain scarce in direct air capture (DAC), limiting reproducibility and making it difficult to separate physical conclusions from implementation choices. We present pyDAC, an open-source Python framework for packed-bed DAC simulation with one dimensional (1D) and two dimensional (2D) axisymmetric formulations built on the same governing framework. The 2D model is validated against independent zeolite 13X breakthrough experiments, including temperature measurements at multiple radial positions. We then use pyDAC to assess the validity of the 1D approximation for a steam-assisted temperature–vacuum swing adsorption cycle using Lewatit® VP OC 1065. At fixed operating conditions and bed volume, aspect ratios τ = L/D (bed-lenght/bed- diameter) from 1/8 to 8 are examined. The 1D model systematically predicts more favorable performance, overestimating productivity by up to 14 % and underestimating equivalent work by up to 13 %; discrepancies remain around 4 % even at τ = 8. The residual difference originates from the early, conduction-dominated wall-heating transient, which a constant wall heat-transfer coefficient cannot reproduce. During multi-objective optimization, however, the bias reverses because the optimizer selects shorter pre-heating steps within this transient. At τ = 1/2, the 1D Pareto front requires a median 30 % more equivalent work at equal productivity, and the sampled 2D-optimal designs become infeasible when re-evaluated in 1D. At τ = 8, the fronts nearly coincide, but the corresponding operating decisions differ. These results show that 1D models remain useful for screening, but selected designs should be verified in 2D when radial heat transfer controls cycle performance or constraint margins.

item.title: Gas-Conditioned Message Passing Graph Neural Network for Permeability Prediction in Polymeric Membranes
item.description: Designing polymeric membranes for diverse gas-separation applications remains a critical challenge. Machine learning (ML) models can significantly accelerate this effort by capturing complex relationships between polymer-gas pairs and enabling permeability prediction over an extended chemical space of gases and polymers. In this work, we present a novel ML framework, the gas-conditioned message passing neural network (GC-MPNN), that jointly combines gas descriptors and polymer chemistry in a fused neural network model. Polymers are represented at the monomer level and encoded as molecular graphs, where node and edge information is propagated through message-passing layers. Six gas species (He, H2, N2, O2, CH4, and CO2) are represented using multiple descriptor sets spanning thermodynamic, kinetic, and electrostatic properties, along with one-hot encodings and combined feature sets that include kinetic plus thermodynamic descriptors and the full physicochemical descriptor set. For each descriptor combination, model hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization within a leave-one-gas-out (LOGO) validation framework. Test performance is then evaluated on the gas species excluded entirely from the corresponding training fold (out-of-training set) and compared across descriptor sets. For most gas species, the model achieves strong predictive performance (R2 ∼ 0.86–0.96), while CO2 remains more challenging in terms of absolute prediction accuracy (R2 ∼ 0.44). Active learning sampling further improves model performance by adding a few labeled samples from the test gas species into the training set. Among the three strategies tested, deep ensemble-based sampling and random sampling show strong improvement, with R2 reaching approximately ∼ 0.95 for all gas species, while evidential regression shows less consistent improvement. The model is further evaluated on a smaller polymer-gas dataset containing hydrocarbon species (C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, and n-C4H10) using the GC-MPNN trained only on the six base gases, achieving moderate to strong Pearson correlations (r ∼ 0.77–0.89) for these out-of-training gases. Overall, this work presents a machine learning model that can learn transferable polymer-gas relationships from known gas species and extend them to previously unseen gases.

item.title: Leveraging Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Fast and Accurate AMBER-Compatible Force Field Parameterization
NEBwalk: A transparent and calculator-agnostic framework for reproducible nudged elastic band workflows with machine-learned potentials and firstprinciples calculators
item.description: The nudged elastic band (NEB) method is established, but a reproducible transition-state calculation requires more than the NEB equations. Path construction, calculator isolation, restart behaviour, convergence monitoring, provenance, failure handling, and the transfer from inexpensive potentials to first-principles checks must remain consistent throughout the workflow. We developed NEBwalk as an open-source, calculator-agnostic Python framework for NEB and climbing-image NEB (CI-NEB) calculations built around the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). NEBwalk v0.11.0 supports improved-tangent NEB forces, variable springs, FIRE optimisation, minimum-image-aware periodic geometry, linear, IDPP, and regularized geodesic-style interpolation, restartable runs, structured result export, fresh calculator construction for each image, MLIP-assisted image selection, DFT-labelled data export, an optional MACE fine-tuning and evaluation handoff, resumable campaign infrastructure, reproducibility bundles, and conservative Quantum ESPRESSO recovery logic. A September 2026 audit re-examined 20 historical system-calculator cases rather than treating old documentation as automatically valid: 13 were re-audited and reconfirmed from surviving output artefacts, while 7 are retained only as historical provenance and excluded from the current quantitative validation claim. Ten artefact-backed vacancy-migration cases also have DOI-traceable literature comparators for the same element, crystal structure, and migration-hop class; because the numerical settings differ, we use these only as physical-scale checks. In two matched-physical-input implementation tests, NEBwalk and ASE differ by no more than 0.04 meV in the barrier and about 0.002 Å in the converged path geometry. A MACEMP-0 H/Cu(111) calculation gives a converged fcc-to-hcp barrier of about 0.126 eV, close to published DFT values of about 0.13-0.15 eV, although the literature itself disagrees on the sign of the small fcc-hcp site splitting. NEBwalk is therefore not presented as a new NEB algorithm or as a replacement for ASE or first-principles engines. Its role is to keep path optimisation, MLIP screening, DFT validation, reproducibility, and failure-aware execution in one inspectable workflow.

item.title: Skeletal Editing of Cycloparaphenylenes by Direct Oxygen Insertion
item.description: Direct modification of the carbon framework of cycloparaphenylenes (CPPs) remains challenging despite the substantial strain stored in these carbon nanorings. Here, we report two complementary chemical methods for inserting an oxygen atom into a C–C bond of pristine [n]CPPs and the methylene-bridged [6]CPP ([6]MCPP) to give the corresponding oxylene derivatives. Treatment with m-chloroperbenzoic acid and copper(II) acetylacetonate affords mono-oxygenated products from [6]–[9]CPP in modest yields. Photocatalytically generated singlet oxygen is more efficient for smaller, more strained nanorings: [6]MCPP is converted to [6]MCPP-oxylene in 58% yield within 0.5 h, whereas the reactivity decreases sharply with increasing CPP size. Density functional theory calculations reveal that oxygen-insertion enthalpies become progressively less exothermic with increasing ring size and correlate linearly with 1/n, providing a thermodynamic context for the observed ring-size dependence. X-ray crystallography and strain analysis further reveal that oxygen insertion redistributes strain across the ring and lowers molecular symmetry. The resulting CPPoxylenes show markedly altered photophysical properties, with [9]CPP-oxylene reaching ΦF = 0.91. Prolonged photocatalysis of [6]MCPP enables a second, regioselective oxygen insertion at the most highly strained remaining C–C bond of the mono-oxylene framework. The resulting dioxylene adopts a more elongated structure and emits blue fluorescence at 414 nm with ΦF = 0.39; timeresolved measurements show that the higher fluorescence efficiency arises primarily from suppression of nonradiative decay. These results establish direct oxygen insertion as a route to skeletal editing of CPPs and connect sequential editing with changes in strain distribution, molecular geometry, and photophysical behavior.

item.title: Reaction-Level Machine Learning for Condition Optimization in Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling
item.description: Selecting the ligand, base and solvent for a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling remains largely empirical, and highthroughput experimentation (HTE) screens are usually mined only for one reaction’s best condition. This study tests whether condition–yield relationships learned from some reactions transfer to reactions a model has never seen. Using a published HTE dataset of 5,760 reactions (15 quinoline couplings × 384 ligandbase–solvent combinations), models were trained in MATLAB on categorical condition descriptors with whole reactions held out: a global strategy trained on 12 reactions and was tested on 3; a focused strategy trained on 3 reactions sharing a boronic acid and was tested on a fourth. Selected models were compared with a majority-class predictor and a no-learning condition-average ranker, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Ranking transferred: high-yield (≥62%) precision–recall AUC was 0.21–0.34 where only 6–8% of conditions were high-yield and 0.92–0.96 where most were, above the base rate on every held-out reaction. However, the condition-average ranker matched the trained models within overlapping confidence intervals on all four held-out reactions, so what transfers is mainly the persistence of good-on-average conditions. At a fixed 62% cut-off, a RUSBoosted ensemble flagged 58–96% of high-yield conditions against 6–27% for the untuned average. Accuracy misled: naive Bayes scored 94.8% where always predicting low yield scores 94.3%. Exact yields did not transfer (external R2 at or below zero on most reactions), and focusing the training set left ranking unchanged (PR-AUC 0.943 vs 0.942). Reaction-level splits, minority-class metrics and a condition-average baseline should be standard when evaluating models on HTE data.

item.title: AutoSolvate 2.0: Automated Preparation of Chemically Diverse Explicit-Solvent Systems for Multiscale Molecular Simulation
item.description: Advanced quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM), machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and hybrid methods provide powerful engines for modeling solution-phase chemistry. Yet before production begins, chemically diverse explicit-solvent systems must be parameterized, assembled at the desired composition, relaxed, equilibrated, and sampled. This preparatory “first mile” remains labor-intensive, requiring multiple software packages and manual customization, particularly for transition-metal complexes, solvent mixtures, and multicomponent electrolytes.Here, we present AutoSolvate 2.0, a modular, open-source framework that converts molecular structures and solution compositions into equilibrated, simulation-ready explicit-solvent ensembles. The new AutoMCPB module automates Metal Center Parameter Builder (MCPB.py)-based parameterization of transition-metal complexes (TMCs), while generalized system representations support multiple solutes and solvents at arbitrary molar, weight, or volume ratios. Standardized wrappers integrate force-field generation, box construction, minimization, heating, equilibration, classical sampling, and microsolvated-cluster extraction. Native classical molecular dynamics (MD) and TeraChem-based QM/MM workflows execute directly; equilibrated coordinates, velocities, trajectories, and clusters provide starting points for external quantum mechanical (QM), other QM/MM, MLIP training, and hybrid machine learning (ML)/classical workflows. JSON, guided command-line, and Model Context Protocol interfaces support high-throughput and agent-assisted use.We demonstrate these capabilities by reproducing the solvent-dependent absorption spectrum of an aqueous transition-metal photosensitizer, the composition-dependent microsolvation of water–acetonitrile mixtures, and characteristic ion-pairing features of a published multicomponent electrolyte simulation. Together, these applications establish AutoSolvate 2.0 as a preparation and initial-sampling layer connecting chemical system specification to classical, quantum, and machine-learning simulations. Rather than competing with higher-accuracy methods, AutoSolvate provides the on-ramp needed to apply them efficiently to complex explicit-solvent systems.

item.title: Breaking Bottlenecks in Solid Electrolyte Discovery With Large Artificial Intelligence Models
