item.title: Text-mined dataset of sol-gel synthesis protocols with phase purity outcomes using large language models
item.description: Sol-gel synthesis is a versatile method for producing inorganic materials that offers advantages such as atomic-level mixing and lower processing temperatures over traditional solid-state methods. Despite these benefits, achieving phase purity remains a challenge due to the process's sensitivity to synthesis parameters such as precursor choice, solvent selection, and heating conditions. Negative results, such as phase-impure outcomes, are essential for understanding sol-gel reaction pathways, but are largely absent from existing curated datasets. This work leverages Gemini 3.0 Flash to construct a text-mined inorganic sol-gel database with phase purity information. The dataset contains ~148,000 synthesis records, including ~28,000 phase-impure entries. All extracted entities achieved F1 scores greater than 0.89. At the record level, 68% of extracted records match human annotation on all evaluated fields. Furthermore, to validate the scientific utility of our dataset, we demonstrate that the aggregated data reproduces previously reported phase-purity trends for BiFeO3 thin films.

item.title: Fully Automated System for Exploring Molecular Dynamics Trajectories
item.description: Molecular dynamics (MD) studies often require separate tools for system preparation, simulation, enhanced sampling, analysis, and reporting, creating opportunities for inconsistent settings and undocumented decisions. We present FastMDXplora, an open-source Python framework built on OpenMM that integrates setup, simulation, analysis, and report phases through a single declarative configuration. A shared schema supports command-line and browser-based graphical interfaces. An optional artificial intelligence (AI) agent generates study configurations from natural-language descriptions, subject to the same validation as user-defined configurations. Each phase records its resolved settings, software versions, and execution environment. When a requested result lacks sufficient support, the software withholds it and reports the reason through a registry of 111 typed refusal codes. Fifteen estimator tests recover analytical benchmarks, including statistical inefficiencies within 2 % of reference values and WHAM reconstruction of analytical free-energy profiles from synthetic umbrella-sampling data with root-mean-square errors below 0.1 kJ mol−1. A labeled corpus of 25 defective and 26 clean studies produces the expected outcomes in all 51 cases. Calibration against ten replicas shows that singlerun standard errors at 20 ns can be up to tenfold smaller than replica-based estimates, even when the estimated correlation time is resolved. The software withholds standard errors when its correlation diagnostics fail, but passing these diagnostics does not establish calibrated uncertainty. In a trypsin–benzamidine case study, interaction analysis reveals differences in the engagement of Asp189 between two ligand charge states that are not distinguished by total contact counts. FastMDXplora provides an integrated framework for reproducible MD studies, combining workflow automation with explicit validation and provenance while preserving the need for independent assessment of sampling and uncertainty. The source code is available at https://github.com/aai-research-lab/FastMDXplora.

item.title: Certifying the Kinetics of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials from Single-Point Energies
item.description: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are validated by force errors on equilibrium configurations, yet activated rates depend on transition regions that equilibrium sampling rarely visits. In a onedimensional metastable double well, the worst-case rate sensitivity to force error grows as eβB/2 with barrier height B; a path-space bound valid at any friction shows that force error certifies rare-event frequencies only to within a factor that grows at the same rate. The leverage density weights energy errors by their influence on reactive transport: it is the normalised dissipation density of the reactive current. For reversible overdamped dynamics, the Dirichlet and Thomson principles give two-sided capacity bounds, converted to metastable rate bounds by basin population corrections. A path representation evaluates their averages from reactive trajectories, committor values and single-point energies. Sampling uses reference paths to assess sampled transitions and model paths to expose additional or overpopulated pathways. In alanine dipeptide, closely matched force errors produce rate changes from 0.49 to 3.5, consistent with estimated intervals. In Li3OCl, mechanism-resolved upper endpoints track six models’ vacancy-hop rates with a systematic underestimation of about 7%. Labels selected from both ensembles improve kinetics even as force errors rise. We propose reporting the energy-error contrast M between the leverage density and the basins, and the spread σν under the leverage density, alongside force error; both are independent of the energy zero.

item.title: Lifetime Sample Tracking (LiST): A data platform for materials science
item.description: The 2D Crystal Consortium Materials Innovation Platform (2DCC-MIP) is a NSF supported national user facility focused on advancing the synthesis of 2D materials, monolayers, surfaces, and interfaces. The need for the facility to organize and share data with users led to the development of an internal data management and analysis engine, the Lifetime Sample Tracking platform (LiST). This infrastructure allows the automated capture, curation, analysis, and dissemination of data ranging from experimental materials synthesis parameters and characterization to theoretical first-principles and ReaxFF molecular dynamics modeling [Nayir et al., 2D Mater. 10, 032002 (2023)]. The system currently hosts synthesis and property data (accessible via a REST API) on ∼20 000 samples produced by the 2DCC grown using a variety of techniques from bulk crystal growth to metal-organic chemical vapor deposition and molecular beam epitaxy, among others. Data used in publications can easily be grouped by the system into data packages that are given digital object identifiers for inclusion with each publication. The LiST platform is now being used by groups outside of the 2DCC as a solution for data curation in materials science. Data management tools, such as LiST, support the materials development process by allowing a closed loop iteration between synthesis, characterization, theory, and targeted materials design. This also enables machine learning research, artificial intelligence analysis, and the potential for autonomous synthesis in the future.

item.title: Complementary Roles of Iodide-Mediated Pathways and Anion Dynamics in Lithium-Ion Transport in Li3PS4-LiI Glasses
item.description: LiI addition enhances lithium-ion transport in sulfide glasses, yet the microscopic mechanisms linking halide incorporation to faster conduction remain unclear. Here, we investigate how LiI promotes Li+ migration in (100−x)Li3PS4–xLiI glasses by resolving changes in local structure, migration energetics, and anion dynamics. A machinelearning potential trained on newly generated ab initio molecular dynamics data and an existing sulfide-electrolyte dataset enables 10 ns simulations of approximately 5000atom glass models at 300 K over a LiI content range of 0–50 mol%. The potential is validated against density functional theory calculations, experimental densities, and X-ray total scattering profiles. Although the PS4 3–units remain intact and their time-averaged inter-unit correlations change little, Li+ diffusivity more than doubles across this composition range, accompanied by increased migration beyond local cage-like regions. To characterize the energetics of these pathways in a disordered environment, we introduce an analysis that combines Voronoi partitioning into P-and I–-centered domains with atomic potentialenergy fluctuations along Li+ trajectories. The resulting statistical local energy-barrier indicators allow comparisons between domain transitions without assigning absolute activation energies. This analysis reveals two complementary effects of LiI addition. Transitions involving I–-centered domains exhibit lower barrier indicators than direct transitions between P-centered domains, identifying favorable I–-mediated migration pathways. LiI addition also lowers the barrier indicators for direct P-to-P transitions, extending its influence beyond pathways that pass through I–-centered domains. Enhanced local translational and rotational dynamics of PS4 3–units accompany this broader reduction, suggesting that anion motion helps facilitate Li+ migration. These findings explain how LiI can enhance transport while largely preserving the average glass structure and highlight the combined roles of local migration pathways and anion dynamics in designing sulfide glass electrolytes.

item.title: Drug Molecular and Route Similarity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented LLM Generation with Knowledge Graph for Semantic Reasoning
item.description: To address the inherent limitations of large language models (LLMs) in chemical synthesis—hallucinations, and low knowledge dense—this study presents a Knowledge Graph–enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework (KG-RAG-LLM) with a multi-scale calculation of molecular and route similarity. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that KG-RAG-LLM significantly mitigates hallucinations, increasing the proportion of concrete chemical information in generated responses to 39.52%–40.87%, drastically outperforming baseline LLMs and standard literature-based RAG pipelines in response completeness and accuracy. To overcome the inability of traditional 2D linear fingerprints to capture 3D spatial properties and reaction path variations, we further developed a multidimensional molecular and route similarity calculation combining SimHash, core similarity, and FCFP, as an alternative to Route CGR representations coupled with UMAP dimensionality reduction. This formulation accurately distinguishes between subtle and distinct synthetic strategies, demonstrating superior precision over traditional clustering methods for fuzzy retrieval of synthetic routes. Overall, this work provides a reliable, knowledge-dense solution for intelligent retrosynthetic Semantic Reasoning.

item.title: Process and Systems Modeling of Hydrothermal Liquefaction for Fuels and Bioproducts from Wet Organic Wastes
item.description: Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) can convert wet organic waste into fuels and bioproducts, but variation in feedstocks and operating conditions can propagate from product yields to system performance and deployment. This study linked machine learning based HTL yield prediction with process simulation, techno-economic analysis (TEA), life cycle assessment (LCA), uncertainty analysis, and surrogate modeling. A literature data set of 402 experiments was used to predict biocrude, aqueous, gas, and solids yields, with 71.8% of predictions within ±5 wt% of experimental values. The predicted yields reproduced 77.1% of internal rate of return (IRR) and 83.2% of GWP100 estimates within ±5% and ±10 kg CO2e/kg, respectively, and were integrated into two deployment configurations (centralized and decentralized HTL) and two product pathways (biobinder/biofuel and sustainable aviation fuel [SAF]). Process and system scale analyses showed that operating conditions strongly affecting HTL performance could have weaker or competing economic effects due to tradeoffs among product yields, water handling, energy requirements, and capital costs. Across representative feedstocks, decentralized biobinder systems achieved median IRRs up to 35.8%, compared with up to 8.0% for decentralized SAF systems. Feedstock price, followed by biocrude quality, and biocrude yield emerged as the leading economic drivers. Monte Carlo filtering identified waste tipping fee thresholds $25.1–196.7 per wet metric tonne for achieving the 10% IRR target. These results show that existing tipping fee structure can support HTL deployment in some cases, while higher tipping fees or additional financial incentives can expand viability and enable higher investment returns.

item.title: Unveiling Hidden Patterns in Electrode‐Electrolyte Interphase Chemistry and Architecture Through Machine Learning‐Assisted Mass Spectrometry Analysis
item.description: Small Methods, EarlyView.

item.title: Building the Data Foundations for the Design and Discovery of Transition Metal Complexes
item.description: The unique chemistry of transition metal complexes (TMCs) enables several advanced technologies in diverse fields including renewable energies, medicine, and catalysis. Machine learning methods can accelerate their rational design but are bounded by limited dataset sizes, restricted chemical scopes, and insufficient quality. This Perspective surveys the current landscape of TMC datasets and investigates how they seek to address these challenges. The analysis focuses on the data curation processes as well as the scope of the properties provided, and their level of theory. Furthermore, the applications and methodological advancements enabled by TMC datasets are reviewed, including the generative design of metal ligands and the evolutionary optimization of TMCs. The Perspective concludes by outlining future directions, with particular emphasis on extending data to broader chemical scopes including non-equilibrium geometries, establishing community-wide data formats and benchmarks, and developing strategies to effectively integrate heterogeneous data sources.

item.title: COSMO-RS-Based Theoretical Investigation of Equilibria in Protic Ionic Liquids
item.description: Ionic liquids have become an increasingly important field of research. A subgroup, protic ionic liquids, have been shown to be excellent solvents even for poorly soluble materials such as cellulose or polyamides. Still, the composition of such liquids, e.g., their ionicity and the nature of formed aggregates, is mostly unknown and experimental attempts to shed light on this have been mostly unsuccessful. Herein, we report the development of the Python-based COSMOPIL program (COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Protic Ionic Liquids) to analyze the composition of protic ionic liquids via theoretical methods based on density functional theory (DFT) and the COSMO-RS (COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents) implicit solvation model. The inputs of experimental data such as dielectric constants is not necessary. The COSMO-PIL program demonstrates the influence of acid/base ratios and residual water on the ionic liquid composition and allows the understanding of the reported poor ionicity of those liquids. Most notably, we explain this “ionicity gap” in protic ionic liquids, as even superbases fail to achieve full acid deprotonation, with a polarity mismatch between anion and cation, requiring residual acid as mediator.

item.title: UpKast: Method, Model, and Database for Large-Scale Cross-Solvent Determination of pKa Values
item.description: The acid dissociation constant, commonly written as pKa, plays a key role in chemistry. However, most pKa measurements have been conducted in only a handful of solvents, resulting in data scarcity for many relevant solvent systems. Herein, we introduce the UpKast-DB, which comprises of pKa estimates for around 3,000 acids and bases in 29 solvents. We constructed UpKast-DB using a quantum-chemical method that integrates solvation free energy calculations with experimental data. Furthermore, we trained a surrogate machine learning model UpKast-ML on the computed values, allowing for rapid and accurate prediction of pKa values beyond the acids and bases presented in UpKast-DB. The quantum-chemical and machine learning methods result in RMSEs of approximately 1 pKa unit relative to experimental values, slightly higher than the typical aleatoric uncertainty of underlying experimental data, but more accurate than many existing experimental measurements (which can have uncertainties up to, and sometimes beyond, 3 pKa units). The data and modeling approaches provide a means of productively augmenting existing pKa data sources, and represent a significant step toward general determination of pKa in any solvent. The dataset and models can be found on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23239570

item.title: CP-GFM-SGX: Topology-Aware Cyclic Peptide Generation and Design with Receptor-Conditioned Structural Evaluation and Experimental KRAS Affinity Optimization
item.description: Cyclic-peptide discovery requires molecular topology, atomic structure, receptor-associated evidence and computational decisions to remain consistent across a multistage workflow. We present CP-GFM-SGX, an all-atom generative AI model for cyclic-peptide design that integrates a topology-aware generative core with a Unified Evidence State Machine (UESM) to track candidate identity, chemical validity, provenance, typed failures and bounded computation. We evaluated three distinct aspects of the system. In Track A, a frozen five-complex known-ligand benchmark with 100 scheduled poses per complex, the native-free FULL route selected a ligand-backbone pose with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) below 2 Å in four of five systems; retrospective best-of-100 evaluation found a sub-2-Å pose in all five (median selected RMSD, 1.72 Å). In Track B, matched true-pocket versus shuffled-pocket comparisons favored the specified pocket in all seven main targets (median of target medians, +172.6 Rosetta energy units; weakest margin, +3.9 for MCL-1–9CDT). An exploratory post-protocol assessor admitted 42/42, 42/42 and 40/42 selected top-K slots in the full, condition-masked and post hoc head-to-tail arms, respectively. In Track C, FULL UESM produced the specified protective outcomes for six deterministic synthetic fault fixtures and one additional missing-evidence case; targeted ablations isolated the roles of provenance and failure propagation. In a separate KRAS G12D–GDP experimental-feedback series, synthesis and SPR/BLI testing of cyclic-peptide analogues guided position-2 basic-side-chain selection and dual-basic-group placement, advancing the reported SPR affinity from approximately 60 µM for CRO-748 to approximately 6 µM for 748-R1 and approximately 1 µM for 748-RK. Comparisons using the 31-dimension Structured Capability and Evidence Grid (SCEG-31D) demonstrate that CP-GFM-SGX exhibits certain superiority over other design platforms in multiple aspects. Together, we evaluate a topology-aware generative artificial intelligence workflow for receptor-focused cyclic-peptide design and show, in a KRAS feedback series, how binding measurements guide iterative chemical optimization.

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 42, October 2026.

item.title: Unleashing AI for preclinical drug development
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping preclinical drug development across target discovery, therapeutic design, synthesis, functional characterization and safety assessment. In this review, we present an integrated view of AI across the preclinical pipeline, beginning with target identification, modality selection and representation learning for molecular, protein, structural, cellular and multimodal data. We then examine major generative modeling paradigms including autoregressive, latent-variable, diffusion, flow-based and guided approaches and their applications across small molecules, peptides, enzymes, antibodies, Tcell receptors and mRNA therapeutics. We discuss how these methods support de novo design, structure- and pocket-conditioned generation, sequence–structure co-design, affinity and activity optimization, developability engineering and synthesis-aware discovery. We further review AI-enabled retrosynthesis, reaction prediction and closed-loop experimental optimization, emphasizing the distinction between computational synthesizability and experimentally executable chemistry. Beyond molecular generation, we organize functional prediction from binding and kinetics through target engagement, pharmacological activity, mechanism of action, pathway response and phenotypic outcome. We also examine singlecell perturbation modeling, organoid-based drug-response prediction, toxicity and off-target assessment, and prospective validation across therapeutic modalities. Across these areas, we highlight the importance of uncertainty estimation, out-of-distribution generalization, reproducibility and experimentally grounded benchmarking. Finally, we discuss how integrating generative AI, mechanistic biology and iterative design–make–test–analyze cycles could transform AI from isolated predictive tools into decision-support systems for preclinical drug development.

item.title: NEVPT2 Multiple Spawning Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Uracil
item.description: The quasidegenerate n-electron valence state second-order perturbation theory (QD-NEVPT2) for complete active space reference wavefunctions has been implemented in the OpenMolcas package. The implementation utilizes the efficient formulation of Kollmar et al. for the electronic energy, which is extended here to the calculation of analytic derivatives. To demonstrate its utility, the method is applied to classical and non-adiabatic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of uracil. The non-adiabatic MD simulations describe the ultrafast deactivation of the initially excited bright ππ∗ state through the S2/S1 conical intersection, demonstrating the applicability of the method to photochemical processes. Furthermore, a machine learning-based analysis of the trajectory data extracts key geometrical parameters that are associated with the magnitude of the time-derivative coupling.

item.title: Direct-Write Printing of Freestanding Prussian Blue Analogue Fibers with Tunable Redox Potentials
item.description: Prussian blue (PB) and its analogues (PBAs) are attractive electrode materials for energy storage because of their chemical tunability, open-framework structures, fast ion transport, and rich redox chemistry. Yet, their practical implementation remains limited due to the challenging processability and the discrete set of redox potentials accessible through conventional compositions. Here, a 3D flow-focusing microfluidic strategy is used for directly synthesizing and printing freestanding PB and PBA composite fibers in a single step, coupling particle formation with their integration into an alginate/carbon-nanotube matrix. The method yields continuous, self-supporting fibers incorporating PB and multiple PBAs (Co, Ni, Cu, Zn), which can be directly written into functional electrode architectures and assembled into working energy storage cells. Beyond processability, the platform enables two complementary routes for voltage design: high-entropy PBAs, which access redox responses distinct from those of conventional single-metal PBAs, and spatially encoded fibers in which different PBAs are integrated within one fiber to generate intermediate and deliberately tuned electrochemical behavior. By exploiting the inherent spatial and temporal control afforded by microfluidic flow focusing, the approach establishes a versatile route toward printed, application-tailored PB and PBA electrodes with programmable operating voltages.

item.title: Lithium Plating-Induced Fracture of Individual Graphite Platelets Revealed by Operando
item.description: Lithium plating is a key barrier to achieving faster charging of lithium-ion batteries; however, fundamental and nanoscale understanding of plating is still being developed, largely due to the dynamic nature of the process. Here, we perform operando electrochemical atomic force microscopy on individual graphite platelets to observe the morphology evolution of plated lithium and graphite electrodes simultaneously. We observe plating-induced fracture of the graphite platelets even in the absence of a porous electrode structure. Unexpectedly, fracture occurs through preferential lithium deposition beneath the particle surface despite lithium-ion transport limitations, pointing to lithium in graphite as the lithium source. Our findings deepen the understanding of the lithium plating process and offer pathways to improvement for fast-charged negative electrodes.

item.title: Data-driven discovery of pH-dependent surfactant behavior in a peptide amphiphile library
item.description: Developing bio-based formulations is essential for reducing the environmental impact of modern surfactants. Peptide amphiphile (PA) surfactants offer a modular platform for developing materials with tailored structures and functions, making them highly attractive to replace existing petrochemical surfactants. However, rationally designing peptide sequences with predictable and tunable surface activity remains challenging. Existing sequence-based models primarily target aggregation and antimicrobial activity and cannot predict surface activity or account for environmental conditions such as pH and temperature. To address this shortcoming, we combine experimental and computational approaches to investigate sequence–property relationships of PAs. We employ automated experimental workflows to generate a consistent dataset of PA surface tension across a range of pHs. Our analyses reveal that the presence of proline most strongly induces surface activity at all pHs. Positively charged residues such as lysine and arginine more strongly introduce surface activity than negatively charged residues. Experimental validation of a machine learning classifier trained on the data collected for our library showed that the machine learning model correctly predicts surface activity in 97% of the sampled predicted surface active sequences. Thereby, we show that machine learning models trained on our dataset generalize across the sequence space, and enable targeted design of surface active PAs in diverse environments.

item.title: Advancing Targeted Nanoparticle mRNA Delivery Using Machine Learning
FMS2Lib: A Machine Learning-Ready Tandem Mass Spectral Library for Nontargeted Analysis of Non-conventional PFAS
item.description: Nontargeted identification of non-conventional per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), including fluorinated pharmaceuticals and pesticides, remains challenging. Existing machine learning models for nontargeted analysis, primarily trained on tandem mass spectra of nonfluorinated compounds, may not generalize well to non-conventional PFAS because of their distinct mass spectrometric chemistry. Here, we established FMS2Lib, an experimental tandem mass spectral library containing 34,686 fluorinated drug-like compounds (F1-4), to support machine learning-based nontargeted PFAS analysis. We demonstrated that training with FMS2Lib substantially improved the performance of existing models for both molecular formula prediction and structure annotation. We further applied these models to identify PFAS in passive samplers from wastewater effluents and surface waters and in high-throughput laboratory biotransformation experiments, revealing dozens of non-conventional PFAS and their biotransformation products. Collectively, FMS2Lib addresses a major data bottleneck in machine learning-based nontargeted analysis of non-conventional PFAS.

item.title: Drude, Where's My Charge? End-to-End Learning of Polarizable Drude Force Fields for Polymer Electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2610.12799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations of solid polymer electrolytes require force fields that are fast enough to converge ion transport over hundreds of nanoseconds, yet accurately describe the ion-polymer interactions that govern it. Fixed-charge force fields meet the first requirement but neglect electronic polarization, an effect often approximated by scaling ionic charges using empirically chosen factors. Here we present AutoDrude, a differentiable framework that parametrizes polarizable Drude force fields directly from DFT energies, forces, and dipoles, with no empirical tuning and at only 1.20 times the cost of a fixed-charge simulation. For PEO-LiTFSI, the dipole-constrained (hard-constraint) AutoDrude model reproduces the experimental ionic conductivity as accurately as the best charge-scaled model (17% versus 16% mean absolute percentage error). We compare the polarizable forcefield to fixed charge ones models by fitting a fixed charge model. Unlike the charge-scaled models tested here, however, AutoDrude also reproduces the dilute-limit cation transference number, its increase with salt concentration, and the absence of Li-TFSI contact ion pairs at low concentration. A penalty-based (soft-constraint) variant yields a closer fit to the DFT reference yet underestimates the conductivity by up to an order of magnitude, demonstrating that closer agreement with DFT training data alone does not guarantee accurate ion transport. These results indicate that although charge scaling can reproduce ionic conductivity the explicit inclusion of polarization is necessary to capture the concentration dependence of cation transport in PEO-LiTFSI.

item.title: Symmetry-Enforced Topology and Van Hove Saddle Points in Hexagonal TiAs
item.description: arXiv:2610.12925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the first successful growth of stoichiometric hexagonal TiAs single crystals (space group $P6_3/mmc$) using chemical vapor transport and investigate their vibrational, electronic, topological, and magnetotransport properties. Polarized Raman spectroscopy identifies all four Raman-active phonon modes ($A_{1g} + E_{1g} + 2E_{2g}$), consistent with the hexagonal crystal symmetry. First-principles calculations reveal nontrivial band topology characterized by a symmetry indicator $\mathbb{Z}_4 = 2$ and a strong topological index $\nu_0 = 1$, together with symmetry-protected fourfold band degeneracies at the nonsymmorphic Brillouin-zone boundary. The Fermi surface exhibits an orbital-dependent crossover from quasi-two-dimensional cylindrical sheets to a corrugated three-dimensional structure along $k_z$. A Van Hove saddle point approximately 0.5 eV below the Fermi level along $\Gamma\text{--}K$ is associated with a neck-disrupting Lifshitz transition and enhanced density of states. Magnetotransport measurements reveal a pronounced twofold angular magnetoresistance, consistent with anisotropic Fermi-surface geometry and open cyclotron orbits. Hall measurements indicate uncompensated, hole-dominated transport, accounting for the absence of extreme magnetoresistance and contributing to the field-orientation-dependent Hall response. These results establish hexagonal TiAs as a platform for exploring the interplay of nonsymmorphic band topology, Van Hove singularities, and anisotropic electronic transport in transition-metal monopnictides.

item.title: High-Throughput Discovery of Chiral Carbon-Boron Semimetals with Weyl Topology and Phonon-Mediated Superconductivity
item.description: arXiv:2610.12965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiral crystals provide a natural platform for unconventional topological fermions, while light-element carbon--boron frameworks are promising for phonon-mediated superconductivity owing to strong covalent bonding and high phonon frequencies. Here, we combine Wyckoff-position-based structure generation with high-throughput first-principles calculations to search for C--B crystals in selected hexagonal chiral space groups. Starting from 972 generated $\mathrm{C}_m\mathrm{B}_n$ structures ($m,n=1\text{--}4$), successive filters based on energetic stability, dynamical stability, electronic metallicity, topological band features, and thermal stability identify six stable candidates: $(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{B}_2)_8$, $(\mathrm{C}\mathrm{B}_2)_3$, $(\mathrm{C}\mathrm{B}_4)_6$, $(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{B}_2)_6$, $(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{B}_3)_6$, and $(\mathrm{C}\mathrm{B}_2)_6$. These materials host diverse topological semimetal states near the Fermi level, including charge-one, charge-two, and charge-three Weyl points, nodal rings, and nodal-surface states. Notably, $(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{B}_2)_8$ exhibits screw-symmetry-protected charge-three Weyl points and strong electron--phonon coupling, yielding a McMillan transition temperature of $31.1\,\mathrm{K}$ for the Coulomb pseudopotential parameter $\mu^* = 0.10$. In addition, $(\mathrm{C}\mathrm{B}_2)_3$ hosts multiple charge-one Weyl points and pronounced anisotropic multiband superconductivity revealed by fully anisotropic Eliashberg calculations. These results extend the materials scope of topological semimetals with phonon-mediated superconductivity to chemically designed chiral light-element structures.

item.title: Electron- and hole-doped superconductivity in two-dimensional electride ZrX$_2$ (X = Cl, Br, I)
item.description: arXiv:2610.13124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) superconducting systems have recently emerged as a frontier in condensed matter physics, driven by their unique physical properties and potential applications. Using first-principles calculations, we show that monolayer ZrX$_2$ (X = Cl, Br, I), which is a family of 2D semiconducting electrides, hosts phonon-mediated superconductivity under both electron and hole dopings. Electron doping in ZrX$_{2}$ can achieve high superconducting transition temperatures at very low concentrations, with ZrBr$_2$ reaching $T_c = 30.0$ K at 0.01 \textit{e}/f.u., followed by ZrCl$_2$ (22.5 K at 0.05 \textit{e}/f.u.) and ZrI$_2$ (18.1 K at 0.01 \textit{e}/f.u.), for which the high $T_c$ originates from the flat conduction band minimum, with Van Hove singularities nearby enhancing the density of states. In contrast, hole doping requires higher concentrations (0.2--0.25 \textit{h}/f.u.) to activate superconductivity, yielding $T_c \sim 2$ K, and approaches a magnetic instability at elevated doping levels. By comparing with InSe and LaBr$_2$, we identify the spatial location and orbital character of excess electrons as key factors determining the strength of hole-doped superconductivity and the nature of competing orders. These findings establish monolayer ZrX$_2$ as a platform for bipolar superconductivity in a 2D electride and provide insights into flat-band engineering for high-$T_c$ superconductors.

item.title: Atomic Edge Resonators Flatten Phonon Bands in Biphenylene Nanoribbons
item.description: arXiv:2610.13342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that H--F edge complexes in biphenylene nanoribbons act as intrinsic atomic resonators, flattening low-frequency phonon branches. With increasing wave vector, flexural and twisting vibrations concentrate at the edges while motion of the carbon backbone is suppressed. Displacement profiles and edge-mass tuning identify a local-resonance mechanism, an atomic counterpart of a tuned mass damper. Combining machine-learned interatomic potentials, frozen-phonon calculations, and density-functional tight binding, we find that weakly dispersive modes contribute substantially to thermal band-gap narrowing. Zero-point motion shifts the calculated gap closure toward the experimentally observed ribbon widths. A hexagonal boron nitride substrate preserves the principal spectral features while reducing thermal renormalization. These results establish edge chemistry as a route to nearly flat phonon bands and connect a local atomic resonance to the electronic response of an entire nanoribbon.

item.title: Improved screening of doped ZrO$_2$ catalysts for CO$_2$ hydrogenation from graph-based machine learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.13795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dopants can tune the activity of zirconia-based CO$_2$ hydrogenation catalysts through changes in adsorbate and transition-state (TS) energetics. Computing these quantities with density functional theory (DFT) becomes expensive when several dopants, reaction intermediates, and TSs must be screened. Here, we further develop the graph-based machine learning method Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Gaussian Process Regression (WWL-GPR): we introduce additional electronic-structure and local-environment features relevant for oxide surfaces and use the resulting model to predict adsorption and TS energies on ZrO$_2$(101) surfaces doped with Al$^{3+}$, Cd$^{2+}$, Ga$^{3+}$, In$^{3+}$, and Zn$^{2+}$. Adsorbate-surface structures are represented as attributed graphs that combine bonds connectivity and features. We benchmark WWL-GPR against thermodynamic scaling relations (TSR) for reaction intermediates and Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relations (BEP) for TSs, and then propagate the predicted energies to microkinetic CH$_3$OH-yield estimates. WWL-GPR consistently improves the prediction of reaction intermediate energetics relative to linear scaling approaches and provides TS estimates that are competitive with BEP-based models. These improvements become especially relevant when the predicted energetics are propagated through the reaction network. Microkinetic calculations show that WWL-GPR-derived energies give CH$_3$OH yields closer to DFT-derived yields than the linear-relation workflow. Degree-of-rate-control analysis links the activity errors to dopant-dependent rate-controlling steps, including HCOO* formation, H$_2$COOH* dissociation, and H$_3$CO* formation. These results support WWL-GPR as a data-efficient surrogate for connecting atomistic energetics with catalyst-screening observables on doped oxide surfaces.

item.title: Phononic Frequency Combs in Twisted Bilayer Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Heterostructures from First Principles
item.description: arXiv:2610.13825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phononic frequency combs are equidistant spectral ladders generated when a driven vibrational mode transfers energy to an autoparametrically excited subharmonic mode through anharmonic intermode coupling. In previous studies, the coupling strength governing this energy transfer has typically been treated as a free parameter, extracted from a fabricated device, or adopted from an earlier calculation for a specific mode pair. As a result, whether a given crystal can support a phononic frequency comb, and the drive strength required to generate it, has not been predictable a priori. Here we obtain the complete parameter set from density functional theory. Twisted bilayers of \MoSSe{} and \MoSMoSe{} at the commensurate angle $21.787^{\circ}$ adopt space group $P3$ in a 42-atom \rootseven{} moir\'e supercell. The second-order force constants provide the mode frequencies; the third-order constants provide the linewidths through the Boltzmann transport equation and hence the quality factors; and the same third-order tensor projected onto the phonon eigenvectors of a chosen mode pair provides the anharmonic couplings $\kt$ and $\kss$. Both bilayers constitute a mode pair within $0.8\%$ of the $2\!:\!1$ resonance with $\omega_1/\omega_2 = 1.9923$ in \MoSSe{} and $1.9943$ in \MoSMoSe{}. By integrating the resulting two-mode equations, both modes generate combs through a discontinuous transition: at $701\,\fth$ in \MoSSe{} the envelope variance rises from $2.1\times10^{3}$ to $1.37\times10^{4}$ and the tooth count of mode 1 from 7 to 16 within a single $5\,\fth$ increment, identifying the onset as subcritical. The spectral entropy peaks \emph{before} this jump, at $341\,\fth$. The two compounds carry comparable coupling, differing by a factor of $1.2$. However, the comb excitation threshold is set by the quality-factors of signal modes: $Q_2 = 672$ for \MoSSe{} and $Q_2 = 3844$ for \MoSMoSe{}.

item.title: Predictive Synthesis of MOFs and COFs
item.description: arXiv:2610.12739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predictive synthesis concerns the prospective modeling of how a targeted structure can be realized. The synthesis of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) intrinsically involves a multidimensional space of interdependent variables, posing a challenge for bench chemists to parameterize and predict. In this Perspective, we discuss the evolution from chemical-intuition-driven experimentation toward the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in the laboratory. By virtue of prior knowledge, uncertainty, and experimental failure in determining what should be attempted next, we envision predictive synthesis progressing from static recipe recommendation toward real-time control and transferable principles of framework formation. In this context, the significance lies in transforming trial-and-error practice into a means of measurable chemical reasoning, thereby accelerating crystalline materials discovery and advancing synthetic chemistry.

item.title: A Generalizable Machine Learning Framework for Half-Heusler Thermoelectrics
item.description: arXiv:2602.01149v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful approach for accelerating the discovery of thermoelectric (TE) materials, yet many models suffer from limited generalizability. Here we present a robust ML framework for predicting the thermoelectric figure of merit (zT) in half-Heusler (hH) compounds, emphasizing prediction of previously unseen compositions. A principal component analysis (PCA)-based train/test splitting strategy is introduced to generate representative partitions of chemical space. Bayesian hyperparameter optimization is combined with correlation-based k-best feature selection for Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models, together with the interpretable SISSO symbolic-regression method. Relative to the full set of 118 input features, the optimized feature subsets reduce the test RMSE by 16-27%. SHAP and SISSO analyses identify temperature, A-site dopant concentration, and A-site heat of vaporization as the most important descriptors of zT. The framework is validated through prediction of previously unexplored compositions, recovery of literature-reported optimal zT values for established hH systems, and first-principles calculations for the new compounds CeCoBi and CeIrBi, which exhibit favorable electronic transport properties. The framework is further applied to high-throughput screening of the doped hH chemical space, covering about 2.46 million elemental substitution combinations across 631 thermodynamically screened parent matrices under stability constraints. This screening yields a concise set of promising candidates for future study. Overall, the work establishes a generalizable workflow for reliable data-driven thermoelectric materials discovery.

item.title: Lee--Yang Zeros and Pseudocritical Drift in J-Q N\'eel Antiferromagnet--Valence-Bond Solid Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2603.15116v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Square-lattice J-Q models provide a sign-problem-free setting for probing the quantum phase transition between N\'eel antiferromagnet and columnar valence-bond solid. We analyze this transition through the scaling of Lee--Yang zeros, computed within stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo by reweighting configurations sampled near criticality in the presence of complex source fields. Benchmark studies of the dimerized Heisenberg model and the checkerboard J-Q model validate the method, yielding stable \(\mathrm{O}(3)\) critical scaling in the former and clear spacetime-volume scaling in the latter, as expected for a first-order transition. Applying the same analysis to the J-Q models, we find a pronounced and systematic drift of the leading-zero scaling with increasing system size, consistent with an extended pseudocritical regime. The Lee--Yang scaling implies an effective scaling dimension \(\Delta_{\phi}\) of the \(\mathrm{SO}(5)\) order-parameter field that decreases with size and is consistent with vanishing in the thermodynamic limit. Such behavior lies below the scalar unitarity bound of any unitary relativistic conformal field theory in \(2{+}1\) dimensions and enforces inverse spacetime-volume scaling of the zeros, the hallmark of a first-order transition. These results support a weakly first-order interpretation of the N\'eel--VBS transition and establish the finite-size Lee--Yang zeros as a sensitive, symmetry-resolved diagnostic of pseudocriticality and transition order in the J-Q family.

item.title: Engineering superconductivity on the surface of Weyl semimetals
item.description: arXiv:2604.26859v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ten years after the experimental discovery of Weyl semimetals, theoretical and experimental work has pointed to the possibility of realizing surface-only superconductivity at relatively high temperatures in these materials. A consensus is developing that this unusual form of superconductivity is supported by surface electronic states unique to Weyl semimetals, known as Fermi arcs. In this work, we show that the topological protection of these exotic states can be exploited to engineer high critical temperatures. Motivated by reports of van Hove singularities on the surface of PtBi$_2$-the first Weyl semimetal in which surface superconductivity was unequivocally linked to its Fermi arcs-we demonstrate how such singularities can be engineered through the deposition of a suitable additional layer. We find that the critical temperature becomes extremely sensitive to the exact value of the chemical potential, and values as large as 20 times the bulk $T_c$ can be achieved. More generally, our results demonstrate how topological protection can be exploited to manipulate surface electronic states, thereby opening experimentally accessible routes toward engineering high-temperature two-dimensional superconductivity and other exotic phases.

item.title: Contrasting $\Gamma$- and K-Valley Moir\'e Physics in Twisted Monolayer/Bilayer WSe$_2$
item.description:
arXiv:2607.18212v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Electronic orbital character plays a central role in determining electronic correlations, spin-orbit coupling, dimensionality, and ultimately the quantum phases of condensed-matter systems. Two-dimensional moir'e materials have emerged as highly tunable platforms for exploring correlated phenomena, but the role of orbital degrees of freedom remains largely unexplored. Here, we identify twisted monolayer/bilayer WSe$_2$ as a platform in which displacement-field tuning enables moir'e physics to be realized in both the $K$ and $\Gamma$ valleys. The distinct orbital characters of these valleys give rise to contrasting correlated phases at moir'e filling factors $
u=1$ and $
u=1/3$. At $
u=1$, the $K$-valley state is a weak insulator, consistent with an antiferromagnetic state near a van Hove singularity in the intermediate-coupling regime, similar to that observed in twisted bilayer WSe$_2$. In contrast, the $\Gamma$-valley state exhibits a pronounced Pomeranchuk effect, consistent with proximity to a Mott transition. At $
u=1/3$, the $K$ valley hosts a robust generalized Wigner crystal, whereas the $\Gamma$-valley state lies near the crystallization boundary and again exhibits a Pomeranchuk effect, with localization enhanced by increasing temperature or magnetic field. Our work highlights the importance of orbital character in defining quantum phases in moir'e systems, and identify the $\Gamma$ valley as a promising platform for exploring correlated phenomena near quantum phase transitions, where competing phases and enhanced fluctuations may give rise to unconventional phases.

item.title: Efficient simulation of second-order phase transitions in quantum anharmonic materials
item.description: arXiv:2608.14292v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a crystal undergoes a second-order structural phase transition, such as in ferroelectrics, Peierls, and charge-density waves, the diverging fluctuations of the order parameter lead to the break- down of the standard phonon quasiparticle picture. Simulating these highly anharmonic regimes is notoriously challenging, as methods such as molecular dynamics suffer from a critical slowdown near the transition point, while the harmonic approximation fails dramatically at saddle points of the energy landscape stabilized by quantum or thermal ionic fluctuations. This work introduces a new approach, based on the variational free-energy principle, to predict critical long-range behavior and dynamical spectra in strongly anharmonic systems, even when quantum ionic fluctuations dominate. The proposed framework builds upon the stochastic self- consistent harmonic approximation but reduces its computational scaling with the number of atoms, N, from O(N^6) to O(N^2) and the memory requirement from O(N^4) to O(N). We benchmark the method on the prototypical lead-free metal-halide perovskite CsSnI3, a promising candidate for photovoltaic engineering, simulating its phase stability and Raman spectrum near the phase transition, where the breakdown of the quasiparticle picture becomes evident. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method by computing the full free-energy Hessian and the critical temperature in a supercell with 1080 atoms. Such simulations would have required tens of thousands of years with the legacy approach; it is now feasible in a few hours on consumer hardware.

item.title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.12151v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by accessing unprecedented length and time scales. While pretrained equivariant graph neural networks achieve robust zero-shot performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, their translation to complex materials dynamics remains fundamentally challenged by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling limits. In this Review, we examine how physics-driven specialization extends the applicability of MLIPs to complex dynamical systems. We systematically evaluate the structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. Through four demanding application contexts - electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture - we establish a framework for observable-specific validation. Highlighting the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, we emphasize that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables. We conclude with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

item.title: Physics-inspired Generative AI models via real hardware-based noisy quantum diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2505.22193v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum Diffusion Models (QDMs) are an emerging paradigm in Generative AI that aims to use quantum properties to improve the performances of their classical counterparts. However, existing algorithms are not easily scalable due to the limitations of near-term quantum devices. Following our previous work on QDMs, here we propose and implement two physics-inspired protocols. In the first, we use the formalism of quantum stochastic walks, showing that a specific interplay of quantum and classical dynamics in the forward process produces statistically more robust models generating sets of MNIST images with lower Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) than using totally classical dynamics. In the second approach, we realize an algorithm to generate images by exploiting the intrinsic noise of real IBM quantum hardware with only four qubits. Our work could be a starting point to pave the way for new scenarios for large-scale algorithms in quantum Generative AI, where quantum noise is neither mitigated nor corrected, but instead exploited as a useful resource.

item.title: Prediction of MOF Adsorption Isotherms and High-Throughput Screening Using a Physics-Informed Membranes Graph Neural Network
item.description: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are prime CO2-capture candidates, but grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) screening is costly when full isotherms, not single uptakes, are required; machine learning surrogates rarely resolve the continuous pressure response. We report a physics-informed pressure-aware multi-task graph neural network (PI-MGNN) to predict CO2 uptake at arbitrary pressure and reconstruct isotherms from structure. From ~130,000 candidates, PCA and K-means select 5,023 representative MOFs, each simulated by GCMC at five pressures spanning 0.1-5.0 MPa, enforcing a continuous pressure response. Crystal graphs are processed by decoupled geometric and electrostatic graph-attention branches with auxiliary supervision, while a Gaussian-expanded pressure query is fused by cross-attention. PI-MGNN attains R2 = 0.977 and MAE = 0.291 mol kg-1; isotherm MAEs are 0.428/0.312/0.330 mol kg-1 for high/medium/low-uptake MOFs, and cross-attention improves accuracy by 6.3%. Attention weights recover the pressure-resolved physics, enabling accurate and interpretable high-throughput screening.

item.title: The Pnictogen Oracle Provider: Multi-Fidelity Graph Landscapes To Benchmark Molecular Optimization
item.description: The informed discovery and inverse design of new molecules and materials is among the most active applications of data-driven procedures, such as statistical learning, to chemical problems. These approaches involve two key aspects: the dataset, and the exploration algorithms. Here, we cover both of these dimensions by introducing POP (Pnictogen Oracle Provider), a platform comprised by an extensive graph database and an optimization toolkit. The database contains almost 200,000 structures for phosphines, amines and arsines at different fidelity levels, explicitly including failed calculations and enforcing a topology based on substituent-level mutation operations. On the other hand, the software toolkit streamlines the application of optimization algorithms (search policies and predictive oracles) to such databases, pushing forward the development of benchmarks. We explore the baseline application of a varied set of such methods—evolutionary algorithms, Bayesian Optimization, LLM-based procedures and multifidelity approaches—to the optimization of a key property: the HOMO-LUMO gap across each of the three ligand families. In this manner, we reveal the relevance of graph topology in the guidance of these algorithms, as well as the performance differences these baseline methods depending on the particularities of each of the ligand families.

item.title: First-principles data for solid-solution Nb–Zr, Ta–Zr, and V–Zr binary alloys with body-centered-cubic structures
item.description: We present three open-access datasets containing density functional theory (DFT) calculations for refractory solid-solution binary alloys niobium–zirconium (NbZr), tantalum–zirconium (TaZr), and vanadium–zirconium (VZr) in 128-atom body-centered-cubic (BCC) supercells. These datasets extend our previously published first-principles collections for NbTa, NbV, TaV, and NbTaV alloys and were generated with the same automated high-throughput workflow based on the Vienna Ab-Initio Simulation Package (VASP). For each of the three NbZr, TaZr, and VZr systems, we uniformly sample 31 chemical compositions across the full composition range in 4-atom increments. For every composition we construct 100 distinct disordered atomic configurations by randomizing the element assignments on the BCC lattice sites. All structures are fully relaxed, and the released data include complete input files, detailed VASP outputs for each relaxation stage, and derived physical quantities such as ground-state formation energy and root mean-squared displacement (RMSD) relative to an ideal BCC reference. These Zr-containing binaries are motivated by our earlier demonstration that graph neural networks (GNNs) trained on binary NbTa, NbV, and TaV data can interpolate formation enthalpies and structural descriptors in ternary NbTaV alloys while dramatically reducing the required number of ternary DFT calculations. The new NbZr, TaZr, and VZr datasets increase the diversity of available binary training data, in particular in systems with larger size mismatch and stronger lattice distortion due to Zr, and are intended to support the development of transferable machine learning (ML) interatomic models for accelerated exploration of high-dimensional multicomponent alloy spaces.

item.title: High-Sensitivity, Dual Ratiometric and Turn-on ABATaRs for Multiplexed Temporal Imaging of Ferroptosis Hallmarks in Living Cells
item.description: We present a computationally-guided workflow for designing dual turn-on and ratiometric Raman sensors. The workflow has been used to rationally design activity-based alkyne tagged Raman, ABATaR, sensors that overcome the inherently low Raman sensitivity via strategic placement of electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups. An ABATaR sensing scaffold designed via the workflow afforded ~ 9000 times higher Raman scattering cross-section than the dimethylsulfoxide C-H stretching-mode. The sensitivity of the scaffold was compared to that of 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) to determine Raman intensity versus EdU, RIE, a parameter used to benchmark Raman probes. An RIE value of 170 was obtained which is one of the highest amongst previously reported monoyne and diyne-based Raman probes. The sensitive ABATaR-scaffold was developed into a dual turn-on and ratiometric Fe2+-sensor that was applied to distinctly quantify endogenous cellular labile Fe2+ ion levels. In a key result, live-cell, temporal imaging with the Fe2+-ABATaR sensor revealed that intracellular labile Fe2+ levels progressively increase with ferroptosis while the total Fe-level remains constant. To demonstrate the generalizability of the design workflow, we synthesized an orthogonal ABATaR-sensor for H2O2. The H2O2-sensor was applied together with the Fe2+-sensor along with inherent Raman peaks for cytochromes to enable simultaneous, multiplexed spontaneous Raman imaging of three distinct ferroptosis hallmarks—labile Fe2+, H2O2, and redox-sensitive cytochrome Raman signals—in living cells. Importantly, the ability to pre-design orthogonal ratiometric Raman sensors and simultaneously track three regulators of ferroptosis via discrete non-overlapping Raman peaks highlights the tremendous potential of Raman sensors toward attaining live cell multiplexed imaging and quantification.

item.title: Multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential for the energetics and finite temperature structure of Pt surfaces and nanoparticles
item.description: Accurate accounting of exposed facets and surface sites is central to understanding metal nanoparticle catalysts, but modelling their structure at finite temperatures is computationally expensive. We benchmark the universal interatomic potential UMA (Universal Model for Atoms, Open Catalyst 2020 task) against Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional theory (PBE-DFT) for Pt. UMA underestimates the surface energies of all 13 facets by 11-17 % and the excess energies of 28 differently shaped nanoparticles, each containing less than 500 atoms, most strongly for small particles. We distill UMA into a compact Deep Potential model by pre-training on UMA labelled bulk and slab data, then fine-tune it on a small PBE-DFT dataset that includes nanoparticles. The resulting multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential (MF-MLIP) gives a surface-energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 2.8 meV Å−2, 21 % lower than a DFT only model trained on the same data. On six nanoparticles, the MF-MLIP improves force accuracy over UMA, reducing the force RMSE by 29-52 %, with the largest gains at surface, edge and vertex atoms. Molecular dynamics at 500 K shows Pt(111) retaining its termination while Pt(100) and Pt(110) change strongly. At 500-700 K, the nanoparticles lose vertex sites and gain edge sites, and some restructure away from their ideal shapes. On the same CPU hardware, the MF-MLIP runs molecular dynamics simulations 60-100 times faster than UMA.

item.title: On the impact of methodological configurations and data variations on chemical recycling life cycle assessment studies
item.description: The comparability of Life Cycle Assessment studies on chemical recycling processes for plastic waste conversion is challenging due to the wide range of investigated feedstocks, datasets, and methodological choices. Thus, this paper investigates the impact of various degrees of freedom within peer-reviewed Life Cycle Assessments of chemical recycling processes on the proposed environmental impact. In detail, methodological degrees of freedom, such as system boundary depth, functional units, allocation methods, and the utilization of substitution credits, as well as data-related degrees of freedom, including the use of plant-level, model-based, literature-derived, or third-party data at different data scales, such as experimental, laboratory, or pilot scale, are considered. Among the investigated Life Cycle Assessment studies, none of them applied the same combination of methodological choices, highlighting the methodological uniqueness of each study. However, changes in either methodological or data-related degrees of freedom substantially affect Life Cycle Assessment results in both magnitude and interpretation: without changing the methodology, data-related degrees of freedom shift the global warming potential for 1 kg of treated waste from 2.5 kg CO2-eq. below that of incineration as the reference waste treatment process to 0.5 kg CO2-eq. above. Utilizing the same database, methodological differences as reported in the investigated studies shift the global The underlined authors contributed equally and share first authorship. warming potential from 2.9 below to 0.3 kg CO2-eq. above the global warming potential of incineration. The same trend is found when comparing the products of chemical recycling to the fossil-based production routes, where the main levers affecting the results were identified as the declaration of products, the handling of side streams, and the choice of energy sources. These findings show that LCA results should not be interpreted on the basis of individual values alone, but in the context of methodological choices, data sources and quality, and sensitivity to both data and methodological assumptions. Without transparency regarding these aspects, reported values are of limited interpretive value and may offer unwanted possibilities for selective interpretation and may ultimately increase the risk of greenwashing in the communication of chemical recycling performance.

item.title: QMzyme: A Python Package for Automated and Systematic QM-based Enzyme Modeling
item.description: We introduce QMzyme, a Python package to automate the generation of Quantum mechanics (QM)-based enzyme models. QM calculations on enzymes are computationally challenging because full enzyme systems typically contain thousands of atoms, placing accurate QM treatments beyond practical computational limits.Therefore, QM-based enzyme studies rely on identifying a subset of atoms that captures the essential chemistry of the reaction environment, enabling tractable yet chemically meaningful calculations. However, constructing these reduced models requires numerous user-defined decisions, including selection of the starting structure, identification of atoms to include in the QM region, and definition of truncation strategies for QM-only models, all of which can substantially influence the resulting calculations. QMzyme aims to provide the community with a flexible and extensible framework for automated, systematic generation of QM-based enzyme models, enabling researchers to more rigorously evaluate how model construction decisions influence computational outcomes while improving reproducibility and transparency across workflows. By facilitating high-throughput generation and analysis of QM enzyme models, QMzyme supports largescale, data-driven investigations of enzyme structure, function, and reactivity. This effort is especially crucial for the creation of large, chemically consistent datasets that can support emergent artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches for accelerated digital discovery in enzymology and biocatalysis.

item.title: Bio-derived ionic conductive Guar Gum hydrogels as distributed circuit elements for analogue signal processing: the case of Resistor-Capacitor filters
item.description: Developing functional electronic materials from renewable resources is a key challenge toward more sustainable electronics. Here, we report on a bio-derived ionic conductive hydrogel based on guar gum and demonstrate its direct integration as a functional circuit element for analogue signal processing. Ionic conductivity is introduced by incorporating sodium chloride into the polysaccharide matrix and systematically tuned through the glycerol and salt contents. Increasing glycerol loading enhances conductivity, while varying NaCl concentration produces a non-monotonic response, with maximum conductivities in the 10-2 S cm-1 range and an optimum salt-loading window. The conductive formulation is subsequently combined with pristine guar gum, used as a dielectric, to fabricate guar gum-based resistor-capacitor elements. Their integration into low-pass and high-pass filters demonstrates frequency-selective operation in the audio range, with cut-off frequencies of 658 and 576 Hz and transition slopes of −17 and +15 dB dec-1, respectively. These results demonstrate that guar gumbased ionic hydrogels can move beyond conventional roles as substrates or electrolytes and directly perform circuit-level functions, providing a simple materials platform for low-frequency analogue electronics.

item.title: Process and Systems Modeling of Hydrothermal Liquefaction for Fuels and
item.description: 17 Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) can convert wet organic waste into fuels and bioproducts, but 18 variation in feedstocks and operating conditions can propagate from product yields to system 19 performance and deployment. This study linked machine learning based HTL yield prediction with 20 process simulation, techno-economic analysis (TEA), life cycle assessment (LCA), uncertainty 21 analysis, and surrogate modeling. A literature data set of 402 experiments was used to predict 22 biocrude, aqueous, gas, and solids yields, with 71.8% of predictions within ±5 wt% of experimental 23 values. The predicted yields reproduced 77.1% of internal rate of return (IRR) and 83.2% of 24 GWP100 estimates within ±5% and ±10 kg CO2e/kg, respectively, and were integrated into two 25 deployment configurations (centralized and decentralized HTL) and two product pathways 26 (biobinder/biofuel and sustainable aviation fuel [SAF]). Process and system scale analyses 27 showed that operating conditions strongly affecting HTL performance could have weaker or 28 competing economic effects due to tradeoffs among product yields, water handling, energy 29 requirements, and capital costs. Across representative feedstocks, decentralized biobinder 30 systems achieved median IRRs up to 35.8%, compared with up to 8.0% for decentralized SAF 31 systems. Feedstock price, followed by biocrude quality, and biocrude yield emerged as the 32 leading economic drivers. Monte Carlo filtering identified waste tipping fee thresholds $25.1–33 196.7 per wet metric tonne for achieving the 10% IRR target. These results show that existing 34 tipping fee structure can support HTL deployment in some cases, while higher tipping fees or 35 additional financial incentives can expand viability and enable higher investment returns. 36

item.title: A PVDF‐Based Composite Solid Electrolyte Enabled by Carbon‐Free LiFePO4 for Stable Lithium Metal Batteries

item.title: Machine Learning of Methacrylated Dextran Phase Separation for Prediction, Transferability, and Adaptation
item.description: Thermoresponsive polymers are promising materials for separations, sensing, drug delivery, and other biomedical applications, but their phase behavior depends on numerous polymer and solution variables, which creates a formulation space that is impractical to explore exhaustively by experiments. Here, we develop machine-learning (ML) models for predicting the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of methacrylated dextran (Dex-MA), a biocompatible polysaccharide-based polymer, using 403 unique experimentally measured formulations spanning polymer molecular weight, degree of methacrylation, concentration, salts, surfactants, and other additives. The dataset is nonuniformly sampled because of practical synthesis constraints and application priorities. Despite this nonuniformity, descriptor-and molecular-embedding-based XGBoost and multilayer perceptron (MLP) models achieved mean absolute errors of 3.6 oC to 3.7 oC and 5.4 oC to 5.7 oC, respectively, for within-domain LCST prediction and mean phase-behavior classification accuracies of 89.4–89.6% and 85.3–86.6%, respectively. However, strong within-domain performance did not uniformly transfer to unseen formulation domains. Systematically withholding entire polymer, surfactant, and salt domains produced domain-dependent losses in predictive accuracy; for example, withholding 86 and 250 kDa Dex-MA increased LCST prediction errors to 11.4 oC and 17.5 oC, respectively, whereas errors for held-out surfactants were 5.6–7.2 oC. Progressive incorporation of target-domain measurements recovered predictive accuracy, but the recovery rate varied substantially with additive and salt identity and polymer molecular weight. This work provides a framework not only for predicting thermoresponsive-polymer phase behavior but also for evaluating model transferability to new formulation domains and guiding experimental data collection for model adaptation.
